title: Expected learning outcomes
text:
A first-cycle course (3MB001, Umeå University) in modern molecular cell biology for year-2 biomedicine students. The verbatim outcomes are in courseplan.md. This page says what each outcome means and where it is taught.


By the end of the course, a student can follow a molecule, a signal or a cell decision through the cell: where a protein is made, how it reaches its compartment, how the cell senses and answers a signal, how it moves, divides and dies. They can also explain how a drug or a disease acts on that path.



Each ELO is examined separately with a 60 % pass bar and one VG question, so each needs enough lectures, quiz questions and study questions of its own.









ELO
Short name
What a student can do
Taught in




1
Cell & methods
Describe the parts of a eukaryotic cell and choose a method (microscopy, fractionation, flow cytometry, perturbation) to answer a cell biology question
The cell and how we study it; a methods slide in every lecture


2
Membranes & transport
Explain bilayer structure and fluidity, membrane proteins, passive and active transport, channels and membrane potential
Membranes and transport


3
Signalling
Describe signal types, receptor classes, second messengers, kinase cascades, feedback and how signals are switched off
Cell signalling


4
Protein handling
Describe protein folding, sorting, translocation, modification, quality control and degradation
Protein handling and organelles


5
Organelles & homeostasis
Compare organelles’ structure and function, and explain how they cooperate to keep the cell in balance (energy, Ca²⁺, pH, lipids, protein load)
Protein handling and organelles (especially mitochondria and organelles compared)


6
Cytoskeleton & motility
Explain actin, microtubules and intermediate filaments, motors, migration and transport, and give examples of methods to study them
Cytoskeleton


7
Cell cycle & division
Describe the cell-cycle control system, checkpoints, mitosis and cytokinesis, and control of cell numbers
Cell cycle and division


8
Cell death
Describe apoptosis (intrinsic and extrinsic), necroptosis, pyroptosis and ferroptosis, and their regulation
Cell death


9
Disease mechanisms
Explain disease as cell biology going wrong: cancer, misfolding, trafficking, channel and mitochondrial defects
Disease mechanisms, plus every lecture’s “Why it matters” slides



The final lecture follows one drug through the cell and revisits all nine ELOs.



These are taught and assessed in the labs and in module 2 (oral presentations, seminars, group problem solving, poster), which are handled outside this site.

ELO 10–12, 17–19 → Module 2 (PPT): oral presentation, group problem solving, discussion, poster for a commissioning party, projects as a working method, own learning needs.
ELO 13–16 → Module 3 (Lab): planning and running experiments, GLP, written report, interpreting results.





Quiz per lecture: short self-check, each question tagged with its ELO.
Study questions per lecture (replacing the programming exercises of the scaffold course): G-level recall and explanation questions and one VG-style question (“predict what happens if…”, “compare…”, “design an experiment to…”), written the way the exam asks them.

title: Quiz: principles of cell communication
text:
Short questions to check your understanding of the lecture Principles of cell communication. Try each on paper first, then open the hint or the answer. The tag after each question shows the learning outcome (ELO) it practises.

Q1. Match each signal to its type of signalling: (a) insulin from the pancreas acting on muscle, (b) histamine from a mast cell acting on a nearby blood vessel, (c) acetylcholine from a nerve ending acting on a muscle fibre, (d) Delta on one cell acting on Notch on the neighbouring cell. Types: contact-dependent, endocrine, paracrine, synaptic. [ELO 3]






Hint





How far does each signal travel, and does it leave the sending cell at all?









Answer






endocrine: a hormone carried in the blood; (b) paracrine: a local mediator acting on nearby cells; (c) synaptic: a neurotransmitter crossing a narrow gap to one target cell; (d) contact-dependent: Delta stays in the membrane of the sending cell, so only touching cells respond.





Q2. Adrenaline binds a receptor in the plasma membrane, while cortisol binds a receptor inside the cell. Why? And which of the two hormones gives the faster response? [ELO 3]






Hint





Which of the two can cross a lipid bilayer? What does the cortisol receptor do once it has bound its hormone?









Answer





Adrenaline is water-soluble and cannot cross the bilayer, so its receptor must sit in the plasma membrane and pass the signal inside. Cortisol is a small fat-soluble steroid that diffuses through the membrane and binds a nuclear receptor, a transcription factor. Adrenaline is faster (seconds): it changes proteins that already exist. Cortisol acts through gene expression, so new RNA and proteins must be made (hours).




Q3. A receptor has \(K_d\) = 2 nM for its hormone. What fraction of the receptors is occupied at 2 nM, 6 nM and 18 nM hormone? [ELO 3]






Hint





Fraction occupied \(= [L]/([L] + K_d)\).









Answer





2/(2+2) = 50 %; 6/(6+2) = 75 %; 18/(18+2) = 90 %. Going from 50 % to 90 % needs nine times more hormone: the binding curve flattens as the receptors fill up.




Q4. Drug A gives a maximal response of 100 % with EC₅₀ = 10 nM. Drug B, acting on the same receptor, gives at most 40 % with EC₅₀ = 1 nM. Which drug is more potent, which has the higher efficacy, and what kind of drug is B? [ELO 3]






Hint





Potency is about how much drug you need; efficacy is about how large the effect can get.









Answer





Drug B is more potent (lower EC₅₀: it works at lower concentrations). Drug A has the higher efficacy (larger maximum). B is a partial agonist: even when it occupies all the receptors, it switches them on only part-way.




Q5. You measure an agonist’s dose–response curve with and without a new antagonist. With the antagonist, the curve moves to the right, but at very high agonist concentrations it reaches the same maximum. What kind of antagonist is it? What would you see with an irreversible antagonist in a tissue without spare receptors? [ELO 3]






Hint





Can extra agonist win back the receptors?









Answer





A competitive (reversible, same-site) antagonist: enough agonist out-competes it, so Emax is unchanged and only the EC₅₀ rises. An irreversible antagonist removes receptors for good; with no spare receptors, the maximum falls, as with a non-competitive antagonist.




Q6. In one tissue, an agonist gives half of its maximal effect when only about 5 % of its receptors are occupied. How is that possible, and is its EC₅₀ higher or lower than its \(K_d\)? [ELO 3]






Hint





What happens to the signal in the steps after the receptor?









Answer





Amplification: each active receptor activates many G proteins, each makes many cAMP molecules, and so on, so a few active receptors are enough for a large response. The other receptors are spare receptors. The EC₅₀ is therefore lower than the \(K_d\). EC₅₀ equals \(K_d\) only if the response is directly proportional to occupancy.




Q7. A mutation makes a GTPase unable to hydrolyse GTP. Is the protein stuck ON or OFF? Which helper protein normally switches it off, and which switches it on? [ELO 3]






Hint





Which nucleotide is bound in the active state?









Answer





Stuck ON: the GTP-bound form is active, and without hydrolysis it never returns to the GDP form. A GAP (GTPase-activating protein) normally speeds up hydrolysis and switches it off; a GEF (guanine nucleotide exchange factor) switches it on by letting GDP out and GTP in. Ras mutations of this kind drive many cancers.




Q8. A patient uses a β₂-agonist inhaler many times a day for weeks, and it works less and less well. Name the phenomenon and two mechanisms in the cell that can cause it. [ELO 3]






Hint





What happens to receptors that are switched on all the time?









Answer





Desensitisation (adaptation; in the clinic called tolerance). Mechanisms: (1) the active receptor is phosphorylated by a receptor kinase and bound by arrestin, which blocks coupling to the G protein (fast); (2) receptors are taken into the cell by endocytosis and some are degraded in lysosomes, so fewer remain on the surface (slower). Changes further down the pathway can add to this.

title: Principles of cell communication
section: About this lecture

title: Principles of cell communication
section: The question: one hormone, many answers
text:
The question: one hormone, many answers


A fright: your adrenal glands release adrenaline into the blood. Within seconds the heart beats faster, the liver releases glucose and blood vessels in the gut contract.
Even in a fright, blood adrenaline reaches only a few nanomolar: about one molecule per 10 billion water molecules. How does a cell detect so little? Why does the same molecule do different things in different cells? And how can a drug block it?


Imagine a sudden fright, for example a car that almost hits you. Within seconds your heart races, you feel your pulse, and your muscles are ready to run. The signal is adrenaline, a small molecule made in the adrenal glands and released into the blood. Every cell in the body is bathed in the same blood, so every cell sees the same adrenaline. Yet the answers are completely different. Heart muscle cells beat faster and stronger. Liver cells break down glycogen and release glucose into the blood, fuel for the muscles. Smooth muscle cells around the blood vessels of the gut contract, so blood goes to the muscles instead of to digestion. And the concentration is tiny: below one nanomolar at rest and a few nanomolar in a fright. Three puzzles guide today’s lecture. First, how can a receptor detect a nanomolar signal? The answer is high-affinity binding plus amplification. Second, why does the same signal do different things? Because cells have different receptors and different machinery behind them. Third, how can a drug change the answer? This is the basis of half of pharmacology, and we finish with beta-blockers and opioids.

title: Principles of cell communication
section: Five ways to send a signal
text:
Five ways to send a signal


Endocrine: a hormone travels in the blood to cells all over the body (insulin, cortisol). Slow to spread, long reach.
Paracrine: a local mediator acts on nearby cells and is quickly destroyed or taken up (histamine, many growth factors).
Autocrine: a cell responds to its own signal; a group of similar cells can reinforce each other (IL-2 from activated T cells).
Contact-dependent: the signal stays on the membrane of the sending cell; only touching cells respond (Delta on one cell, Notch on the next).
Synaptic: a nerve cell releases a neurotransmitter across a narrow gap to one target cell (acetylcholine): fast and private.


Cells signal over very different distances. In endocrine signalling, a gland releases a hormone into the blood, which carries it to almost every cell. Insulin from the pancreas and cortisol from the adrenal cortex are examples. Because the hormone is diluted in about five litres of blood, its concentration is low, so the receptors must bind it very tightly. In paracrine signalling the signal acts locally, on cells a few cell diameters away. Histamine released from mast cells in an allergic reaction is an example; the signal does not get far because it is broken down, taken up or bound to the matrix. Autocrine signalling is a special case: the cell has receptors for its own signal. Activated T cells make the growth factor interleukin 2 and respond to it themselves, which amplifies the immune response. In contact-dependent signalling the signal molecule stays anchored in the membrane; Delta and Notch, which you meet in the lecture on signals that decide cell fates, are the classic pair. Synaptic signalling is the extreme of local signalling: a nerve ending releases a neurotransmitter into a gap of about 20 nanometres, and only the cell on the other side responds, within milliseconds.

title: Principles of cell communication
section: Where is the receptor? On the surface or inside
text:
Where is the receptor? On the surface or inside


Water-soluble signals (most hormones, peptides, growth factors, neurotransmitters) cannot cross the lipid bilayer. Their receptors sit in the plasma membrane and pass the message inside.
Small fat-soluble signals (steroid hormones such as cortisol and oestrogen, thyroid hormone, vitamin D) diffuse through the membrane and bind intracellular receptors, which act as transcription factors.


The first question about any signal is where its receptor is, and the answer follows from chemistry you know from the membrane lecture. The lipid bilayer stops charged and polar molecules. Adrenaline, insulin and growth factors are water-soluble, so they cannot enter the cell. Their receptors are transmembrane proteins: the signal binds outside, the receptor changes shape, and the change is passed to proteins inside the cell. Because these relay proteins already exist, the response can start within seconds. Steroid hormones are different. Cortisol, oestrogen and testosterone are made from cholesterol, are small and hydrophobic, and diffuse straight through the membrane. Thyroid hormone and vitamin D act in the same way. Their receptors are inside the cell, in the cytosol or the nucleus. When the hormone binds, the receptor binds DNA and changes which genes are transcribed. New messenger RNA and new proteins must be made, so these responses take hours. A side note: a few gases, such as nitric oxide, also cross membranes and act directly on an enzyme inside the cell.

title: Principles of cell communication
section: Three classes of cell-surface receptor
text:
Three classes of cell-surface receptor


Ion-channel-coupled: the receptor is a channel; binding opens it. You met the acetylcholine receptor in the lecture on ion channels. Fastest: milliseconds.
G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs): seven helices cross the membrane; the active receptor switches on a G protein, which switches on enzymes or channels. Largest family: about 800 genes in humans.
Enzyme-coupled: a single-pass receptor that is itself an enzyme (often a tyrosine kinase) or recruits one. Binding brings two receptors together (insulin, growth factors).


Cell-surface receptors come in three classes, and each gets its own detail later. Ion-channel-coupled receptors, also called ligand-gated channels, are the simplest: the receptor is a channel, and the signal opens it. You met the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor in the lecture on ion channels: two acetylcholine molecules bind and sodium flows in. This is the fastest kind of signalling, used at synapses. G-protein-coupled receptors are the largest family of membrane proteins in our genome, about 800 genes, of which about half are smell receptors. All have the same fold, a chain that crosses the membrane seven times. When a signal binds, the receptor changes shape and activates a G protein on the inside, which then changes the activity of enzymes or channels. The next lecture is about them. Enzyme-coupled receptors cross the membrane once. Most are kinases themselves, or bind a kinase. When the signal binds, two receptors come together and phosphorylate each other on tyrosines, which starts a cascade; that is the lecture on kinase cascades. Receptors of all three classes are major drug targets.

title: Principles of cell communication
section: Intracellular receptors: a hormone becomes a transcription factor
text:
Intracellular receptors: a hormone becomes a transcription factor







Glucocorticoid receptor (green) on DNA: DNA-binding domain (DBD) and ligand-binding domain (LBD) with the drug dexamethasone in its pocket and a co-activator (red). Crystal structures.


Nuclear receptors: about 48 in humans; receptors for steroids (cortisol, oestrogen, testosterone), thyroid hormone, vitamin D and retinoic acid.
Without hormone, some wait in the cytosol (the glucocorticoid receptor, held by chaperones), others sit on DNA in the nucleus.
The hormone binds a pocket in the ligand-binding domain; the receptor changes shape, binds DNA response elements and recruits co-activators: target genes switch on (or off).
Response in hours, lasting long after the hormone is gone. Drugs: prednisolone (anti-inflammatory), tamoxifen (breast cancer).



Intracellular receptors form one protein family, the nuclear receptors, with about 48 members in humans. Each has a DNA-binding domain and a ligand-binding domain. The ligand-binding domain has a deep pocket that fits a small hydrophobic hormone. The glucocorticoid receptor, which binds cortisol, waits in the cytosol, held in an inactive form by chaperone proteins. When cortisol binds, the receptor releases the chaperones, moves into the nucleus and binds short DNA sequences called response elements near its target genes. There it recruits co-activator proteins that open chromatin and help RNA polymerase start transcription. Other nuclear receptors are already bound to DNA and switch from repressor to activator when the hormone arrives. Note the logic: the receptor is a transcription factor whose activity is controlled by a small molecule, which links to what you know about gene regulation. Because new RNA and proteins must be made, the response takes hours, and it lasts for hours or days. Many drugs act here: synthetic glucocorticoids such as prednisolone dampen inflammation, and tamoxifen blocks the oestrogen receptor in breast cancer, which returns in the lecture on signals that decide cell fates.

title: Principles of cell communication
section: Recap: binding is an equilibrium; Kd measures affinity
text:
Recap: binding is an equilibrium; Kd measures affinity

\text{R} + \text{L} \rightleftharpoons \text{RL} \qquad K_d = \frac{[\text{R}][\text{L}]}{[\text{RL}]} \qquad \text{fraction occupied} = \frac{[\text{L}]}{[\text{L}] + K_d}

Kd is the concentration that fills half the receptors. Low Kd = high affinity. Hormone receptors: Kd about 0.1–10 nM.
On a log axis the curve is an S: from 10 % to 90 % occupied takes an 81-fold rise in concentration.


This is a recap from chemistry. A ligand L and a receptor R form a complex RL, and the reaction reaches an equilibrium. The dissociation constant K d is the equilibrium constant written for the complex falling apart, so it has units of concentration. A small K d means the complex rarely falls apart: high affinity. If you rearrange the equation, the fraction of receptors occupied is L over L plus K d. When the free ligand concentration equals K d, exactly half the receptors are occupied. That is the definition to remember. On a linear axis the curve is a hyperbola that rises steeply and then flattens. Pharmacologists almost always plot the concentration on a log axis, because concentrations span many orders of magnitude. On a log axis the same curve becomes an S shape, symmetric around K d. At one tenth of K d about 9 percent of the receptors are occupied, at K d 50 percent, at ten times K d 91 percent. Receptors for hormones typically have a K d in the nanomolar range, which matches the low hormone concentrations in blood. This is the first half of the answer to the question of how a cell detects so little signal.

title: Principles of cell communication
section: How do we know? Counting receptors with a radioactive drug
text:
How do we know? Counting receptors with a radioactive drug


1970s: Robert Lefkowitz used radioactively labelled drugs to find the β-adrenergic receptor, then thought by many to be just an idea. Specific binding was saturable, tight and matched the drugs’ effects.
Specific binding = total − non-specific. Its curve gives Bmax (how many receptors) and Kd (how tightly they bind).
Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2012 (Lefkowitz and Kobilka, for GPCRs).


How do we know that receptors exist and how tightly they bind? Until the 1970s, a receptor was an abstract idea: something on the cell that a drug must act on. Robert Lefkowitz and others made it concrete with radioligand binding. You mix cell membranes with a radioactively labelled drug at a known concentration, let binding reach equilibrium, then pour the mixture through a filter. The membranes stay on the filter with whatever is bound to them, and the free drug is washed away. Counting the radioactivity tells you how much is bound. Some binding is non-specific: the drug sticks to lipids and other proteins. To measure it, you run a second tube with a thousand-fold excess of unlabelled drug, which fills all real receptors, so the remaining radioactivity is non-specific. Subtract it, and the specific binding curve saturates: there is a fixed number of receptors, B max, and the half-saturating concentration is K d. Binding that is saturable, high-affinity and matches the potency of drugs in tissue is the signature of a real receptor. Lefkowitz used this approach to find and then purify the beta-adrenergic receptor, and he shared the 2012 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Brian Kobilka.

title: Principles of cell communication
section: From binding to response: the dose–response curve
text:
From binding to response: the dose–response curve


Measure a response (heart rate, cAMP, contraction) at many concentrations; plot it against log concentration.
Emax: the largest response the drug can give. EC₅₀: the concentration that gives half of Emax.
Potency = how little drug you need (a low EC₅₀). Drug A is 100× more potent than drug B, but both reach the same maximum.


Binding is not yet a response. A pharmacologist measures what the cell or tissue does: how fast an isolated heart beats, how much cAMP a cell makes, how strongly a muscle strip contracts. You measure this at many drug concentrations and plot the response against the log of the concentration. The result is again an S-shaped curve, the dose–response curve, the most important graph in pharmacology. Two numbers describe it. E max is the plateau, the largest response that drug can give in that system. EC 50, the effective concentration 50 percent, is the concentration that gives half of E max. The EC 50 measures potency: a drug with a low EC 50 works at low concentration. In the figure, drug A has an EC 50 of 1 nanomolar and drug B of 100 nanomolar. Drug A is a hundred times more potent, but both give the same maximal effect. Potency is not the same as being a better drug; a less potent drug can be given at a higher dose. What matters clinically is whether the drug reaches a useful effect at a dose without too many side effects.

title: Principles of cell communication
section: Agonists, partial agonists and antagonists
text:
Agonists, partial agonists and antagonists


Binding (affinity) and switching the receptor on (efficacy) are two different properties.
Full agonist: binds and switches on fully (adrenaline, morphine). Partial agonist: binds but switches on only part-way, even at 100 % occupancy (buprenorphine). Antagonist: binds, switches nothing on, and blocks the site (naloxone, beta-blockers). Try it: Demo: dose–response.


A drug can do two separate things. It can bind the receptor, which is its affinity, measured by K d. And once bound, it can switch the receptor on more or less well, which is its efficacy. A full agonist binds and switches the receptor fully on; the natural hormone is usually a full agonist. A partial agonist binds but switches the receptor on only part of the way: even when every receptor is occupied, the response stays below the maximum. Buprenorphine, used against pain and in the treatment of opioid addiction, is a partial agonist at the opioid receptor. An antagonist binds but has no efficacy at all. On its own it does nothing visible, flat on the graph. Its effect appears only when an agonist is present: it occupies the binding site and keeps the agonist out. The three drugs in the figure have the same affinity, so their curves are centred at the same concentration; only efficacy differs. A useful picture: affinity is how well a key fits the lock, efficacy is how far it turns the lock. There are also inverse agonists, which switch off receptors that are slightly active without any signal. Try the demo: you can compare morphine, buprenorphine and naloxone.

title: Principles of cell communication
section: Antagonists: shift or flatten; IC₅₀
text:
Antagonists: shift or flatten; IC₅₀


Competitive antagonist (same site, reversible): more agonist can out-compete it. The curve shifts right; Emax is unchanged.
Non-competitive antagonist (another site, or irreversible): more agonist cannot help. Emax falls.
IC₅₀: the antagonist concentration that removes half of the response, at a stated agonist concentration. More agonist → higher IC₅₀.


Antagonists come in two main kinds, and the dose–response curve tells them apart. A competitive antagonist binds the same site as the agonist, reversibly. Agonist and antagonist compete for the receptors, and the law of mass action decides who wins. If you add more agonist, you can always overcome the antagonist; you just need more. So the curve moves to the right, parallel, and reaches the same maximum. The shift depends on how much antagonist there is relative to its own K d: at ten times its K d the agonist curve shifts about eleven-fold. A non-competitive antagonist binds somewhere else and stops the receptor from working, or it binds the same site irreversibly, with a covalent bond. Then extra agonist cannot help, because those receptors are lost. The maximum falls. The third panel shows how an antagonist is usually tested in drug development: keep the agonist at a fixed concentration and add more and more antagonist. The concentration that halves the response is the IC 50, the inhibitory concentration 50 percent. Note that the IC 50 of a competitive antagonist is not a constant of the drug: with more agonist present, you need more antagonist.

title: Principles of cell communication
section: Amplification: a few receptors, a large response
text:
Amplification: a few receptors, a large response


Each active molecule activates many of the next: an enzyme cascade. One adrenaline–receptor pair can lead to thousands of phosphorylated proteins.
Consequence: a full response may need only a few % of the receptors occupied. The rest are spare receptors, and EC₅₀ is lower than Kd.


The second half of the answer to the question of how a cell detects so little signal is amplification. One active receptor does not activate one G protein; it activates many, one after the other, while the hormone stays bound. Each activated G protein switches on an enzyme, adenylyl cyclase, which makes many molecules of the small messenger cAMP. cAMP activates protein kinase A, and each kinase molecule phosphorylates many target proteins. The numbers in the figure are rounded and only illustrate the principle; each step multiplies. You will see this cascade in detail in the next lecture. Amplification has a consequence you can see on a dose–response curve. If a small fraction of occupied receptors is enough for a full response, the response curve lies to the left of the binding curve. In the figure, half of the maximal response needs only about 5 percent of the receptors. The other receptors are called spare receptors, or the receptor reserve. So the EC 50 is often much lower than the K d. EC 50 equals K d only in the simplest case, when the response is directly proportional to occupancy. Remember this when you compare binding and functional data.

title: Principles of cell communication
section: Molecular switches: phosphorylation and GTPases
text:
Molecular switches: phosphorylation and GTPases


Phosphorylation: a kinase adds a phosphate from ATP to serine, threonine or tyrosine; a phosphatase removes it. About 500 kinases in the human genome.
GTP-binding proteins are ON with GTP and turn themselves OFF by hydrolysing it. A GEF switches them on; a GAP speeds up switching off. Examples: G proteins, Ras.
Every switch needs an off route. A switch that cannot turn off causes disease (Ras mutations in cancer, cholera toxin).


Inside the cell, signals are carried by proteins that act as switches. There are two main kinds. The first is phosphorylation. A protein kinase transfers a phosphate group from ATP onto a serine, threonine or tyrosine side chain of a target protein. The large negative charge changes the protein’s shape or creates a docking site for other proteins, so the protein is switched on, or sometimes off. A protein phosphatase removes the phosphate again. The human genome has about 500 kinases, which shows how central this switch is. The second kind are GTP-binding proteins. With GTP bound they are on; with GDP bound they are off. They switch themselves off, because they slowly hydrolyse their GTP to GDP. Two kinds of helper proteins control the timing: a guanine nucleotide exchange factor, GEF, lets GDP out and GTP in, which switches the protein on. A GTPase-activating protein, GAP, speeds up hydrolysis, which switches it off. Activated receptors often act as GEFs. The heterotrimeric G proteins and the small protein Ras are both GTPases. The off route is as important as the on route: Ras that cannot hydrolyse GTP drives many cancers, and cholera toxin locks a G protein in the on state.

title: Principles of cell communication
section: Integration and feedback: cells compute
text:
Integration and feedback: cells compute


Integration: a cell receives many signals at once. Proteins that need two inputs act like an AND gate; the answer depends on the combination of signals.
Negative feedback: the output switches off its own cause. Keeps responses short or stable, and lets the cell adapt.
Positive feedback: the output reinforces itself. Makes all-or-none decisions that stay on (dividing, differentiating).


A cell does not receive one signal at a time. It sits in a bath of hormones, local mediators and contact signals, and it has to combine them. Integration happens where pathways meet. Some proteins are switched on only when two signals arrive together, for example when a protein needs two phosphorylations by two different kinases, or a kinase needs both a lipid messenger and calcium. Such a protein works like an AND gate in a computer. Feedback loops shape the response in time. In negative feedback, a product of the pathway inhibits an earlier step. The result is a response that rises and then settles to a lower, stable level, even if the signal stays on; this is one way cells adapt. You will see negative feedback in the kinase cascade lecture, where it explains why some cancer drugs lose effect. In positive feedback, a product activates its own production. Then a small push beyond a threshold flips the system completely on, and it stays on even when the signal falls. Cells use positive feedback for decisions that must be all or none, such as entering cell division, which you meet in the cell-cycle lectures.

title: Principles of cell communication
section: Adaptation: when the signal stays on
text:
Adaptation: when the signal stays on


Under a constant signal, the response fades: the cell becomes less sensitive (desensitisation). A stronger signal gives a new response.
Ways to adapt: the active receptor is phosphorylated and blocked by arrestin (seconds to minutes); receptors are taken into the cell (minutes to hours) and degraded; downstream proteins adapt.
Seen in the clinic as tolerance: opioids need higher doses over time; frequent β₂-agonist inhaler use works less well.


If a signal stays on, most cells do not keep responding at the same level. The response rises quickly and then falls, although the signal is still there. The cell has become less sensitive, which is called adaptation or desensitisation. If the signal then becomes stronger, the cell responds again. This lets cells detect changes in a signal over a wide range of concentrations, as your eyes adapt from sunlight to a dark room. There are several mechanisms. Fast: a special kinase phosphorylates the active receptor, and a protein called arrestin binds the phosphorylated receptor and blocks the G protein from coupling; you meet this in the next lecture. Slower: receptors are pulled into the cell by endocytosis, which you met in the endocytosis lecture, and some are degraded in lysosomes, so fewer receptors remain. Changes further downstream also contribute. In medicine, adaptation appears as tolerance. Patients who take opioids for a long time need higher doses for the same pain relief, and asthma patients who use a beta-2 agonist inhaler very often find that it works less well. In the demo, you can remove receptors and see what happens to the dose–response curve.

title: Principles of cell communication
section: Fast and slow responses
text:
Fast and slow responses


Fast (milliseconds to minutes): the signal changes proteins that are already there: opens channels, switches enzymes, starts secretion or contraction.
Slow (hours to days): the signal changes gene expression; new proteins must be made. This is how cells change what they are.
Many signals do both: adrenaline acts in seconds via enzymes, and later changes genes via the same pathway.


The speed of a response tells you a lot about its mechanism. The fastest responses are electrical: a ligand-gated channel opens within a millisecond, and the membrane voltage changes immediately. Next come responses that work through second messengers and protein phosphorylation. They take seconds to minutes, because a few enzymatic steps are needed, but nothing new has to be made. Secretion of stored hormones, muscle contraction and changes in cell shape belong here. The slowest responses involve gene expression. The signal must reach the nucleus, the gene must be transcribed, the RNA processed, exported and translated, and the protein must fold and reach its place. That takes from about half an hour to many hours. Decisions about cell division, differentiation and cell death take hours to days. The difference is the reason why adrenaline acts within seconds and cortisol within hours. Many pathways have both a fast and a slow arm. Protein kinase A, activated by adrenaline, quickly phosphorylates metabolic enzymes, and it also phosphorylates a transcription factor that changes gene expression over the following hours.

title: Principles of cell communication
section: Why it matters: receptors are the main drug targets

title: Principles of cell communication
section: Why it matters: opioids, naloxone and beta-blockers
text:
Why it matters: opioids, naloxone and beta-blockers



Morphine, fentanyl: full agonists at the μ-opioid receptor (a GPCR). They relieve pain, but in overdose they stop breathing.
Buprenorphine: a partial agonist with very high affinity. Its effect on breathing reaches a ceiling, so it is safer; used to treat opioid addiction. It also displaces full agonists.
Naloxone: a competitive antagonist. A nasal spray or injection pushes the opioid off the receptors and restarts breathing within minutes. It wears off faster than many opioids, so the patient must be watched.
Beta-blockers (metoprolol): competitive antagonists at the β₁-adrenergic receptor of the heart. They shift the curve for adrenaline to the right: lower heart rate and blood pressure.







A naloxone kit handed out to the public (New Brunswick, Canada): naloxone, syringes and instructions.


Here the vocabulary saves lives. Morphine and fentanyl are full agonists at the mu-opioid receptor, a GPCR on nerve cells in the pain pathways and in the brainstem centres that control breathing. They relieve pain, but too much shuts down breathing, which is how people die of an overdose. Buprenorphine is a partial agonist with very high affinity. Because its maximal effect is lower, the depression of breathing reaches a ceiling, and buprenorphine is used as a safer substitute in the treatment of opioid addiction. Its high affinity has another consequence: it pushes full agonists off the receptor, and in someone who is dependent on heroin it can cause sudden withdrawal. Naloxone is a competitive antagonist. Given as a nasal spray or an injection, it displaces the opioid and restores breathing within minutes. Because it is competitive, a large opioid dose may need a large naloxone dose, and because naloxone is cleared within about an hour, the opioid can take over again, so the patient must be observed. Beta-blockers such as metoprolol are competitive antagonists at the beta-1 receptor in the heart. They shift the dose–response curve for adrenaline and noradrenaline to the right, so the heart rate and blood pressure fall. In the demo you can try all of these.

title: Principles of cell communication
section: Summary
text:
Summary

Cells signal over long distances (endocrine), short distances (paracrine, autocrine, synaptic) or by contact. Water-soluble signals use cell-surface receptors (ion-channel-coupled, GPCR, enzyme-coupled); small fat-soluble signals use intracellular receptors that regulate genes.
Binding is an equilibrium: Kd is the concentration that fills half the receptors. A dose–response curve gives Emax (efficacy) and EC₅₀ (potency); IC₅₀ measures an inhibitor.
Agonists switch receptors on, partial agonists only part-way, antagonists block. Competitive antagonists shift the curve; non-competitive ones lower the maximum.
Signals are amplified by cascades of molecular switches (kinases and phosphatases, GTPases with GEFs and GAPs), integrated, shaped by feedback, and adapt when they stay on.
Changing existing proteins is fast (seconds); changing gene expression is slow (hours). Receptors are the targets of a large part of all drugs.

Read more (optional): Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell, 7th ed., ch. 15.
Image credits

Five take-home points. First, cells signal over different distances, and the chemistry of the signal decides where its receptor is: water-soluble signals bind receptors in the plasma membrane, of three classes; small fat-soluble signals cross the membrane and bind nuclear receptors that act on genes. Second, binding is an equilibrium described by K d, and the dose–response curve, plotted on a log axis, gives you E max and EC 50; for an inhibitor you measure the IC 50. Third, affinity and efficacy are different: a full agonist switches the receptor fully on, a partial agonist part-way, and an antagonist not at all; competitive antagonists shift the curve to the right, non-competitive antagonists lower its maximum. Fourth, the cell amplifies, combines and shapes signals with molecular switches and feedback loops, and it adapts to a signal that stays on. Fifth, changing existing proteins takes seconds, while changing genes takes hours. In the next lecture we open the box of the G-protein-coupled receptor and follow the signal from the receptor to second messengers.

title: Study questions: sorting proteins to the right compartment
text: Study questions in the style of the written exam. Write your answer first (a few sentences, or a labelled sketch where it helps), then compare with the model answer. Each question is tagged with its learning outcome (ELO). Questions tagged [VG] are of the kind used for the higher grade: predict, compare, explain an unexpected result or design an experiment.

title: Study questions: sorting proteins to the right compartment
section: G-level questions
text:
G-level questions
1. What is a sorting signal? Describe three different sorting signals: where each sits on the protein, what it looks like, and where it sends the protein. [ELO 4]






Model answer





A sorting signal is a part of a protein that is recognised by a receptor and decides where the protein goes, like a zip code on a parcel. Most are short stretches of amino acids in which the pattern matters more than the exact sequence. Examples: the ER signal peptide, at the N-terminus, 15–30 amino acids with a hydrophobic core, sends the protein into the ER and is cut off. The NLS, a short basic stretch (e.g. PKKKRKV) almost anywhere in the protein, sends it into the nucleus and stays. PTS1, the last three amino acids (-SKL), sends it into peroxisomes. Others: the mitochondrial presequence (N-terminal positively charged amphipathic helix, cut off in the matrix), KDEL (C-terminal, returns proteins to the ER), the NES (leucine-rich, export from the nucleus), and the mannose-6-phosphate signal, which is a patch on the folded surface rather than a linear sequence.




2. Describe the three ways in which proteins move between compartments. Use the idea of topology (cytosol side and lumen side) to explain why each compartment uses the kind of transport it does. [ELO 4, 5]






Model answer





Gated transport between cytosol and nucleus: the nucleoplasm and the cytosol are one space joined by nuclear pores, so no membrane is crossed; the pore lets small molecules diffuse and lets large folded proteins through only when bound to a transport receptor. Transmembrane transport from the cytosol into the ER, mitochondria and peroxisomes: these are separate spaces, so the protein must cross a membrane through a protein translocator, usually as an unfolded chain (peroxisomes import folded proteins). Vesicular transport from the ER onwards: the ER, Golgi, endosomes, lysosomes and the outside are all on the lumen side, so vesicles can bud from one and fuse with the next and carry proteins without any membrane crossing.




3. Describe the import of a protein with an NLS into the nucleus, step by step. Include the roles of importin α, importin β, the FG repeats and Ran. [ELO 4]






Model answer





In the cytosol, importin α binds the NLS and importin β binds importin α. Importin β interacts with the FG repeats, the disordered Phe-Gly-rich chains that fill the pore channel, and the complex passes through the pore with the cargo folded (about 10 ms). In the nucleus, Ran-GTP binds importin β, the complex changes shape and releases importin α and the cargo. Importin β returns to the cytosol bound to Ran-GTP; there RanGAP makes Ran hydrolyse GTP, Ran-GDP lets go and importin β is free again (importin α is returned by its own exportin). Because Ran-GTP is made in the nucleus by RanGEF on chromatin and destroyed in the cytosol, the cargo is always released on the nuclear side: import is one-way.




4. Compare nuclear import and nuclear export. What is the same, and what is opposite? [ELO 4]






Model answer





Same: both use soluble transport receptors (karyopherins) that pass the FG meshwork of the pore with folded cargo, and both use the Ran-GTP gradient, so both get their energy from Ran’s GTP hydrolysis. Opposite: importins bind cargo (with an NLS) in the cytosol, where Ran-GTP is absent, and release it when Ran-GTP binds in the nucleus. Exportins (e.g. XPO1/CRM1) bind cargo (with a leucine-rich NES) in the nucleus together with Ran-GTP, and release it in the cytosol when GTP is hydrolysed.




5. Describe how a protein made in the cytosol reaches the mitochondrial matrix. Name the complexes and the forces involved. [ELO 4, 5]






Model answer





The precursor is made on free ribosomes and kept unfolded by cytosolic Hsp70 chaperones (post-translational import). Its N-terminal presequence, a positively charged amphipathic helix, binds receptors of the TOM complex in the outer membrane. The chain passes the TOM channel and, at a contact site, the TIM23 channel in the inner membrane. The membrane potential across the inner membrane (about 150–180 mV, matrix negative) pulls the positive presequence in, and mitochondrial Hsp70 pulls the rest using ATP. The matrix processing peptidase removes the presequence, and the protein folds. A hydrophobic segment after the presequence can stop transfer in TIM23 and leave the protein in the inner membrane.




6. How does peroxisomal import differ from import into mitochondria and the ER? [ELO 4, 5]






Model answer





Peroxisomal matrix proteins carry PTS1 (C-terminal -SKL) and are recognised after translation by the cytosolic receptor PEX5, which docks on the peroxisome membrane and takes the cargo in. Unlike the ER and mitochondria, peroxisomes import proteins fully folded, even oligomers, and the receptor enters with its cargo and is recycled. The ER imports during translation (co-translational, SRP-dependent) and mitochondria import unfolded chains through TOM and TIM using the membrane potential. Defects in the PEX genes stop import (Zellweger syndrome).




7. Explain what happens to (a) a soluble ER protein with a C-terminal KDEL, (b) a lysosomal enzyme with a mannose-6-phosphate signal patch, and (c) a soluble protein with only an ER signal peptide. [ELO 4]






Model answer





All three enter the ER lumen by their signal peptide and leave the ER in COPII vesicles. (a) The KDEL protein reaches the cis-Golgi, where the KDEL receptor binds it and returns it to the ER in COPI vesicles: retrieval, so at steady state it is in the ER. (b) In the cis-Golgi an enzyme recognises the signal patch and adds a phosphate to mannose; in the trans-Golgi network the M6P receptor binds the tag, and clathrin-coated vesicles carry it to endosomes, where the acid pH releases it; it ends up in lysosomes. (c) With no further signal it follows the default route through the Golgi and is secreted.




8. Describe an experiment that shows that a protein is imported into mitochondria rather than just bound to their surface. [ELO 1, 4]






Model answer





Make the precursor in a test tube with radioactive amino acids; incubate with isolated mitochondria; then add a protease, which cannot cross membranes and digests everything outside. Analyse by SDS-PAGE and autoradiography. An imported protein is protected from the protease and is often shorter (presequence removed). Controls: without mitochondria the precursor is digested; an uncoupler (CCCP), which collapses the membrane potential, blocks import, so the protein is digested; detergent dissolves the membranes and makes the protein sensitive again, showing that protection was due to the membranes.

title: Study questions: sorting proteins to the right compartment
section: VG-level questions
text:
VG-level questions
9. [VG] A researcher adds the SV40 NLS to the C-terminus of human serum albumin, which has an N-terminal ER signal peptide. She expects the protein in the nucleus, but finds it in the culture medium. Explain the result, and propose one change to the construct that would put it in the nucleus. [ELO 4]






Model answer





The ER signal peptide is read first, by SRP, while the protein is still being translated. The ribosome is brought to the ER and the whole chain, including the NLS, is threaded into the ER lumen. Importins are in the cytosol and never see the NLS, so it has no effect; with no other signal the protein follows the default route and is secreted into the medium. To send it to the nucleus, remove the signal peptide: the protein is then finished in the cytosol and the NLS can be read by importin α. (Albumin is about 66 kDa, so without an NLS it would stay mainly in the cytosol; with the NLS it is imported. It may fold less well in the cytosol, which is another thing to check.)




10. [VG] A patient’s fibroblasts secrete large amounts of several lysosomal enzymes into the culture medium, and their lysosomes are full of undigested material. The enzymes themselves have normal sequences. (a) Propose which step is defective. (b) Predict what happens if you add purified, correctly tagged lysosomal enzyme to the medium, and explain. [ELO 4, 9]






Model answer






All the enzymes are normal but go to the wrong place, so the shared sorting step is broken: the enzyme in the cis-Golgi that adds the mannose-6-phosphate tag (the GlcNAc phosphotransferase), as in I-cell disease. Without M6P, the M6P receptor in the trans-Golgi network cannot bind the enzymes, and they follow the default route and are secreted. (A defective M6P receptor would give a similar picture.) (b) Some M6P receptors are also on the plasma membrane. Tagged enzyme added to the medium binds them, is taken up by endocytosis and delivered to lysosomes, so the stored material should be degraded. This is the principle of enzyme replacement therapy for lysosomal storage diseases (endocytosis lecture).





11. [VG] Design an experiment to test whether a new 80 kDa protein, which has a short basic stretch in the middle, is imported into the nucleus because of that stretch. Say what result you expect if the hypothesis is right, and include the controls. [ELO 1, 4]






Model answer





Make GFP fusions and express them in cultured cells; image living cells by fluorescence microscopy with a DNA stain (e.g. Hoechst) to mark the nucleus, and quantify the nuclear/cytosolic ratio in many cells. Constructs: (1) the full protein–GFP: if the hypothesis is right, it is nuclear. (2) The same protein with the basic stretch mutated (e.g. lysines to alanine or threonine): it should stay cytosolic (necessary). (3) The basic stretch alone fused to a large cytosolic reporter (e.g. GFP fused to a large enzyme, or two to three GFPs in a row, too big to diffuse): it should become nuclear (sufficient). Controls: GFP alone (small, spreads everywhere) and the large reporter without the stretch (cytosolic). A dominant-negative or depleted importin α/β, or a drug that blocks import, should keep construct 1 out of the nucleus.

title: Study questions: sorting proteins to the right compartment
section: Explore
text:
Explore
Demo: zip-code game. Build a protein from sorting signals: an N-terminal ER signal peptide or mitochondrial presequence, a transmembrane (TM) segment, an NLS, a C-terminal KDEL or PTS1, and a mannose-6-phosphate signal patch; choose whether the protein is small (like GFP) or large. Or start from a real protein. Predict where it ends up, then press Run and follow its route on the cell map. Time runs in real time by default (the clock shows minutes since translation began); choose a faster speed if you do not want to wait, or “Show the end now”. The result box explains the outcome, greys out signals that have no effect, and says why.
The rules are the textbook ones: the ER decision is made during translation, and a signal works only on the side of the membrane where its receptor is. Combinations that real cells resolve in complicated ways (e.g. two cytosolic signals on one protein) are marked not predicted rather than given an invented answer. The times are typical, rounded values.



E1. Choose Albumin. Predict, then run it at real time for one minute: what happens first, and where is the ribosome? Then speed up. Where does albumin end, and how long does the whole route take? Now add KDEL at the C-terminus and run again. Where does it end, and does KDEL stop the protein from leaving the ER? [ELO 4]
E2. Compare GFP alone, the same protein made large, and GFP + NLS. Where does each end up, and why? Which one is the “necessary and sufficient” experiment from the lecture? [ELO 4]
E3. Choose Cathepsin D. Predict and run. Then remove its ER signal peptide (N-terminus: none) and run again. What happens to the M6P signal, and why? [ELO 4]
E4. [VG] Predict first. (a) Add an NLS to Albumin. (b) Add KDEL to the LDL receptor. For each, write down your prediction with a reason before you run. Then explain why the extra signal has no effect in both cases, using the word topology. [ELO 4, 5]
E5. [VG] Choose Citrate synthase and add an NLS. The game says “not predicted”. Why is this combination not decided by a simple rule? Design an experiment that would tell you where such a protein really goes. [ELO 1, 4]
E6. Give a protein a mitochondrial presequence and a TM segment. Where does it end up, and which way does it face? Compare the time it takes with the route of the LDL receptor to the plasma membrane. Why is one so much faster? [ELO 4, 5]






Solutions





E1. In the first minute the ribosome makes the chain; SRP takes the ribosome to the ER, and the chain enters the ER while it is made (the ribosome moves to the ER and lets go after translation). Albumin is secreted: ER (folding, about 5 min) → COPII vesicle to the Golgi (about 10 min) → through the Golgi (about 20 min) → secretory vesicle to the plasma membrane (about 10 min), about 46 min in total. With KDEL it ends in the ER lumen after about 21 min: it still leaves the ER in a COPII vesicle, and is brought back from the cis-Golgi by the KDEL receptor in a COPI vesicle. KDEL does not stop exit; it works by retrieval.
E2. GFP alone (27 kDa) ends in the cytosol and nucleus: it has no signal, but is small enough to diffuse through the pores (it spreads in about 10 min in the game). The large version stays in the cytosol: too big for the pores and no NLS. GFP + NLS ends in the nucleus (importins carry it in; it builds up over a few minutes). The test of sufficiency is “large protein” versus “large protein + NLS” (try making GFP + NLS large too): the NLS alone moves an unrelated protein. Necessity would be a mutated NLS, which the game shows as removing the NLS.
E3. Cathepsin D with its signal peptide goes ER → Golgi (where it gets the M6P tag) → endosome → lysosome, about 61 min. Without the signal peptide it is made and stays in the cytosol; the M6P patch is greyed out. The M6P tag is added by an enzyme in the cis-Golgi lumen; a protein that never enters the ER never meets it, so the patch has no effect. (Real cathepsin D would also fold badly in the cytosol.)
E4. (a) Albumin + NLS is still secreted. The signal peptide is read first, during translation, so the whole chain, NLS included, is in the ER lumen. Importins are in the cytosol: the NLS is on the wrong side of the membrane. (b) LDL receptor + KDEL still goes to the plasma membrane. With the signal peptide first and one TM segment, the N-terminal part is in the lumen and the C-terminal tail is in the cytosol (a type I membrane protein). KDEL is at the C-terminus, so it faces the cytosol, and the KDEL receptor, which binds in the lumen, never sees it. In both cases a signal works only on the side of the membrane where its receptor is: that is topology. (ER membrane proteins use a different retrieval signal in their cytosolic tail.)
E5. Both the presequence and the NLS are read in the cytosol, by different receptors (TOM and importins), so they compete for the same newly made protein. Which wins depends on how strong each signal is, how fast the protein folds (mitochondrial import needs an unfolded chain, nuclear import works on folded protein) and the amounts of the receptors; real proteins like this are often found in both places. An experiment: express a GFP fusion of the protein in cells and image with a mitochondrial marker (e.g. MitoTracker or a red mitochondrial protein) and a DNA stain; quantify the fraction in each. Confirm with cell fractionation (nuclear, mitochondrial and cytosolic fractions, Western blot with marker proteins for each fraction), and mutate each signal in turn to see which one is needed for each location.
E6. It goes to the inner mitochondrial membrane: the presequence starts import into the matrix through TOM and TIM23, and the TM segment stops transfer in TIM23 and moves sideways into the inner membrane, with the N-terminus in the matrix and the C-terminal part in the intermembrane space. It takes about 2 min, compared with about 46 min for the LDL receptor. Mitochondrial import is a direct, post-translational crossing of two membranes from the cytosol, while the plasma membrane is reached through the whole secretory pathway: folding and quality control in the ER, vesicle steps to and through the Golgi, and a vesicle to the surface.
