title: Quiz: protein life and death
text:
Short questions to check your understanding of the lecture Protein life and death: folding, modification and degradation. Try each on paper first, then open the hint or the answer. The tag after each question shows the learning outcome (ELO) it practises.

Q1. Anfinsen showed that a purified protein can refold by itself in a test tube. Why do cells still need chaperones? Give two reasons. [ELO 4]






Hint





Compare a test tube with the cytosol, and think about how a new chain is made.









Answer






The cytosol is crowded (about 200–300 g protein per litre), so exposed hydrophobic stretches easily meet and stick to other chains. (2) A new chain is made slowly, one amino acid at a time, so for a long time a partly made chain shows hydrophobic stretches but cannot yet fold. Also, stress (heat) unfolds proteins that were already folded. Chaperones bind exposed hydrophobic stretches and prevent wrong contacts; they do not carry information about the final shape.





Q2. Hsp70 binds its substrate tightly in one nucleotide state and loosely in the other. Which is which, and why does Hsp70 need ATP at all? [ELO 4]






Hint





Think of the lid.









Answer





With ADP bound the lid is closed and Hsp70 holds the chain tightly; with ATP the lid is open and binding is loose and fast. ATP binding and hydrolysis drive the cycle of binding and release: each release gives the chain a new chance to fold, and each rebinding covers its sticky stretches. Without the cycle Hsp70 would either never bind or never let go.




Q3. What is special about the structure of amyloid compared with an amorphous aggregate, and why can amyloid “spread”? [ELO 4] [ELO 9]






Hint





Look at the direction of the β-strands relative to the fibril.









Answer





Amyloid is ordered: each chain forms β-strands lying across the fibril, and strands from many chains stack along it (cross-β), held by backbone hydrogen bonds. This makes fibrils very stable. A fibril end acts as a seed that converts new misfolded chains into the same structure, and broken fibrils make new seeds, which can move to other cells. An amorphous aggregate is a disordered tangle without this template.




Q4. A kinase phosphorylates an enzyme on a serine and the enzyme becomes active. Name the enzyme that switches it off again, and explain how one phosphate can change activity. [ELO 4]






Hint





What does a phosphate group carry?









Answer





A protein phosphatase removes the phosphate (by hydrolysis). The phosphate carries two negative charges and is large; it attracts positive and repels negative side chains nearby, which can move a loop, open the active site or create (or block) a binding surface for another protein. The switch is fast and reversible and needs no new protein synthesis.




Q5. Put these in the correct order for marking a protein for destruction, and say what each does: E2, proteasome, E1, E3. Which of them gives the specificity? [ELO 4]






Hint





Humans have 2 of one, about 40 of another and about 600 of a third.









Answer





E1 activates ubiquitin using ATP → E2 carries the activated ubiquitin → E3 binds both the E2 and the substrate (through its degron) and moves ubiquitin onto a lysine of the substrate; repeated rounds build a Lys48 chain → the 26S proteasome binds the chain, removes the ubiquitin, unfolds the protein and cuts it into peptides. The E3s (about 600 in humans) give the specificity.




Q6. Two proteins are both present at 1000 molecules per cell. Protein A has a half-life of 30 min, protein B of 30 h. Which one is made faster? What happens to each within 2 hours after the gene is switched off? [ELO 4]






Hint





At steady state \(P = k_s/k_d\), and \(k_d = \ln 2 / t_{1/2}\).









Answer





At steady state \(k_s = k_d P\), so A is made 60 times faster than B (its \(k_d\) is 60 times larger). After the gene is switched off, A falls by half every 30 min: after 2 h (4 half-lives) about 1/16, about 60 molecules, are left. B loses only about 4.5 % in 2 h (\(e^{-0.023 \times 2} \approx 0.955\)), about 955 molecules left. Short-lived proteins can be changed quickly.




Q7. In a cycloheximide chase you add a proteasome inhibitor together with cycloheximide, and the protein now disappears much more slowly. What do you conclude? Why can you not run the experiment for 48 hours? [ELO 1] [ELO 4]






Hint





What else besides your protein depends on new protein synthesis?









Answer





The protein is degraded mainly by the proteasome (most likely after ubiquitination). A long experiment is not reliable because cycloheximide stops all protein synthesis: short-lived proteins, including regulators of degradation itself, disappear, the cell becomes stressed and eventually dies. Results over more than a few hours no longer describe a normal cell; a pulse-chase avoids this.




Q8. Bortezomib and lenalidomide are both used in multiple myeloma and both act on the ubiquitin–proteasome system. How do their mechanisms differ? [ELO 4] [ELO 9]






Hint





One blocks, the other redirects.









Answer





Bortezomib blocks the proteasome (the β5 active site in the 20S core): degradation of many proteins slows, misfolded antibody chains pile up in the protein-loaded myeloma cell, and the cell dies by apoptosis. Lenalidomide redirects an E3 ligase: it binds cereblon and acts as a molecular glue, so cereblon tags new substrates (IKZF1 and IKZF3) for destruction; the myeloma cells need these transcription factors to survive.

title: Protein life and death: folding, modification and degradation
section: About this lecture

title: Protein life and death: folding, modification and degradation
section: The question: why do some proteins live for minutes, and others for your whole life?
text:
The question: why do some proteins live for minutes, and others for your whole life?



Cataract: the lens of this eye has become cloudy.


The crystallins in your eye lens were made before you were born. They are never replaced. Over decades they are damaged, unfold and clump: the lens turns cloudy (cataract).
The tumour suppressor p53 is made all the time but lives only 5–20 minutes. When DNA is damaged, the cell stops destroying it, and p53 builds up within an hour.
Most proteins in a growing human cell live hours to a few days.

How does a cell decide which protein to destroy, and when? And how does a protein keep its shape at all?


Look at this eye. The lens should be clear, but here it is milky white: a cataract. The lens is made of tightly packed cells that lost their nucleus and organelles early in life. They are filled with proteins called crystallins, which were made when you were an embryo and never replaced. Over sixty or seventy years, UV light and chemical damage slowly unfold some crystallins. Unfolded proteins stick together, and the clumps scatter light. Cataract is the most common cause of blindness worldwide. Compare this with p53, the protein that stops a cell from dividing when its DNA is damaged. A cell makes p53 all the time, but destroys each molecule within minutes. When DNA is damaged, the cell simply stops destroying it, and p53 rises fast. So the lifetime of a protein is not an accident: it is controlled, and control of destruction is as important as control of synthesis. Today we ask how proteins keep their shape, how the cell marks proteins for destruction, and how this sets the amount of each protein.

title: Protein life and death: folding, modification and degradation
section: Recap: a protein’s fold is only just stable
text:
Recap: a protein’s fold is only just stable


The amino acid sequence contains the information for the fold (Anfinsen). The hydrophobic side chains are buried in a core.
A folded protein is only slightly more stable than the unfolded chain: often only 20–60 kJ/mol, the energy of a few hydrogen bonds. Heat, mutations or damage can unfold it.
A chain that is partly folded shows hydrophobic patches. It can fold, stick to other chains (aggregate), or be destroyed. This lecture is about these three fates.


This is a recap from biochemistry, with one new point. Christian Anfinsen showed in the 1950s and 60s that a purified, unfolded enzyme can refold by itself in a test tube: the sequence contains all the information for the shape. In the folded protein the hydrophobic side chains are hidden in the core, away from water. The new point is that the folded state is only marginally stable. The difference in free energy between the folded and unfolded protein is typically twenty to sixty kilojoules per mole, about as much as a few hydrogen bonds. So proteins breathe, partly unfold and refold, all the time, and a small push from heat or a mutation can tip the balance. A partly folded chain has a problem: its hydrophobic patches are exposed. Such a chain has three possible futures, shown in the diagram. It can fold, often with help. It can stick to other exposed chains and form an aggregate. Or the cell can recognise it as damaged and destroy it. The rest of the lecture follows these three paths, and how the cell chooses between them.

title: Protein life and death: folding, modification and degradation
section: Folding in a crowded cytosol
text:
Folding in a crowded cytosol



Painting of the cytoplasm at molecular scale, drawn from known structures. Blue: ribosomes; long tubes: cytoskeleton filaments.


The cytosol holds about 200–300 g of protein per litre: macromolecules fill a quarter or more of the volume.
A new chain leaves the ribosome one amino acid at a time, about 5 per second in human cells. A 500-residue protein needs about 2 minutes; it cannot fold until a whole domain is out.
Meanwhile its hydrophobic stretches are exposed, among thousands of other sticky surfaces. Crowding makes sticking more likely.
Chaperones bind exposed hydrophobic stretches, prevent wrong contacts and give the chain time and space to fold. Many are heat shock proteins (Hsp): the cell makes more of them when stress unfolds proteins.



Anfinsen’s experiments were done in dilute solution in a test tube. A cell is very different. This painting by David Goodsell shows the inside of a cell at the scale of molecules, drawn from real structures. Every space is filled: ribosomes in blue, filaments of the cytoskeleton, and thousands of other proteins. The cytosol contains two to three hundred grams of protein per litre, which is like a thick syrup. In such a crowded space, molecules are pushed together, which makes them stick to each other more easily. The second problem is time. A ribosome adds about five amino acids per second, so a large protein takes minutes to make, and a domain cannot fold properly until the whole domain has left the ribosome. During that time, the growing chain shows hydrophobic stretches to its neighbours. The solution is a set of proteins called molecular chaperones. They do not contain information about the final shape. They simply bind exposed hydrophobic stretches and release them again, so that wrong contacts are prevented. Many chaperones were first found as heat shock proteins, because cells make more of them after a heat shock, when many proteins unfold.

title: Protein life and death: folding, modification and degradation
section: Hsp70: hold and release, powered by ATP
text:
Hsp70: hold and release, powered by ATP


Hsp70 binds short hydrophobic stretches of an unfolded chain, often while it is still on the ribosome. With ATP: open, loose binding. With ADP: lid closed, tight grip.
Each round of binding and release gives the chain a new chance to fold. Helpers: J-proteins (Hsp40) bring chains and start ATP hydrolysis; exchange factors reload ATP.
Hsp70 also unfolds aggregates (with Hsp110) and hands hopeless cases to an E3 ligase for destruction.


Hsp70 is the main all-purpose chaperone of the cytosol, and it works by a cycle of binding and release. It has two parts: a domain that binds ATP and a domain that binds the substrate chain, with a lid. Follow the cycle from step one. With ATP bound, the lid is open and Hsp70 binds chains loosely. A helper called a J-protein, or Hsp40, brings an unfolded chain and stimulates Hsp70 to split its ATP. In step two, with ADP bound, the lid closes over a short hydrophobic stretch of the chain, and Hsp70 holds it tightly. That stretch is now covered and cannot stick to anything else. In step three, a nucleotide exchange factor removes the ADP, and new ATP binds. In step four the lid opens and the chain is released. If it folds, fine. If it still shows hydrophobic stretches, Hsp70 binds it again. So Hsp70 uses ATP not to fold the protein, but to give it many chances. If a chain never folds, Hsp70 can pass it to an E3 ubiquitin ligase, which marks it for destruction. We meet E3s later today.

title: Protein life and death: folding, modification and degradation
section: Chaperonins: a folding cage
text:
Chaperonins: a folding cage











A barrel of two rings (7 or 8 subunits each). A misfolded chain enters the ring, a lid closes, and it folds alone in a protected chamber for about 10 s (an ATP timer).
Bacteria: GroEL with the lid GroES (structure above). Human cytosol: TRiC (CCT), needed for actin and tubulin; mitochondria: Hsp60.


Some proteins need more than Hsp70. For these, cells have chaperonins: large barrel-shaped machines with a cavity inside. The structure at the top is the bacterial chaperonin GroEL, seen from the end and from the side, with its lid, GroES, in green. GroEL is two rings of seven subunits stacked back to back. The cartoon shows how it works. A misfolded chain binds to hydrophobic patches at the rim of an open ring. Then ATP and the lid bind. This changes the shape of the ring: the inside wall becomes water-loving, the chain is released into the closed chamber, and it can fold there alone, without meeting any other chain. This is sometimes called the Anfinsen cage, because inside it the protein is in the same situation as in Anfinsen’s test tube. After about ten seconds, ATP hydrolysis acts as a timer, the lid comes off and the protein leaves, folded or not. If not, it can enter again. Human cells have a chaperonin called TRiC in the cytosol, which is essential for folding actin and tubulin, the building blocks of the cytoskeleton, and Hsp60 in mitochondria.

title: Protein life and death: folding, modification and degradation
section: When folding fails: aggregates and amyloid
text:
When folding fails: aggregates and amyloid





Model of an amyloid fibril: β-strands (arrows) from many chains stacked into one long sheet.


Amorphous aggregates: tangles of misfolded chains, often cleared by chaperones and degradation.
Amyloid: ordered fibrils in which chains of any sequence stack as cross-β sheets. Very stable, they seed their own growth. About 50 human diseases involve amyloid.


What happens when chaperones and degradation cannot keep up? Misfolded chains stick to each other. Often they form disordered clumps, called amorphous aggregates, which chaperones can sometimes pull apart. But some proteins form a special, highly ordered aggregate: amyloid. In an amyloid fibril, each chain forms a flat β-strand that lies across the fibril, and strands from thousands of chains stack on top of each other, just under half a nanometre apart, held by hydrogen bonds between their backbones. The model on the right shows this sheet of stacked strands. Because the backbone is the same in every protein, almost any chain can form amyloid under some conditions. Fibrils grow from their ends: a fibril end acts as a seed and recruits new misfolded chains, and when fibrils break, the pieces become new seeds. This is why amyloid can spread, and in prion diseases even pass from one animal to another. Small clumps of a few chains, called oligomers, may be more toxic to cells than the large fibrils. Amyloid is found in Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, type 2 diabetes and about fifty other diseases.

title: Protein life and death: folding, modification and degradation
section: A protein as a switch: phosphorylation
text:
A protein as a switch: phosphorylation


A protein kinase moves the end phosphate of ATP onto serine, threonine or tyrosine; a protein phosphatase removes it. Humans have about 500 kinases and about 150 phosphatases.
The phosphate carries two negative charges: it changes the protein’s shape, its activity, its partners or its location, within seconds.
Reversible and fast: the cell’s most common way to switch proteins in signalling (the signalling lectures) and the cell cycle.


A folded protein is often not simply active. Many proteins can be switched between two states, and the most common switch is phosphorylation. A protein kinase takes the end phosphate from ATP and attaches it to the hydroxyl group of a serine, threonine or tyrosine side chain. The phosphate is large and carries two negative charges. It can attract positively charged side chains nearby and repel negative ones, which can pull a loop into a new position, open an active site, or create a new binding surface for another protein. A protein phosphatase removes the phosphate again with water. The switch is therefore fully reversible, and the balance of kinase and phosphatase activity decides how much of the protein is in the on state. Humans have about five hundred protein kinases and fewer phosphatases, and most proteins are phosphorylated at some time. Phosphorylation is fast, within seconds, and does not need new protein to be made. That is why it dominates signalling, which you will meet in the signalling lectures, and the cell cycle. Kinase inhibitors are one of the largest groups of cancer drugs.

title: Protein life and death: folding, modification and degradation
section: More marks: acetylation, ubiquitination, methylation
text:
More marks: acetylation, ubiquitination, methylation


Each mark has writers (add it), erasers (remove it) and readers (proteins that bind the mark and act).
Marks combine: one phosphate can create a binding site for an E3 ligase, so the protein is ubiquitinated and destroyed (next slides).
Many other modifications exist (sugars, lipids); the sugars added in the ER and Golgi come in those lectures.


Phosphorylation is not the only mark. Lysine side chains, with their positive charge, can carry several. Acetylation adds an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to a lysine and removes its positive charge. On histones this loosens the grip of the histone on negatively charged DNA and opens chromatin for transcription, which you met in gene regulation. Acetylation also changes the activity of many enzymes in the cytosol and mitochondria, linking them to the cell’s metabolic state. Deacetylases remove the mark; some deacetylase inhibitors are used against lymphoma. Methylation adds one to three methyl groups to lysine or arginine without changing the charge; it is read by proteins that bind the methylated site, especially on histones. Ubiquitination attaches a whole small protein, ubiquitin, to a lysine. A chain of ubiquitins is the signal for destruction, but single ubiquitins and other chain types have other jobs. The general idea is the same for all marks: enzymes write them, other enzymes erase them, and reader proteins bind them and act. Marks also combine: phosphorylation can create the signal that leads to ubiquitination, as we will see.

title: Protein life and death: folding, modification and degradation
section: Ubiquitin tagging: E1, E2, E3
text:
Ubiquitin tagging: E1, E2, E3


Ubiquitin (Ub) is a small protein of 76 amino acids, found in all eukaryotes (“ubiquitous”).
E1 activates it with ATP, E2 carries it, E3 picks the substrate and links Ub to one of its lysines. Repeated rounds build a chain. Deubiquitinases can remove it again.
The chain type is a code: Lys48 chains send a protein to the proteasome; single Ub and Lys63 chains are signals (e.g. for endocytosis, the endocytosis lecture).


How does the cell mark a protein for destruction? It attaches ubiquitin, a small, very stable protein of seventy-six amino acids. Three kinds of enzyme work in a relay. E1, the activating enzyme, uses ATP to attach ubiquitin to itself. E1 passes the ubiquitin to an E2, the conjugating enzyme. The E2 then teams up with an E3, the ligase, which binds the target protein, the substrate. The E3 positions the substrate so that the ubiquitin is transferred onto one of its lysine side chains. Ubiquitin itself has seven lysines, so a second ubiquitin can be added onto the first, and so on, building a chain. Notice the numbers: humans have two E1s, about forty E2s, but about six hundred E3s. The E3s recognise different substrates, so they provide the specificity, much as kinases do for phosphorylation. The type of chain matters. A chain of four or more ubiquitins linked through lysine 48 is read by the proteasome and means destroy. A single ubiquitin, or chains linked through lysine 63, act as signals, for example to send a membrane protein into endocytosis, which comes in the endocytosis lecture.

title: Protein life and death: folding, modification and degradation
section: Degrons: what decides that a protein is destroyed?

title: Protein life and death: folding, modification and degradation
section: The proteasome: a shredder with a gate
text:
The proteasome: a shredder with a gate





Structure of the yeast 26S proteasome: 20S core (blue–yellow rings) and 19S cap (red), each subunit in its own colour.

26S proteasome: about 2.5 MDa, many thousands per cell, in the cytosol and nucleus.
The 19S cap binds the Ub chain, removes and recycles the ubiquitin, and unfolds the protein with ATP.
The 20S core cuts it inside a closed chamber into short peptides, which cytosolic peptidases turn into amino acids.



The proteasome is where ubiquitinated proteins end. It is a huge complex, about two and a half megadaltons, and every cell has many thousands of them in the cytosol and the nucleus. The structure on the right, and the cartoon on the left, show its two parts. The core particle, 20S, is a barrel of four stacked rings of seven subunits. The two inner rings, the beta rings, carry six protease active sites, all facing the inside of the barrel. The two outer alpha rings form a gate. Because the active sites are hidden inside, a normal folded protein in the cytosol is safe: it cannot get in. The cap, 19S, is the gatekeeper. Its receptors bind the lysine-48 ubiquitin chain. Enzymes in the cap remove the ubiquitin, which is reused. A ring of six ATPases then grips the protein, unfolds it, and threads it as a single chain into the core. Inside, the chain is cut into peptides of about three to twenty-five amino acids, which other enzymes in the cytosol break down to amino acids. Some peptides are shown on the cell surface to the immune system, which you will meet in immunology.

title: Protein life and death: folding, modification and degradation
section: Turnover: synthesis and degradation set the amount
text:
Turnover: synthesis and degradation set the amount


\dfrac{dP}{dt} = k_s - k_d\,P: molecules are made at rate k_s; each is destroyed with probability k_d per hour, so t_{1/2} = \ln 2 / k_d.
Steady state: P_{ss} = k_s / k_d. The time to get there depends only on k_d: half-way after one half-life. Short-lived proteins respond fast. Try it: Demo: protein turnover


Now we can put synthesis and destruction together with one equation. The amount of protein P changes as the rate of synthesis, k s, minus the rate of degradation. Degradation is first order: each molecule has the same chance per hour of being destroyed, k d, so the total rate is k d times P. The half-life is the natural log of two divided by k d. At steady state the two rates are equal, and P equals k s divided by k d. Look at the plot. Both proteins end up at the same amount, almost three thousand molecules per cell. The blue one is made ten times faster but also destroyed ten times faster. The difference is how quickly they get there. The time to reach steady state depends only on the degradation rate: half-way after one half-life, ninety percent after about three point three half-lives. So a protein with a two-hour half-life responds to a change within hours, while one with a twenty-hour half-life needs days. This is why regulators such as transcription factors, cyclins and p53 are short-lived: high turnover costs energy but makes them fast. In growing cells, dilution by cell division adds to k d. The demo lets you try all this.

title: Protein life and death: folding, modification and degradation
section: How do we know? Cycloheximide chase
text:
How do we know? Cycloheximide chase


Cycloheximide blocks the eukaryotic ribosome: k_s = 0, so P(t) = P_0\,e^{-k_d t}. On a log scale the decay is a straight line; read t_{1/2} where the band is 50 %.
Add a proteasome inhibitor too: if the decay slows, the protein is degraded by the proteasome. Caution: cycloheximide stops all synthesis, which stresses the cell, so only short experiments (hours) can be trusted.


How do we measure a half-life in a real cell? The simplest method is a cycloheximide chase. Cycloheximide is a small molecule from a soil bacterium that blocks elongation on eukaryotic ribosomes. Add it to cultured cells and no new protein is made. From that moment the amount of each protein can only fall, and it falls exponentially with its own degradation rate. Collect cells at several times, separate the proteins by SDS gel electrophoresis, and detect your protein with an antibody on a Western blot. A stable protein such as actin serves as a control that equal amounts were loaded. Plot the band intensity on a logarithmic scale against time: the points fall on a straight line whose slope is minus k d, and the half-life is where the band has fallen to half. Here the protein has a half-life of two hours. A useful variation is to add a proteasome inhibitor together with cycloheximide. If the protein now disappears more slowly, it is degraded by the proteasome. The weakness of the method is that stopping all protein synthesis harms the cell: short-lived regulators vanish, and after many hours the cell’s behaviour changes. So results over long times are unreliable.

title: Protein life and death: folding, modification and degradation
section: How do we know? Pulse-chase labelling
text:
How do we know? Pulse-chase labelling


Pulse: a short time with a labelled amino acid (radioactive ³⁵S-methionine, or today often a heavy-isotope or clickable amino acid). Only molecules made in this window are labelled.
Chase: excess normal amino acid. Follow the labelled cohort over time; the cell itself keeps working normally.
Modern versions with mass spectrometry measured thousands of half-lives at once: the median protein in cultured mouse cells lives about 2 days.


A second method avoids the drug. In a pulse-chase experiment you give cells a short pulse, for example ten minutes, of an amino acid that carries a label. Classically this was methionine with radioactive sulfur-35. Every protein made during those ten minutes carries the label; proteins made before or after do not. Then you chase: you replace the medium with one that contains a large excess of normal methionine, so any new protein is unlabelled. At each time point you lyse the cells, pull out your protein with an antibody, run a gel and expose it to film. The labelled band fades as the labelled molecules are destroyed, and you can read the half-life as before. Because nothing is blocked, the cell works normally. The same design can show where a protein goes and how it is processed, for example a change in size when sugars are added; the secretion lectures use it to follow proteins through the ER and Golgi. Today, labels with heavy isotopes and mass spectrometry measure the turnover of thousands of proteins in one experiment. In mouse fibroblasts the median half-life was about two days, while many regulators lived less than an hour.

title: Protein life and death: folding, modification and degradation
section: Why it matters: bortezomib in multiple myeloma
text:
Why it matters: bortezomib in multiple myeloma



Bone marrow smear from a patient with multiple myeloma: many plasma cells (purple, round, nucleus to one side).



Multiple myeloma: a cancer of plasma cells, which make huge amounts of antibody.
Bortezomib (2003) blocks the β5 site of the proteasome (the proteasome slide). Misfolded protein piles up and the myeloma cell dies. Newer: carfilzomib, oral ixazomib.



Our first drug acts on the proteasome directly. Multiple myeloma is a cancer of plasma cells, the cells that make antibodies. The smear on the left shows bone marrow full of them. Each plasma cell secretes thousands of antibody molecules every second, made in the endoplasmic reticulum. Some of them always misfold; these are pulled back out of the ER into the cytosol and destroyed by the proteasome, a process you meet in the ER lecture. Myeloma cells therefore depend heavily on their proteasomes. Bortezomib is a small molecule with a boronic acid group that binds the active threonine of the beta-5 site inside the proteasome core, the site shown in orange on the proteasome slide. When it is partly blocked, misfolded proteins pile up, the unfolded protein response cannot cope, and the myeloma cell kills itself by apoptosis. Normal cells, which make far less protein for export, survive better. Bortezomib was approved in 2003 and, together with other drugs, has more than doubled survival in myeloma. Its side effects, such as nerve damage, show that all cells need their proteasomes. You meet the testing of such drugs in the course on clinical trials and drug development.

title: Protein life and death: folding, modification and degradation
section: Why it matters: drugs that hijack E3 ligases
text:
Why it matters: drugs that hijack E3 ligases


Thalidomide (1957) caused severe limb malformations in about 10 000 children. Fifty years later its target was found: the E3 component cereblon. Thalidomide, lenalidomide and pomalidomide are molecular glues: cereblon now tags new substrates (for myeloma cells, IKZF1 and IKZF3; in embryos, SALL4).
PROTACs are designed glues: remove a disease protein instead of only blocking it. One drug molecule destroys many targets. The first are in late clinical trials (e.g. against the oestrogen receptor in breast cancer).


The second application turns the ubiquitin system into a tool. Thalidomide was sold from 1957 as a sleeping pill and against morning sickness. Taken in early pregnancy it caused severe malformations, especially missing or shortened limbs, in about ten thousand children, and it was withdrawn in 1961. Decades later, related drugs, lenalidomide and pomalidomide, turned out to work well against multiple myeloma. In 2010 the target was found: cereblon, the substrate-recognising part of an E3 ligase. The drug sits in a pocket of cereblon and creates a new surface that grabs proteins cereblon never binds alone. In myeloma cells these are the transcription factors IKZF1 and IKZF3, which the cancer cells need; they are ubiquitinated and destroyed. In the embryo, one of the new substrates is SALL4, a transcription factor needed for limb development, which explains the birth defects. Such drugs are called molecular glues. PROTACs are designed versions: two binding heads joined by a linker, one for the target, one for an E3. They can remove proteins that have no druggable active site, and because the drug is released after each round, one molecule can destroy many targets.

title: Protein life and death: folding, modification and degradation
section: Why it matters: misfolding in Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s
text:
Why it matters: misfolding in Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s



Alzheimer’s disease: an amyloid plaque (pink, centre) in the hippocampus.


Parkinson’s disease: a Lewy body (brown, α-synuclein) in a neuron.


Alzheimer’s: amyloid plaques of Aβ peptide outside neurons, and tangles of hyperphosphorylated tau inside them.
Parkinson’s: α-synuclein amyloid in Lewy bodies kills dopamine neurons. Some inherited forms break parkin, an E3 ligase.
Neurons never divide, so they cannot dilute damaged protein; chaperone and proteasome capacity decline with age.
Antibodies that clear Aβ (lecanemab, donanemab) slow early Alzheimer’s modestly.



Misfolding and amyloid return in the most common neurodegenerative diseases. On the left is brain tissue from a person with Alzheimer’s disease. The pink, fluffy structure in the centre is an amyloid plaque, made mainly of a peptide called amyloid beta, which is cut from a larger membrane protein. Inside neurons, the protein tau, which normally binds microtubules, becomes heavily phosphorylated, lets go, and forms tangles: a protein switch gone wrong. In the middle is a neuron from a person with Parkinson’s disease. The brown ball is a Lewy body, full of the protein alpha-synuclein in amyloid form; these neurons, which make dopamine, slowly die. Some inherited forms of Parkinson’s are caused by mutations in parkin, an E3 ubiquitin ligase, which links the disease to today’s machinery. Why neurons? They live as long as we do and never divide, so they cannot dilute damaged protein into daughter cells, and the capacity of chaperones and proteasomes declines with age. Antibodies that remove amyloid beta, lecanemab and donanemab, are now approved; they slow decline in early Alzheimer’s somewhat, but do not stop it. You meet these diseases again in Sjukdomslära.

title: Protein life and death: folding, modification and degradation
section: Summary
text:
Summary

A protein’s fold is only just stable. In the crowded cytosol, chaperones prevent wrong contacts: Hsp70 binds and releases hydrophobic stretches using ATP; chaperonins fold proteins inside a closed cage.
Chains that fail can aggregate; amyloid is an ordered, self-seeding cross-β fibril found in Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s and many other diseases.
Reversible marks turn proteins into switches: phosphorylation (kinase/phosphatase), acetylation, methylation and ubiquitination, each written, erased and read by proteins.
E1–E2–E3 enzymes attach Lys48 ubiquitin chains to proteins with a degron; the 26S proteasome unfolds them and cuts them into peptides.
The amount of a protein is set by synthesis and degradation: P_{ss} = k_s/k_d, reached in a few half-lives, measured by cycloheximide chase and pulse-chase. Drugs block (bortezomib) or redirect (lenalidomide, PROTACs) this system.

Read more (optional): Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell, 7th ed., ch. 3 and 6.
Image credits

Five take-home points. First, folding is risky in a crowded cell because new chains expose hydrophobic stretches; chaperones such as Hsp70 and the chaperonins give chains time and space to fold, using ATP, without carrying any information about the final shape. Second, when folding fails, chains aggregate, and amyloid fibrils are a particularly stable, self-seeding form of aggregate behind many diseases. Third, proteins are switched on and off by reversible chemical marks, with phosphorylation as the most common; each mark has enzymes that add it, enzymes that remove it and proteins that read it. Fourth, the ubiquitin–proteasome system destroys proteins selectively: E3 ligases recognise degrons, attach lysine-48 ubiquitin chains, and the proteasome unfolds and cuts the tagged protein. Fifth, every protein’s amount is a balance of synthesis and degradation; short-lived proteins can change quickly, and we measure lifetimes with cycloheximide chase and pulse-chase. The ER lecture follows proteins into the endoplasmic reticulum, where folding, quality control and degradation have their own special machinery.

title: Study questions: organelles compared
text: Study questions in the style of the written exam. Write your answer first (a few sentences, a table or a labelled sketch where it helps), then compare with the model answer. Each question is tagged with its learning outcome (ELO). Questions tagged [VG] are of the kind used for the higher grade: predict, compare, explain an unexpected result or design an experiment.
crumbs: Organelles compared: keeping the cell in balance

title: Study questions: organelles compared
section: G-level questions
text:
G-level questions
1. Describe the structure of the nuclear envelope: its membranes, the space between them, the pores and the lamina. Explain why the nucleus is a separate compartment for proteins but not for ions. [ELO 5]






Model answer





The envelope has two membranes. The outer membrane is continuous with the ER, and the space between the two membranes (perinuclear space) is continuous with the ER lumen. At the nuclear pores the two membranes join; large pore complexes fill these openings. Under the inner membrane lies the lamina, a mesh of lamin filaments (intermediate filaments, A- and B-type) that gives shape and stiffness, anchors chromatin and connects through the envelope to the cytoskeleton. Pores let ions and small molecules diffuse freely, so pH and Ca²⁺ are the same as in the cytosol. Proteins and RNA above about 40 kDa pass only with a signal (NLS or NES) and transport receptors, so for them the nucleus is a separate compartment.




2. Describe peroxisomes: structure, how their proteins arrive, and three things they do. [ELO 5]






Model answer





Small organelles (0.1–1 µm) with one membrane and no DNA. Their proteins are made on free ribosomes in the cytosol and imported after translation, even in the folded state; most carry a C-terminal tag SKL (PTS1), recognised by a receptor and imported by the PEX machinery. Jobs: (1) oxidases use O₂ and produce H₂O₂, which catalase destroys; (2) β-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids (C22 and longer), which are then passed to mitochondria; (3) the first steps of plasmalogen synthesis (ether lipids, abundant in myelin); in liver also bile-acid synthesis. New peroxisomes form by growth and division or bud from the ER.




3. How does a lipid droplet form, and how does its surface differ from the membrane of other organelles? Give two functions of lipid droplets. [ELO 5]






Model answer





Enzymes in the ER membrane make neutral lipids (triglycerides, cholesterol esters). These collect between the two leaflets of the ER membrane, form a lens, and bud towards the cytosol. The droplet is covered by a single phospholipid layer (the cytosolic leaflet), not a bilayer, because the core is oil. Functions: store energy (fatty acids released by lipases and burned in mitochondria) and membrane building blocks; protect the cell by trapping excess free fatty acids, which would otherwise damage membranes.




4. What is an organelle contact site? Describe how Ca²⁺ moves from the ER to mitochondria at a contact site, and what it does there. [ELO 5]






Model answer





A contact site is a region where two organelle membranes are held 10–30 nm apart by tether proteins without fusing; molecules pass between them but each lumen stays separate. At ER–mitochondria contacts, IP₃ receptor channels release Ca²⁺ from the ER into the narrow gap, where its concentration becomes much higher than in the bulk cytosol. Ca²⁺ crosses the outer mitochondrial membrane (VDAC) and enters the matrix through the mitochondrial Ca²⁺ uniporter (MCU), driven by the negative matrix potential. In the matrix it activates dehydrogenases of the citric acid cycle, so ATP production rises when the cell is active. Prolonged Ca²⁺ overload opens a pore in the mitochondria and can trigger apoptosis.




5. Give the approximate pH of the cytosol, the ER, the trans-Golgi, the lysosome and the mitochondrial matrix. Explain how the lumen of the lysosome is acidified and give two reasons why acidity is useful there. [ELO 5]






Model answer





Cytosol 7.2; ER 7.2; trans-Golgi ≈ 6.0; lysosome 4.5–5; mitochondrial matrix ≈ 8. A V-type H⁺-ATPase in the membrane uses ATP to pump H⁺ into the lumen; Cl⁻ (or another counter-ion) follows to keep the voltage low, so pumping can continue. The steady pH depends on the number of pumps and on H⁺ leaks. Uses: lysosomal hydrolases work best at low pH (and are almost inactive at pH 7.2, a safety lock if a lysosome leaks); low pH helps unfold proteins for digestion; in endosomes, low pH makes receptors release their cargo (e.g. LDL from its receptor, enzymes from the M6P receptor).




6. Free Ca²⁺ in the cytosol is about 0.1 µM, in the ER about 0.5 mM and outside the cell 1–2 mM. Name the pumps that keep these differences, and explain why the low cytosolic level is important for signalling. [ELO 5]






Model answer





SERCA (sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca²⁺-ATPase) pumps Ca²⁺ from the cytosol into the ER; PMCA (plasma membrane Ca²⁺-ATPase) and the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger move Ca²⁺ out of the cell. Because the resting cytosolic level is 5 000–10 000 times lower than in the stores and outside, opening a few Ca²⁺ channels raises cytosolic Ca²⁺ ten- to a hundred-fold within milliseconds. This makes Ca²⁺ a fast, strong signal (secretion, contraction, gene expression). The pumps then return it to rest, ending the signal.




7. Explain the unfolded protein response as a homeostatic feedback loop: what is sensed, by what, and which four corrections bring the system back? What happens if the stress is not resolved? [ELO 4] [ELO 5]






Model answer





The variable is the load of unfolded proteins in the ER lumen relative to the folding capacity. Three ER membrane sensors, IRE1, PERK and ATF6, detect unfolded proteins. Corrections: (1) less translation of new proteins (PERK phosphorylates eIF2α); (2) more chaperones; (3) more ER-associated degradation (ERAD) of misfolded proteins; (4) more ER membrane (larger ER). Load falls and capacity rises, so the sensors switch off again: negative feedback. If the stress cannot be resolved, the same pathways switch to apoptosis (e.g. via the transcription factor CHOP), removing the cell.

after translation; N-terminal presequence (amphipathic helix), TOM/TIM, unfolded
after translation; C-terminal SKL (PTS1), PEX import, can be folded


Main job
fold and modify membrane and secreted proteins; make lipids; Ca²⁺ store
ATP by oxidative phosphorylation; Ca²⁺ buffer; start apoptosis
oxidations (H₂O₂ + catalase); very-long-chain fatty acids; plasmalogens







9. Explain how stereology (point counting) estimates the volume fraction of mitochondria in a cell from electron micrographs. [ELO 1] [ELO 5]






Model answer





A grid of test points is laid over EM sections. One counts the points that fall on mitochondria and the points that fall on the reference space (the cell). Points on mitochondria ÷ points on the cell estimates the area fraction of mitochondria in the section. By the Delesse principle, the average area fraction over random sections equals the volume fraction. Many sections from many cells are needed, because single sections are not random (a section through the centre of the nucleus overestimates it) and cells differ. More points per section reduce counting error; more sections and cells reduce sampling error.




10. Describe the molecular cause of Hutchinson–Gilford progeria and explain how lonafarnib acts. [ELO 5] [ELO 9]






Model answer





Lamin A is made as prelamin A, which gets a farnesyl lipid at its C-terminal end; this holds it at the inner nuclear membrane. The protease ZMPSTE24 then cuts off the last 15 amino acids together with the lipid, and mature lamin A joins the lamina. In progeria a single, new point mutation in LMNA activates a hidden splice site; 50 amino acids are lost, including the cleavage site. The protein, progerin, keeps its farnesyl lipid permanently, stays stuck on the membrane and distorts the lamina: nuclei are misshapen, chromatin and DNA repair are disturbed, and cells (especially in blood vessels) age early. Lonafarnib inhibits farnesyltransferase, so less progerin is farnesylated; nuclear shape improves and survival increases by a few years on average.

title: Study questions: organelles compared
section: VG-style questions
text:
VG-style questions
11. [VG] A child has low muscle tone, seizures and an enlarged liver. A blood test shows high levels of very-long-chain fatty acids. (a) Which organelle do you suspect, and why? (b) Electron micrographs of liver cells show membrane sacs but no normal peroxisomes, and the enzyme catalase is found in the cytosol fraction after centrifugation. What kind of defect does this point to? (c) Predict what happens to plasmalogen levels and explain why the brain is affected. [ELO 5] [ELO 9]






Model answer






Peroxisomes: in humans they are the only site where very-long-chain fatty acids are shortened, so their accumulation points to a peroxisomal defect (Zellweger spectrum or a single-enzyme defect).
The membranes are present (“ghosts”) but the matrix enzymes such as catalase stay in the cytosol. So the enzymes are made but cannot be imported: a defect in the import machinery, i.e. a PEX gene (most often PEX1), not in one enzyme. A single-enzyme defect would leave normal-looking peroxisomes with catalase inside. This is Zellweger syndrome.
Plasmalogens will be low, because their synthesis starts with peroxisomal enzymes. Plasmalogens are abundant in myelin and nerve-cell membranes; together with toxic very-long-chain fatty acids, their lack disturbs brain development and myelination, which explains the low muscle tone and seizures.





12. [VG] A researcher expresses a Ca²⁺ sensor targeted to the mitochondrial matrix and stimulates cells with a hormone that releases Ca²⁺ from the ER through IP₃ receptors. Matrix Ca²⁺ rises quickly and strongly. (a) The mitochondrial uniporter has a low affinity for Ca²⁺ (it needs about 10 µM to work well), but the cytosolic Ca²⁺ rises only to about 1 µM. Explain the result. (b) Predict the effect on the matrix Ca²⁺ signal and on ATP production if the tethers between ER and mitochondria are removed. (c) Design a control experiment showing that the matrix Ca²⁺ comes from the ER. [ELO 1] [ELO 5]






Model answer






The ER releases Ca²⁺ into the narrow gap (10–30 nm) at ER–mitochondria contact sites. There, close to the open IP₃ receptors, the local Ca²⁺ concentration is far higher (tens of µM) than the average in the bulk cytosol measured by a cytosolic sensor. These microdomains are enough to drive the low-affinity uniporter.
Without tethers, the gap widens and Ca²⁺ dilutes into the cytosol before it reaches the mitochondria: the matrix Ca²⁺ rise will be smaller and slower, while the cytosolic signal may be similar. Matrix Ca²⁺-activated dehydrogenases of the citric acid cycle are less stimulated, so the increase in ATP production during stimulation is reduced (lipid transfer from the ER would also suffer over time).
Empty the ER store first with thapsigargin (SERCA blocker) in Ca²⁺-free medium, or block IP₃ receptors; the hormone should then no longer raise matrix Ca²⁺. Measure cytosolic Ca²⁺ in parallel (a second sensor) to show that the effect is on the ER release. As a further control, block the uniporter (MCU knock-down): cytosolic Ca²⁺ rises, matrix Ca²⁺ does not.

title: Study questions: organelles compared
section: Explore
text:
Explore
Demo: measure the organelles. The same HeLa cell slice as in the cell explorer, now with a Measure mode. An orange counting frame and a grid of yellow test points lie over the electron micrograph. Choose an organelle under Mark, then tap every point that lies on it (zoom in to decide; tap a marked point again to unmark it). Unmarked points count as cytosol. Check my count compares your marks with the outlines (red rings: points to look at again) and fills in the computer’s count and the exact area of the outlines in the frame. Count all for me marks every point from the outlines. You can change the frame, the grid spacing and the grid position, and colour the organelles by pH or Ca²⁺; point at (or tap) any place to read the pH and free Ca²⁺ of that compartment. The table compares everything with the volume fractions from the cell tour (a liver cell).









About the model and the numbers





The image and outlines are real data (OpenOrganelle jrc_hela-2, FIB-SEM, CC BY 4.0), but the outlines are machine predictions checked by eye: small vesicles and endosomes below about 200 nm, and peroxisomes, are not outlined, and parts of the ER are missed. Where outlines overlap, the smaller organelle counts. The nucleolus and the nuclear envelope count as nucleus; the centrosome counts as cytosol. pH and Ca²⁺ are typical textbook values for mammalian cells, not measurements in this cell. The volume fractions in the table are for a liver cell; HeLa cells are different. This is one slice through one cell, so it is a demonstration of the method, not a measurement of HeLa cells.



E1. [ELO 5] Start with the frame Whole cell (centre) and the 2 µm grid. Mark the mitochondria, then press Check my count. What fraction of the points falls on mitochondria, and how does it compare with the outline area and with the cell-tour value for a liver cell (about 20 %)? Then Count all for me and look at the nucleus. Why is the nucleus share in this frame so much larger than the 5–10 % in the cell-tour table?
E2. [ELO 1] Predict first: how much will your mitochondria estimate change if you count again with the grid in a new position? Press Move the grid five times (with Count all for me each time) and write down the mitochondria percentage. Then do the same with the 1 µm and the 0.5 µm grid (a few grid positions each). How does the spread of the estimates change, and why? What does this cost?
E3. [ELO 5] Compare the three frames (use Count all for me and the outline area). Where do the mitochondria take up the largest share of the area? What does this tell you about choosing where to measure?
E4. [ELO 5] Choose Colour by pH, then Colour by Ca²⁺, and point at (or tap) a mitochondrion, an endosome or lysosome, the ER, the nucleus and the cytosol. Which compartments differ most from the cytosol in pH, and which in Ca²⁺? Find a rule that links the Ca²⁺ level to the topology of the compartment (lumen side or cytosol side). Why does the lipid droplet have no value?
E5. [VG] [ELO 1, 5] In this slice the ER outlines cover only about 5 % of the frame, but the cell-tour table says the ER is 10–15 % of a cell’s volume. Give at least two possible reasons, at least one about the method and one about the biology. Then predict how the ER and mitochondria fractions would change in a pancreatic acinar cell (which secretes digestive enzymes) and in a plasma cell (which secretes antibodies), and say how you would test your prediction with the same method.






Solutions





E1. With the starting grid (120 points), 13 points fall on mitochondria: 10.8 %. The outline area of mitochondria in the frame is 7.5 %, so the point count is about 3 percentage points off, which is normal for so few points (see E2). Both are well below the ~20 % of a liver cell: HeLa cells are cancer cells grown in culture, which make much of their ATP by glycolysis and have fewer mitochondria than a liver cell. The nucleus takes 42 points (35 %), and 34 % of the outline area, far above 5–10 %. The frame is placed around the nucleus and the slice passes through its middle, where its cross-section is largest; much of the thin cytoplasm at the cell edges is outside the frame. A volume fraction needs random sections through many cells; a chosen section through the centre of one nucleus is not random.
E2. At 2 µm, the five new grid positions give 5.4, 6.7, 7.8, 7.8 and 4.7 % mitochondria (6, 8, 10, 10 and 6 points out of 112–128): together with the first grid (10.8 %) the estimates scatter from about 5 to 11 % around the outline area of 7.5 %. With the 1 µm grid (about 470–500 points) the six grid positions give 4.9–9.1 %, and with 0.5 µm (1922 points) 6.7–7.8 %, close to the outline area. (Your exact numbers depend on how often you pressed Move the grid; the spread is what matters.) The counting error falls roughly as \(1/\sqrt{n}\): for a fraction \(p\) counted with \(n\) points, the standard error is \(\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}\), about 2.4 percentage points for 120 points and 0.6 for 1922. The cost is time: by hand, 16 times more points is 16 times more work. In practice, stereologists use a moderate number of points per section (100–200) and spend the effort on more sections and more cells, because the differences between sections and cells (E3) are usually larger than the counting error.
E3. Outline areas: whole cell (centre) 7.5 %, cytoplasm, left 9.7 %, cytoplasm above the nucleus 16.2 % mitochondria. The band of cytoplasm between the nucleus and the upper cell edge is packed with mitochondria, while the large frame is diluted by the nucleus. The answer depends on where you look. To measure a whole cell (or a tissue) without bias, sections and frames must be placed systematically at random, not where the organelle looks interesting, and the reference space must be defined (whole cell or only cytoplasm).
E4. pH: the endosomes and lysosomes are the most acidic (6.5 down to 4.5, red), the Golgi is mildly acidic (6.0–6.7), the mitochondrial matrix is alkaline (≈ 8, blue); the nucleus and ER are like the cytosol (7.2). Ca²⁺: the ER, Golgi and lysosomes hold 0.1–0.8 mM, thousands of times more than the cytosol, nucleus and mitochondrial matrix (≈ 0.1 µM at rest). Rule: compartments on the lumen side (ER, Golgi, endosomes and lysosomes, topologically equivalent to the outside of the cell) keep high Ca²⁺ like the outside (1–2 mM), pumped in by SERCA and other pumps; compartments on the cytosol side (nucleus, connected through pores) keep it low. Mitochondria are a third space: low at rest, but they take up Ca²⁺ during a signal. The lipid droplet is oil with a single phospholipid layer and no water inside, so pH and Ca²⁺ do not exist there.
E5. Method: the ER is a network of thin tubes and sheets, often only 30–60 nm across; the machine segmentation misses many tubes and smooth ER, and edges of thin objects are hard to outline, so the ER area is underestimated; in a single plane, many tubes are cut obliquely and look fainter. The cell-tour value is for a liver cell, and one section of one cell is not a random sample. Biology: HeLa cells are not specialised secretory cells; they have less rough ER than a liver cell. Prediction: a pancreatic acinar cell and a plasma cell are packed with rough ER (ER fraction much higher, often a quarter or more of the cytoplasm), with mitochondria a smaller share; acinar cells also have many secretory granules. Test: take EM sections of these cell types (pancreas tissue; plasma cells from a lymph node or culture), place frames systematically at random, count points on ER, mitochondria and cytoplasm in many sections from several cells and animals, and compare the volume fractions with confidence intervals.

title: Quiz: myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell
text:
Short questions to check your understanding of the lecture Myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell. Try each on paper first, then open the hint or the answer. The tag after each question shows the learning outcome (ELO) it practises.

Q1. In the cross-bridge cycle of myosin II, which step needs (a) ATP binding, (b) ATP hydrolysis, (c) phosphate release? [ELO 6]






Hint





Think of three verbs: let go, cock, pull.









Answer






ATP binding makes the head let go of actin. (b) ATP hydrolysis (ADP and Pi stay bound) re-cocks the lever while the head is detached. (c) Phosphate release, after the head binds actin again, triggers the power stroke, which pulls the actin filament 5–10 nm. ADP then leaves and the head is in the rigor state until the next ATP binds.





Q2. Why do muscles become stiff a few hours after death (rigor mortis)? [ELO 6]






Hint





Which step of the cycle cannot happen without ATP?









Answer





After death the cells run out of ATP. Myosin heads can still finish their stroke and stay bound to actin, but without ATP they cannot let go. All heads end up locked to actin in the rigor state, so the filaments cannot slide and the muscle is stiff. (Rigor passes later, when the proteins are broken down.)




Q3. A muscle fibre contracts from a sarcomere length of 2.6 µm to 2.2 µm. What happens to the length of (a) the A band, (b) the I band, (c) the H zone? What does this tell us? [ELO 6]






Hint





The A band is the length of the thick filaments.









Answer






The A band stays the same (1.6 µm, the thick-filament length). (b) The I band shrinks (from 0.5 µm to 0.3 µm on each side). (c) The H zone shrinks (from 0.55 µm to 0.15 µm). Neither filament changes length; they slide past each other and overlap more. This is the sliding-filament model (Huxley and Hanson; Huxley and Niedergerke, 1954).





Q4. Why does a muscle fibre stretched to a sarcomere length of 3.65 µm produce no active force, even when it is fully stimulated? [ELO 6]






Hint





Add up the filament lengths: thick 1.6 µm, thin 1.0 µm on each side, plus the Z-disc.









Answer





At 3.65 µm the thin filaments have been pulled completely out of the thick filaments (1.6 + 2 × 1.0 + 0.05 µm). No myosin head faces a thin filament, so no cross-bridges can form and no force is made. Force on the descending limb is proportional to the filament overlap, which is the evidence that every cross-bridge adds a small, independent force (Gordon, Huxley and Julian, 1966).




Q5. Describe how a rise in cytosolic Ca²⁺ switches on contraction in skeletal muscle. Where does the Ca²⁺ come from, and how does the muscle relax? [ELO 6]






Hint





Two proteins sit on the thin filament; one covers the binding sites, the other binds Ca²⁺.









Answer





An action potential opens Ca²⁺ channels in the sarcoplasmic reticulum (the ER of muscle). Cytosolic Ca²⁺ rises from about 0.1 µM to about 10 µM. Ca²⁺ binds troponin C; troponin changes shape and moves tropomyosin away from the myosin-binding sites on actin. Cocked myosin heads can now bind and run the cross-bridge cycle. To relax, SERCA pumps use ATP to move Ca²⁺ back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, and tropomyosin covers the sites again.




Q6. Match each myosin to its job: (a) muscle myosin II, (b) non-muscle myosin II, (c) myosin V. Jobs: carries pigment granules along actin; pinches a dividing cell in two; makes a sarcomere shorten. [ELO 6]






Hint





Myosin II always works as a bipolar filament that pulls; one of the three is a single two-headed walker with a cargo-binding tail.









Answer






Muscle myosin II: makes a sarcomere shorten (thick filaments pull thin filaments towards the M-line). (b) Non-muscle myosin II: pinches a dividing cell in two (contractile ring; it also pulls the rear of a migrating cell). (c) Myosin V: carries pigment granules (and vesicles) along actin, in 36 nm steps.





Q7. Give three differences between intermediate filaments and actin filaments. [ELO 6]






Hint





Think about nucleotides, polarity, motors and mechanics.









Answer





Intermediate filaments (1) bind no nucleotide (actin binds ATP); (2) have no polarity, because their tetramers are antiparallel (actin has plus and minus ends); (3) have no motor proteins walking on them (actin has myosins); (4) are rope-like: they can be stretched to two or three times their length, while actin filaments break after a few per cent stretch; (5) are tissue-specific (keratins, vimentin, desmin, neurofilaments, lamins), while actin is in every cell. Diameter: about 10 nm, versus 7 nm for actin.




Q8. Why do mutations in keratin 5 or 14 cause blisters, and why is one mutant copy enough? [ELO 6] [ELO 9]






Hint





Which cells make keratin 5 and 14? What does a mutant subunit do to a filament it is built into?









Answer





Keratin 5 and 14 form the intermediate filament network of the basal cells of the epidermis, anchored to desmosomes and hemidesmosomes. A mutant keratin is built into the same filaments as the normal protein and spoils them (a dominant-negative effect), so even with one normal gene copy the network collapses into clumps. Without a working network, basal cells break under friction, and the skin above separates: a blister (epidermolysis bullosa simplex).
