title: Myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell
section: The question: how does a muscle shorten?
text:
The question: how does a muscle shorten?



Human skeletal muscle, thin section, transmission electron microscopy. Each repeat of dark and light bands is one sarcomere, about 2.5 µm long.


Skeletal muscle is striped (striated): the same unit repeats thousands of times along each fibre.
When a muscle contracts, each unit shortens by up to a third, in milliseconds.
But no filament in the unit gets shorter. How can a structure shorten if none of its parts do?
And a second puzzle: your skin is rubbed and stretched all day, but it does not tear. What holds cells together under force?



This is an electron micrograph of a thin slice through human skeletal muscle. You can see long parallel structures, the myofibrils, and along each of them a regular pattern of dark and light bands with thin dark lines. One repeat, from one thin dark line to the next, is a sarcomere. It is about two and a half micrometres long, and a single muscle fibre contains many thousands of them in a row. When you lift a cup, every sarcomere shortens a little, all at the same time, and the shortenings add up. In the 1950s, researchers measured the filaments inside the sarcomere during contraction and found something surprising: the filaments themselves did not shorten at all. So how does the sarcomere shorten? The answer is a molecular motor, myosin, which makes filaments slide past each other. The second puzzle of today is the opposite of movement: strength. Skin cells are pulled and rubbed all day without tearing. In the second half of the lecture you will see that a different filament system, the intermediate filaments, makes this possible.
crumbs: Myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell

title: Myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell
section: Myosin: one motor domain, many jobs
text:
Myosin: one motor domain, many jobs


Every myosin has a motor domain that binds actin and ATP, and a lever arm that swings. The tail decides the job.
Myosin II has a long tail; many tails bundle into a thick filament with heads at both ends. It pulls actin filaments towards each other: contraction.
Myosin V has long lever arms and a tail that binds cargo; it walks along actin.


Myosins are a large family. Humans have about forty myosin genes, grouped into classes by their tails. They all share the same kind of motor domain, the head. It binds actin and ATP, and it changes shape as it breaks down ATP. Behind the motor domain sits a lever arm, a long helix stabilised by small proteins called light chains. A small shape change in the motor domain is amplified by the lever arm into a swing of several nanometres, a bit like a short movement of your wrist giving a long movement at the end of a fishing rod. The tail decides what the myosin does. Myosin II, on the left, has a long coiled-coil tail. Hundreds of tails pack together into a thick filament, with heads pointing outwards at both ends and a bare zone in the middle. Because the two halves point in opposite directions, a myosin II filament pulls actin filaments towards its centre. That is how muscle contracts, and how a cell pinches itself in two. Myosin V, on the right, has two heads with long lever arms and a tail that grabs a vesicle or pigment granule; it walks along actin like the kinesin you met on microtubules. Almost all myosins walk towards the plus end of actin.
crumbs: Myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell

title: Myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell
section: The cross-bridge cycle: ATP lets go, hydrolysis cocks, phosphate release pulls
text:
The cross-bridge cycle: ATP lets go, hydrolysis cocks, phosphate release pulls

1 Without nucleotide the head is locked on actin (rigor). 2 ATP binding releases the head. 3 ATP hydrolysis cocks the lever (ADP·Pi stays bound). 4 The head binds actin, Pi leaves, and the lever swings: the power stroke (≈ 5–10 nm). ADP leaves, and we are back at 1.

This cycle is the heart of the lecture, so go through it slowly. Start at panel 1, top left. The head is bound tightly to actin and carries no nucleotide. This is the rigor state. Panel 2: ATP binds to the head. This changes the shape of the actin-binding cleft, and the head lets go of actin. So ATP is needed for release, not for the pull. Panel 3: while detached, the head hydrolyses ATP to ADP and phosphate, which both stay bound. The energy of hydrolysis is used to swing the lever back into a cocked position, like pulling back the string of a bow. Panel 4: the cocked head binds to a new site on actin. Binding makes phosphate leave, and this triggers the power stroke: the lever swings back and pulls the actin filament five to ten nanometres towards the centre of the sarcomere. Then ADP leaves, and the head is in rigor again, ready for the next ATP. One ATP, one stroke. Remember the three words: binding releases, hydrolysis cocks, phosphate release pulls. If ATP runs out, as after death, heads get stuck in panel 1: muscles become stiff. This is rigor mortis.
crumbs: Myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell

title: Myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell
section: The sarcomere: the unit of contraction
text:
The sarcomere: the unit of contraction












Human skeletal muscle (TEM): Z-discs (dark diagonal bars), A bands (dark), I bands (light).


Thin filaments (actin, about 1 µm) are anchored in the Z-disc with their plus ends, and point towards the middle.
Thick filaments (myosin II, 1.6 µm) sit in the middle, held at the M-line.
A band = length of the thick filaments. I band = only thin filaments. H zone = only thick filaments.



Here is the sarcomere in detail, a micrograph on the left and our diagram on the right. A sarcomere runs from one Z-disc to the next. The Z-disc is a dense protein plate that anchors the thin filaments, which are actin filaments, about one micrometre long. Their plus ends are in the Z-disc, so the minus ends point towards the middle. In the middle sit the thick filaments, made of myosin II, 1.6 micrometres long, held in register by proteins at the M-line. In the light microscope and the electron microscope, the region with thick filaments looks dark: this is the A band. The regions on each side with only thin filaments look light: the I bands. The middle part of the A band that thin filaments do not reach is the H zone. A giant elastic protein, titin, runs from the Z-disc to the M-line and keeps the thick filament centred; we will not go into it. Notice the polarity: myosin heads walk towards the plus end of actin, so the heads in each half pull their thin filaments towards the M-line. Both Z-discs are pulled towards the centre, and the sarcomere shortens.
crumbs: Myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell

title: Myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell
section: How do we know? The filaments slide
text:
How do we know? The filaments slide


1954, two papers in the same issue of Nature: A. F. Huxley and R. Niedergerke (interference light microscopy of living fibres) and H. E. Huxley and J. Hanson (phase contrast and EM of myofibrils).
During contraction the A band keeps its length; the I band and H zone shrink. So the filaments keep their length and slide past each other: the sliding-filament model.


How do we know that filaments slide? In 1954, two groups published side by side in Nature. Andrew Huxley and Rolf Niedergerke used a special light microscope to watch single living frog muscle fibres. Hugh Huxley and Jean Hanson, who were not related to Andrew, looked at isolated myofibrils with phase-contrast microscopy and electron microscopy. Both measured the bands at different sarcomere lengths. The result was the same. The A band, which is the length of the thick filaments, stayed at 1.6 micrometres whether the muscle was stretched or contracted. The I bands and the H zone, the regions where the two kinds of filament do not overlap, got shorter. The only explanation is that both filaments keep their length and slide past each other, so the overlap increases. This was a major change in thinking: before, many believed that contraction was a folding or coiling of long protein chains. The sliding-filament model then asked a new question: what makes the filaments slide? The answer, the cross-bridges between thick and thin filaments, came over the following decades.
crumbs: Myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell

title: Myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell
section: How do we know? Force depends on filament overlap
text:
How do we know? Force depends on filament overlap


Gordon, Huxley and Julian, 1966: hold single frog muscle fibres at fixed sarcomere lengths, stimulate, measure force.
Long sarcomere: force falls in a straight line with the overlap, to zero at 3.65 µm. So force comes from the heads that face a thin filament: each cross-bridge adds a little force.
Short sarcomere: thin filaments collide, thick filaments hit the Z-discs: force falls again. Try it: Demo: sarcomere


If force comes from cross-bridges between overlapping filaments, then force should depend on how much the filaments overlap. In 1966, Gordon, Andrew Huxley and Julian tested this with great care. They took single fibres from frog muscle, held a short segment at a fixed sarcomere length with a feedback system, stimulated the fibre and measured the force. The result is the length–tension curve. Above 2.25 micrometres, force falls in a straight line as the sarcomere gets longer, and it reaches zero at 3.65 micrometres. That is exactly the length where thin filaments are pulled out of the thick filaments: 1.6 plus two times one micrometre, plus the Z-disc. Between 2.0 and 2.25 there is a plateau, where every myosin head faces a thin filament; the bare zone has no heads, so a little extra overlap there adds nothing. Below 2.0, thin filaments from the two halves cross and get in each other’s way, and below about 1.65 the thick filaments press against the Z-discs, so force falls steeply. The shape of this curve follows from the filament lengths: strong evidence that each head adds its own small force. You can explore this in the demo.
crumbs: Myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell

title: Myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell
section: The switch: Ca²⁺, troponin and tropomyosin
text:
The switch: Ca²⁺, troponin and tropomyosin


At rest, tropomyosin lies along the actin filament and covers the myosin-binding sites. Heads are cocked but cannot bind.
A nerve signal opens Ca²⁺ channels in the sarcoplasmic reticulum (the ER of muscle). Ca²⁺ rises from 0.1 µM to about 10 µM, binds troponin, and troponin pulls tropomyosin aside: heads bind and pull.
This is the Ca²⁺ signal from the ion-channels lecture. Ca²⁺ pumps (SERCA) take it back: relaxation.


A muscle must not contract all the time, so the cross-bridge cycle needs a switch. In skeletal and heart muscle, the switch sits on the thin filament. Tropomyosin is a long rod-shaped protein that lies in the groove of the actin filament, covering seven actins. At rest it covers the sites where myosin heads bind. Every seven actins there is a troponin complex attached to tropomyosin. One of its subunits, troponin C, binds calcium. When a motor nerve fires, an action potential spreads over the muscle cell membrane and into the cell, and calcium channels in the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which is the ER of muscle, open. Remember from the ion-channels lecture that cytosolic calcium is kept around 0.1 micromolar, ten thousand times lower than in the ER. Now calcium floods out and rises about a hundred-fold. Calcium binds troponin C, troponin changes shape, and tropomyosin rolls away from the binding sites. The cocked heads bind, and the cycle runs. To relax, calcium pumps called SERCA use ATP to pump calcium back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Notice the two jobs of ATP in muscle: release of the heads, and removal of calcium. The full story of excitation and contraction comes in the course on organ structure and function.
crumbs: Myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell

title: Myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell
section: Non-muscle myosin II: the cell’s own muscle
text:
Non-muscle myosin II: the cell’s own muscle


Every cell has myosin II, in small bipolar minifilaments that pull on actin.
Contractile ring in cell division: a ring of actin and myosin II pinches the cell in two (more in the mitosis lecture).
Migration: at the cell rear, myosin II contracts and pulls the tail forward, while actin polymerisation pushes the front (the actin lecture).
Switched on by phosphorylation of its light chain (by a kinase activated by Ca²⁺–calmodulin, or by Rho kinase), not by troponin.


Myosin II is not only for muscle. Every cell in your body makes non-muscle myosin II. It forms small bipolar filaments of a few dozen molecules, called minifilaments, which work just like a tiny piece of muscle: they pull actin filaments of opposite polarity towards each other. Two examples. First, cell division. At the end of mitosis, a ring of actin filaments and myosin II forms under the plasma membrane at the equator of the cell. Myosin pulls the actin filaments past each other, the ring tightens like a purse string, and the cell is pinched in two. You will meet the contractile ring again in the mitosis lecture. Second, migration. In the actin lecture you saw that a migrating cell pushes its front forward by actin polymerisation. That is only half of moving. The rear must follow, and here myosin II contracts and pulls the tail forward and detaches it from the surface. Non-muscle cells have no troponin. Instead, myosin II is switched on when a small regulatory light chain on the head is phosphorylated, either by a kinase activated by calcium and calmodulin, or by Rho kinase, which you will meet in the signalling lectures. Smooth muscle uses the same switch.
crumbs: Myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell

title: Myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell
section: Myosin V: a cargo carrier on actin
text:
Myosin V: a cargo carrier on actin


Myosin V walks hand over hand along actin, 36 nm per step, one ATP per step, for many steps before it falls off.
Long distances: microtubules and kinesin/dynein. The last few micrometres in the actin-rich cortex: myosin V.
Example: pigment cells (melanocytes) hand pigment granules to skin cells. No myosin V (Griscelli syndrome type 1): granules pile up in the cell centre, hair is silvery.


Myosin V shows that myosin can also be a transporter. Its two heads are joined by long lever arms, each stabilised by six light chains. The heads take turns: while one head is bound, the other swings forward, 36 nanometres, and binds the next site. Thirty-six nanometres is not a random number: it is the distance at which the twisted actin filament repeats, so the motor walks straight along one face of the filament. A myosin V molecule takes many steps before it lets go; such a motor is called processive, like kinesin. Why would a cell need two transport systems? Microtubules are the long-distance highways: kinesin carries cargo from the cell centre to the periphery. Near the plasma membrane, the cytoplasm is full of a dense mesh of actin, the cortex, and here myosin V takes over and moves the cargo the last few micrometres. Pigment cells in the skin are the classic example. They make pigment granules and carry them out to the tips of their extensions, from where they are handed to skin cells. In patients without functional myosin V, in a rare disease called Griscelli syndrome, the granules pile up around the nucleus and the hair looks silvery.
crumbs: Myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell

title: Myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell
section: Intermediate filaments: built like a rope
text:
Intermediate filaments: built like a rope


A long α-helical rod with a head and a tail. Two rods form a coiled-coil dimer; two dimers lie side by side, antiparallel, in a tetramer.
Tetramers pack side by side and end to end into a rope 10 nm thick: between actin (7 nm) and microtubules (25 nm), hence “intermediate”.
No nucleotide, no polarity, no motors. Their job is strength, not movement.


Now the third filament system. Intermediate filaments got their name from their diameter, about ten nanometres, between actin and microtubules. They are built in a completely different way. Each protein has a long central rod domain, an alpha helix about 45 nanometres long, with flexible head and tail domains at the ends. Two rods wind around each other into a coiled-coil dimer, with both heads at the same end. Two dimers then lie side by side, pointing in opposite directions and slightly staggered. This antiparallel tetramer looks the same from both ends, so the filament built from it has no polarity. Eight tetramers associate side by side into a short unit-length filament, and these join end to end and compact into the final filament. Compare this with actin and microtubules. Intermediate filaments bind no ATP or GTP, so they have no built-in dynamic instability or treadmilling. They have no plus and minus ends, so no motor protein can walk on them. They are regulated mainly by phosphorylation, for example during mitosis. And because many long helices are packed side by side and overlap, the filament behaves like a rope: flexible, but very hard to break.
crumbs: Myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell

title: Myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell
section: Intermediate filament families: one per tissue
text:
Intermediate filament families: one per tissue



Cytokeratin filaments in a human epithelial cell (immunofluorescence). The network spans the cytoplasm around the nucleus (dark).









Family
Where
Note




Keratins (type I + II pairs)
epithelia: skin, gut, liver
the largest family, about 50 genes


Vimentin
fibroblasts, white blood cells, endothelium



Desmin
muscle
links Z-discs to each other


Neurofilaments
nerve axons
set the axon diameter


Nuclear lamins
inside the nucleus, all cells
the nuclear lamina (organelles-compared lecture)



Pathologists use the IF type to find where a tumour came from: keratin = carcinoma (epithelium), vimentin = sarcoma.


Humans have about seventy intermediate filament genes, and different cell types use different ones. Keratins are the largest family, with about fifty genes. They come in two types, acidic and basic, and a keratin filament always contains one of each, as a pair. Epithelial cells, in skin, gut lining or liver, are full of keratin. The image shows a keratin network in a cultured epithelial cell: a dense meshwork around the dark nucleus that spreads to the cell edges. Vimentin is the typical intermediate filament of cells of mesenchymal origin, such as fibroblasts and endothelial cells. Desmin is found in muscle, where it links neighbouring Z-discs and keeps myofibrils in register. Neurofilaments fill nerve axons and set their diameter, which affects how fast signals travel. The nuclear lamins are different: they line the inside of the nuclear envelope and form the nuclear lamina, which you met in the lecture comparing organelles. Because the type of intermediate filament is so tissue-specific, pathologists stain tumours for it. A tumour that makes keratin came from an epithelium and is a carcinoma, even if it sits in a lymph node or a bone.
crumbs: Myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell

title: Myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell
section: Mechanical strength: a network riveted to its neighbours
text:
Mechanical strength: a network riveted to its neighbours


Keratin filaments end in desmosomes (rivets between cells) and hemidesmosomes (rivets to the basal lamina). The filaments of one cell are linked to those of the next: the whole sheet shares the load.
Intermediate filaments can be stretched to two or three times their length before breaking, and they get stiffer as they stretch. Actin filaments and microtubules break much earlier.
The nuclear lamina does the same for the nucleus.


How do intermediate filaments make a tissue strong? In an epithelium, the keratin filaments of each cell end in two kinds of junction. Desmosomes are button-like junctions between neighbouring cells: on each side, a dense plaque inside the cell anchors keratin filaments, and adhesion proteins cross the gap between the cells and hold on to each other. Hemidesmosomes are half of this: they anchor the bottom of the cell to the basal lamina, the sheet of extracellular matrix below the epithelium. The tissue is therefore one continuous network, from cell to cell and down to the matrix. When you rub your skin, the force does not land on one cell; it is spread over thousands. The filaments themselves are tough. Single intermediate filaments can be stretched to two or three times their length before they break, and they become stiffer the more they are stretched, like a rope. Actin filaments and microtubules are stiff, but break after a stretch of a few per cent. The nucleus has its own intermediate filament net, the lamina, which protects the DNA when cells squeeze through narrow spaces. The junctions themselves come back in the course on organ structure and function.
crumbs: Myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell

title: Myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell
section: How do we know? Watching filaments turn over: FRAP and TIRF
text:
How do we know? Watching filaments turn over: FRAP and TIRF


FRAP (from the membrane-structure lecture; FRAP lab): bleach a GFP-tagged filament protein in a spot, watch fluorescence return. Fast return = subunits exchange quickly (actin, myosin II); slow = a stable network (keratin).
TIRF microscopy: only a ≈ 100 nm layer above the glass is lit. Sharp images of adhesions, single motors and filaments at the bottom of a cell or in a test-tube assay, with almost no background.


This and the next slide gather the main methods for the whole cytoskeleton block. FRAP, fluorescence recovery after photobleaching, you met in the membrane-structure lecture. Here, you express a filament protein fused to GFP, bleach a small spot with a strong laser, and watch how fast fluorescence comes back. Recovery means that bleached subunits leave the filaments and fresh, fluorescent subunits from the cytosol take their place. Actin in a lamellipodium, or myosin II in the contractile ring, recovers within seconds: these structures are rebuilt all the time. A keratin network recovers over many minutes or longer: it is much more stable, although it still exchanges subunits. TIRF, total internal reflection fluorescence microscopy, solves a different problem. If you shine a laser through the glass at a steep enough angle, it is totally reflected. A thin field of light, the evanescent field, still leaks about 100 nanometres into the sample. Only molecules in this thin layer light up. TIRF gives very sharp images of focal adhesions at the bottom of a cell, and in a test tube it lets you watch single fluorescent myosin or kinesin molecules walk along filaments fixed on the glass.
crumbs: Myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell

title: Myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell
section: How do we know? Measuring forces: traction-force microscopy and optical tweezers
text:
How do we know? Measuring forces: traction-force microscopy and optical tweezers


Traction-force microscopy: grow cells on a soft gel with beads. From how far the beads move and how stiff the gel is, calculate the forces each adhesion feels (nanonewtons). Block myosin II (blebbistatin) and the forces vanish.
Optical tweezers: a focused laser holds a bead like a spring. Attach an actin filament and let one myosin pull: each step is one power stroke, a few nanometres and a few piconewtons.


Cell biology is usually about chemistry, but the cytoskeleton is about mechanics, so we need to measure forces. Traction-force microscopy measures the forces a whole cell exerts on its surroundings. The cell grows on a soft gel of known stiffness that contains fluorescent beads. When the cell pulls on its adhesions, the gel is deformed and the beads move. You image the beads with the cell, then remove the cell and image them again in their relaxed positions. From the displacement field and the stiffness of the gel, a computer calculates a map of forces, typically nanonewtons per adhesion. If you add blebbistatin, a drug that blocks myosin II, most of these forces disappear: so they come from myosin pulling on actin. Optical tweezers work at the level of a single molecule. A tightly focused laser beam traps a small plastic bead; the bead behaves as if held by a spring, so its displacement tells you the force. In the classic experiment, an actin filament is stretched between two trapped beads and lowered onto a single myosin. Each time the myosin binds and strokes, the beads jump a few nanometres. This is how the step sizes and forces of myosin II, myosin V and kinesin were measured.
crumbs: Myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell

title: Myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell
section: Why it matters: mavacamten, a drug that parks myosin heads
text:
Why it matters: mavacamten, a drug that parks myosin heads




Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM): about 1 in 500 people. Often a mutation in cardiac myosin (MYH7) or a myosin-binding protein. Fewer heads are parked, so too many cross-bridges cycle: the heart pulls too hard, relaxes poorly, and its wall thickens.
Mavacamten (approved 2022) binds the myosin motor domain, slows its ATPase and parks heads: fewer cross-bridges (back to the cycle slide). Too high a dose weakens the heart, so the dose is adjusted with ultrasound.







Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: the wall of the left ventricle is thickened (illustration).


Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the most common inherited heart disease, affecting about one person in five hundred. The heart muscle wall, especially of the left ventricle, becomes thick and stiff. It can block the outflow of blood, cause shortness of breath and, in young people, sudden death during exercise. Many patients carry a mutation in the beta cardiac myosin heavy chain or in myosin-binding protein C, which normally helps to hold heads still. In a relaxed heart, many myosin heads are folded back onto the thick filament in a parked state, the super-relaxed state, which uses ATP very slowly. Many HCM mutations release heads from this state. More heads cycle, the heart contracts too strongly, uses too much energy and relaxes poorly, and over years the wall thickens. Mavacamten is the first drug designed to act directly on the sarcomere. It binds the motor domain of cardiac myosin, slows phosphate release and stabilises the parked state. Fewer heads form cross-bridges, so force is reduced, as in step four of the cycle. Because too much inhibition makes the heart pump too weakly, patients are checked with ultrasound and the dose is adjusted. You can test this in the demo. Drug development of this kind returns in the course on clinical trials and drug development.
crumbs: Myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell

title: Myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell
section: Why it matters: epidermolysis bullosa simplex, when keratin breaks
text:
Why it matters: epidermolysis bullosa simplex, when keratin breaks




Mutations in keratin 5 or 14, the keratin pair of the basal layer of the skin. Usually dominant: the mutant protein poisons the filament it joins.
Keratin forms clumps instead of a network. Basal cells tear under friction, and the skin above lifts off as a blister.



Blisters on the hands of a person with epidermolysis bullosa simplex.


Epidermolysis bullosa simplex shows what happens when an intermediate filament network fails. The basal layer of the skin, the layer of dividing cells that sits on the basal lamina, makes keratin 5 and keratin 14, which pair up to form filaments. In the 1990s, it was shown that most patients with this disease carry a point mutation in one of these two genes, often in the conserved ends of the rod domain that are needed for filaments to join end to end. The disease is usually dominant. Each patient also makes normal keratin, but the mutant protein is built into the same filaments and spoils them, so one bad copy is enough. In basal cells, keratin forms clumps instead of a network linked to desmosomes and hemidesmosomes. The cells look normal until the skin is rubbed. Then basal cells break open, the layers above lift off, and fluid fills the gap: a blister. In mild forms, blisters appear on hands and feet after walking or work, especially in warm weather; severe forms start at birth. There is no cure yet; care means protecting the skin. The link between keratin and the disease was confirmed in mice with a mutant keratin 14, which had blistering skin. More in Sjukdomslära.
crumbs: Myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell

title: Myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell
section: Summary
text:
Summary

Myosins share a motor domain that binds actin and ATP; the tail decides the job. Myosin II pulls (muscle, contractile ring, cell rear); myosin V carries cargo.
Cross-bridge cycle: ATP binding releases the head, hydrolysis cocks the lever, Pi release gives the power stroke. No ATP = rigor.
In the sarcomere, thick and thin filaments slide; force follows filament overlap (length–tension curve). Ca²⁺ on troponin moves tropomyosin and switches contraction on.
Intermediate filaments (keratins, vimentin, desmin, neurofilaments, lamins) are non-polar ropes that, linked by desmosomes and hemidesmosomes, give cells and tissues mechanical strength.
Methods: FRAP, TIRF, traction-force microscopy, optical tweezers. Disease and drugs: mavacamten parks myosin heads in HCM; mutant keratin 5/14 gives blistering skin (EBS).

Read more (optional): Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell, 7th ed., ch. 16.
Image credits

Five take-home points to close the cytoskeleton block. First, myosins are actin motors with a common motor domain; the tail decides whether a myosin pulls, like myosin II, or carries, like myosin V. Second, the cross-bridge cycle: ATP binding releases the head from actin, ATP hydrolysis re-cocks the lever, and phosphate release on binding to actin drives the power stroke. Without ATP, heads stay stuck: rigor. Third, the sarcomere shortens because filaments slide, not because they shorten; the force depends on how many heads face a thin filament, which gives the length–tension curve, and calcium binding to troponin moves tropomyosin to let heads bind. Fourth, intermediate filaments are rope-like, non-polar and have no motors; through desmosomes and hemidesmosomes they make a tissue one mechanical unit. Fifth, we have a toolbox: FRAP for turnover, TIRF for the cell bottom and single molecules, traction-force microscopy and optical tweezers for forces. And two medical lessons: a drug can treat a heart disease by parking motor heads, and a single mutant keratin can make skin fall apart. Next block: how cells divide, where actin, myosin and microtubules all come back.
crumbs: Myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell

title: Study questions: microtubules and motor proteins
text: Study questions in the style of the written exam. Write your answer first (a few sentences, or a labelled sketch where it helps), then compare with the model answer. Each question is tagged with its learning outcome (ELO). Questions tagged [VG] are of the kind used for the higher grade: predict, compare, explain an unexpected result or design an experiment.

title: Study questions: microtubules and motor proteins
section: G-level questions
text:
G-level questions
1. Describe the structure of a microtubule, from the tubulin dimer to the tube. Explain what is meant by its polarity. [ELO 6]






Model answer





The building block is a dimer of α- and β-tubulin (8 nm long), each binding a GTP. Dimers join head to tail into a protofilament; 13 protofilaments lie side by side and close into a hollow tube about 25 nm wide. Because every dimer points the same way, the two ends differ: the plus end, with β-tubulin exposed, grows and shrinks fast; the minus end, with α-tubulin exposed, is slower and in cells is usually capped and anchored. This polarity is what motor proteins read to know which way to walk.




2. Explain dynamic instability. Use the terms GTP cap, catastrophe and rescue, and sketch the length of one microtubule over time. [ELO 6]






Model answer





Each microtubule end switches at random between slow growth and fast shrinkage. Dimers are added as GTP-tubulin; GTP on β-tubulin is hydrolysed shortly afterwards. A growing end therefore carries a GTP cap, which keeps the protofilaments straight. The GDP-tubulin lattice behind it is strained. If the cap is lost by chance, the protofilaments peel outward and the microtubule shrinks rapidly: a catastrophe. If a shrinking end regains a cap, it starts growing again: a rescue. The sketch is a saw-tooth: long sloping rises (growth), steep falls (shrinkage), with sharp turns at catastrophes and rescues. Dynamic instability needs no other protein (it is seen with pure tubulin), but MAPs tune it in cells.




3. Describe the centrosome and explain how it organises the microtubules of a fibroblast. [ELO 6]






Model answer





The centrosome sits next to the nucleus. It has two centrioles at right angles (each a barrel of nine triplet microtubules) surrounded by pericentriolar material, which contains many γ-tubulin ring complexes. Each ring is a template for the 13 protofilaments of a new microtubule and caps its minus end. So in a fibroblast the minus ends are anchored at the centrosome and the plus ends grow outward to the cell edge: a radial aster. Plus-end motors (kinesin) therefore carry cargo outward, minus-end motors (dynein) inward. The centrosome is duplicated once per cycle, and the two copies form the spindle poles in mitosis.




4. Compare the microtubule arrays in a fibroblast, the axon of a neuron and an epithelial cell. Why does the array matter for transport? [ELO 6]






Model answer





Fibroblast: radial aster from the centrosome; minus ends central, plus ends at the periphery. Axon: microtubules are not attached to the centrosome, and all have their plus end towards the axon tip (dendrites have mixed directions). Epithelial cell: bundles run from apical to basal, minus ends near the apical surface. Motors walk in one direction only (kinesin to plus, dynein to minus), so the array decides where cargo goes: in the axon kinesin delivers to the synapse and dynein returns to the cell body; in the epithelium, motors can sort vesicles to the apical or basolateral side.




5. Name four kinds of microtubule-associated proteins (MAPs) by what they do, with one example each. [ELO 6]






Model answer





Stabilisers bind along the lattice, reduce catastrophes and space microtubules (tau in axons, MAP2 in dendrites). Plus-end tracking proteins ride on growing ends and recruit other proteins (EB1). Destabilisers pull dimers off the ends or keep free dimers away (kinesin-13; stathmin). Severing enzymes cut microtubules with ATP and make new ends (katanin, spastin). Cells shift the balance, for example towards more catastrophes when they enter mitosis.




6. Compare kinesin and cytoplasmic dynein: direction, structure, energy use and typical cargo. [ELO 6]






Model answer





Kinesin (most kinds) walks to the plus end; it has two globular heads, a long stalk and a tail that binds cargo; there are about 45 kinesin genes in humans. It carries vesicles, mitochondria and mRNA particles outward, for example down the axon. Cytoplasmic dynein walks to the minus end; it is much larger (about 1.4 MDa), each head is a ring of ATPase domains, and it needs dynactin and an adaptor to carry cargo far; one main form does most minus-end transport (endosomes, Golgi membranes, retrograde signals, viruses going to the nucleus). Both hydrolyse ATP to take steps and both are processive.




7. Explain how kinesin walks, and describe one experiment that measured its step size. [ELO 6]






Model answer





Kinesin walks hand over hand. With both heads bound, ATP binds the front head; its neck linker docks and throws the rear head forward by 16 nm to the next binding site. The new front head binds and releases ADP; the new rear head hydrolyses its ATP and lets go. One head is always bound, so the motor is processive (about a hundred steps before it falls off). Each step moves the cargo 8 nm (one dimer) and uses one ATP; at about 100 steps per second, kinesin moves about 1 µm/s. Optical trap: a laser holds a plastic bead carrying one kinesin; the motor walks on a microtubule fixed to glass and pulls the bead; its position, measured to ~1 nm, rises in 8-nm steps, and the motor stalls at about 6 pN.




8. Describe the structure of the axoneme of a motile cilium and explain how it beats. How does a primary cilium differ? [ELO 6]






Model answer





The axoneme has nine doublet microtubules around two single central microtubules (9 + 2), and grows from a basal body (a centriole). Each doublet carries inner and outer dynein arms that walk on the neighbouring doublet, pushing the doublets to slide. Links between doublets and the anchoring at the base prevent sliding apart, so the force becomes bending; dynein activity alternates around the ring, so the cilium beats. A primary cilium (one per cell in most cells) is 9 + 0, has no dynein arms and does not move; it is a sensory antenna, for example for urine flow in kidney tubules.

title: Study questions: microtubules and motor proteins
section: VG-style questions
text:
VG-style questions
9. [VG] A patient has chronic bronchitis since childhood, is infertile and has the heart on the right side. An electron micrograph of airway cilia shows doublets without outer arms. Explain how one defect can cause all three findings. Why would a mutation in polycystin give a different disease? [ELO 6]






Model answer





The missing outer arms are axonemal dyneins, so the patient has primary ciliary dyskinesia. Without dynein the doublets do not slide, so motile cilia and flagella do not beat. Airways: cilia normally sweep mucus and trapped bacteria upward; without the beat mucus stays and infections recur. Infertility: sperm flagella use the same axoneme and dynein, so sperm cannot swim. Heart on the right: in the early embryo, rotating cilia in a small pit (the node) drive a leftward flow of fluid that tells the embryo which side is left; without it, left and right are decided at random, so about half of patients have mirrored organs. Polycystin works in the non-moving primary cilium of kidney tubule cells as a sensor of flow, not as a motor. Its loss leaves motility intact but disturbs signalling, so tubule cells keep proliferating and form cysts (polycystic kidney disease).




10. [VG] Paclitaxel stabilises microtubules and vinblastine depolymerises them. A student says: “They do opposite things, so a patient given both should be fine.” Explain why the student is wrong. Then predict what each drug does to EB1-GFP comets in a cultured cell. [ELO 6]






Model answer





Cells need microtubules that are dynamic, not a particular amount of polymer. The spindle depends on microtubules that grow, shrink, search for kinetochores and pull; both drugs suppress dynamic instability (at clinical doses both mainly freeze the ends), so each alone arrests cells in mitosis, and together they do not cancel: both still block the dynamics, and both disturb axonal transport (neuropathy). EB1-GFP: EB1 marks growing ends. With paclitaxel, catastrophes become rare and the lattice is locked, so microtubules become long and stable, many reach the cell edge and stop, and the comets become fewer and dimmer because few ends are growing. With vinblastine, the ends cannot add tubulin, so comets disappear (and at high doses the microtubule array itself disappears).




11. [VG] Design an experiment to test whether a newly discovered motor protein walks towards the plus or the minus end of microtubules, and whether it uses ATP. [ELO 6]






Model answer





Purify the motor (for example with a tag) and use a gliding assay with polarity-marked microtubules: microtubules with a brightly labelled short seed at the minus end, grown from the seed with dimmer tubulin (or grown from centrosomes, whose minus ends are known). Stick the motor to glass, add the microtubules and ATP, and film them. A plus-end-directed motor pushes the microtubule so that its minus end leads (the motor walks towards the plus end, so the filament moves the opposite way); a minus-end motor makes the plus end lead. Alternatively, label the motor itself and film single molecules walking on surface-bound marked microtubules. For energy use: repeat without ATP, with a non-hydrolysable analogue (AMP-PNP) and with ADP only; a motor that needs ATP hydrolysis stops (often stuck tightly with AMP-PNP). Measure speed at several ATP concentrations: speed rising and saturating with ATP shows the ATP dependence. An optical trap could then measure the step size and stall force.

title: Study questions: microtubules and motor proteins
section: Explore
text:
Explore
Demo: dynamic instability. Tab 1 shows a cell seen from above with 40 microtubules growing from the centrosome. A green dash marks each growing end (as EB1-GFP would), a red dot each shrinking end. Tap a microtubule to follow it in the kymograph (distance from the centrosome across, time downwards: green = growing, red = shrinking). Below are the counts of catastrophes and rescues since you last pressed Reset counts, and the four rates of the model. Tab 2 compares how long cargo needs to move along an axon by diffusion and by kinesin. Time runs at 1× real time; choose a faster speed for long runs. The random events differ between runs, so your counts will differ a little from the solutions; count for at least 5 minutes of model time.



E1. Tab 1, free tubulin 10 µM. Watch one microtubule in the kymograph for a few minutes (choose 5× or 10×). Describe what a growth phase, a catastrophe and a rescue look like. Then press Reset counts, let 5 minutes of model time pass, and read the catastrophes and rescues per microtubule per minute and the mean length. [ELO 6]
E2. Predict first. What happens to growth speed, catastrophes and the mean length if you lower the free tubulin to 5 µM, or raise it to 20 µM? Check it. At about which concentration does the model change from “bounded” to “unbounded”? Why does a microtubule grow longer on average when tubulin is higher, although it still has catastrophes? [ELO 6]
E3. Back at 10 µM, tick taxol, wait 2 minutes and count again. Then untick taxol and tick vinblastine. Describe the array in each case. Which of the four rates does each drug change? [ELO 6]
E4. [VG] Taxol makes microtubules longer and vinblastine makes them disappear, yet both are used to kill dividing cancer cells. Use your observations in E3 and the EB1 comets to explain why. Then set free tubulin to 3 µM with taxol ticked: what do you see, and what does this tell you about how taxol changes the tubulin concentration needed for growth? [ELO 6]
E5. Tab 2, vesicle, kinesin 1 µm/s. Run the race across a cell at 1× real time. Then read the table for 1 mm and 1 m. Repeat with protein. Over what distance do diffusion and the motor take equally long for each cargo? How many ATP does one kinesin use to carry a vesicle 1 m? [ELO 6]
E6. [VG] Predict first. How fast would a motor need to walk to bring a vesicle from the spinal cord to the foot (1 m) in one day? Is this possible for kinesin (use the slider)? Untick ATP: what happens to the kinesin, and why does a neuron with too little ATP (for example with failing mitochondria) lose its synapses first at the far end? [ELO 6]






Solutions





E1. Growth is a sloping green edge moving slowly to the right (12 µm/min: the end moves out 1 µm every 5 s). A catastrophe is a sharp turn: the edge turns red and moves back towards 0 about twice as fast (24 µm/min). A rescue is a turn from red back to green before the microtubule reaches the centrosome; if it reaches 0, a new microtubule starts after a few seconds. Over 5 minutes the model gives about 1.1–1.3 catastrophes and 0.5–0.6 rescues per microtubule per minute, and a mean length of about 8–9 µm. (The “bounded” readout says 13 µm: that is the average for a microtubule in a cell without an edge that is never empty; in the demo some microtubules are empty or stalled at the edge.)
E2. At 5 µM growth slows to about 5 µm/min, catastrophes become more frequent (about 2 per microtubule per minute: a slowly growing end has a small GTP cap and loses it more easily), rescues are rarer, and the mean length falls to about 2 µm: a small, sparse array near the centrosome. At 20 µM growth is about 25 µm/min, catastrophes are fewer (about 0.9–1 per minute), and the mean length rises to about 16 µm, with 4–10 microtubules touching the cell edge. The model switches from bounded to unbounded at about 14.5 µM (the readout shows “unbounded” from 15 µM). In the Dogterom–Leibler model a microtubule is unbounded when the length gained in growth phases, \(v_g/f_\text{cat}\) per phase, outweighs the length lost in shrinkage phases, \(v_s/f_\text{res}\). Higher tubulin raises \(v_g\) and lowers \(f_\text{cat}\), so each growth phase adds more than each shrinkage phase removes; the average end drifts outward until the cell edge stops it.
E3. Taxol: within a minute or two almost all microtubules (35–40 of 40) reach the cell edge and stay there; the mean length is about 25 µm. Taxol lowers the catastrophe rate tenfold, slows shrinkage and raises rescues; the few catastrophes left (about 0.3 per microtubule per minute) happen at the edge and are rescued almost at once, so the kymograph shows a nearly straight vertical line at 25 µm. Green comets vanish because the ends at the edge are stalled, not growing. Vinblastine: the microtubules shrink back to the centrosome and only tiny stubs appear and vanish; the mean length is about 0.1 µm. Vinblastine lowers the growth speed tenfold (1.2 µm/min) and makes catastrophes more frequent. (In the demo vinblastine is a high dose; at low doses both drugs mainly freeze the ends.)
E4. A dividing cell must build a spindle whose microtubules grow, shrink and search the cell until they capture every chromosome, and then shorten to pull the chromosomes apart. With taxol the microtubules are long but frozen: they no longer have catastrophes, so they cannot search or pull. With vinblastine they cannot grow. In both cases the spindle fails, the spindle checkpoint keeps the cell in mitosis, and the cell dies (the mitosis lecture). In both cases the EB1 comets, the sign of growing, searching ends, disappear. At 3 µM with taxol the microtubules still grow out to the edge and stay (the readout says unbounded), while without taxol 3 µM gives only short microtubules (mean about 0.7 µm). Taxol lowers the tubulin concentration needed for net growth (the critical concentration), because it stops the GDP lattice from falling apart: in a cell it pulls free tubulin into stable polymer.
E5. Vesicle (D = 0.1 µm²/s): across a cell the kinesin arrives after 10 s; the diffusing copies spread only about √(2Dt) ≈ 1.4 µm in 10 s, and the average time to diffuse 10 µm is 8.3 min (a few of the 40 copies arrive earlier by chance). Over 1 mm: diffusion 58 days, kinesin 17 min. Over 1 m: diffusion about 160 000 years, kinesin 12 days. Protein (D = 5 µm²/s): across a cell both take about 10 s; 1 mm: diffusion 28 h, kinesin 17 min; 1 m: diffusion about 3000 years, kinesin 12 days. Equal times at \(x = 2D/v\): 10 µm for a protein, 0.2 µm for a vesicle. So small proteins can diffuse across an ordinary cell, but vesicles and organelles need motors at almost any distance. ATP: 1 m / 8 nm = 125 million steps, so 125 million ATP for one kinesin (in reality a cargo is carried by several motors that take turns).
E6. 1 m in one day is 10⁶ µm in 86 400 s, about 12 µm/s. The slider stops at 5 µm/s, the top of fast axonal transport, which gives 2.3 days; kinesin cannot go much faster because each step needs one ATP cycle (about 100 per second, 8 nm each). Without ATP the kinesin stops where it is and stays bound to the microtubule (in a real cell it would be stuck in a tightly bound state), so nothing arrives. The far end of the axon depends on a constant supply of new vesicles, membrane proteins and mitochondria; if ATP falls, transport slows everywhere, and the part that is reached last, the synapses at the end of the longest axons, suffers first. This is why diseases of mitochondria and of motors, and drugs such as vincristine, often show up first as problems in the feet.

title: Quiz: seeing cells (microscopy)
text:
Short questions to check your understanding of the lecture Seeing cells: microscopy. Try each on paper first, then open the hint or the answer. The tag after each question shows the learning outcome (ELO) it practises.

Q1. A student says: “If I use a 100× objective and a 20× eyepiece instead of a 10× eyepiece, I will be able to see ribosomes in a light microscope.” Is the student right? [ELO 1]






Hint





What does the eyepiece change: the size of the image or the amount of detail in it? How big is a ribosome compared with the resolution limit?









Answer





No. A stronger eyepiece only magnifies the image more; it does not improve resolution. Resolution is set by the wavelength of light and the numerical aperture of the objective, and is about 200 nm for the best light microscope. A ribosome is about 25 nm, so it stays below the limit. Extra magnification just makes the blur bigger (“empty magnification”).




Q2. Using \(d \approx 0.61\,\lambda / \mathrm{NA}\), which change gives better (smaller) resolution: (a) blue light (450 nm) instead of red light (650 nm), or (b) a dry objective with NA 0.75 instead of an oil objective with NA 1.4? [ELO 1]






Hint





Smaller \(\lambda\) and larger NA both make \(d\) smaller.









Answer






improves resolution: shorter wavelength gives smaller \(d\) (about 196 nm with NA 1.4 instead of about 283 nm). (b) makes it worse: a lower NA collects light from a narrower cone, so \(d\) grows (for 500 nm light, about 407 nm with NA 0.75 instead of about 218 nm with NA 1.4).





Q3. Why can unstained living cells be seen clearly in a phase-contrast microscope but hardly at all in a bright-field microscope? [ELO 1]






Hint





Cells absorb very little light. What else happens to light that passes through a nucleus or a membrane?









Answer





Cells are mostly water and absorb little visible light, so in bright field the light passes through almost unchanged. But dense parts of the cell (higher refractive index) slow the light down, giving a phase shift that the eye cannot see. Phase-contrast optics turn these phase differences into differences in brightness, so the nucleus and the cell edges become visible without stain.




Q4. A fluorophore is excited at 490 nm and emits at 520 nm. What is the Stokes shift, and why is it essential for fluorescence microscopy? [ELO 1]






Hint





Think of the filter cube: what would happen if the emitted light had the same colour as the excitation light?









Answer





The Stokes shift is the difference between the excitation and emission peaks, here 30 nm. Emitted light has a longer wavelength because some energy is lost as heat before emission. Because the colours differ, the dichroic mirror and emission filter can block the very bright excitation light and pass only the weak emitted light. Without the shift, the glow would be lost in the excitation light.




Q5. You want to follow how fast a vesicle protein moves in a living neuron. Should you use immunofluorescence or a GFP fusion protein? Give one reason and one thing you must check. [ELO 1] [ELO 6]






Hint





What must you do to cells before antibodies can get inside?









Answer





A GFP fusion protein. Immunofluorescence needs the cells to be fixed and permeabilised, so they are dead and nothing moves. A GFP fusion is made by the living cell itself. You must check that the GFP tag does not change the protein: it should still work and be in the same place as the untagged protein (for example, compare with antibody staining in fixed cells).




Q6. What does the pinhole in a confocal microscope do, and what do you gain from it? [ELO 1]






Hint





Where is light from the focal plane focused, and where is light from other depths focused?









Answer





The pinhole sits where light from the focal plane comes to a sharp point, so that light passes. Light from planes above and below is spread out at the pinhole and mostly blocked. You gain a sharp optical section (about 0.5–1 µm thick) without out-of-focus haze, and by refocusing step by step you can build a 3D stack without cutting the sample.




Q7. Match each question to the best method: (i) the shape of microvilli on the surface of an intestinal cell; (ii) the atomic structure of a purified membrane pump; (iii) how the ER membrane is arranged next to a mitochondrion inside a cell, at nanometre detail. Methods: TEM, SEM, single-particle cryo-EM. [ELO 1]






Hint





Which method shows surfaces, which shows thin slices through a cell, and which averages many copies of one purified molecule?









Answer






SEM: a scanned beam shows the 3D surface. (ii) Single-particle cryo-EM: many images of the purified protein in thin ice are averaged into a map, often better than 0.3 nm. (iii) TEM of thin sections (or cryo-electron tomography of a frozen cell) shows membranes inside the cell at about 1–2 nm.





Q8. In a figure, protein A (green) and protein B (red) give yellow in the merged confocal image. The authors conclude “A binds B”. What is wrong with this conclusion? [ELO 1]






Hint





How close must two proteins be to look like one spot in a confocal image? How big is a protein?









Answer





Yellow only means the two signals are in the same spot within the resolution limit, about 200 nm, which is about 40 protein diameters. A and B could be in the same organelle without touching. To claim binding you need other evidence, for example co-immunoprecipitation (next lecture), or a method with much better resolution. You should also check the controls (for example cells lacking A) and that the signal does not leak from one channel into the other.
