At pH 4, when the particle is made, it is positive and binds the negative RNA. In blood at pH 7.4 it is almost neutral, which makes it less toxic. After the particle is taken up by endocytosis, the endosome becomes acidic, the lipid becomes positive again, pairs with negative lipids of the endosome membrane, and disturbs it, so some RNA escapes into the cytosol. The helper phospholipid, DSPC, and cholesterol give structure. The PEG-lipid controls particle size and stops particles sticking together. Patisiran, approved in 2018, carries a small interfering RNA that destroys transthyretin mRNA in liver cells; misfolded transthyretin causes a hereditary amyloidosis. The COVID-19 vaccines use the same design with mRNA. You meet vaccines again in Immunologi, and drug development in Kliniska prövningar och läkemedelsutveckling.

title: Membrane structure
section: Why it matters: liposomal doxorubicin (Doxil)
text:
Why it matters: liposomal doxorubicin (Doxil)


Doxorubicin blocks topoisomerase II and kills dividing cells, but damages the heart (dose-limiting).
In a rigid, PEG-coated liposome (approved 1995), it circulates for days. Tumour vessels are leaky (EPR effect), heart capillaries are tight: less heart damage, new side effect in the skin (hand–foot syndrome).
Caveat: EPR is strong in mouse tumours but varies a lot between human tumours; survival is similar to free drug.


Doxorubicin is an old and effective cancer drug. It inserts between DNA bases and traps topoisomerase II on cut DNA, which kills dividing cells. Its big problem is the heart: above a lifetime dose it damages heart muscle, even years later. Liposomal doxorubicin packs the drug into a liposome of about ninety nanometres, a small bilayer vesicle. The lipids are saturated phospholipid plus cholesterol, so the bilayer is stiff and the drug does not leak out. Inside, the drug is loaded with a gradient and forms a crystal. The outside carries a PEG coat that hides the particle from phagocytes, so it circulates for days instead of being cleared in minutes. Most normal capillaries, including those of the heart, have a tight wall, so the particle stays in the blood. Many tumour vessels have gaps of hundreds of nanometres and poor lymph drainage, so particles leak in and stay: the enhanced permeability and retention, or EPR, effect. In patients, Doxil causes much less heart damage. But be honest: EPR was found in fast-growing mouse tumours, it varies widely in human tumours, and in trials survival was similar to free doxorubicin. The gain is mainly safety. Clinical trials return in Kliniska prövningar och läkemedelsutveckling.

title: Membrane structure
section: Summary
text:
Summary

Membrane lipids self-assemble into a sealed bilayer because of the hydrophobic effect. The plasma membrane mixes glycerophospholipids, sphingolipids and cholesterol.
The bilayer is a two-dimensional liquid: fast lateral diffusion, rare flip-flop. Tail length, double bonds, cholesterol and temperature set its fluidity.
The two leaflets differ (asymmetry): flippases keep PS inside; scramblases expose it as an “eat me” or “clot here” signal.
Proteins are integral (α-helices or β-barrels; predicted from hydropathy plots; extracted with detergents), lipid-anchored or peripheral. FRAP, cell fusion and freeze-fracture EM show a fluid mosaic with domains and fences.
Drug carriers use the same rules: lipid nanoparticles for RNA, PEG-liposomes for doxorubicin.

Read more (optional): Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell, 7th ed., ch. 10.
Image credits

Let us go back to the red blood cell that squeezes through a capillary. Its membrane is a bilayer that forms and reseals by itself because water pushes the tails together. It is a liquid in its own plane, so it can bend and flow, but polar molecules and ions cannot cross its oily core, so it is a barrier. The cell tunes its fluidity with tail length, double bonds and cholesterol, and it keeps the two leaflets different with flippases; when a cell dies or a platelet is activated, scramblases expose PS as a signal. Proteins sit in the membrane in a few defined ways, and the rules of the bilayer, twenty hydrophobic residues for a helix, explain how we can predict them and how detergents take them out. FRAP, cell fusion and freeze-fracture are the evidence for this fluid mosaic, with domains such as the region fenced off by tight junctions. Finally, the same rules let us build drug carriers. The next lecture asks the question this one leaves open: if the bilayer blocks ions and sugars, how do they get across? The answer is transporters and pumps.

title: Study questions: enzyme-coupled receptors and kinase cascades
text: Study questions in the style of the written exam. Write your answer first (a few sentences, or a labelled sketch where it helps), then compare with the model answer. Each question is tagged with its learning outcome (ELO). Questions tagged [VG] are of the kind used for the higher grade: predict, compare, explain an unexpected result or design an experiment.

title: Study questions: enzyme-coupled receptors and kinase cascades
section: G-level questions
text:
G-level questions
1. Describe, step by step, how binding of EGF to its receptor leads to activation of Ras. Name the proteins and domains involved. [ELO 3]






Model answer






EGF binds the extracellular part of the EGF receptor and brings two receptor chains together (dimerisation).
The two kinase domains, now close together, phosphorylate each other (trans-autophosphorylation): first in the activation loop, which makes the kinases fully active, then on several tyrosines in the cytosolic tails.
The phosphotyrosines are docking sites. The adaptor Grb2 binds one with its SH2 domain. Grb2 holds the GEF SOS, which is thereby brought to the plasma membrane.
At the membrane SOS meets Ras, which is held there by a lipid anchor. SOS makes Ras release GDP; GTP, which is abundant in the cytosol, binds. Ras-GTP is active.





2. Compare the two kinds of molecular switch used in RTK signalling, phosphorylation and GTP binding. For each, say what turns it on and what turns it off, with one example from the lecture. [ELO 3]






Model answer





Phosphorylation: a kinase transfers a phosphate from ATP to a Ser, Thr or Tyr; a phosphatase removes it. The phosphate changes the shape of the protein or creates a binding site. Example: MEK phosphorylates ERK on a Thr and a Tyr; dual-specificity phosphatases (DUSPs) remove them. Or: RTK tyrosines phosphorylated, then bound by SH2 proteins.
GTP binding: a GTPase is on with GTP and off with GDP. A GEF turns it on by exchanging GDP for GTP; a GAP turns it off by speeding up GTP hydrolysis. Example: Ras, turned on by SOS and off by GAPs such as neurofibromin.
In both, the “off” state is reached by an enzyme reaction, so the length of the signal is controlled by the balance of the two enzymes.




3. Draw the Ras–MAP kinase cascade from the receptor to the nucleus. For each step, say what kind of molecule it is and how it activates the next. What does ERK do in the nucleus? [ELO 3]






Model answer





Active RTK (phosphotyrosines) → Grb2 (adaptor, SH2) → SOS (GEF) → Ras (small GTPase; Ras-GTP binds RAF) → RAF (Ser/Thr kinase, MAPKKK; phosphorylates MEK on two serines) → MEK (dual-specificity kinase, MAPKK; phosphorylates ERK on a Thr and a Tyr) → ERK (MAP kinase; active only when both sites are phosphorylated).
Active ERK phosphorylates many proteins in the cytosol and enters the nucleus, where it phosphorylates transcription factors. Immediate early genes (e.g. FOS, MYC) are transcribed within minutes; their products turn on later genes, including cyclin D, which lets the cell enter the cell cycle.




4. Explain how the PI3K–Akt pathway helps a cell survive and grow. Include PIP₃, the PH domain, PTEN and two targets of Akt. [ELO 3]






Model answer





PI3K docks on phosphotyrosines of an active RTK (SH2 domains of its regulatory subunit; Ras-GTP also helps) and phosphorylates the membrane lipid PIP₂ to PIP₃. Akt binds PIP₃ with its PH domain, is brought to the membrane, and is phosphorylated and activated by PDK1 and mTORC2. Active Akt (1) phosphorylates and inactivates BAD and other pro-apoptotic proteins, so the cell survives; (2) activates mTORC1 (via TSC and Rheb), which increases protein synthesis and cell growth; (in muscle and fat cells it also sends GLUT4 to the surface after insulin). PTEN removes the 3-phosphate from PIP₃ and so switches the pathway off; loss of PTEN in cancer keeps Akt active.




5. Describe the JAK–STAT pathway. How does it differ from the Ras–MAP kinase pathway? [ELO 3]






Model answer





Cytokine receptors (e.g. for interferons, IL-6, erythropoietin) have no kinase domain; a JAK tyrosine kinase is bound to each receptor tail. The cytokine brings two receptor chains together; the JAKs phosphorylate each other and tyrosines on the receptor. A STAT protein docks on a phosphotyrosine with its SH2 domain and is phosphorylated by JAK on one tyrosine. Two phosphorylated STATs bind each other (each SH2 domain binds the other’s phosphotyrosine), the dimer enters the nucleus and binds DNA as a transcription factor.
Differences: the kinase is associated, not part of the receptor; there is no GTPase and no kinase cascade: the protein phosphorylated at the receptor is itself the transcription factor. The route is shorter and amplifies less.




6. List four ways in which a growth-factor signal through the Ras–MAP kinase pathway is switched off. Which of them is a negative feedback, and what does it do to the time course of ERK activity? [ELO 3]






Model answer






Receptor endocytosis and degradation in lysosomes (and dephosphorylation of the receptor by tyrosine phosphatases). (2) GAPs speed up GTP hydrolysis by Ras. (3) Phosphatases remove the phosphates from MEK and ERK (e.g. DUSPs). (4) Negative feedback: active ERK phosphorylates SOS and RAF and makes them less active; ERK also induces transcription of DUSP genes.

The feedback (4, and the induced DUSPs) is driven by the output itself. It makes ERK activity rise to a peak within minutes and then fall to a lower plateau although the growth factor is still there.




7. What is a phospho-specific antibody? Describe a western blot experiment that shows that EGF activates ERK within minutes, and name the controls. [ELO 1] [ELO 3]






Model answer





A phospho-specific antibody is raised against a peptide that carries a phosphate at a particular site, and selected so that it binds the protein only when that site is phosphorylated. It therefore reports the active form (e.g. ERK phosphorylated on Thr202 and Tyr204).
Experiment: starve cultured cells of serum (so that the pathway is off), add EGF, and lyse dishes of cells at 0, 2, 5, 10, 30 and 60 min. Run equal amounts of protein on SDS-PAGE, blot, and stain with anti-phospho-ERK. Controls: the same blot (or a parallel one) stained with anti-total-ERK, to show that the amount of ERK does not change and only its phosphorylation does; a loading control (actin or tubulin); a lane without EGF; optionally a lane with a MEK inhibitor, which should remove phospho-ERK. Expected: phospho-ERK appears within 2 min, peaks at about 5–10 min and then declines.




8. Explain how imatinib works in chronic myeloid leukaemia. Start with the chromosome change. [ELO 3] [ELO 9]






Model answer





In CML, chromosomes 9 and 22 exchange pieces (translocation t(9;22)); the shortened chromosome 22 is the Philadelphia chromosome. At the joint, the start of the BCR gene is fused to most of the ABL tyrosine kinase gene. The BCR part makes the fusion protein form oligomers, so the kinase is always active; the cells divide and survive without the normal signals, and too many white blood cells are made. Imatinib is a small molecule that binds the ATP pocket of ABL (in its inactive shape). Without ATP, BCR-ABL cannot phosphorylate its substrates, so the signal stops and the leukaemia cells stop dividing and die. Normal cells, which do not depend on ABL, are largely spared. Imatinib (2001) was the first targeted cancer drug; most patients now survive long term.

title: Study questions: enzyme-coupled receptors and kinase cascades
section: VG-style questions
text:
VG-style questions
9. [VG] A tumour carries a KRAS G12V mutation. (a) Explain at the molecular level why this Ras is “stuck on”. (b) Predict whether an EGFR inhibitor, a RAF inhibitor (vemurafenib) or a MEK inhibitor will reduce ERK activity in these cells, and explain why. [ELO 3] [ELO 9]






Model answer






Ras switches off by hydrolysing GTP, which is very slow unless a GAP puts a catalytic arginine into the active site. Glycine 12 lies next to that site; any larger side chain (here valine) blocks the GAP’s arginine, so GAP-stimulated hydrolysis no longer works. Ras stays GTP-bound (active) without any input from the receptor.
EGFR inhibitor: little effect, because the block is upstream of the mutation; Ras is active without the receptor. RAF inhibitor (vemurafenib): does not work, and can even increase ERK. Vemurafenib is made for the monomeric BRAF V600E; with active Ras, RAF works as dimers, and drug binding to one RAF in a dimer can activate the other (paradoxical activation). MEK inhibitor: reduces ERK, because MEK lies downstream of Ras. General rule: an inhibitor must act at or below the mutated step. (In practice, MEK inhibitors alone work poorly in KRAS-mutant tumours, partly because of feedback relief and the PI3K branch; new KRAS G12C inhibitors such as sotorasib target the mutant protein itself.)





10. [VG] BRAF V600E melanomas often respond to vemurafenib, but BRAF V600E colon cancers hardly do. Colon cells have much more EGFR signalling than melanocytes. Use the idea of negative feedback to explain the difference, and propose a better treatment for the colon cancer. Then describe an experiment with cultured colon cancer cells that would test your explanation. [ELO 1] [ELO 3] [ELO 9]






Model answer





Explanation: In BRAF V600E cells, ERK is very active, so the negative feedback from ERK keeps SOS, Ras and wild-type RAF strongly suppressed; the mutant BRAF itself ignores the feedback. Vemurafenib blocks V600E-BRAF and ERK falls. Lower ERK means less feedback, so the brake on the upstream pathway is released. In a melanoma cell there is little receptor input, so not much happens. In a colon cancer cell, EGFR is active: with the brake released, EGFR activates Ras, Ras makes RAF dimers, and vemurafenib inhibits these poorly. ERK comes back, and the tumour keeps growing.
Better treatment: combine the BRAF inhibitor with an EGFR blocker (e.g. the antibody cetuximab; this combination, with encorafenib, is now used) and/or a MEK inhibitor, which acts below RAF.
Experiment: treat BRAF V600E colon cancer cells with vemurafenib and lyse them at 0, 1, 4 and 24 h. Western blot with phospho-ERK, total ERK, phospho-EGFR and a loading control (and a Ras-GTP pull-down assay if available). Prediction: phospho-ERK falls first, then rises again, while phospho-EGFR and Ras-GTP increase. Add an EGFR inhibitor (or knock EGFR down by siRNA/CRISPR): the rebound should disappear and the cells should stop dividing (count cells or measure proliferation). Compare with a melanoma cell line, which should show little rebound.




11. [VG] Students compare two signals: receptor occupancy and active (doubly phosphorylated) ERK, both measured over a range of growth-factor concentrations. ERK is half-maximal at a ten times lower growth-factor concentration than the receptor, and its curve is much steeper. (a) Explain both observations. (b) Why could a steep, switch-like response be useful for a decision such as cell division? (c) Predict how a strong negative feedback would change the ERK dose–response curve. [ELO 3]






Model answer






Sensitivity (left shift): amplification. Each active kinase activates many molecules of the next, so a small fraction of active receptors is enough to switch on a large fraction of ERK. Steepness: MEK and ERK each need two phosphorylations, and the kinases and phosphatases work close to saturation, so at each level a small change in input tips the balance from mostly off to mostly on. The steepness compounds level by level (Hill coefficient about 4–5 for ERK versus 1 for binding).
Division is an all-or-none decision. A switch-like response ignores small, noisy changes in growth factor, but gives a clear “go” above a threshold, so cells do not start the cell cycle halfway.
Negative feedback reduces the maximum ERK level and makes the curve less steep (more graded) and shifts it, because the more ERK is active, the more it suppresses its own input. (In the demo: Hill coefficient falls from about 4 to about 1.3.) Feedback trades switch-like behaviour for robustness.

title: Study questions: enzyme-coupled receptors and kinase cascades
section: Explore
text:
Explore
The demo is a small model of the cascade growth factor → RTK → Ras → RAF → MEK → ERK. On the left, the cascade is coloured by how much of each protein is active at the time you choose. The upper plot shows activity over 90 minutes after growth factor is added; tap or drag in the plot (or use the slider) to move the time cursor. The table gives the percentage active and the number of active molecules per cell. The lower plot shows the steady state at every growth-factor dose, with the half-maximal dose and steepness (Hill coefficient \(n_H\)) below it. You can add three inhibitors (dose in multiples of their IC₅₀), before or 30 min after the growth factor, switch the negative feedback (active ERK slowly inhibits SOS and RAF) on and off, and add an oncogenic mutation. When a drug is present, a dotted line shows ERK without the drugs, and the box under the table gives the effect at steady state.
A qualitative model with illustrative numbers. MEK and ERK are each phosphorylated twice by enzymes near saturation, in the spirit of Huang and Ferrell (1996). It is one pathway out of a network: no PI3K branch, scaffolds or nuclear transport, one lumped feedback, simple drug binding. The RAF inhibitor blocks BRAF V600E well, but Ras-driven RAF dimers about 100 times less, and at moderate doses it activates them up to 1.5 times (paradoxical activation). The curves are computed at once; there is no animation.





E1. Choose Feedback off. In the lower plot, compare the receptor and ERK curves. At what growth-factor dose is each half-maximal, and what are their Hill coefficients? Set the dose to 0.1 ng/mL: what percentage of receptors and of ERK is active? Explain both differences with two properties of the cascade. [ELO 3]
E2. Choose Normal cell + growth factor (feedback on). Read ERK at the peak and at 60 min, and when the peak occurs. Then untick the feedback. What changes in the time course and in the dose–response curve? What would you expect to see on a phospho-ERK western blot with and without the feedback? [ELO 1] [ELO 3]
E3. [VG] Predict first: a MEK inhibitor at its IC₅₀ is added 30 min after the growth factor. Will it remove a larger or a smaller fraction of ERK activity in a cell with feedback than in one without? Then run MEK inhibitor at 30 min, no feedback and … with feedback. Read the percentage of ERK activity removed, and look at RAF and Ras before and after the drug. Explain what you see. [ELO 3]
E4. Choose Ras G12V (stuck on). Is ERK active without growth factor? Now try each inhibitor alone at 10× IC₅₀ (use Remove all drugs between tries). Which one works, which one does nothing, and which one makes ERK more active? Explain each with where the drug acts relative to the mutation. [ELO 3] [ELO 9]
E5. [VG] Choose BRAF V600E melanoma (no growth factor) and add the RAF inhibitor at 10× IC₅₀. Then choose BRAF V600E + vemurafenib, with EGF. Compare ERK. Untick the feedback in the second case: what happens, and what does this tell you about why the drug fails? Find two ways (one or two drugs) to bring ERK below 30 %. Relate this to the treatment of BRAF V600E colon cancer. [ELO 3] [ELO 9]






Solutions





E1. Receptor: half-maximal at about 1 ng/mL (the K_d), \(n_H\) = 1.0. ERK: half-maximal at about 0.09 ng/mL (11 times less) with \(n_H\) ≈ 4. At 0.1 ng/mL only 9 % of the receptors are bound, but 53 % of ERK is active (and at 0.2 ng/mL, 17 % against 80 %). The left shift comes from amplification: each active kinase activates many molecules of the next, so a few active receptors are enough to switch on much of the ERK. The steepness comes from the double phosphorylations of MEK and ERK by enzymes working near saturation; it grows from level to level (MEK \(n_H\) ≈ 2, ERK ≈ 4). ERK switches from off to on over a small change in growth factor.
E2. With feedback, ERK peaks at about 85 % after 5–6 min and falls to about 45–50 % by 30 min, then stays there (a small dip and rebound on the way). Without feedback, ERK rises to about 85 % and stays there. The dose–response curve with feedback is lower (maximum about 59 %) and much less steep (\(n_H\) ≈ 1.3 instead of 4). On a western blot, phospho-ERK with feedback would be strongest at 5–10 min and weaker at 30–60 min (as in real cells after EGF); without feedback it would stay strong. Total ERK would be the same in all lanes.
E3. Without feedback, the drug removes about 59 % of ERK activity (85 % → 35 %); RAF and Ras do not change. With feedback, it removes only about 46 % (49 % → 27 %), and the time course shows ERK dropping to about 7 % within a few minutes and then climbing back to 27 %. At the same time RAF rises from about 39 % to 56 % and Ras from about 44 % to 54 %. Explanation: the inhibitor lowers ERK, ERK no longer brakes SOS and RAF, so more MEK is phosphorylated, which partly overcomes the drug. Relief of negative feedback blunts the inhibitor. At 3× IC₅₀ the drug wins in both cases (only 5–9 % left): feedback relief raises the dose needed.
E4. Yes: without any growth factor, Ras is about 67 % GTP-bound and ERK about 65 % active. RTK inhibitor: no effect (ERK stays 65 %), because the receptor is upstream of the mutated Ras. MEK inhibitor: works (ERK about 0 % at 10× IC₅₀, 4 % at 3×), because MEK is downstream of Ras. RAF inhibitor: ERK rises to about 78 %. In Ras-mutant cells RAF works as Ras-driven dimers, which the drug blocks poorly; at moderate doses drug binding to one RAF activates the partner (paradoxical activation). This is why vemurafenib is not given to patients with RAS-mutant tumours, and why patients on it can get new skin tumours from cells with RAS mutations. Rule: the drug must act at or below the mutated step, and must actually bind the active form of its target.
E5. Melanoma without growth factor: the RAF inhibitor at 10× takes ERK from 88 % to about 0 %. The cells depend on V600E-BRAF, and there is little other input. With EGF, the same dose leaves about 69 % of ERK active: the drug barely works. Look at Ras: before the drug, the strong ERK signal kept Ras suppressed by feedback (about 28 % active although half of the receptors are bound); with the drug, ERK falls, the brake is released and Ras rises (35 %), and the RAF activity now comes from Ras-driven wild-type RAF dimers, which the drug blocks poorly (and even activates). With the feedback switched off, the drug does nothing at all (88 % with and without): the receptor input fully replaces the blocked mutant. So the drug fails because of the receptor, and the feedback is what kept that receptor input hidden before treatment. Two ways below 30 %: add the RTK inhibitor at 10× (ERK about 26 %), or add a MEK inhibitor at 3× (ERK about 6 %; a MEK inhibitor alone at 10× gives about 1 %). In patients, BRAF V600E colon cancer is treated with a BRAF inhibitor plus the EGFR antibody cetuximab (encorafenib + cetuximab), and melanoma with a BRAF + MEK inhibitor combination.

title: Quiz: ion channels and membrane potential
text:
Short questions to check your understanding of the lecture Ion channels and membrane potential. Try each on paper first, then open the hint or the answer. The tag after each question shows the learning outcome (ELO) it practises.

Q1. A membrane protein moves 500 molecules of glucose per second. Another moves 10 million K⁺ ions per second. Which is a channel and which is a transporter? Give one more property that tells them apart. [ELO 2]






Hint





Does the protein change shape for every molecule, or is it an open pore?









Answer





The glucose mover is a transporter (10²–10⁴ per second: it binds, changes shape and releases each molecule). The K⁺ mover is a channel (up to 10⁸ ions per second through an open pore). Other differences: a transporter is never open to both sides at once and can be coupled to ATP or another gradient to move a solute uphill; a channel only lets ions flow down their electrochemical gradient.




Q2. Na⁺ is smaller than K⁺. Why can it not pass through the K⁺ channel’s selectivity filter? [ELO 2]






Hint





What does an ion have to lose before it enters the narrow filter, and what does the filter give back?









Answer





To enter the narrow filter, an ion must lose its shell of water, which costs energy. For K⁺, the filter’s backbone carbonyl oxygens sit at the same distance as the water oxygens did, so the cost is paid back. Na⁺ is smaller; the rigid filter cannot close in on it, so the oxygens are too far away to replace its water. Losing water without being paid back costs too much, so Na⁺ stays out.




Q3. Match each channel to how it is opened: (a) voltage-gated Na⁺ channel, (b) nicotinic acetylcholine receptor, (c) Piezo2. Gating types: ligand, mechanical force, voltage. [ELO 2]






Hint





One has a charged sensor helix, one binds a transmitter, one responds to stretch of the membrane.









Answer






voltage: positive charges in a sensor helix move when the membrane depolarises. (b) ligand: two acetylcholine molecules bind and open the pore. (c) mechanical force: membrane tension pulls on its blades; Piezo2 senses touch.





Q4. Use the Nernst equation (\(E = \frac{61.5\text{ mV}}{z}\log_{10}\frac{c_\text{out}}{c_\text{in}}\) at 37 °C) to calculate \(E_\text{K}\) if K⁺ is 150 mM inside and 15 mM outside. [ELO 2]






Hint





The ratio out/in is 0.1. What is log₁₀(0.1)?









Answer





\(E_\text{K} = 61.5 \times \log_{10}(15/150) = 61.5 \times (-1) =\) −61.5 mV. A tenfold gradient of a singly charged ion gives about 61.5 mV. The sign is negative because K⁺ is higher inside: the inside must be negative to hold K⁺ back.




Q5. The resting membrane potential of a cell is −70 mV, \(E_\text{K}\) is −89 mV and \(E_\text{Na}\) is +67 mV. Why is the resting potential so much closer to \(E_\text{K}\) than to \(E_\text{Na}\)? [ELO 2]






Hint





Which channels are open at rest?









Answer





At rest, many K⁺ leak channels are open and very few Na⁺ channels. The membrane potential is a weighted average of the equilibrium potentials, weighted by permeability (the Goldman idea). K⁺ dominates, so the potential lies near \(E_\text{K}\), pulled a little towards \(E_\text{Na}\) by the small Na⁺ leak.




Q6. During an action potential, why does the voltage fall again after the peak, and why can a second action potential not start immediately? [ELO 2]






Hint





Two things happen to two kinds of voltage-gated channels after the peak.









Answer





The voltage-gated Na⁺ channels inactivate (a part of the channel plugs the pore from inside), and slower voltage-gated K⁺ channels open, so K⁺ flows out and the voltage falls towards \(E_\text{K}\). Inactivated Na⁺ channels cannot reopen until the membrane has been negative for a short time: the refractory period. This also makes the signal travel in only one direction along an axon.




Q7. In a cell-attached patch-clamp recording, the current jumps between 0 and −2 pA and never stays in between. What does this tell you, and about how many ions per second pass through the channel when it is open? (Charge of one ion: 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.) [ELO 1] [ELO 2]






Hint





1 A = 1 C/s. Divide the current by the charge of one ion.









Answer





The square steps show one channel switching between fully open and fully closed; there is no half-open state. 2 × 10⁻¹² C/s ÷ 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C ≈ 1.25 × 10⁷, about 12 million ions per second through one protein molecule.




Q8. Two patients have cystic fibrosis. Patient A is homozygous for G551D, patient B for F508del. Ivacaftor alone helps A a lot but B very little. Explain. [ELO 2] [ELO 9]






Hint





Where is the CFTR protein in each patient, and what does a potentiator do?









Answer





G551D CFTR reaches the plasma membrane but its gate rarely opens. Ivacaftor is a potentiator: it increases the time the channel is open, so it fixes this defect. F508del CFTR misfolds in the ER and is degraded, so almost none reaches the surface; a potentiator has nothing to act on. Patient B needs correctors (elexacaftor, tezacaftor) to help the protein fold and reach the membrane, plus the potentiator, because rescued F508del also gates poorly.

title: Ion channels and membrane potential
section: About this lecture

title: Ion channels and membrane potential
section: The question: every cell is a small battery
text:
The question: every cell is a small battery


Put a fine electrode into almost any animal cell: the inside is about 70 mV more negative than the outside.
The membrane is only 5 nm thick, so the electric field across it is huge: about 14 million volts per metre.
Where does the voltage come from? How can a protein pore pass K⁺ but not the smaller Na⁺? And why does a child with cystic fibrosis taste salty?


If you push a very fine glass electrode into a cell and compare it with a second electrode in the fluid outside, the voltmeter reads about minus 70 millivolts. The inside is negative. That sounds small, a twentieth of a torch battery. But the membrane is only about 5 nanometres thick. Seventy millivolts across five nanometres is about fourteen million volts per metre, an electric field strong enough to move charged parts of proteins inside the membrane. Look also at the ion concentrations: potassium is about thirty times higher inside, sodium more than ten times higher outside. You saw in the transport lecture that the sodium-potassium pump builds these gradients. Today we connect the gradients to the voltage. Three puzzles guide the lecture. First, where does the voltage come from? Second, a potassium channel lets potassium through ten thousand times better than sodium, although sodium is the smaller ion. How? Third, an old European saying warned that a child who tastes salty when kissed will die young. We now know this is cystic fibrosis, a disease of one chloride channel.

title: Ion channels and membrane potential
section: Channels and transporters: two ways across
text:
Channels and transporters: two ways across
Recap: the bilayer stops ions; the Na⁺/K⁺ pump uses ATP to keep K⁺ high inside and Na⁺ high outside.

A channel is fast because nothing has to change shape for each ion. It can only let ions flow down their electrochemical gradient: passive transport.

In the transport lecture you met transporters. A transporter binds its solute, changes shape, and releases the solute on the other side. It is never open to both sides at the same time, which is why it can couple the movement of one solute to ATP or to another gradient, and pump uphill. The price is speed: each cycle needs a shape change, so a transporter moves a hundred to ten thousand molecules per second. A channel is different. When it is open, it is a water-filled pore through the membrane, and ions stream through one after another, up to a hundred million per second. That is close to the speed of free diffusion. But a channel can never pump: ions only go downhill, from high to low electrochemical potential. Channels have two more properties. They are selective: most let only one kind of ion through, for example potassium, sodium, calcium or chloride. And they are gated: they switch between open and closed, and the cell controls the switch. Rate, selectivity and gating are the three words to remember.

title: Ion channels and membrane potential
section: How do we know? The structure of a K⁺ channel
text:
How do we know? The structure of a K⁺ channel







KcsA, a bacterial K⁺ channel (PDB 1K4C). Two of the four subunits are shown. K⁺ ions (purple) and water (red) sit in the selectivity filter, sites S1–S4.


1998: Roderick MacKinnon’s group solved the first atomic structure of an ion channel by X-ray crystallography: KcsA from the bacterium Streptomyces.
Four identical subunits form a ring around a central pore, like the staves of a barrel.
Most of the pore is wide and lined with water. Only a short part near the outside, the selectivity filter (about 1.2 nm long), is narrow.
The filter is lined by backbone carbonyl oxygens (C=O) of the sequence TVGYG, the same in K⁺ channels from bacteria to humans.
Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2003 (MacKinnon, with Peter Agre for water channels).



For decades, physiologists knew from electrical measurements that potassium channels were very selective and very fast, and they could not explain how both were possible. The answer came from a structure. Roderick MacKinnon chose a simple potassium channel from a soil bacterium, KcsA, because it could be made in large amounts and crystallised. In 1998 his group solved the structure by X-ray crystallography. The image shows two of the four identical subunits; the other two, in front and behind, are removed so you can see into the pore. Each subunit has two long helices that cross the membrane. The four subunits make a ring, and the pore runs down the middle. Most of the pore is wide and full of water. Near the outer end it narrows into the selectivity filter. Here, the protein backbone, not the side chains, points its carbonyl oxygen atoms into the pore. The filter sequence, threonine, valine, glycine, tyrosine, glycine, is conserved in potassium channels of bacteria, plants and humans. You can see four ion sites, with potassium ions and water molecules alternating. MacKinnon shared the 2003 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

title: Ion channels and membrane potential
section: The selectivity filter: why K⁺ passes and Na⁺ does not
text:
The selectivity filter: why K⁺ passes and Na⁺ does not


In water, every ion is wrapped in a shell of water molecules. To enter the narrow filter, the ion must lose its water, which costs energy.
For K⁺ (radius 0.13 nm), the filter’s carbonyl oxygens sit exactly where the water oxygens were: the energy is paid back.
Na⁺ is smaller (0.10 nm). The rigid filter cannot close in on it, so losing water is not paid back. Na⁺ stays out: about 1 in 10 000 ions that pass is Na⁺.


Here is the solution to the puzzle. An ion in water is never naked. Water molecules turn their partly negative oxygen atoms towards a positive ion and hold it tightly. Pulling these water molecules off costs a lot of energy. The selectivity filter is too narrow for an ion with its water shell, so an ion can only enter if it gives up its water. For potassium, the filter offers a perfect replacement. The carbonyl oxygens of the protein backbone are held by the rigid structure at the same distance from the ion as the water oxygens were. The potassium ion trades water oxygens for protein oxygens and hardly notices the change. Sodium is smaller. In water its shell is tighter. In the filter, the oxygens are too far away to touch it, and the filter is too stiff to close in. So for sodium, entering the filter means losing water without getting anything back. That costs too much, and sodium stays out. Speed comes from the same structure: two potassium ions sit in the filter at a time, and they repel each other, so one pushes the next one through.

title: Ion channels and membrane potential
section: Gating: three ways to open a channel
text:
Gating: three ways to open a channel


Voltage-gated: positive charges in a voltage-sensor helix are pulled by the membrane field. When the inside becomes less negative, the sensor moves and opens the gate.
Ligand-gated: a molecule binds and opens the pore. Two acetylcholine molecules open the receptor on a muscle cell; Na⁺ flows in.
Mechanically gated: tension in the membrane opens Piezo, a large three-bladed channel (Nobel Prize 2021, Patapoutian). Piezo2 lets you feel touch.


Most channels are closed most of the time and open only for a few milliseconds when they get a signal. There are three main kinds of signal. Voltage-gated channels have a voltage sensor: a helix that crosses the membrane and carries a positive charge at every third amino acid. At rest, the negative inside pulls these charges inwards. When the membrane depolarises, that is, the inside becomes less negative, the sensor moves outwards and pulls the gate open. Voltage-gated sodium channels in nerve and muscle open this way. Ligand-gated channels open when a molecule binds. The nicotinic acetylcholine receptor at the junction between nerve and muscle is a ring of five subunits; when two acetylcholine molecules bind, the pore opens and lets sodium and potassium through, mostly sodium in. Mechanically gated channels respond to force. The Piezo channels have three long blades that sit in the membrane; when the membrane is stretched, the blades flatten and the central pore opens. Piezo2 in skin nerve endings makes touch possible, and Piezo1 senses blood flow in vessels. You will meet more ligand-gated channels in the signalling lectures.

title: Ion channels and membrane potential
section: Two forces on an ion: the electrochemical gradient
text:
Two forces on an ion: the electrochemical gradient


Concentration: more K⁺ inside than outside pushes K⁺ out.
Voltage: a negative inside pulls positive ions in (and pushes negative ions out).
Together they make the electrochemical gradient. The ion flows until the two forces are equal: the equilibrium potential of that ion.


An ion feels two forces at once. The first is the concentration gradient, which you know from diffusion: potassium is about thirty times more concentrated inside, so potassium ions that find an open channel tend to leave. The second is the electrical force. Potassium is positive, and a negative inside pulls it back. The sum of these two is called the electrochemical gradient. Imagine you open only potassium channels. Potassium starts to flow out. Each ion that leaves takes a positive charge with it and leaves a negative charge behind, so the inside becomes more negative, and the electrical pull back grows. At some voltage the two forces balance. Ions still cross in both directions, but as many go in as come out, so there is no net flow. That voltage is the equilibrium potential of potassium, written E sub K. For potassium it is about minus 90 millivolts. Every ion has its own equilibrium potential, set by its own concentrations. On the next slide we calculate it from Gibbs energy.

title: Ion channels and membrane potential
section: The Nernst equation from ΔG
text:
The Nernst equation from ΔG
You know \Delta G = \Delta G^\circ + RT\ln Q. Move 1 mol of ion from outside to inside:

Same ion on both sides, so \Delta G^\circ = 0 and Q = c_\text{in}/c_\text{out}. Chemical part: \;RT \ln \dfrac{c_\text{in}}{c_\text{out}}
Moving charge z across the membrane potential V = V_\text{in} - V_\text{out} adds electrical work: \;zFV
Total: \quad \Delta G = RT \ln \dfrac{c_\text{in}}{c_\text{out}} + zFV
At equilibrium \Delta G = 0. Solve for V:

E_\text{ion} = \frac{RT}{zF}\,\ln\frac{c_\text{out}}{c_\text{in}}
R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, T = 310 K (37 °C), F = 96 485 C mol⁻¹, so RT/F \approx 26.7 mV. In base-10 logarithm: E \approx \dfrac{61.5\text{ mV}}{z}\,\log_{10}\dfrac{c_\text{out}}{c_\text{in}}: 61.5 mV per tenfold gradient for a +1 ion.

You already know this from chemistry, so we only need three steps. Take one mole of an ion and move it from outside to inside. The chemical part of the Gibbs energy is RT ln Q, where Q is the inside concentration over the outside concentration; delta G zero is zero because the ion is the same chemical on both sides. The new part is electrical. Moving a mole of charge z through a voltage V costs z times F times V, where F, the Faraday constant, is the charge of one mole of electrons, about 96 thousand coulombs. Add the two. If delta G is negative, the ion flows in by itself; if positive, it flows out. At equilibrium, delta G is zero, and solving for V gives the Nernst equation. Notice the shape: the equilibrium potential depends only on the ratio of the concentrations and the charge of the ion. At body temperature RT over F is about 26.7 millivolts. A handy rule: for a singly charged ion, each tenfold concentration difference gives about 61.5 millivolts. The sign of z matters: for chloride, z is minus one, and for calcium, plus two.

section: Nernst with numbers
text:
Nernst with numbers
