E_\text{K} ≈ −89 mV: K⁺ would stop flowing out when the inside is 89 mV negative.
E_\text{Na} ≈ +67 mV: Na⁺ would keep flowing in until the inside is 67 mV positive.
The resting cell (−70 mV) is close to E_\text{K} and far from E_\text{Na}. So at rest K⁺ leaks out slowly, and Na⁺ is pulled in strongly whenever a Na⁺ channel opens.

Typical mammalian values; concentrations differ between cell types.

Let us put in numbers. Potassium: inside 140 millimolar, outside 5. The ratio out over in is 0.036; its natural log is about minus 3.3; times 26.7 gives minus 89 millivolts. Sodium: inside 12, outside 145. The ratio is about 12, the log is 2.5, so plus 67 millivolts. Sodium is in equilibrium only when the inside is strongly positive. Chloride has a negative charge, so we divide by minus one, and E for chloride is about minus 64, close to the resting potential. Calcium has a huge gradient, twenty thousand fold, and a charge of two, which gives about plus 130 millivolts. Now compare each number with the real resting potential, minus 70. The difference between the membrane potential and E tells you the driving force. For potassium the difference is small, so potassium leaks out slowly. For sodium the difference is about 140 millivolts, so the moment a sodium channel opens, sodium rushes in. For calcium the driving force is even bigger. This driving force is the energy store that channels spend. The exact concentrations vary between cells, so treat these as typical values.

title: Ion channels and membrane potential
section: How the resting potential arises
text:
How the resting potential arises


Pump: the Na⁺/K⁺ pump (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in per ATP) builds and keeps the gradients.
Leak: the resting membrane has many open K⁺ leak channels, few open Na⁺ channels. K⁺ leaves; the large negative molecules inside cannot follow.
Charge: the thin layer of extra charge at the membrane is the membrane potential. Concentrations hardly change.


Put the pieces together. Step one: the sodium-potassium pump, from the transport lecture, uses ATP to move three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in. This builds the gradients. The pump itself makes the inside only a few millivolts more negative, because it moves more positive charge out than in, but that is not the main source of the voltage. Step two: the resting membrane contains potassium leak channels, which are open most of the time. Potassium ions flow out down their concentration gradient. Their partners inside, mostly negatively charged proteins, phosphates and other organic molecules, are too large and cannot follow. Step three: every potassium ion that leaves adds one positive charge outside and leaves one negative charge inside. These charges collect in a thin layer on both faces of the membrane, and the voltage builds up until it stops further net potassium loss, close to E K. Surprisingly few ions are needed: in a typical cell, fewer than one potassium ion in ten thousand has to leave. So the voltage changes quickly, but the concentrations stay almost the same.

title: Ion channels and membrane potential
section: The voltage follows the most open channels
text:
The voltage follows the most open channels


At rest the membrane is mostly permeable to K⁺, so the resting potential (about −70 mV) lies close to E_\text{K}, pulled a little towards E_\text{Na} by a small Na⁺ leak.
This weighted average is the Goldman equation. Learn the idea, not the formula: more open channels for an ion = voltage closer to that ion’s E. Try it: the cell battery.
Open many Na⁺ channels, and the voltage swings towards E_\text{Na}. That is the action potential.
Change the K⁺ outside, and the resting potential changes: high blood K⁺ is dangerous for the heart.


If only potassium channels were open, the membrane potential would sit exactly at E K, minus 89. Real resting membranes also let through a little sodium and some chloride. The membrane potential then becomes a kind of weighted average of the equilibrium potentials, where the weights are the permeabilities, that is, how many channels for each ion are open. This is the Goldman equation. We will not use its formula, but the idea is powerful. At rest, potassium dominates, so the resting potential is close to E K, a bit less negative because of the small sodium leak. If the cell suddenly opens many sodium channels, sodium dominates and the voltage swings towards E Na. That is what happens in an action potential, next slide. The same idea explains a clinical fact. If potassium in the blood rises, E K becomes less negative, the resting potential of heart muscle cells moves up, and the heart’s rhythm can fail. Doctors watch blood potassium carefully for this reason. You will meet the heart in detail in the course on organ structure and function.

title: Ion channels and membrane potential
section: The action potential in one slide
text:
The action potential in one slide

An all-or-none spike of about 1 ms: voltage-gated Na⁺ in, then voltage-gated K⁺ out. Na⁺ channel inactivation makes a short refractory period, so the signal only travels forwards along an axon. Only a tiny number of ions move; the pump restores the gradients later.

Nerve and muscle cells use the voltage to send fast signals. Follow the numbers. One: something, for example a synaptic input, makes the membrane less negative. If it reaches the threshold, about minus 55 millivolts, enough voltage-gated sodium channels open to start a positive feedback loop. Two: sodium rushes in, which depolarises the membrane more, which opens more sodium channels. Within half a millisecond the voltage swings to about plus 35, towards E Na. Three: the sodium channels inactivate. A part of the channel on the inside plugs the pore, even though the voltage is still positive. At the same time, slower voltage-gated potassium channels open. Potassium flows out, and the voltage falls. Four: because many potassium channels are still open, the voltage briefly goes below the resting level, towards E K. Inactivated sodium channels cannot reopen until the membrane has been negative for a while, so a second spike cannot start at once. This refractory period makes the spike travel in one direction along an axon. The whole spike moves very few ions. The full neuroscience comes in the course on organ structure and function.

title: Ion channels and membrane potential
section: How do we know? Patch clamp
text:
How do we know? Patch clamp



A glass pipette (left, blue-grey) sealed onto a neuron in a brain slice (hippocampus), seen by DIC microscopy.







Press a polished glass pipette onto a cell and apply gentle suction. The glass seals to the membrane so tightly (gigaseal) that the only current is through channels in the patch under the tip.
Cell-attached recording: the cell stays intact; you measure currents of a few picoamperes.



How could anyone see one channel? Erwin Neher and Bert Sakmann solved this in the late 1970s with patch clamp. You pull a glass tube into a fine pipette with a tip about one micrometre wide, fill it with salt solution and put a wire inside. Under a microscope you press the tip against a cell, as in the photograph, and suck gently. The membrane seals to the glass with an electrical resistance of more than a gigaohm, a billion ohms. Because almost no current can leak around the seal, any current you measure must flow through the few channels in the small patch of membrane under the tip. A sensitive amplifier holds the voltage constant, the clamp, and measures the tiny current. This configuration, with the cell still intact, is called cell-attached. You can also tear the patch off to study the inside face, or break the patch to record from the whole cell, the whole-cell configuration used in most drug tests today. Neher and Sakmann received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1991.

title: Ion channels and membrane potential
section: Watching one protein open and close
text:
Watching one protein open and close

Single-channel recording (inside-out patch) of BK channels, a Ca²⁺-activated K⁺ channel. Dashed lines: 0, 1, 2 or 3 channels open. Each step is the current through one channel.

The current jumps in square steps: a channel is either fully open or closed. No half-open state.
One step of 2 pA = 2 × 10⁻¹² C/s ÷ 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C ≈ 12 million ions per second through one protein.
Open times are random, milliseconds long. Gating signals change the probability of being open, not the size of the step.


This is what patch clamp gives you. The trace shows the current through a patch that contains three potassium channels. The current does not change smoothly. It jumps between fixed levels: zero, one, two or three channels open. Each jump is one protein molecule changing its shape. This was the first time anyone had watched a single protein molecule work, in real time. Let us calculate what a step means. A current of two picoamperes is two times ten to the minus twelve coulombs per second. Divide by the charge of one ion, 1.6 times ten to the minus nineteen coulombs, and you get about twelve million ions per second through one channel, the high rate we promised on the channel slide. Notice also that each channel opens and closes at random. A gating signal, such as voltage or a ligand, does not open a channel halfway. It changes the probability that the channel is open. When you record from a whole cell with thousands of channels, these random steps add up to the smooth currents seen in textbooks. Drug companies use automated patch clamp to test thousands of compounds on channels.

title: Ion channels and membrane potential
section: Channels in non-excitable cells: CFTR moves salt and water
text:
Channels in non-excitable cells: CFTR moves salt and water




CFTR is a Cl⁻ channel in the apical (top) membrane of epithelia: airways, gut, pancreas, sweat glands. It opens when phosphorylated by protein kinase A and when it binds ATP.
Cells cannot pump water. They secrete salt (Cl⁻ through CFTR, Na⁺ between the cells), and water follows by osmosis. This keeps the airway surface wet, so cilia can clear mucus.







Human CFTR, cryo-EM (PDB 5UAK).


Channels are not only for nerves. Here is one in an epithelium, a sheet of cells that lines the airways, gut and glands. The airway surface is covered by a thin liquid layer, with mucus on top. Cilia beat in the liquid and move the mucus, with trapped dust and bacteria, up and out of the lungs. Cells cannot pump water directly. Instead they move salt, and water follows by osmosis, partly through water channels. The key protein is CFTR, a chloride channel in the apical membrane, the side that faces the airway. When the cell is stimulated, protein kinase A phosphorylates CFTR, ATP binds, and the channel opens. Chloride flows out into the airway, down its electrochemical gradient. Sodium follows between the cells, attracted by the negative charge, and water follows the salt. The structure on the right, solved by cryo-EM, shows the two membrane domains on top and the two ATP-binding domains below, in the cytosol. CFTR belongs to the family of ABC transporters, but it evolved into a channel. In cystic fibrosis, this channel is missing or broken, the liquid layer dries out, and mucus becomes thick.

title: Ion channels and membrane potential
section: Ca²⁺ channels: making a signal
text:
Ca²⁺ channels: making a signal


Pumps keep cytosolic Ca²⁺ 10 000 times lower than outside and in the ER. Opening a few Ca²⁺ channels therefore makes a large, fast rise.
Ca²⁺ binds proteins that change shape and act: neurotransmitter release, muscle contraction, insulin secretion, gene expression.
Channels in the plasma membrane (voltage- or ligand-gated) and in the ER membrane (opened by second messengers). More in the signalling lectures.


Calcium is special. Cells keep free calcium in the cytosol extremely low, about 100 nanomolar, while outside the cell and inside the ER lumen it is around a millimolar or more: a gradient of ten thousand times. Pumps in the plasma membrane and in the ER membrane work all the time to keep it so. Because the resting level is so low, opening even a few calcium channels raises cytosolic calcium ten- or a hundred-fold within milliseconds. Calcium then binds proteins such as calmodulin or synaptotagmin, which change shape and switch on a process. In a nerve terminal, voltage-gated calcium channels open when the action potential arrives, and calcium triggers the release of neurotransmitter. In muscle, calcium triggers contraction. In pancreatic beta cells, it triggers insulin secretion. Calcium can also be released from the ER through channels that open when a second messenger binds. So here a channel is not used to make a voltage, but to make a chemical signal. You will meet these pathways again in the signalling lectures and in the lecture comparing organelles. Calcium-channel blockers are common drugs for high blood pressure.

title: Ion channels and membrane potential
section: Why it matters: cystic fibrosis and drugs matched to the defect
text:
Why it matters: cystic fibrosis and drugs matched to the defect




Cystic fibrosis: both copies of the CFTR gene mutated. Thick mucus, lung infections, blocked pancreas.
F508del: one amino acid missing; CFTR misfolds in the ER and is degraded (the ER lecture). Carried by about 9 in 10 patients.



G551D: CFTR reaches the surface, but the gate does not open.
Elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (one combination, approved 2019): two correctors plus a potentiator. Lung function improves markedly.



Cystic fibrosis is one of the most common severe inherited diseases in people of European descent. It is recessive: both copies of the CFTR gene carry a mutation. Without working CFTR, the airway liquid layer becomes thin, mucus is thick and sticky, and bacteria grow in the lungs; the pancreas ducts also block. More than two thousand mutations are known, but they fall into a few types of molecular defect, and that is the key to treatment. The most common, F508del, deletes one phenylalanine. The protein folds badly in the ER, quality control recognises it, and it is degraded, so almost none reaches the surface. You will learn this quality control in the ER lecture. Drugs called correctors, such as elexacaftor and tezacaftor, bind the protein while it folds and help it reach the membrane. Another mutation, G551D, gives a protein that reaches the membrane but rarely opens. A potentiator, ivacaftor, binds CFTR and holds the gate open longer. Since F508del protein that reaches the surface also gates poorly, the combination of two correctors and a potentiator works for most patients. You will meet drug development like this in Kliniska prövningar och läkemedelsutveckling.

title: Ion channels and membrane potential
section: Why it matters: salty sweat, and blocking Na⁺ channels
text:
Why it matters: salty sweat, and blocking Na⁺ channels




Lidocaine (local anaesthetic, dentist) crosses the membrane, then blocks the Na⁺ channel pore from inside. No action potentials in pain fibres.
Tetrodotoxin from pufferfish plugs the outer mouth. It blocks all nerve signals: deadly.







Sweat test: Cl⁻ in sweat ≥ 60 mmol/L means cystic fibrosis.





Pufferfish (Takifugu). Its toxin is made by bacteria.


Two more examples link this lecture to the clinic. First, the sweat test. In the sweat gland duct, CFTR normally takes chloride back from the sweat into the body, and sodium follows, so sweat on the skin is only a little salty. Without CFTR the salt stays in the sweat. A sweat test collects sweat from the arm, and a chloride level of 60 millimoles per litre or more indicates cystic fibrosis; this is the old saying about the salty kiss. Second, sodium channels as drug targets. If voltage-gated sodium channels cannot open, no action potential can start. Lidocaine, the local anaesthetic used by dentists, crosses the membrane in its uncharged form, becomes charged inside the cell and binds inside the pore. It binds best to channels that open often, so active pain fibres are blocked first. Tetrodotoxin, from the pufferfish, is a toxin that plugs the outer mouth of the sodium channel. A tiny amount stops nerve signals to the breathing muscles. Disease mechanisms like these return in Sjukdomslära, and the development of channel drugs in Kliniska prövningar och läkemedelsutveckling.

title: Ion channels and membrane potential
section: Summary
text:
Summary

Channels are open pores: fast (up to 10⁸ ions/s), selective and gated (voltage, ligand, mechanical force). Transporters are slower but can pump.
The K⁺ channel filter selects K⁺ over the smaller Na⁺ because its carbonyl oxygens replace the water shell of K⁺ exactly, but not of Na⁺.
Each ion has an equilibrium potential from \Delta G = RT\ln(c_\text{in}/c_\text{out}) + zFV = 0: the Nernst equation. E_\text{K} ≈ −89 mV, E_\text{Na} ≈ +67 mV.
The resting potential (≈ −70 mV) comes from the pump’s gradients plus open K⁺ leak channels, so it lies near E_\text{K}. Opening Na⁺ channels gives the action potential. Patch clamp shows single channels opening and closing.
Channels work in all cells: CFTR drives salt and water secretion, Ca²⁺ channels make signals. Drugs match the defect: CFTR correctors and potentiators, lidocaine on Na⁺ channels.

Read more (optional): Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell, 7th ed., ch. 11.
Image credits

Five take-home points. First, channels are pores that let ions flow down their electrochemical gradient, very fast, and they are selective and gated; transporters are slower but can couple to energy and pump. Second, selectivity comes from structure: the potassium channel filter replaces the water around a potassium ion with protein oxygens at exactly the right distance, which does not work for the smaller sodium ion. Third, the Nernst equation is just Gibbs energy with an electrical term; set delta G to zero and you get the equilibrium potential, which you should be able to calculate. Fourth, the resting potential arises because the pump makes the gradients and the resting membrane is mainly permeable to potassium; when sodium channels open, the voltage swings towards E Na, which is the action potential. Patch clamp lets us record a single channel. Fifth, all cells use channels: CFTR for salt and water secretion, calcium channels for signals. Knowing the exact molecular defect lets us choose the drug. Next we leave the plasma membrane and follow proteins into the compartments of the cell.

title: Quiz: G-protein-coupled receptors and second messengers
text:
Short questions to check your understanding of the lecture G-protein-coupled receptors and second messengers. Try each on paper first, then open the hint or the answer. The tag after each question shows the learning outcome (ELO) it practises.

Q1. Adrenaline never enters a liver cell, yet it changes the cell’s metabolism within seconds. What crosses the membrane: the hormone, an ion, or something else? [ELO 3]






Hint





Think about what the receptor protein does when the hormone binds on the outside.









Answer





Nothing crosses. The receptor is a seven-helix membrane protein. Hormone binding outside changes the shape of the helix bundle, which opens a pocket on the cytosolic face. The G protein binds there and is activated. The information crosses the membrane as a change in protein shape.




Q2. What exactly does an active GPCR do to the G protein? Why is it called a GEF? [ELO 3]






Hint





Does the receptor add a phosphate to GDP?









Answer





It opens Gα’s nucleotide pocket so that GDP leaves; GTP, which is about ten times more abundant in the cytosol, then binds. The receptor only catalyses the exchange of guanine nucleotides: a guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF). It does not phosphorylate anything, and after release of Gα–GTP it can activate the next G protein.




Q3. Match each Gα type to its main effect: Gs, Gi, Gq. Effects: (a) activates phospholipase C-β; (b) inhibits adenylyl cyclase; (c) activates adenylyl cyclase. [ELO 3]






Hint





s = stimulatory, i = inhibitory.









Answer





Gs → (c): more cAMP. Gi → (b): less cAMP (its βγ also opens K⁺ channels). Gq → (a): PLC-β cuts PIP₂ into IP₃ and DAG; IP₃ releases Ca²⁺ from the ER.




Q4. How does cAMP activate protein kinase A? How many cAMP molecules are needed to release one catalytic subunit? [ELO 3]






Hint





PKA is R₂C₂. Each R subunit binds two cAMP.









Answer





The regulatory (R) subunits block the catalytic (C) subunits. Four cAMP bind the two R subunits, which change shape and release the two C subunits as active kinases. So two cAMP per C subunit: this step does not amplify. The amplification is at enzyme steps: the receptor, adenylyl cyclase, and the kinases.




Q5. Phospholipase C-β cuts PIP₂ into two products. Name them, say where each goes, and what each does. [ELO 3]






Hint





One product is water-soluble, the other is a lipid.









Answer





IP₃ is water-soluble: it diffuses through the cytosol and opens the IP₃ receptor, a Ca²⁺ channel in the ER membrane, so cytosolic Ca²⁺ rises from about 100 nM to about 1 µM. DAG is a lipid and stays in the plasma membrane, where it activates protein kinase C together with Ca²⁺.




Q6. List four ways the cAMP pathway is switched off after adrenaline has gone. [ELO 3]






Hint





One off-switch for each active molecule: receptor, Gα, cAMP, phosphorylated proteins.









Answer






The hormone dissociates and is removed; active receptors are also phosphorylated by GRK and bound by arrestin (desensitisation) and taken in by endocytosis. (2) Gα hydrolyses GTP to GDP and rejoins βγ. (3) Phosphodiesterases turn cAMP into AMP. (4) Protein phosphatases remove the phosphates that PKA added.





Q7. Cholera toxin modifies Gαs so it cannot hydrolyse GTP. Why does this cause watery diarrhoea? [ELO 3] [ELO 9]






Hint





Follow the chain: Gαs → cAMP → PKA → which chloride channel?









Answer





Once Gαs is switched on, it stays on. Adenylyl cyclase keeps making cAMP, PKA stays active and keeps the CFTR Cl⁻ channel open in the apical membrane of gut cells. Cl⁻ flows into the gut, Na⁺ follows, and water follows by osmosis: litres of fluid are lost. Oral rehydration (salt + glucose, absorbed by SGLT) replaces it.




Q8. Metoprolol is a β-blocker. Is it an agonist or an antagonist? What happens to cAMP in heart muscle cells when adrenaline is present? [ELO 3] [ELO 9]






Hint





It binds the same pocket as adrenaline.









Answer





A competitive antagonist: it occupies the β₁ receptor without activating it, so fewer receptors are bound by adrenaline. Less Gs is activated, cAMP and PKA activity stay lower, and the heart beats more slowly and with less force. Because it is competitive, very high adrenaline levels can partly overcome the block.

title: G-protein-coupled receptors and second messengers
section: About this lecture

title: G-protein-coupled receptors and second messengers
section: The question: one hormone, many effects, all from outside
text:
The question: one hormone, many effects, all from outside


Fright or exercise: the adrenal gland releases adrenaline (epinephrine) into the blood. Within seconds the heart beats faster and the liver releases glucose.
Adrenaline is water-soluble: it cannot cross the membrane. It binds a receptor on the outside.
How does the signal cross the membrane? Why is the response so large and so fast, and how does it stop? And why does cholera, a gut infection, cause litres of watery diarrhoea?


Imagine you are startled. Your adrenal glands release adrenaline into the blood. Within seconds your heart beats faster and harder, and your liver breaks down its glycogen store and releases glucose into the blood, fuel for your muscles. Adrenaline is a small, charged, water-soluble molecule. It cannot cross the lipid bilayer, so it never enters the liver cell. It binds a receptor protein on the outer surface, and the message must cross the membrane by a change in the shape of that protein. The numbers are striking. Adrenaline in the blood is in the nanomolar range, yet a liver cell can release millions of glucose molecules per second. So the signal must be amplified on the way. And when the danger has passed, the response must stop within minutes, so the signal must also be switched off. Keep the fourth puzzle in mind: cholera bacteria in the gut make a toxin that hijacks exactly this machinery. We solve it at the end of the lecture.

title: G-protein-coupled receptors and second messengers
section: GPCRs: seven helices across the membrane
text:
GPCRs: seven helices across the membrane




One protein chain crosses the membrane seven times (7TM). N-terminus outside, C-terminus inside. Drawn unrolled here; in reality the helices form a bundle.
The ligand binds outside or in a pocket between the helices; the G protein binds the cytosolic face.
About 800 human GPCRs: receptors for hormones, neurotransmitters, light (rhodopsin), smell and taste (about half are odorant receptors).







β₂-adrenergic receptor (gold) bound to its G protein (green, blue, purple), from X-ray crystallography (PDB 3SN6).


All GPCRs share one architecture. A single polypeptide chain crosses the membrane seven times as alpha helices, so they are also called seven-transmembrane receptors. The N-terminus is outside the cell, the C-terminus inside. The diagram unrolls the chain so you can count the helices; in the real protein the seven helices pack into a barrel-like bundle. Small ligands such as adrenaline bind in a pocket between the helices, reached from the outside; large protein hormones bind to the outer loops and the N-terminus. The cytosolic face, with its loops and the C-terminal tail, binds the G protein. The image on the right is a real structure: the beta-2 adrenergic receptor in gold, in complex with its G protein, solved by X-ray crystallography. The human genome encodes about 800 GPCRs. About half of them are odorant receptors in the nose. Others detect light in the eye, taste, hormones and neurotransmitters. One family, one design, hundreds of signals.

title: G-protein-coupled receptors and second messengers
section: Activation: the receptor swaps GDP for GTP
text:
Activation: the receptor swaps GDP for GTP


Agonist binding shifts the helices: helix 6 swings outwards (about 1.4 nm in the β₂ receptor), opening a pocket on the cytosolic side.
The Gα subunit’s C-terminal helix inserts into that pocket. This pulls open Gα’s nucleotide site: GDP leaves, and GTP (10 × more abundant in the cytosol) enters.
So the active receptor is a GEF (guanine nucleotide exchange factor) for the G protein. It then lets go and activates the next one.


How does binding outside change anything inside? The receptor is not rigid. When an agonist binds in the pocket between the helices, it stabilises a slightly different arrangement of the bundle. The largest movement is on the cytosolic side: helix 6 swings outwards, by about 1.4 nanometres in the beta-2 receptor, and a cavity opens. The G protein’s alpha subunit fits into this cavity with its C-terminal helix. This contact is transmitted through Gα to its nucleotide-binding site, which opens. GDP falls out. In the cytosol GTP is about ten times more abundant than GDP, so GTP binds next, and Gα closes around it in its active shape. In the language of the principles lecture, the receptor acts as a guanine nucleotide exchange factor, a GEF. Note what the receptor does not do: it does not add the phosphate, it only lets GDP out. Once Gα holds GTP, it lets go of the receptor, and the receptor, still bound to its hormone, can activate another G protein.

title: G-protein-coupled receptors and second messengers
section: The trimeric G protein is a switch with a timer
text:
The trimeric G protein is a switch with a timer


Three subunits: Gα (binds GDP or GTP) and the tight pair Gβγ. Both are anchored to the membrane by lipid tails.
With GTP, Gα separates from βγ: both halves can switch on targets.
Gα is itself a slow GTPase: after seconds to minutes it hydrolyses GTP and switches off. RGS proteins speed this up for many G proteins.


The G protein has three subunits, alpha, beta and gamma, which is why it is called trimeric or heterotrimeric. Beta and gamma never separate, so we treat them as one unit, βγ. Both Gα and βγ carry lipid anchors, so the whole cycle happens on the inner surface of the plasma membrane. At rest, Gα holds GDP and sits with βγ. An active receptor exchanges GDP for GTP. Gα with GTP changes shape and leaves βγ. Now both halves are free to bind target proteins in the membrane: enzymes or ion channels. Here is the clever part. Gα is an enzyme that slowly hydrolyses its own GTP to GDP and phosphate. This is a built-in timer. For Gs, the GTP lasts on average ten to twenty seconds. Then Gα–GDP rebinds βγ, and the switch is off. Proteins called RGS proteins, regulators of G-protein signalling, act as GTPase-activating proteins and can make the timer much faster. Remember from the principles lecture: a GTPase switch is on with GTP and off with GDP. This is the same idea.

title: G-protein-coupled receptors and second messengers
section: Three main kinds of G protein: Gs, Gi, Gq
text:
Three main kinds of G protein: Gs, Gi, Gq


The receptor decides which G protein is used; the Gα type decides the effect. The same hormone can act through different receptors: adrenaline uses β (Gs), α₂ (Gi) and α₁ (Gq) receptors.
Simplified: there are more Gα types (e.g. G₁₂/₁₃, and transducin in the eye), and βγ has its own targets.


Humans have sixteen genes for Gα, but three families do most of the work we need. Gs, s for stimulatory, activates adenylyl cyclase, the enzyme that makes cyclic AMP. Gi, i for inhibitory, inhibits adenylyl cyclase, so cyclic AMP falls; in neurons and the heart its βγ subunits also open potassium channels, which makes the cell harder to excite. Gq activates a different enzyme, phospholipase C beta, which makes two messengers, IP₃ and diacylglycerol, and leads to a rise in cytosolic calcium. Which G protein a cell uses depends on the receptor. That is why one hormone can have opposite effects in different tissues. Adrenaline acting on beta receptors in the heart uses Gs and makes the heart beat harder. The same adrenaline acting on alpha-1 receptors in the smooth muscle of skin blood vessels uses Gq and constricts the vessel. This is a simplified map: there are more Gα families, for example transducin in the retina, and βγ has its own targets. But Gs, Gi and Gq will carry us through this lecture.

title: G-protein-coupled receptors and second messengers
section: The cAMP pathway: adenylyl cyclase, cAMP and PKA
text:
The cAMP pathway: adenylyl cyclase, cAMP and PKA


Adenylyl cyclase (in the plasma membrane) turns ATP into cyclic AMP. Phosphodiesterases (PDEs) turn cAMP into AMP. Resting cAMP is low (about 0.1 µM), stimulated several µM.
PKA (protein kinase A) is held inactive by its regulatory (R) subunits. Four cAMP bind the R subunits, and two catalytic (C) subunits are released.
Free C phosphorylates Ser/Thr on target proteins: fast effects on enzymes and channels (seconds), slow effects on genes via CREB (hours).


Here is the Gs pathway in detail. Active Gαs binds adenylyl cyclase, a large enzyme in the plasma membrane, and switches it on. Adenylyl cyclase converts ATP into cyclic AMP, a small, water-soluble molecule that diffuses through the cytosol. This is the second messenger: the hormone was the first messenger. Cyclic AMP is destroyed by phosphodiesterases, which open the ring to give plain AMP. The balance between cyclase and phosphodiesterase sets the cAMP level, and the phosphodiesterases also make sure cAMP falls quickly when the cyclase stops. The main target of cAMP is protein kinase A. PKA is a complex of two regulatory and two catalytic subunits. The regulatory subunits block the active sites. Each regulatory subunit binds two cAMP molecules, so four in total; the regulatory subunits change shape and release the two catalytic subunits, which are now active kinases. They phosphorylate serines and threonines on many proteins. Some effects are fast, like switching on enzymes for glycogen breakdown, or opening CFTR, which you met in the ion-channel lecture. Others are slow: PKA enters the nucleus and phosphorylates the transcription factor CREB, which switches on genes over hours.

title: G-protein-coupled receptors and second messengers
section: Amplification: from one hormone to thousands of molecules
text:
Amplification: from one hormone to thousands of molecules


Gain comes from steps where one active molecule acts on many: the receptor (one G protein after another), adenylyl cyclase, the kinases and the enzymes they switch on.
Binding steps do not amplify: four cAMP free two C subunits of PKA.
In the liver, the glycogen cascade has two more kinase steps after PKA, so a few hormone molecules can release millions of glucose molecules.


Let us count. One hormone molecule keeps one receptor active for as long as it stays bound. While active, the receptor catalyses GDP–GTP exchange on one G protein after another, so it switches on several to many G proteins: with the numbers in our demo model, about eight at a time. Each active Gαs switches on one adenylyl cyclase, which is an enzyme that makes many cAMP molecules per second. That is the largest gain in this cascade. The next step looks like a loss: four cAMP molecules are needed to release two catalytic subunits of PKA. Binding does not amplify; only catalysis does. But each PKA catalytic subunit is an enzyme. In the liver, PKA phosphorylates phosphorylase kinase, which phosphorylates glycogen phosphorylase, which cuts glucose units off glycogen, so each step multiplies again. The exact numbers depend on the cell and are illustrative here. The principle is not: enzymes in series multiply the signal, so a nanomolar hormone can move the metabolism of a whole organ. Amplification also has a price: a cascade that amplifies must be switched off at every step.

title: G-protein-coupled receptors and second messengers
section: Gq: IP₃ releases Ca²⁺, DAG recruits PKC
text:
Gq: IP₃ releases Ca²⁺, DAG recruits PKC


Phospholipase C-β cuts the membrane lipid PIP₂ into IP₃ (soluble) and DAG (stays in the membrane).
IP₃ opens the IP₃ receptor, a Ca²⁺ channel in the ER. Cytosolic Ca²⁺ rises from about 100 nM to about 1 µM.
PKC (protein kinase C) moves to the membrane when Ca²⁺ rises and becomes active when it also binds DAG.


Now the Gq branch. Active Gαq switches on phospholipase C beta. Its substrate is a minor membrane lipid, phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate, PIP₂ for short, which has a sugar-phosphate head group in the inner leaflet. Phospholipase C cuts PIP₂ into two messengers at once. The head group, inositol trisphosphate or IP₃, is water-soluble and diffuses into the cytosol. The rest, diacylglycerol or DAG, is a lipid and stays in the membrane. IP₃ binds the IP₃ receptor, a calcium channel in the ER membrane. You know from the ion-channel lecture that cytosolic calcium is kept at about 100 nanomolar, ten thousand times lower than in the ER. So when the channels open, calcium floods out and the cytosolic level rises roughly tenfold within a second. Calcium and DAG then work together. Protein kinase C binds calcium, moves to the membrane, and becomes fully active when it also binds DAG there. This is a coincidence detector: both messengers are needed. Calcium has many other targets, and the most important is calmodulin, on the next slide.

title: G-protein-coupled receptors and second messengers
section: Ca²⁺ acts through calmodulin
text:
Ca²⁺ acts through calmodulin







Calmodulin with four Ca²⁺ ions (black spheres), wrapped around a helix of its target, myosin light-chain kinase.


Calmodulin is a small, abundant protein with four Ca²⁺ binding sites. They fill when Ca²⁺ rises towards 1 µM.
With Ca²⁺ bound, calmodulin wraps around a helix of its target and switches it on:

CaM-kinase II: a kinase in neurons (memory);
myosin light-chain kinase: smooth muscle contraction;
adenylyl cyclases and phosphodiesterases: cross-talk with cAMP.

Ca²⁺ signals often come as spikes or oscillations: the cell can code strength in their frequency.
Pumps (SERCA in the ER, PMCA in the plasma membrane) bring Ca²⁺ back to 100 nM.



Calcium itself does nothing until it binds a protein. The main calcium sensor in every eukaryotic cell is calmodulin, a small protein of about 150 amino acids with four calcium-binding sites. These sites have an affinity in the micromolar range, so at resting calcium they are mostly empty, and when calcium rises towards one micromolar they fill. Calcium-bound calmodulin changes shape, exposing sticky hydrophobic surfaces, and wraps around a helix in its target protein, as you see in the structure, where calmodulin grips a peptide from myosin light-chain kinase. That kinase then phosphorylates myosin in smooth muscle, and the muscle contracts. Another target, calcium-calmodulin-dependent kinase II, is abundant in synapses and is important for memory. Calmodulin also regulates some adenylyl cyclases and phosphodiesterases, so the calcium and cAMP pathways talk to each other. Calcium signals are often brief spikes, repeated as oscillations, and cells can read the frequency. Pumps in the ER and plasma membrane, which you met in the transport lectures, constantly return calcium to 100 nanomolar and end each spike.

title: G-protein-coupled receptors and second messengers
section: How do we know? Finding and seeing the receptor
text:
How do we know? Finding and seeing the receptor



1970s: Robert Lefkowitz used radioactive ligands to show that receptors are real, countable proteins in the membrane, and purified the β-adrenergic receptor.
1986: his group, with Brian Kobilka, cloned the gene. Its sequence showed seven hydrophobic helices, like rhodopsin, the light receptor: one family for hormones and light.
2007–2011: Kobilka’s group solved the crystal structure of the β₂ receptor, and then of the receptor caught in the act of activating Gs (PDB 3SN6, the structure two slides back).
Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2012. Today cryo-EM gives new GPCR–G protein structures every week, and drugs are designed against them.



Brian Kobilka (left) and Robert Lefkowitz at the Nobel Prize ceremony in Stockholm, December 2012.


For a long time receptors were an abstract idea: something on the cell that a drug must bind. Robert Lefkowitz made them concrete. In the 1970s his group labelled adrenaline-like drugs with radioactive isotopes and measured how much bound to membranes: a saturable number of high-affinity sites, which they could count and purify. Then, in 1986, Lefkowitz’s group, with Brian Kobilka as a young researcher, cloned the gene for the beta-2 adrenergic receptor. The sequence was a surprise: seven stretches of hydrophobic amino acids, just like rhodopsin, the light receptor of the eye. This showed that hormone receptors and light receptors belong to one family. Kobilka then spent twenty years trying to crystallise the receptor, which is floppy and unstable outside the membrane. In 2007 his group solved its structure, and in 2011 they caught the receptor bound to its G protein in the active state, the structure you saw earlier. Lefkowitz and Kobilka shared the 2012 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Today cryo-electron microscopy produces such structures routinely, and they guide drug design.

title: G-protein-coupled receptors and second messengers
section: How do we know? Watching second messengers live
text:
How do we know? Watching second messengers live





Retinal glial cells loaded with the Ca²⁺ dye fura-2: before ATP, a few seconds after adding ATP (which acts on a Gq-coupled receptor), and later. Blue = low Ca²⁺, red = high.



Ca²⁺ imaging: a dye (fura-2) or a genetically encoded sensor (GCaMP: GFP + calmodulin) gets brighter or changes colour when it binds Ca²⁺.
FRET sensor for cAMP (right): cAMP opens the sensor, so less energy passes from CFP to YFP; the blue/yellow ratio reads cAMP.





How do we know that calcium rises, and how fast, in a living cell? We make it visible. The images at the top show glial cells from the retina loaded with fura-2, a fluorescent dye that changes its excitation spectrum when it binds calcium; the colours show the calcium level, blue low and red high. Before stimulation the cells are blue. A few seconds after ATP is added, which acts on P2Y receptors that couple to Gq, many cells turn green to red, and the signal then fades as pumps clear the calcium. Today we often use genetically encoded sensors such as GCaMP, a fusion of GFP and calmodulin that becomes brighter when calcium binds, so we can image calcium in a specific cell type in a living animal. For cAMP we use FRET sensors, shown bottom right. A cAMP-binding domain, here from the protein Epac, sits between two fluorescent proteins, CFP and YFP. Without cAMP they are close: light absorbed by CFP is passed to YFP by FRET, and the sensor glows yellow. When cAMP binds, the sensor opens, FRET drops and more blue light comes out. The blue-to-yellow ratio reads cAMP in real time.

title: G-protein-coupled receptors and second messengers
section: Switching off: every step has its own off-switch
text:
Switching off: every step has its own off-switch


A signal is only useful if it ends. Each active state decays on its own: GTP hydrolysis in Gα, PDE for cAMP, phosphatases for the phosphorylated targets, pumps for Ca²⁺.
The signal lasts as long as the slowest off-step allows. Block one off-switch and the signal outlasts the hormone.
This is why the PDE inhibitors caffeine and theophylline raise cAMP (theophylline was used for asthma).


We have built a powerful amplifier. Now we need the brakes. A signal that cannot end carries no information about time: the cell must know not only that adrenaline came, but also that it has gone. Every step of the cascade has its own way back. The hormone is removed from the blood, taken up or broken down. Gα hydrolyses its GTP. Phosphodiesterases destroy cyclic AMP. Protein phosphatases remove the phosphates that PKA added. In the calcium branch, pumps in the ER and plasma membrane return calcium to 100 nanomolar, IP₃ is dephosphorylated, and DAG is converted to other lipids. Because these steps are in series, the signal can last only as long as the slowest of them allows. If you slow down one off-switch, the signal outlasts the hormone. Methylxanthines such as caffeine and theophylline inhibit phosphodiesterases. At the doses in coffee, caffeine acts mainly on adenosine receptors, another GPCR, but at higher doses PDE inhibition raises cAMP; theophylline was used to relax airway smooth muscle in asthma. Next: the receptor’s own off-switch.

title: G-protein-coupled receptors and second messengers
section: Desensitisation: GRK, arrestin and endocytosis
text:
Desensitisation: GRK, arrestin and endocytosis


GRK (G-protein-coupled receptor kinase) phosphorylates only active receptors on their tail. Arrestin binds the phosphorylated tail and blocks G-protein coupling: the receptor is desensitised, even with hormone bound.
Arrestin is also an adaptor for clathrin: the receptor is taken into the cell by endocytosis (the endocytosis lecture). In the endosome it is recycled (resensitised) or sent to the lysosome (fewer receptors).
Result: under constant hormone the response fades (minutes), and with long drug use tolerance develops.


The receptor has an off-switch of its own, and it acts only on receptors that are in use. G-protein-coupled receptor kinases, GRKs, recognise the active shape of the receptor and phosphorylate serines and threonines on its cytosolic tail. The phosphorylated tail is bound by arrestin. Arrestin sits on the same cytosolic face that the G protein needs, so the receptor can no longer activate G proteins, even though the hormone is still bound. This is desensitisation, and it takes seconds to minutes. Arrestin does more: it also binds clathrin and its adaptor, so the receptor is collected into a clathrin-coated pit and taken into the cell by endocytosis, which you will meet in detail in the endocytosis lecture. In the endosome the hormone dissociates, the phosphates are removed, and the receptor is either recycled to the surface, ready to signal again, or sent to the lysosome and degraded. Repeated or constant stimulation therefore reduces the number of receptors on the surface. This is one cause of drug tolerance: patients need higher doses of some drugs, such as opioids, to get the same effect.

title: G-protein-coupled receptors and second messengers
section: The off-rates set the shape of the signal
text:
The off-rates set the shape of the signal


Left: a 1-minute hormone pulse. A slow GTPase or a PDE inhibitor makes cAMP rise higher and last longer after the hormone has gone.
Right: 5 minutes of hormone. With GRK + arrestin, cAMP peaks and then falls although the hormone is still there.
Curves from a simple model with illustrative numbers. Try it: Demo: GPCR cascade


Here is what the off-switches do to the time course of cAMP, computed with the simple model in the demo for this lecture. On the left, the hormone is present for one minute, shaded blue. In the normal cell, black, cAMP rises within about twenty seconds, stays up while the hormone is there, and falls back within a minute after it has gone. If Gα hydrolyses its GTP five times more slowly, orange, active Gα accumulates: cAMP rises higher and stays up long after the hormone has gone. If a drug inhibits the phosphodiesterase, dashed, cAMP rises much higher and also falls more slowly. On the right, the hormone stays for five minutes. Without arrestin, dashed grey, cAMP rises to a plateau and stays there as long as the hormone is present. With GRK and arrestin, purple, cAMP peaks and then falls, although the hormone is still present: the receptors are being desensitised. The cell responds to a change in hormone more than to a constant level. These are illustrative numbers, not data, but the shapes are what experiments show. In the demo you can change each rate yourself.

title: G-protein-coupled receptors and second messengers
section: Why it matters: cholera toxin locks Gs on
text:
Why it matters: cholera toxin locks Gs on





Vibrio cholerae, electron microscope (negative stain).


Cholera toxin attaches ADP-ribose to Gαs, which then cannot hydrolyse GTP: Gs stays on, cAMP stays high in gut cells. PKA opens CFTR; Cl⁻, Na⁺ and water pour into the gut: several litres a day.
Treatment: oral rehydration (water + salt + glucose), which uses the SGLT Na⁺–glucose symporter that cholera leaves intact.


Now the puzzle from the start. Vibrio cholerae lives in contaminated water. In the small intestine it makes cholera toxin, a protein with one A subunit and a ring of five B subunits. The B ring binds a ganglioside on the gut cell surface, the toxin is taken into the cell, and part of the A subunit reaches the cytosol. There it is an enzyme: it transfers an ADP-ribose group from NAD onto Gαs. Modified Gαs can still bind GTP, but it can no longer hydrolyse it. The timer is broken, so every Gαs that is switched on stays on. Adenylyl cyclase runs continuously, cAMP stays high, and PKA keeps CFTR, the chloride channel from the ion-channel lecture, open. Chloride flows into the gut, sodium and water follow, and the patient loses several litres of fluid a day. Without treatment, dehydration can kill within a day. The treatment is simple and cheap: oral rehydration solution. It works because the SGLT sodium–glucose symporter from the transport lecture still works, and water follows the absorbed salt and sugar. Pertussis toxin, from the whooping-cough bacterium, modifies Gαi instead: its receptors can no longer activate it, so the brake on cyclase is lost.

title: G-protein-coupled receptors and second messengers
section: Why it matters: three drug classes acting on GPCRs
text:
Why it matters: three drug classes acting on GPCRs


About one third of approved drugs act on GPCRs. β-blockers are antagonists: they occupy the receptor without activating it. Opioids and GLP-1 drugs are agonists.
Semaglutide is GLP-1 made long-lasting: natural GLP-1 lasts minutes; semaglutide resists breakdown and binds albumin, so one injection lasts a week.
You meet these drugs again in Organs struktur och funktion (heart, pancreas) and Kliniska prövningar och läkemedelsutveckling.


Three drug classes show the range. Beta-blockers such as metoprolol are antagonists at beta-1 adrenergic receptors in the heart. They bind the pocket but do not activate the receptor, so adrenaline cannot act; Gs, cAMP and PKA stay lower, the heart beats more slowly and less forcefully, and blood pressure falls. They are used for high blood pressure, angina, heart failure and after heart attacks. Opioids such as morphine and fentanyl are agonists at the mu-opioid receptor, which couples to Gi. In pain-signalling neurons, Gαi lowers cAMP, and βγ opens potassium channels and closes calcium channels at the nerve terminal, so less transmitter is released and less pain signal reaches the brain. The same receptors in the brainstem slow breathing, which makes overdoses deadly, and desensitisation contributes to tolerance. Semaglutide is an agonist at the GLP-1 receptor, a Gs-coupled receptor on pancreatic beta cells. Extra cAMP increases insulin release only when glucose is high, so the risk of low blood sugar is small. It also acts in the brain to reduce appetite. Natural GLP-1 is destroyed within minutes; semaglutide carries an amino-acid change and a fatty-acid chain that binds albumin, so it lasts about a week.

title: G-protein-coupled receptors and second messengers
section: Summary
text:
Summary

GPCRs have seven transmembrane helices. An agonist shifts the helices; the active receptor is a GEF that swaps GDP for GTP in the trimeric G protein.
Gα–GTP and βγ switch on targets: Gs ↑ cAMP, Gi ↓ cAMP, Gq → PLC-β → IP₃ (Ca²⁺ from the ER) + DAG (with Ca²⁺ activates PKC). Ca²⁺ acts through calmodulin.
cAMP frees the catalytic subunits of PKA, which phosphorylate enzymes, channels and transcription factors. Enzymes in series amplify the signal.
Every step is switched off: GTP hydrolysis, phosphodiesterase, phosphatases, Ca²⁺ pumps; GRK + arrestin desensitise the receptor and lead to endocytosis.
Ca²⁺ imaging and FRET sensors show these signals live. Toxins and drugs act on single steps: cholera toxin (Gs stuck on), β-blockers, opioids, semaglutide.

Read more (optional): Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell, 7th ed., ch. 15.
Image credits

Five take-home points. First, GPCRs are seven-helix receptors; the hormone changes the shape of the bundle, and the active receptor acts as an exchange factor that loads GTP onto the G protein. Second, the G protein is a timed switch; its alpha type decides the output: Gs raises cAMP, Gi lowers it, and Gq splits PIP₂ into IP₃, which releases calcium from the ER, and DAG, which with calcium activates protein kinase C; calcium itself acts through calmodulin. Third, cAMP activates protein kinase A by releasing its catalytic subunits, and the chain of enzymes amplifies a few hormone molecules into a large response. Fourth, a signal must end: GTP hydrolysis, phosphodiesterases, phosphatases and pumps reset the messengers, and GRK and arrestin desensitise the receptor and send it into endocytosis. Fifth, we can watch these signals in living cells, and many toxins and drugs act on exactly one step. In the next lecture we meet the other big class of surface receptors, the enzyme-coupled receptors and their kinase cascades.

title: Study questions: the Golgi and the secretory pathway
text: Study questions in the style of the written exam. Write your answer first (a few sentences, or a labelled sketch where it helps), then compare with the model answer. Each question is tagged with its learning outcome (ELO). Questions tagged [VG] are of the kind used for the higher grade: predict, compare, explain an unexpected result or design an experiment.
crumbs: The Golgi and the secretory pathway

title: Study questions: the Golgi and the secretory pathway
section: G-level questions
text:
G-level questions
1. Describe the route of a secreted protein from its synthesis to the outside of the cell. Name each compartment and say which kind of carrier moves it between them. [ELO 4]






Model answer





The protein is made by ribosomes on the rough ER and enters the ER lumen during synthesis. After folding and quality control it leaves the ER in COPII-coated vesicles and reaches the ERGIC (ER–Golgi intermediate compartment). From there it enters the cis Golgi and crosses the stack (cis → medial → trans), mainly by cisternal maturation: the cisterna that contains it matures while COPI vesicles bring Golgi enzymes back. In the trans-Golgi network (TGN) it is sorted; a protein with no special signal leaves in a constitutive carrier (vesicle or tubule) that fuses with the plasma membrane, releasing the protein outside. In a cell with regulated secretion it may instead be stored in a secretory granule until a Ca²⁺ signal. Throughout, the protein stays in the lumen of membrane compartments and never crosses a membrane after the ER.




2. Explain how a COPII vesicle forms at the ER. Include the role of the small GTPase and how cargo is selected. [ELO 4]






Model answer





A GEF in the ER membrane (Sec12) loads GTP onto the small GTPase Sar1. Sar1-GTP inserts an amphipathic helix into the cytosolic leaflet, which starts to bend the membrane, and recruits the inner coat (Sec23/24). The inner coat binds sorting signals in the cytosolic tails of membrane cargo (for example a di-acidic DxE signal) and of cargo receptors, which in turn bind soluble cargo in the lumen. The outer coat (Sec13/31) forms a cage that shapes the bud, and the vesicle pinches off. GTP hydrolysis by Sar1 then releases the coat, so the vesicle can fuse and the coat proteins can be reused. Because the GEF is only in the ER, COPII coats form only there.




3. Compare the three main vesicle coats: where does each work, which way does it carry cargo, and what switches it on? [ELO 4]






Model answer














Coat
Where
Direction
Switch




COPII
ER exit sites
forward: ER → ERGIC/Golgi
Sar1


COPI
ERGIC, Golgi
backward: Golgi → ER, and between cisternae
ARF1


Clathrin (with adaptors AP1, AP2)
TGN, plasma membrane
TGN → endosomes; plasma membrane → endosomes (endocytosis)
ARF1 at the TGN



All three bend the membrane and select cargo through binding of sorting signals (directly, or through adaptors in the case of clathrin). All are released after the vesicle forms.




4. Describe how SNARE proteins fuse a vesicle with its target membrane, and what NSF does. [ELO 4]






Model answer





The vesicle carries a v-SNARE (e.g. VAMP/synaptobrevin) and the target membrane carries t-SNAREs (e.g. syntaxin and SNAP-25). When the vesicle has been tethered close to the target, the SNARE motifs (one from the v-SNARE, three from the t-SNAREs) wind together into a four-helix bundle. Assembly zips from the end far from the membranes towards the membranes, pulling the two bilayers into contact; the energy released overcomes the repulsion between them and the lipids merge (fusion). Afterwards all four helices sit in the same membrane (a cis-SNARE complex). The ATPase NSF, with its adaptor α-SNAP, uses ATP to pull the complex apart, so the SNAREs can be used again. Different SNARE pairs work at different membranes, which adds specificity on top of Rabs and tethers.




5. What are Rab GTPases, and how do they help a vesicle find the right target membrane? [ELO 4]






Model answer





Rabs are a family of about 60 small GTPases in human cells. In the GTP-bound form a Rab is anchored to a membrane by a lipid tail and binds effector proteins; in the GDP form it is removed into the cytosol by GDI. A GEF switches it on at the right membrane and a GAP switches it off. Each compartment and vesicle type carries its own Rabs (e.g. Rab1 between ER and Golgi, Rab27 on secretory granules), so Rabs work as address labels or membrane identity markers. Effectors on the target, especially tethers (long coiled-coil golgins or multi-subunit complexes such as the exocyst), bind the Rab-GTP on an arriving vesicle and catch it, holding it close enough for the SNAREs to pair.




6. What happens to N-linked glycans in the Golgi, and why are the processing enzymes arranged in a particular order through the stack? [ELO 4, 5]






Model answer





The glycan arrives from the ER as a high-mannose tree (trimmed during ER quality control). In the cis Golgi mannosidases remove more mannose; in the medial Golgi N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) is added and more mannose removed; in the trans Golgi galactose and finally sialic acid are added, giving a complex glycan. Each step needs the product of the step before, and each enzyme sits in the cisterna where its substrate arrives, so the stack works like an assembly line: cis enzymes first, trans enzymes last. The Golgi also adds O-linked sugars, builds proteoglycans and marks lysosomal enzymes with mannose-6-phosphate. Once a glycan has passed the medial Golgi it is resistant to Endo H, which is used to test whether a protein has reached the Golgi.




7. Compare constitutive and regulated secretion: which cells use them, how is the cargo stored, and what triggers release? [ELO 4, 5]






Model answer





Constitutive secretion happens in every cell, all the time: carriers from the TGN fuse with the plasma membrane as soon as they arrive, delivering secreted proteins (collagen, albumin, antibodies) and new membrane proteins and lipids. It is the default route for proteins without a sorting signal, and it is not stored. Regulated secretion happens only in specialised cells (endocrine cells such as β cells, exocrine cells such as pancreatic acinar cells, neurons, mast cells). The cargo aggregates in the TGN and is packed into secretory granules, which mature (acidify, concentrate their content, cut prohormones) and are stored, some docked at the plasma membrane. Release needs a signal that raises cytosolic Ca²⁺; the Ca²⁺ sensor synaptotagmin triggers SNARE-driven fusion.




8. How are lysosomal enzymes sorted away from secreted proteins in the trans-Golgi network? [ELO 4]






Model answer





In the cis Golgi, lysosomal enzymes are recognised by a phosphotransferase that adds a phosphate to mannose on their N-linked glycans: the mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) tag. In the TGN, the M6P receptor, a transmembrane protein, binds the tagged enzymes on the lumen side, and its cytosolic tail is collected by AP1 and clathrin into vesicles that go to endosomes. In the more acidic endosome (pH about 6) the enzyme lets go of the receptor and moves on to the lysosome; the receptor returns to the TGN for another round. Enzymes that lack the tag are not captured and are secreted by the default route.
crumbs: The Golgi and the secretory pathway

title: Study questions: the Golgi and the secretory pathway
section: VG-style questions
text:
VG-style questions
9. [VG] A yeast sec mutant grows at 25 °C but stops secreting at 37 °C, and its cells fill with small vesicles. A second mutant fills with ER membranes at 37 °C. Predict what you would see in the double mutant at 37 °C, and explain how such experiments revealed the order of the steps in the secretory pathway. What kind of proteins might the two genes encode? [ELO 1, 4]






Model answer





The double mutant would fill with ER, like the ER-block mutant alone. Its block comes earlier in the pathway: if cargo cannot leave the ER, no vesicles that would later fail to fuse with the plasma membrane are ever made. So the earlier block decides the phenotype (it is “epistatic”), and comparing double mutants lets you place each gene in the sequence of steps: ER exit before Golgi before post-Golgi vesicles. The vesicle-accumulating gene probably encodes something needed for vesicle targeting or fusion at the plasma membrane, such as a Rab (Sec4), a SNARE (Sec9, related to SNAP-25) or a tether subunit (exocyst). The ER-block gene probably encodes a part of the COPII machinery (e.g. Sec12, the Sar1 GEF, or a coat protein) or something needed for every fusion event, such as NSF (Sec18). Temperature-sensitive alleles are essential here, because a complete loss of secretion would kill the cell, so the mutant could not be grown.




10. [VG] You want to know whether a new drug candidate blocks transport from the ER to the Golgi, or a later step. Design a live-cell imaging experiment, with controls, and say what result would point to each answer. [ELO 1, 4]






Model answer





Use a synchronised cargo wave: cells expressing a RUSH reporter (a GFP-tagged cargo with a streptavidin-binding peptide, held on an ER hook with streptavidin), or VSVG-GFP ts045 held in the ER at 40 °C. Add the drug (and a solvent-only control) for a short time, then release the cargo with biotin (or shift to 32 °C) and image every minute for an hour. Mark the Golgi with a second colour (e.g. a red Golgi enzyme) and measure the green fluorescence in the ER, the Golgi and at the cell surface (surface: an antibody against an outside epitope on non-permeabilised cells, or a pH-sensitive GFP). Controls: solvent only (normal wave: Golgi peak after about 10–20 min, surface after 30–60 min); brefeldin A or the 15 °C block as a known ER-to-Golgi block; the 20 °C block as a known TGN block; cell viability, to rule out a general toxic effect. Interpretation: if the drug blocks ER exit, the cargo stays in the ER-like network and the Golgi never lights up (as with BFA or 15 °C; with 15 °C, cargo collects in ERGIC puncta). If it blocks a later step, the cargo reaches the Golgi on time but stays there or in the TGN (like 20 °C), and the surface signal does not rise. If it blocks fusion at the plasma membrane, cargo accumulates in vesicles near the cell edge. A biochemical check: Endo H resistance of the cargo over time tells you when it reaches the medial Golgi.




11. [VG] Patients with I-cell disease secrete their lysosomal enzymes into the blood. Yet enzyme replacement therapy, in which a recombinant lysosomal enzyme is given into the blood, works for several other lysosomal storage diseases. Explain both observations with the mannose-6-phosphate pathway, and predict whether giving a normal lysosomal enzyme (with M6P) by infusion could help a patient with I-cell disease. [ELO 4, 9]






Model answer





In I-cell disease the phosphotransferase that adds M6P in the cis Golgi is missing, so all lysosomal enzymes lack the tag, are not bound by the M6P receptor in the TGN and leave the cell by constitutive secretion: the blood has high enzyme levels while the lysosomes are empty of enzymes. In other storage diseases, only one enzyme is missing, and the cell’s sorting machinery is intact. Some M6P receptors also sit at the plasma membrane: they bind M6P-tagged enzymes from the blood and take them in by endocytosis, delivering them to endosomes and lysosomes. Recombinant enzymes made with M6P on their glycans therefore reach the lysosomes of the patient’s cells. In I-cell disease, an infused enzyme with M6P could in principle be taken up the same way, because the patient’s M6P receptors are normal. But the patient lacks M6P on dozens of different lysosomal enzymes, so replacing one would fix only a small part of the problem; replacing all of them is not practical. (Treatment is currently mainly supportive, with haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation tried in some patients.)

title: Study questions: the Golgi and the secretory pathway
section: Explore
text:
Explore
A pulse-chase in a cartoon cell, RUSH-style. A green fluorescent cargo is held in the ER by a hook. Press Release cargo (add biotin) and the whole wave leaves together. The dots show where the cargo is (a ring around a dot = a vesicle or granule); the graph shows the fraction of the cargo in each compartment over time. Choose the cargo (a membrane protein that goes to the surface, a hormone stored in secretory granules, or a lysosomal enzyme), set the temperature (37, 20 or 15 °C) and add brefeldin A, botulinum/tetanus toxin or a Ca²⁺ stimulus at any time; each change is marked on the graph. Time runs at 1× real time by default, like a real experiment; the cargo takes about an hour to pass, so use the speed menu (for example 60×) for the tasks. This is a qualitative compartment model: each step moves a fixed fraction of the cargo per minute, with illustrative rates; the times are of the right order, not measured values for one protein. For each task, press Reset, make the settings, then press Release. Small differences (±2 %) from the solutions come from when you click.



E1. Membrane protein, 37 °C. Release the cargo and follow it for 60 minutes. When does the Golgi signal peak, and what fraction of the cargo is in the Golgi stack at that moment? When has half of the cargo reached the cell surface? Why is the Golgi never filled with all of the cargo at once? [ELO 4]
E2. Predict first. Set 15 °C before release and run for 90 minutes. Where will the cargo collect, and why there? Then set 37 °C: what happens? [ELO 4]
E3. [VG] Predict first. Reset, set 20 °C, release and run for 90 minutes. Where does the cargo collect? Then switch to 37 °C and measure how long it takes until half of the cargo is at the surface. Compare with E1 (half at the surface measured from release at 37 °C). Why do cell biologists often use a 20 °C block before imaging the last step of secretion? [ELO 1, 4]
E4. Membrane protein, 37 °C. Release and let the wave run for 20 minutes, then add brefeldin A. Watch for 20 minutes. What happens to the Golgi and to the cargo that was in it? What happens to the cargo in the TGN and at the surface? Then remove brefeldin A and watch for another 20 minutes. Explain with ARF1 and COPI. [ELO 4, 5]
E5. [VG] Predict first. Choose the hormone cargo, 37 °C. Release and wait 60 minutes: where is the hormone, and how much has been secreted? Then switch on the Ca²⁺ stimulus and read the secreted fraction after 1, 5 and 10 minutes. Describe the shape of the secretion curve and explain it with docked and reserve granules. Which feature of this curve is lost early in type 2 diabetes? [ELO 4, 5, 9]
E6. [VG] Add the toxin before release and repeat (a) the membrane protein for 60 minutes, (b) the hormone with a Ca²⁺ stimulus at 60 minutes, and (c) the lysosomal enzyme for 60 minutes. Where does the cargo end up in each case? Why is the lysosomal route not blocked? Finally, choose the lysosomal enzyme without the toxin and untick “M6P tag on the enzyme”: where does the enzyme go now, and which disease does this model? [ELO 4, 9]






Solutions





E1. Half of the cargo has left the ER after about 6 minutes. The Golgi stack peaks after about 11 minutes, holding only about 35 % of the cargo; the TGN peaks a little later (about 30 % at 20 minutes). Half of the cargo is at the surface after about 28 minutes, and about 95 % after an hour. These times are of the same order as real VSVG and RUSH experiments (Golgi after 10–20 min, surface within an hour). The Golgi never holds everything at once because the wave spreads out: each step is random for each molecule, so some cargo leaves the Golgi before the last cargo has left the ER. The cargo is like a group of runners who start together but spread out along the course.
E2. At 15 °C the cargo leaves the ER slowly (every step is slower in the cold) and collects in the ERGIC: about 90 % after 90 minutes (in the model, about 7 % is still in the ER), and none reaches the Golgi. At 15 °C transport from the ERGIC to the Golgi stops, so cargo accumulates just before that step; this is how the ERGIC was first identified as a separate station (it looks like a set of dots near the Golgi). When you warm to 37 °C, the cargo moves into the Golgi within a few minutes (the Golgi peaks at nearly 60 % about 5 minutes after warming, much higher than the 35 % in E1), then on to the TGN and the surface as a sharp wave (about half at the surface 20 minutes after warming).
E3. At 20 °C the cargo passes the ER and the Golgi slowly but cannot leave the TGN: after 90 minutes about 86 % is in the TGN (11 % still in the Golgi) and none at the surface. After the shift to 37 °C, 10 % is at the surface after about 3 minutes and half after about 10 minutes (about 22 % at 5 min, 49 % at 10 min, 79 % at 20 min). From release at 37 °C (E1), half took about 28 minutes, and the first 10 % alone took 14 minutes. The 20 °C block collects the cargo at one station, so the last step starts from the same place at the same moment: a sharper, synchronised wave that separates the TGN-to-surface step from the earlier ones. (Real 20 °C blocks are usually 1–2 hours, often with a protein-synthesis inhibitor so that no new cargo enters.)
E4. At 20 minutes about 26 % of the cargo is in the Golgi, 30 % in the TGN and 25 % at the surface. With brefeldin A the Golgi fades within about 5 minutes (the banner says it has merged into the ER), and the cargo in the Golgi and ERGIC returns to the ER: after 20 minutes in BFA, about 34 % of the cargo is in the ER, nothing is in the Golgi, about 27 % stays in the TGN and the surface stops rising at about 39 % (the cargo already in vesicles still arrives). BFA blocks the GEF that activates ARF1; without ARF1-GTP, COPI coats (and the ARF1-dependent clathrin/AP1 coats at the TGN) cannot form. The Golgi is kept apart from the ER only by constant traffic, so its membranes tubulate and fuse with the ER. In the model, cargo cannot leave the ER in BFA, and the TGN (which in real cells merges with endosomes, not with the ER) keeps its cargo. After washout the Golgi re-forms in about 10–20 minutes and the cargo moves on: about 60 % is at the surface 20 minutes after washout. In a real experiment, the cargo that went back to the ER now carries Golgi-modified (Endo H-resistant) glycans although it sits in the ER, which was one of the clues that Golgi enzymes really move into the ER.
E5. After 60 minutes almost all of the hormone (about 95 %) is in secretory granules and only about 1 % has been secreted: regulated cargo is stored, not released. With the Ca²⁺ stimulus, secretion is about 14 % after 1 minute, 26 % after 5 minutes and 35 % after 10 minutes: a fast first phase followed by a slower second phase (if you keep Ca²⁺ high, about 50 % after 20 minutes). The first phase is the docked granules (about a fifth of the stored granules in the model), which fuse within a minute or two once Ca²⁺ rises. The second phase is limited by how fast reserve granules move to the membrane and dock. When the stimulus stops, secretion stops. In β cells, insulin release has the same two phases, and loss of the first phase is one of the earliest signs of type 2 diabetes.
E6. (a) The membrane protein reaches the end of the pathway but does not fuse: after 60 minutes about 95 % sits in vesicles docked at the plasma membrane and 0 % is at the surface. Docking needs Rabs and tethers, which the toxin does not touch; fusion needs the SNARE zipper, which is cut. (b) The hormone is stored in granules as before (about 95 % at 60 min), but with Ca²⁺ nothing is secreted (0 % after 10 and 20 minutes): docked granules cannot fuse. (c) The lysosomal enzyme still reaches the lysosomes (about 93 % after 60 min). Vesicles to endosomes and lysosomes fuse with different SNAREs that the toxin does not cut; botulinum and tetanus toxins cut only the SNAREs of exocytosis (VAMP, SNAP-25, syntaxin of the plasma membrane). In a real body the toxins act only in nerve cells, because only neurons have the receptors that take the toxin in. Without the M6P tag, the enzyme is not captured in the TGN and follows the default constitutive route: about 95 % is secreted after 60 minutes and the lysosomes get none. This models I-cell disease (mucolipidosis II), in which the enzyme that adds M6P is missing.

title: Quiz: signalling that shapes tissues and decides fates
text:
Short questions to check your understanding of the lecture Signalling that shapes tissues and decides fates. Try each on paper first, then open the hint or the answer. The tag after each question shows the learning outcome (ELO) it practises.

Q1. In the Wnt pathway, what happens to β-catenin in a cell that receives no Wnt, and what happens when Wnt arrives? [ELO 3]






Hint





β-catenin is made all the time. The question is whether it survives.









Answer





Without Wnt, the destruction complex (APC, Axin, GSK3) phosphorylates β-catenin; it is ubiquitylated and destroyed by the proteasome, so it never reaches the nucleus, and TCF keeps its target genes off with a repressor. When Wnt binds Frizzled and its co-receptor, the destruction complex is blocked, β-catenin builds up, enters the nucleus and turns TCF into an activator (targets such as MYC and cyclin D1).




Q2. Hedgehog signalling is called a “double negative”. Explain what this means with Patched and Smoothened. [ELO 3]






Hint





Which protein inhibits which, and what does Hedgehog inhibit?









Answer





Patched inhibits Smoothened (keeps it out of the primary cilium), and Hedgehog inhibits Patched. So Hedgehog activates Smoothened by inhibiting its inhibitor. Active Smoothened in the cilium stops Gli from being cut into a repressor, and whole Gli activates the target genes. A consequence: a cell that loses Patched behaves as if Hedgehog were always present.




Q3. Notch signalling has no second messenger and no kinase cascade. How does the signal reach the nucleus, and why can it not be amplified? [ELO 3]






Hint





Two proteases are involved. What happens to the receptor itself?









Answer





Delta on the neighbouring cell binds Notch and pulls on it. Notch is then cut twice: by an ADAM protease outside the membrane and by γ-secretase inside the membrane. The freed Notch intracellular domain goes to the nucleus and, with CSL, activates target genes (the Hes repressors). Each receptor is cut once and used up: one ligand–receptor contact gives one signalling molecule, and no enzyme in between multiplies it.




Q4. Put these steps of TGF-β signalling in order: (a) SMAD2/3 binds SMAD4; (b) the type II receptor phosphorylates the type I receptor; (c) the SMAD complex binds DNA with a partner transcription factor; (d) TGF-β binds and brings the two receptors together; (e) the type I receptor phosphorylates SMAD2/3. [ELO 3]






Hint





The receptors are serine/threonine kinases. Which one is activated first?









Answer





d → b → e → a → c. The ligand brings the receptors together, type II activates type I, type I phosphorylates SMAD2/3, phosphorylated SMAD2/3 binds SMAD4, and the complex enters the nucleus and binds DNA together with other transcription factors.




Q5. A patient takes a proteasome inhibitor (used against multiple myeloma). Predict the effect on NF-κB signalling after TNF-α stimulation, and explain. [ELO 3]






Hint





What holds NF-κB in the cytosol, and how is it removed?









Answer





NF-κB stays in the cytosol and its target genes stay off. TNF-α still activates IKK, which phosphorylates IκB, and IκB gets ubiquitylated, but the proteasome cannot destroy it. So IκB keeps covering the nuclear entry signal of NF-κB. (Blocking NF-κB, whose targets include anti-apoptosis genes, is thought to be part of how such drugs kill myeloma cells.)




Q6. Why can cortisol act on a receptor inside the cell, while adrenaline needs a receptor on the cell surface? How does this affect how fast each acts? [ELO 3]






Hint





Think about which molecules cross a lipid bilayer, and what the receptor does after binding.









Answer





Cortisol is a small, fat-soluble steroid that diffuses across the plasma membrane and binds a nuclear receptor (the glucocorticoid receptor), which is itself a transcription factor. Adrenaline is polar and cannot cross the membrane, so it acts on a GPCR on the surface. Adrenaline’s effects come in seconds (second messengers change existing proteins). Cortisol’s effects need transcription and translation, so they start after an hour or more and last longer.




Q7. What is a morphogen, and how can one morphogen give three different cell types in a row of identical cells? [ELO 3]






Hint





Concentration falls with distance from the source; target genes have thresholds.









Answer





A morphogen is a signal made by a group of source cells that spreads and forms a concentration gradient. Cells read the local concentration. If target genes need different threshold concentrations, cells close to the source (above both thresholds) switch on one set of genes, cells in the middle another, and distant cells a third. Example: Sonic hedgehog from the floor of the neural tube gives different neuron types in order.




Q8. Tamoxifen and oestradiol bind the same pocket of the oestrogen receptor. Why does tamoxifen block the receptor in breast cancer cells instead of activating it? [ELO 3] [ELO 9]






Hint





What must the receptor recruit, besides binding DNA, to switch genes on?









Answer





Oestradiol makes a part of the receptor (a helix, the “lid”) close over the pocket, which forms the binding site for coactivators. Tamoxifen fills the pocket but its long side arm pushes the lid aside, so no coactivator can bind; the receptor cannot switch on the growth genes, and oestradiol is kept out. ER-positive breast cancer cells that depend on oestrogen stop growing.
