title: Signalling that shapes tissues and decides fates
section: The question: why does one cell become a hair cell, and its neighbour not?
text:
The question: why does one cell become a hair cell, and its neighbour not?

Inner ear (cochlea) of a mouse embryo, scanning electron micrograph. Each V-shaped tuft is the hair bundle of one hair cell. Between them, hidden below, are supporting cells.

In the inner ear, every hair cell (it detects sound) is surrounded by supporting cells. No two hair cells touch.
All these cells came from one sheet of identical cells with the same genes and the same surroundings.
So how does a cell “know” what to become, and how do neighbours end up different?


Look at this picture of the developing inner ear of a mouse, taken with a scanning electron microscope. The rows of V-shaped tufts are the hair bundles of hair cells, the cells that turn sound vibrations into nerve signals. What you cannot see is that every hair cell sits in a ring of supporting cells, so hair cells never touch each other. The pattern is very regular. Yet all of these cells came from one sheet of cells that looked the same, had the same genome and sat in the same environment. Something had to break the symmetry: one cell becomes a hair cell, its neighbours become supporting cells. The answer is cell–cell signalling that changes gene expression. In this case it is the Notch pathway, and we will see how a simple feedback between neighbours gives exactly this kind of spaced pattern. More generally, a handful of pathways, used again and again, decide cell fates in every tissue. They also cause disease when they get stuck in the on position.
crumbs: Signalling that shapes tissues and decides fates

title: Signalling that shapes tissues and decides fates
section: Recap and plan: a signal ends at a transcription factor
text:
Recap and plan: a signal ends at a transcription factor


Recap: a transcription factor binds an enhancer and recruits coactivators or corepressors. A cell fate is a stable set of genes that are on.
In every pathway today the factor already exists in the cell, but is kept inactive. The signal frees it, in one of five ways.
Many targets are the pathway’s own off-switches (negative feedback).


A short recap from gene regulation. A transcription factor binds a specific DNA sequence in an enhancer and recruits coactivators, which open chromatin and help RNA polymerase, or corepressors, which do the opposite. A cell type, or cell fate, is in this sense a stable combination of genes that are on. Now the new idea. In all six pathways today, the transcription factor is already made and waiting in the cell, but it is held inactive. The signal does not make the factor; it frees it. There are five ways to do that, listed on the right, and we will meet each one. Wnt and NF-κB stop destroying their factor. Notch cuts its factor out of the membrane. TGF-β phosphorylates its factor. Hedgehog stops turning its factor into a repressor. And for nuclear receptors, the hormone binds the transcription factor directly. Notice one more common feature: among the target genes are almost always inhibitors of the same pathway. That negative feedback keeps the response limited in time and strength.
crumbs: Signalling that shapes tissues and decides fates

title: Signalling that shapes tissues and decides fates
section: Wnt: stop destroying β-catenin
text:
Wnt: stop destroying β-catenin


Without Wnt, a destruction complex (APC, Axin, GSK3) phosphorylates β-catenin; it is then ubiquitylated and destroyed by the proteasome. TCF sits on DNA as a repressor.
Wnt binds its receptor Frizzled: the complex is blocked, β-catenin builds up, enters the nucleus and turns TCF into an activator.
Wnt keeps stem cells in the gut lining dividing.


Wnt is a secreted lipid-modified protein that acts on nearby cells. The key player inside the cell is β-catenin. Without Wnt, β-catenin is made all the time but destroyed within minutes. A destruction complex built on the scaffold proteins Axin and APC holds β-catenin while the kinase GSK3 phosphorylates it. The phosphorylated β-catenin is recognised by a ubiquitin ligase, gets a ubiquitin chain and is broken down by the proteasome, which you met in the protein-degradation lecture. In the nucleus, the DNA-binding factor TCF sits on its target genes together with a repressor, so they stay off. When Wnt binds its receptor Frizzled and a co-receptor, the destruction complex is pulled to the membrane and blocked. β-catenin is no longer destroyed, builds up, enters the nucleus, displaces the repressor and turns TCF into an activator. Targets include MYC and cyclin D1, which drive cell division, and AXIN2, which builds more destruction complex: negative feedback. In the adult, Wnt from the surrounding tissue keeps the stem cells at the bottom of each intestinal crypt dividing. Remember the name APC: it comes back in the colorectal cancer slide.
crumbs: Signalling that shapes tissues and decides fates

title: Signalling that shapes tissues and decides fates
section: Hedgehog: a receptor that works in the primary cilium
text:
Hedgehog: a receptor that works in the primary cilium


Most of our cells have one primary cilium, a short antenna. Hedgehog signalling happens there.
Without Hedgehog, Patched keeps Smoothened out of the cilium; the transcription factor Gli is cut into a repressor.
Hedgehog binds Patched: Smoothened enters the cilium, Gli stays whole and activates genes. A double negative: the signal inhibits an inhibitor.


Hedgehog is named after a fruit-fly mutant whose larvae are covered in spiky bristles. Mammals have three Hedgehog proteins; Sonic hedgehog is the best known. The surprise of the last twenty years is where this pathway works: in the primary cilium. Most of our cells carry one primary cilium, a single short projection built on microtubules that does not beat but acts as a signalling antenna. Without Hedgehog, the receptor Patched sits in the cilium and keeps a second membrane protein, Smoothened, out and inactive. The transcription factor Gli is then partly cut by the proteasome into a short form that represses target genes. When Hedgehog binds Patched, Patched leaves the cilium and is degraded. Smoothened moves into the cilium and becomes active. Gli is no longer cut; the whole protein goes to the nucleus as an activator. Note the logic: the signal inhibits Patched, and Patched inhibits Smoothened, a double negative. Among the target genes are Patched itself, a negative feedback, and Gli1. People with defective cilia, called ciliopathies, have malformations partly because Hedgehog signalling fails.
crumbs: Signalling that shapes tissues and decides fates

title: Signalling that shapes tissues and decides fates
section: TGF-β: a receptor kinase phosphorylates SMADs
text:
TGF-β: a receptor kinase phosphorylates SMADs


TGF-β brings two receptor serine/threonine kinases together. Type II phosphorylates type I; type I phosphorylates SMAD2/3.
Phosphorylated SMADs bind SMAD4, enter the nucleus and work with other transcription factors, so the answer depends on the cell type.
Switched off by phosphatases and the inhibitor SMAD7 (a target gene). In epithelial cells TGF-β stops division; many cancers lose this response.


TGF-β, transforming growth factor beta, is a family of more than thirty secreted proteins, including the bone morphogenetic proteins, BMPs. The receptors resemble the receptor tyrosine kinases from the kinase-cascade lecture, but they are serine/threonine kinases, and the path to the nucleus is very short. The ligand, a dimer, brings together two kinds of receptor. The type II receptor phosphorylates and activates the type I receptor. The type I receptor then phosphorylates the transcription factors SMAD2 and SMAD3. Phosphorylated SMAD2/3 binds SMAD4, the complex enters the nucleus and binds DNA. SMADs bind DNA weakly, so they work together with other transcription factors that each cell type has. That is why TGF-β can stop division in an epithelial cell, make a fibroblast produce collagen, or calm down an immune cell. The response ends when phosphatases remove the phosphates, and when the target gene SMAD7 blocks the receptor. In normal epithelium TGF-β stops the cell cycle through inhibitors such as p15 and p21. Many cancers lose this brake, for example by mutations in SMAD4 in pancreatic cancer.
crumbs: Signalling that shapes tissues and decides fates

title: Signalling that shapes tissues and decides fates
section: Morphogens: one signal, several fates
text:
Morphogens: one signal, several fates


A morphogen is a signal made at one place that spreads and forms a concentration gradient. Cells read their distance from the source as a concentration.
Different thresholds switch on different genes: high, middle and low give three fates.
Example: Sonic hedgehog from the floor of the neural tube makes several kinds of spinal cord neurons in order. Wnt, BMP (TGF-β family) and retinoic acid also act as morphogens.


How can one signal make several cell types? By its concentration. A morphogen is a signal that is made by a small group of source cells, spreads through the tissue and is broken down or captured on the way. The result is a gradient: high near the source, low far away. Each cell reads the local concentration, and because target genes have different thresholds, a cell close to the source switches on a different set of genes from a cell further away. In the diagram, two thresholds divide a row of identical cells into three fates. A classic real example: in the embryo, the floor of the neural tube makes Sonic hedgehog. The cells closest to it become floor-plate cells, and the next ones become different kinds of neurons in a fixed order: one kind of interneuron, then motor neurons, then other interneurons further away. Cells also measure how long they have been exposed, not only how much. This one slide is a simplification of a large field: developmental biology. The same signals reappear in the adult, for example in the gut crypt, and in the course on organ structure and function.
crumbs: Signalling that shapes tissues and decides fates

title: Signalling that shapes tissues and decides fates
section: Notch: the receptor is cut
text:
Notch: the receptor is cut


Delta (the signal) is a membrane protein: Notch signalling needs direct contact between cells.
Binding and pulling lets two proteases cut Notch: ADAM outside, then γ-secretase inside the membrane. The freed Notch tail goes to the nucleus and turns the factor CSL into an activator.
No amplification and no second messenger: one receptor, one signal.


Notch is the simplest pathway of all, and the most direct. Both the signal and the receptor are membrane proteins, so only cells that touch can talk. The signal is Delta, or its relative Jagged, on the sending cell. When Delta binds Notch on the receiving cell, the sending cell pulls Delta inwards by endocytosis. This pulling force stretches Notch and exposes a site that an ADAM protease cuts, just outside the membrane. The remaining stump is now a substrate for γ-secretase, a protease that cuts proteins inside the membrane. That cut releases the Notch intracellular domain, the Notch tail. The tail moves into the nucleus and binds the DNA-binding protein CSL. Without Notch, CSL sits on its targets with corepressors; with the Notch tail, it becomes an activator. The main targets are the Hes genes, which encode repressors. Notice that nothing amplifies this signal: each receptor is cut once and used up. So the strength of the signal depends on how many Delta molecules the neighbours show. γ-secretase also cuts other proteins, including the amyloid precursor protein of Alzheimer’s disease.
crumbs: Signalling that shapes tissues and decides fates

title: Signalling that shapes tissues and decides fates
section: Lateral inhibition: neighbours become different
text:
Lateral inhibition: neighbours become different


Notch signalling lowers Delta in the receiving cell (through Hes repressors). So a cell with a bit more Delta silences its neighbours, which then send less Delta back.
The loop amplifies tiny random differences: a salt-and-pepper pattern of Delta-high cells (hair cells, neurons) among Notch-high cells (supporting cells). Try it: Notch lateral inhibition.


Now we can explain the inner-ear pattern. Delta activates Notch in the neighbour. Active Notch, through the Hes repressors, switches off Delta and the genes for becoming a hair cell or a neuron in that same cell. Follow the loop between two neighbours, A and B, that start almost equal. If A has a little more Delta, B gets a little more Notch signal and makes a little less Delta. Then A receives less Notch signal and makes even more Delta. The small difference grows until A is Delta-high and B is Notch-high. This is called lateral inhibition, and it is a double-negative feedback loop between cells. In a whole sheet, each cell competes with all its neighbours, and the result is a salt-and-pepper pattern: isolated Delta-high cells, each surrounded by Notch-high cells. The pattern on the right was calculated with a standard mathematical model, Collier and colleagues 1996, from a nearly uniform start with small random differences. You can run this model yourself in the demo, change the strength of the feedback, knock out Notch in a patch, or add a γ-secretase inhibitor.
crumbs: Signalling that shapes tissues and decides fates

title: Signalling that shapes tissues and decides fates
section: How do we know? Remove Notch and see what goes wrong
text:
How do we know? Remove Notch and see what goes wrong

Fruit-fly wings. A: normal. B: the fly CSL protein (Su(H)) removed in patches of the wing: the wing edge is lost in notches.

Genetics: flies with half the Notch gene have notched wings (1910s). Embryos with no Notch make too many neurons and little skin: every cell takes the “default” fate.
Mosaics: a patch of Notch-negative cells in a normal tissue becomes all neural; its normal neighbours are inhibited.
Drugs: a γ-secretase inhibitor in the inner ear of a mouse turns supporting cells into extra hair cells.
Models: the Collier model predicts the spacing from the feedback alone.


How do we know that Notch does lateral inhibition? The first clue came from fly genetics more than a hundred years ago. Flies that carry only one working copy of the Notch gene have notches at the edge of the wing, which gave the gene its name. Embryos with no Notch at all die with far too many neurons and almost no skin: without lateral inhibition, every cell in a group that could become neural does so. The picture shows a modern version: in B, the fly’s CSL protein, called Suppressor of Hairless, was removed in patches of the wing, and the wing margin, which needs Notch signalling, is lost in those places. A second type of experiment is the genetic mosaic: make a patch of cells without Notch in a normal animal. The patch cells cannot be inhibited, so they all take the neural fate, while normal cells next to the patch are inhibited by them. A third is pharmacology: blocking γ-secretase with an inhibitor in the inner ear of a mouse turns some supporting cells into new hair cells. That result raised hopes for treating deafness. Finally, mathematical models show that the feedback alone is enough to make the pattern.
crumbs: Signalling that shapes tissues and decides fates

title: Signalling that shapes tissues and decides fates
section: NF-κB: release by destroying the inhibitor
text:
NF-κB: release by destroying the inhibitor


At rest, IκB holds NF-κB in the cytosol by covering its nuclear entry signal.
Inflammation signals activate the kinase IKK. It phosphorylates IκB, which is ubiquitylated and destroyed by the proteasome. Free NF-κB enters the nucleus within minutes.
Targets: cytokines, adhesion molecules, anti-apoptosis proteins and IκB itself (negative feedback).


NF-κB is the master switch of inflammation. It is a dimer of transcription factors kept in the cytosol by an inhibitor protein, IκB. IκB covers the nuclear localisation signal of NF-κB, so NF-κB cannot enter the nucleus. Signals of danger, such as the cytokines TNF-α and interleukin-1, or lipopolysaccharide from bacteria, act through their receptors on a kinase complex called IKK. IKK phosphorylates IκB on two serines. This marks IκB for a ubiquitin ligase, IκB gets a ubiquitin chain, and the proteasome destroys it. You saw this machinery in the protein-degradation lecture; here it is the switch of a signalling pathway, the same logic as β-catenin but the other way round: there the factor was destroyed, here its inhibitor is. Freed NF-κB enters the nucleus within minutes, because no new protein needs to be made. Its targets include cytokines that call immune cells, adhesion molecules on blood vessels, and proteins that stop apoptosis. One target is the IκB gene: new IκB enters the nucleus, pulls NF-κB out again and ends the response. You meet NF-κB again in immunology.
crumbs: Signalling that shapes tissues and decides fates

title: Signalling that shapes tissues and decides fates
section: Nuclear receptors: the receptor is the transcription factor
text:
Nuclear receptors: the receptor is the transcription factor


Steroid hormones (cortisol, oestradiol, testosterone), thyroid hormone, vitamin D and retinoic acid are small and fat-soluble: they cross the membrane.
They bind nuclear receptors inside the cell. The hormone–receptor pair binds a hormone response element in DNA and recruits coactivators.
The shortest path from signal to gene: no second messenger. The effect takes hours and needs new protein.


The last pathway has no relay at all. Steroid hormones such as cortisol, oestradiol and testosterone, and also thyroid hormone, vitamin D and retinoic acid, are small and hydrophobic, so they diffuse through the plasma membrane, as you saw in the membrane-transport lecture. Their receptors are inside the cell, and they are themselves transcription factors. Humans have 48 of these nuclear receptors. Each has a DNA-binding domain and a ligand-binding pocket. Take the glucocorticoid receptor, which binds cortisol. Without hormone it sits in the cytosol, held by the chaperone HSP90. Cortisol enters the pocket, the chaperone falls off, two receptors pair up, enter the nucleus and bind a hormone response element, a short DNA sequence near target genes. The hormone also changes the shape of the receptor so that it recruits coactivators. Other receptors, such as the oestrogen receptor and the thyroid hormone receptor, are already in the nucleus and on DNA, and the hormone switches them from repressor to activator. Because the response needs transcription and translation, it starts after an hour or more and lasts long.

title: Signalling that shapes tissues and decides fates
section: How do we know? Reporter genes read out a pathway
text:
How do we know? Reporter genes read out a pathway


Put binding sites for the pathway’s transcription factor in front of a gene for luciferase (light) or GFP (green fluorescence).
The signal measures pathway activity in cells, tissues or living animals. Control: the same construct with mutated sites.
Used to find pathway components in genetic screens and to screen drugs that block a pathway.


How do we measure whether a pathway is on? We could measure each of its target genes, but they differ between cell types. A simpler approach is a reporter gene. We build a piece of DNA with several copies of the binding site for the pathway’s transcription factor, here TCF for the Wnt pathway, in front of a weak promoter and the gene for luciferase, the enzyme that makes fireflies glow. We put this construct into cells. Without signal, little luciferase is made. With Wnt, β-catenin and TCF bind the sites and the cells make light that we measure in a plate reader. The essential control is the same construct with mutated binding sites: if that one also lights up, the effect does not go through TCF. Colon cancer cells with a broken APC gene light up without any Wnt, which shows that their pathway is stuck in the on position. Similar reporters exist for Notch, NF-κB, SMADs and nuclear receptors, and with GFP instead of luciferase one can watch the pathway in living embryos. Drug companies use reporter cells to screen thousands of compounds for pathway inhibitors.

title: Signalling that shapes tissues and decides fates
section: Six pathways, one logic
text:
Six pathways, one logic









Pathway
Signal
Factor is freed by
Off-switch (feedback)




Wnt
secreted, local
no longer destroyed (β-catenin)
Axin2, destruction complex


Hedgehog
secreted, gradient
no longer cut into a repressor (Gli)

TGF-β/BMP
secreted, gradient
phosphorylated by the receptor (SMADs)
SMAD7, phosphatases


Notch
membrane-bound (contact)

Hes repressors, receptor used up


NF-κB

Nuclear receptors
steroid, thyroid hormone
hormone binds the factor
hormone breakdown




The same signal gives different answers in different cells: the answer depends on which genes are open and which partner factors are present (competence). A few pathways, many fates.


Here is the whole lecture on one slide. For each pathway, ask the same four questions: what is the signal, how is the transcription factor freed, and how is the pathway switched off. Wnt and NF-κB both use the proteasome, but in opposite ways: Wnt stops destroying the factor, NF-κB destroys the inhibitor. Notch and Hedgehog both involve cutting proteins: Notch cuts its receptor to free the factor, Hedgehog stops cutting its factor into a repressor. TGF-β is the shortest kinase path. Nuclear receptors skip the membrane altogether. And in every row there is negative feedback. A last point. Development uses only about seven major pathways to make hundreds of cell types. How can that work? Because the answer depends on the receiving cell. A cell’s history has already opened some enhancers and closed others, and it already has certain partner transcription factors. The same Wnt signal can therefore make a gut stem cell divide and a neural cell choose a fate. This readiness to respond in a specific way is called competence. The kinase-cascade lecture showed cross-talk between pathways; the same is true here.

title: Signalling that shapes tissues and decides fates
section: Why it matters: cancers with a pathway stuck on
text:
Why it matters: cancers with a pathway stuck on








APC is mutated in about 80 % of colorectal cancers. Inherited APC mutations (familial adenomatous polyposis) give hundreds of polyps by early adulthood.
In basal cell carcinoma, the most common skin cancer, Patched or Smoothened is mutated. Vismodegib blocks Smoothened, for tumours that cannot be removed by surgery.







Familial adenomatous polyposis: hundreds of small polyps (endoscopy).


Pathways that tell cells to divide during development are dangerous when they are stuck on in the adult. Wnt first. Remember the destruction complex with APC. About four out of five colorectal cancers have a mutation in APC that cuts the protein short, so β-catenin is never destroyed and TCF target genes such as MYC stay on, even without any Wnt. People who inherit one broken APC copy have familial adenomatous polyposis: the second copy is lost in many gut cells, and hundreds of polyps grow, as in the picture. Without surgery to remove the colon, cancer is almost certain. No drug yet targets this pathway in colorectal cancer, because it is hard to replace a missing brake. Hedgehog is the success story. In basal cell carcinoma, the cancer of the skin’s basal cells, most tumours have lost Patched or carry an activating Smoothened mutation. Vismodegib, the first Smoothened inhibitor, was approved in 2012 for tumours that cannot be operated on. The first known Smoothened blocker was cyclopamine, a toxin from a wild lily that causes one-eyed lambs; vismodegib was later found by screening for drug-like inhibitors. Resistance appears when Smoothened mutates so that the drug no longer binds, or when the fault lies further down. More on cancer in Sjukdomslära.

title: Signalling that shapes tissues and decides fates
section: Why it matters: hormone receptors as drug targets
text:
Why it matters: hormone receptors as drug targets








About 70 % of breast cancers carry the oestrogen receptor (ER) and grow on oestrogen. Tamoxifen fills the hormone pocket but blocks the coactivator site: ER stays off in breast tissue.
Corticosteroids (prednisolone, dexamethasone) activate the glucocorticoid receptor. It blocks NF-κB and turns on IκB: inflammation genes go off. The same receptor in other tissues gives the side effects (high blood sugar, bone loss).







Breast cancer stained for ER: brown nuclei carry the receptor.


Nuclear receptors are among the most successful drug targets, because a small molecule can enter the same pocket as the hormone. About seven out of ten breast cancers have the oestrogen receptor, and their growth depends on oestrogen. Pathologists test every breast tumour by staining for the receptor, as in the picture: brown nuclei mean ER-positive. Tamoxifen binds the hormone pocket, but its long side arm pushes aside the helix that normally closes over the pocket and forms the site for coactivators. So the receptor binds DNA but cannot switch genes on in breast tissue. In some other tissues, such as the uterus, tamoxifen partly activates the receptor, which is why it is called a selective oestrogen receptor modulator. Corticosteroids are synthetic versions of cortisol and among the most used drugs in medicine, for asthma, rheumatic disease and transplant rejection. They activate the glucocorticoid receptor, which binds NF-κB and blocks its genes, and also switches on the IκB gene. That connects two slides of today. The glucocorticoid receptor is in almost every tissue, which explains the side effects. You meet these drugs again in immunology and in drug development.
crumbs: Signalling that shapes tissues and decides fates

title: Signalling that shapes tissues and decides fates
section: Summary
text:
Summary

Fate-deciding pathways end at a transcription factor that is already in the cell but kept inactive. The signal frees it: by stopping its destruction (Wnt/β-catenin), cutting it out of the membrane (Notch), phosphorylating it (TGF-β/SMAD), stopping its conversion to a repressor (Hedgehog/Gli in the primary cilium), destroying its inhibitor (NF-κB/IκB) or binding it directly (nuclear receptors).
Each pathway turns on a gene-expression programme and its own negative feedback; the answer depends on the cell’s competence.
Morphogen gradients give different fates at different concentrations; lateral inhibition by Notch makes neighbours different and gives salt-and-pepper patterns.
Pathways stuck on cause cancer (APC in colorectal cancer, Patched/Smoothened in basal cell carcinoma); drugs act at the receptor: vismodegib, tamoxifen, corticosteroids.

Read more (optional): Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell, 7th ed., ch. 15 (and ch. 21–22 for development and stem cells).
Image credits

Four take-home points. First, for every pathway in this lecture, find the transcription factor and ask how the signal frees it. There are five answers: stop destroying it, cut it out of the membrane, phosphorylate it, stop turning it into a repressor, or let the hormone bind it directly; for NF-κB, destroy its inhibitor. Second, the factor switches on a set of genes, a programme, which includes inhibitors of the same pathway, so the response is limited. Which genes respond depends on the history of the cell. Third, two simple ideas explain much of how tissues get their patterns: a morphogen gradient read at different thresholds, and lateral inhibition between neighbours through Notch. Fourth, these pathways are drug targets and cancer genes. Learn the four examples: APC and colorectal cancer, Smoothened and vismodegib, the oestrogen receptor and tamoxifen, and the glucocorticoid receptor and corticosteroids. This ends the signalling block. In the cytoskeleton lectures you will see signals again, now steering cell shape and movement.

title: Study questions: the endoplasmic reticulum
text: Study questions in the style of the written exam. Write your answer first (a few sentences, or a labelled sketch where it helps), then compare with the model answer. Each question is tagged with its learning outcome (ELO). Questions tagged [VG] are of the kind used for the higher grade: predict, compare, explain an unexpected result or design an experiment.

title: Study questions: the endoplasmic reticulum
section: G-level questions
text:
G-level questions
1. Describe how a secreted protein gets from a free ribosome in the cytosol into the ER lumen. Name SRP, the SRP receptor, the translocon and signal peptidase, and say what each does. [ELO 4]






Model answer





Translation starts on a free ribosome. When the N-terminal signal sequence (a positive part, a hydrophobic core of about 6–15 amino acids, and a cut site) comes out of the ribosome, the signal recognition particle (SRP) binds it and pauses translation. SRP with the ribosome binds the SRP receptor in the ER membrane, next to the translocon (Sec61). The ribosome is handed to the translocon, GTP is hydrolysed and SRP is released. Translation continues and the chain is threaded through the translocon into the lumen while it is made (co-translational translocation). Signal peptidase, with its active site in the lumen, cuts off the signal sequence. The protein folds in the lumen.




2. What is the difference between a stop-transfer sequence and a signal-anchor sequence? Draw a type I, a type II and a type III single-pass membrane protein in the ER membrane, with N, C, the lumen and the cytosol. [ELO 4]






Model answer





Both are hydrophobic segments of about 20 amino acids that end up as a transmembrane helix. A stop-transfer arrives while the chain is already being translocated (after a signal sequence): it stops translocation and leaves the translocon sideways, so what follows stays in the cytosol. A signal-anchor is the first hydrophobic segment of a protein without a cleavable signal sequence: it is bound by SRP, starts translocation and stays in the membrane; its orientation is set by the positive charges next to it, which stay in the cytosol. Type I: cleaved signal sequence + stop-transfer; N-terminus in the lumen, C-terminus in the cytosol (LDL receptor). Type II: signal-anchor with positive charges before it; N in the cytosol, C in the lumen (transferrin receptor). Type III: signal-anchor with positive charges after it; N in the lumen, C in the cytosol (cytochrome P450).




3. Explain why a membrane protein that faces the ER lumen with its N-terminus has its N-terminus outside the cell when it reaches the plasma membrane. Why do all sugar chains on the cell surface face outwards? [ELO 4, ELO 5]






Model answer





Vesicles bud from one membrane and fuse with the next without the protein flipping or crossing a membrane. The side of the membrane that faces the ER lumen faces the vesicle lumen, then the Golgi lumen, and when the last vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane its lumen opens to the outside. So the lumen side becomes the outside (topology from the cell tour). N-glycans are added only in the ER lumen (by OST) and O-glycans and further sugars in the Golgi lumen, so all sugar chains end up on the outside of the cell.




4. Describe how disulfide bonds and N-linked glycans are added in the ER. Why are disulfide bonds typical of secreted proteins and rare in cytosolic proteins? [ELO 4]






Model answer





Disulfide bonds: the ER lumen is oxidizing. PDI passes a disulfide bond to two cysteines of the new chain, and it can also break wrong pairs so the correct ones form (PDI is re-oxidised by Ero1, using O₂). The cytosol is reducing (glutathione), so disulfides are rare there. Secreted proteins must survive outside the cell, and disulfides make them stable. N-glycans: a block of 14 sugars (2 GlcNAc, 9 mannose, 3 glucose) is built on the lipid dolichol in the ER membrane. Oligosaccharyltransferase (OST), next to the translocon, transfers the whole block to an asparagine in the sequence N-X-S/T (X not proline) while the chain enters the lumen. The block is then trimmed in the ER and modified in the Golgi.




5. Explain the calnexin cycle. What happens to a glycoprotein that never folds? [ELO 4]






Model answer





After the sugar block is added, glucosidases I and II remove two of the three glucoses. With one glucose, the protein binds calnexin (membrane) or calreticulin (lumen), lectin chaperones that hold it and help it fold (with the PDI-like ERp57). Glucosidase II removes the last glucose and the protein is released. UGGT checks it: if it is still unfolded, UGGT adds a glucose back and the protein binds calnexin again. Folded proteins are not re-glucosylated and can leave for the Golgi. During the cycles, a mannosidase slowly removes mannoses: a timer. A protein that never folds ends up with trimmed mannoses, is recognised by ERAD factors and is degraded by ERAD: retrotranslocation to the cytosol, ubiquitination, the proteasome.




6. What is the unfolded protein response? Describe the three branches and the overall effect on the cell. [ELO 4, ELO 5]






Model answer





A signalling response to too many unfolded proteins in the ER. Three ER membrane sensors are held inactive by BiP; unfolded proteins pull BiP away. IRE1 (kinase and RNase) splices XBP1 mRNA → transcription factor XBP1 → genes for chaperones, ERAD and lipid synthesis. PERK phosphorylates eIF2α → general translation falls (less load), while ATF4 is made. ATF6 moves to the Golgi, is cut by proteases, and its cytosolic part enters the nucleus as a transcription factor for chaperone genes. Overall: less protein in, more folding capacity, more degradation, more ER. If the stress cannot be resolved, prolonged UPR (e.g. via CHOP) triggers apoptosis.




7. List three functions of the smooth ER and give a cell type where each is important. [ELO 5]






Model answer






Lipid synthesis: phospholipids and cholesterol for all membranes (every cell); steroid hormones in adrenal cortex, Leydig cells of the testis and ovary cells. (2) Drug and toxin metabolism by cytochrome P450 enzymes in liver cells (hepatocytes); the smooth ER expands with long-term exposure to some drugs. (3) Ca²⁺ store: SERCA pumps fill it, IP₃ receptors or ryanodine receptors release Ca²⁺ as a signal; most developed as the sarcoplasmic reticulum of muscle cells, where released Ca²⁺ triggers contraction.





8. In cystic fibrosis with the ΔF508 mutation, CFTR is made but hardly any reaches the plasma membrane. Explain why, using ER quality control, and explain how a “corrector” drug helps. [ELO 4, ELO 9]






Model answer





ΔF508 removes one phenylalanine from the first nucleotide-binding domain of CFTR. The protein folds slowly and incompletely. ER quality control (chaperones, the calnexin cycle and other checks) keeps it in the ER, and ERAD sends it back to the cytosol, where it is ubiquitinated and degraded by the proteasome. So almost none reaches the apical membrane, although the mutant channel can still conduct some Cl⁻ if it gets there. A corrector (e.g. elexacaftor, tezacaftor) binds CFTR during folding and stabilises it, so more molecules pass quality control and reach the surface; a potentiator (ivacaftor) then helps the channel open.

title: Study questions: the endoplasmic reticulum
section: VG-level questions
text:
VG-level questions
9. [VG] A protein has, from N to C: a cleavable signal sequence, a 100-amino-acid domain, hydrophobic segment H1, a 30-amino-acid loop, hydrophobic segment H2, and a 200-amino-acid domain with two N-X-S/T sites. (a) Predict its topology in the ER membrane and which sites are glycosylated. (b) Predict what happens if the signal sequence is deleted and H1 has positive charges on its N-terminal side. (c) Design an experiment to test your prediction in (a). [ELO 4, ELO 1]






Model answer






The signal sequence starts translocation and is cut off: the 100-aa domain is in the lumen. H1 arrives while the chain is going in: stop-transfer, so the 30-aa loop is in the cytosol. H2 arrives with the chain in the cytosol: start-transfer, so the 200-aa domain goes into the lumen. Result: two TM segments, both ends in the lumen (later outside the cell); the two N-X-S/T sites in the C-terminal domain are in the lumen and are glycosylated.
Without the signal sequence the 100-aa domain is made in the cytosol. H1 is now the first hydrophobic segment: a signal-anchor. Positive charges before it keep the N-terminal domain in the cytosol; the loop goes into the lumen. H2 is then a stop-transfer, and the 200-aa domain stays in the cytosol: both ends cytosolic, and the two sites are not glycosylated. The topology is inverted.
Make the protein in a cell-free system with microsomes (or in cells and then isolate microsomes). Glycosylation: compare the size with and without Endo H or PNGase F (or mutate the N-X-S/T sites); a shift shows the domain was in the lumen. Protease protection: add a protease to sealed microsomes; lumenal parts survive, the cytosolic loop is cut; detergent as a control digests everything. Antibodies against an N- or C-terminal tag show which fragment survives. In intact cells, antibodies against the N- or C-terminal tag bind without permeabilisation only if that end is outside.





10. [VG] Cells are treated with tunicamycin, which blocks the first step of building the N-glycan precursor. Predict what happens over the next hours to: (a) the size of a secreted glycoprotein on a gel, (b) how much of it is secreted, (c) the level of spliced XBP1 mRNA and the phosphorylation of eIF2α, (d) the cells after 24 hours of high dose. Explain each prediction. [ELO 4, ELO 5]






Model answer






Smaller: no N-glycans are added (each N-glycan adds about 2 kDa). (b) Less secreted: many glycoproteins fold poorly without their glycans and cannot use the calnexin cycle, so they are kept in the ER and degraded by ERAD. (c) Unfolded proteins pile up, BiP is pulled off the sensors, and the UPR is activated: more spliced XBP1 (IRE1) and more phosphorylated eIF2α (PERK); ATF6 is also cut. Western blots and RT-PCR of XBP1 splicing are standard read-outs. (d) If the stress cannot be resolved, the prolonged UPR (CHOP and other signals) triggers apoptosis: many cells die. Tunicamycin (and the SERCA blocker thapsigargin, which empties the ER of Ca²⁺) are standard tools to cause ER stress in the lab.





11. [VG] A biotech company makes a therapeutic IgG1 in CHO cells. After a change in the bioreactor process, the antibody has the same amino acid sequence, but more of its Fc glycans carry core fucose, and the patients’ response falls. Explain the link between the ER and Golgi of the producer cell and the drug’s effect, and say why regulators require glycan analysis of every batch. [ELO 4, ELO 9]






Model answer





The heavy chain gets one N-glycan at Asn297 in the ER (OST, en bloc), and the glycan is trimmed and rebuilt in the Golgi, where fucosyltransferase adds the core fucose. How complete each step is depends on the cell’s enzymes, nutrients, time in the Golgi and growth conditions, so process changes alter the glycan pattern while the sequence stays the same. The Fc glycan shapes the Fc part and its binding to Fc receptors. Antibodies without core fucose bind FcγRIIIa on natural killer cells much more strongly, so they kill antibody-coated tumour cells better (ADCC). More fucose → weaker ADCC → lower effect for an antibody that works by killing cells. Glycans also affect half-life and immunogenicity (non-human sugars from some cell lines can cause allergic reactions, as with cetuximab and α-gal). Therefore the glycan profile is a critical quality attribute that must be measured and kept within limits for every batch and for biosimilars.

title: Study questions: the endoplasmic reticulum
section: Explore
text:
Explore
Demo: topology builder. Build a protein from segments, or pick a real example, then press ▶ Make it. A ribosome makes the chain at about 5 amino acids per second (1× real time; choose a faster speed, or press Next step, to skip ahead). Watch SRP bring the ribosome to the translocon, the segments insert into the ER membrane, the signal sequence get cut off and the N-glycans appear (sugar symbols: blue square GlcNAc, green circle mannose, blue circle glucose, yellow galactose, purple sialic acid). Then follow the protein by vesicle to the Golgi and the cell surface. The close-up always shows the cytosol on top: watch which side the sugars and the termini end up on. Tap a TM segment in your protein to change its type. The Result table appears once the protein is in the ER; it also gives the result of two classic topology tests (protease protection of microsomes, Endo H). The rules are the textbook ones, simplified (see the note under the demo).



E1. Choose LDL receptor (type I) and press ▶ Make it. Watch the first 20 seconds at 1×: when does SRP bind, and when does translation continue? Then use Next step (or a faster speed) to follow the protein to the cell surface. Where are its N-terminus, its C-terminus and its two N-glycans in the ER, and at the cell surface? What do the protease test and the Endo H test give in the ER, and after the Golgi? [ELO 4]
E2. Predict first. Compare the transferrin receptor (type II) with the LDL receptor. Both cross the membrane once. Which way round is each, and what in the sequence decides it? Then build your own protein: + signal-anchor, + before, then + domain (150 aa). Predict the topology, make it, then tap the signal-anchor to change it to “+ after” and make it again. Which real protein in the examples has the second topology, and why does it have no N-glycans? [ELO 4]
E3. Predict first. Run the β2-adrenergic receptor (7 TM) and GLUT1 (12 TM). Where are the two ends of each? State a rule that links the number of TM segments and the sides of the N- and C-terminus. Use it to predict the ends of CFTR before you run it. [ELO 4]
E4. [VG] Predict first. Clear the protein and build: + stop-transfer, then + domain (150 aa): a “stop-transfer” with nothing before it. What will happen? Make it and read the note in the Result. Then build + signal sequence, + domain (150 aa), + signal-anchor, + before, + short loop. What does the signal-anchor do here? What do these two results tell you about how the translocon “reads” a hydrophobic segment? [ELO 4]
E5. [VG] Choose CFTR, tick misfolded (disease mutation) and make it (use Next step). Where does the protein end, and what does the Endo H test show? Compare with normal CFTR. Explain why a patient with ΔF508 has almost no CFTR in the plasma membrane even though the topology is correct, and which step a corrector drug changes. Then do the same with α1-antitrypsin: what is the consequence for the liver and for the lungs? [ELO 4, ELO 9]






Solutions





E1. For the first 11 s the free ribosome makes the chain: the 21-amino-acid signal sequence is fully out of the ribosome when about 56 amino acids have been made (the exit tunnel holds about 35). SRP binds, translation pauses, and the ribosome is carried to the SRP receptor and the translocon (about 4 s in the demo, an illustrative value). Then translation continues, the 767-amino-acid LDL-binding domain is threaded into the lumen, and the signal sequence is cut off. The stop-transfer stops translocation and the 50-amino-acid tail stays in the cytosol. Translation of all 860 amino acids takes about 3 minutes. Result: type I, N-terminus in the ER lumen, C-terminus in the cytosol; both N-glycans on the lumenal domain. At the cell surface: N-terminus and glycans outside the cell, C-terminal tail in the cytosol (this tail is what the endocytosis machinery binds). Protease test on microsomes: 50 aa cut (the cytosolic tail), 767 aa protected. Endo H: sensitive while the protein is in the ER (high-mannose glycans), resistant after the Golgi has rebuilt the glycans into complex glycans. This is how a lab tells whether a protein has left the ER. The whole trip takes about 30 minutes in the demo (typical: tens of minutes).
E2. LDL receptor: cleaved signal sequence + stop-transfer → N outside, C inside (type I). Transferrin receptor: no cleaved signal; its only TM segment is a signal-anchor with positive charges before it → the N-terminal 61 amino acids stay in the cytosol, the 671-amino-acid domain goes into the lumen with its 3 N-glycans → N inside, C outside (type II). What decides: whether there is a cleavable signal sequence, and, for a signal-anchor, the side of the positive charges (positive-inside rule). Your own protein: “+ before” gives type II (N cytosol, domain in the lumen, 1 N-glycan; the demo assumes one N-X-S/T site per lumenal domain). Changed to “+ after”: type III, N-terminus in the lumen (only the end of the helix), the 150-aa domain in the cytosol, no glycans, because N-glycans are added only in the lumen. The real example is cytochrome P450 3A4: N-terminal signal-anchor with charges after it, its large enzyme domain in the cytosol, no N-glycans; it stays in the ER.
E3. β2-adrenergic receptor: 7 TM, N outside (with its 2 N-glycans), C in the cytosol (where kinases and arrestin bind it). GLUT1: 12 TM, both ends in the cytosol, 1 N-glycan on the first outside loop. Rule: each TM segment switches the side, so an odd number puts N and C on opposite sides, an even number on the same side. CFTR has 12 TM segments and its first one is a signal-anchor with N in the cytosol, so both ends are in the cytosol, together with its two ATP-binding domains (NBD1, NBD2) and the R domain: 1143 of its 1480 amino acids are cytosolic, 85 lumenal (its 2 N-glycans are on outside loop 4).
E4. The “stop-transfer” is the first hydrophobic segment, and nothing is being translocated when it comes out of the ribosome, so it cannot stop anything. SRP binds it and it acts as a signal-anchor; its positive charges are after it (like every stop-transfer, whose C-terminal side faces the cytosol), so the N-terminus goes into the lumen: a type III protein with the 150-aa domain in the cytosol. In the second protein, the signal sequence has already started translocation when the “signal-anchor” arrives, so it acts as a stop-transfer: a type I protein (N and the glycosylated domain in the lumen, 20-aa loop in the cytosol). Conclusion: there is no special stop or start sequence. A hydrophobic segment of about 20 amino acids is simply a TM helix that leaves the translocon sideways through the lateral gate. Its role depends on where the chain is when it arrives: going into the lumen → it stops; in the cytosol → it starts. Only for the first one do the flanking charges decide the orientation. (In real proteins charges also influence later segments; the demo simplifies.)
E5. Misfolded CFTR goes through the same insertion; its topology is correct (12 TM, both ends cytosolic). But in the ER it does not pass quality control: it is held by chaperones (the calnexin cycle sees it as unfolded), and after about 10 more minutes it is pulled back into the cytosol, ubiquitinated and degraded by the proteasome (ERAD); the map shows it never reaches the Golgi. Endo H stays sensitive (its glycans were never rebuilt in the Golgi), whereas normal CFTR becomes Endo H-resistant after the Golgi. On a western blot this is the classic difference between “band B” (ER form) and “band C” (mature form) of CFTR. In ΔF508 the problem is folding, not topology: one missing phenylalanine destabilises NBD1, so ER quality control destroys almost all of the protein, although it could still work partly as a channel. A corrector acts at this step: it stabilises the folding protein so more of it passes quality control and reaches the plasma membrane. α1-antitrypsin (Z variant) is secreted when normal; misfolded, it is kept in the ER. In the demo it is all degraded; in patients part of it forms polymers in the hepatocyte ER (the PAS-positive globules), which damage the liver (cirrhosis), and only about 10–15 % reaches the blood, too little to inhibit neutrophil elastase in the lungs (emphysema).

title: Quiz: endocytosis, lysosomes and autophagy
text:
Short questions to check your understanding of the lecture Endocytosis, lysosomes and autophagy. Try each on paper first, then open the hint or the answer. The tag after each question shows the learning outcome (ELO) it practises.

Q1. Put these steps of clathrin-mediated endocytosis in order: dynamin cuts the neck; the coat is removed; adaptors bind receptor tails; clathrin forms a curved lattice; the vesicle fuses with an early endosome. [ELO 4]






Hint





Cargo is chosen first, the coat can only come off once the vesicle is free.









Answer





Adaptors bind receptor tails → clathrin forms a curved lattice (pit) → dynamin cuts the neck → the coat is removed → the vesicle fuses with an early endosome. The adaptors (AP2) choose the cargo by its tail signal, clathrin bends the membrane, dynamin uses GTP to pinch off the vesicle, and only an uncoated vesicle can fuse.




Q2. Fruit flies with the shibire mutation are paralysed within seconds at 29 °C and recover when cooled. What do you expect to see in their nerve endings at 29 °C, and why does this stop nerve signals? [ELO 4]






Hint





shibire is a temperature-sensitive mutation in dynamin. Synaptic vesicles are made again from membrane taken back by endocytosis.









Answer





Many deep coated pits with long necks that cannot pinch off, and very few synaptic vesicles. Dynamin does not work at 29 °C, so endocytosis stops at the last step. Nerve endings release their synaptic vesicles but cannot recycle the membrane into new vesicles, so they run out of transmitter vesicles and signalling stops.




Q3. The LDL receptor releases LDL in the endosome, but the transferrin receptor does not release transferrin there. Both receptors still recycle to the surface. What happens to LDL, to iron and to transferrin? [ELO 4] [ELO 5]






Hint





What does acid do in each case? What stays in the membrane, and what is free in the lumen?









Answer





Acid frees LDL from its receptor; LDL stays in the endosome lumen and goes on to the lysosome, where it is digested and its cholesterol released. Acid frees iron from transferrin; iron is transported into the cytosol. The empty transferrin stays bound to its receptor at acid pH and returns with it to the surface, where at pH 7.4 it lets go and can pick up iron again.




Q4. Order the compartments by pH, from highest to lowest: lysosome, early endosome, cytosol, late endosome. Which protein makes these differences? [ELO 5]






Hint





The further along the endocytic route, the more acid.









Answer





Cytosol (7.2) > early endosome (6.0–6.5) > late endosome (5.0–5.5) > lysosome (4.5–5). The V-ATPase, an ATP-driven proton pump, pumps H⁺ from the cytosol into the lumen. Later compartments have more pumps and are more acidic.




Q5. A lysosomal enzyme lacks the mannose-6-phosphate tag. Where does it end up, and why? [ELO 4]






Hint





Lysosomal enzymes start in the ER, like secreted proteins. What is the “default” route out of the Golgi?









Answer





It is secreted out of the cell. Without M6P, the M6P receptors in the trans Golgi network cannot collect it into clathrin vesicles to the endosomes, so it follows the default secretory route to the surface. This is what happens to most lysosomal enzymes in I-cell disease, where the enzyme that adds the tag is missing.




Q6. Why does a small leak from one lysosome not digest the cytosol? [ELO 5]






Hint





Compare the pH of the two compartments.









Answer





Lysosomal hydrolases are acid hydrolases: they work best at pH 4.5–5 and are much less active at the cytosol’s pH of about 7.2. A small amount that leaks out is therefore nearly inactive (and the cytosol also contains inhibitors of some of them). Large leaks, however, can kill a cell.




Q7. A cell is starved of amino acids. What happens to mTORC1 and to autophagy, and how does this help the cell? [ELO 5]






Hint





mTORC1 is a growth switch that blocks autophagy when nutrients are plentiful.









Answer





mTORC1 becomes inactive, so its block on autophagy is lifted and autophagy increases. Autophagosomes enclose parts of the cytosol and old organelles and deliver them to lysosomes, which break them down and return amino acids and other building blocks to the cytosol. The cell survives the starvation by recycling itself. The drug rapamycin has the same effect.




Q8. How does a PCSK9 antibody lower blood LDL? Use the words recycling and lysosome. [ELO 4] [ELO 9]






Hint





What does PCSK9 normally do to the LDL receptor after endocytosis?









Answer





PCSK9 binds the LDL receptor on liver cells and stays bound in the acidic endosome, which stops the receptor recycling and sends it to the lysosome to be destroyed. The antibody catches PCSK9 in the blood before it binds, so receptors keep recycling, more receptors are at the cell surface, and more LDL is taken out of the blood (about 50–60 % lower LDL).

title: Endocytosis, lysosomes and autophagy
section: About this lecture

title: Endocytosis, lysosomes and autophagy
section: The question: why do some teenagers have heart attacks?
text:
The question: why do some teenagers have heart attacks?



Hands of an 18-year-old with familial hypercholesterolaemia. The lumps over the knuckles are xanthomas: cholesterol deposits in tendons. She had a heart attack at 18.


Familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH): blood LDL cholesterol 2–3× normal in about 1 in 250 people, 4–6× in the rare children with two faulty genes.
Cholesterol builds up in arteries: heart attacks at 30–40, or in childhood.
The cells of these patients can make cholesterol normally. Yet they cannot take LDL out of the blood.
In 1973 Michael Brown and Joseph Goldstein asked: how does a cell take in a particle of 20 nm from the blood? The answer opened the field of receptor-mediated endocytosis.



Look at these hands. The lumps over the knuckles and along the tendons are xanthomas, deposits of cholesterol that build up when the blood cholesterol has been very high for a long time. The patient was an 18-year-old woman who had already had a heart attack. She has familial hypercholesterolaemia, one of the most common inherited diseases: about one person in 250 carries one faulty gene, and these people have about twice the normal LDL cholesterol from birth. Children who inherit two faulty genes can have four to six times normal levels and may have heart attacks before they are ten. In the early 1970s Michael Brown and Joseph Goldstein found that cells from these patients could make cholesterol perfectly well, but could not take up LDL, the cholesterol-carrying particle of the blood. Finding out why led them to the LDL receptor and to a general mechanism by which cells take in specific molecules: receptor-mediated endocytosis. They received the Nobel Prize in 1985. By the end of this lecture you will be able to explain the disease, and three kinds of drugs that treat it.

title: Endocytosis, lysosomes and autophagy
section: Ways into the cell: a map
text:
Ways into the cell: a map


Endocytosis: the plasma membrane folds in and pinches off a vesicle. Small vesicles (clathrin), large gulps of fluid (macropinocytosis), whole bacteria (phagocytosis).
Everything meets in endosomes, which sort: back to the surface or on to the lysosome. Autophagy delivers material from inside the cell.
Recap from the Golgi lecture: vesicles are shaped by a coat, find their target with Rab proteins and fuse with SNAREs. The same machinery works here.


Here is the whole lecture on one map. At the top is the plasma membrane. On the left, a clathrin-coated pit pinches off a small vesicle, about a tenth of a micrometre wide. In the middle, the membrane throws up a ruffle and closes around a large gulp of fluid: macropinocytosis. On the right, a white blood cell wraps its membrane around a bacterium: phagocytosis. Vesicles from the surface fuse with the early endosome, a sorting station. From there, much of the membrane and many receptors go back to the surface, the recycling route. What stays behind matures into a late endosome and then reaches the lysosome, where it is digested. New digestive enzymes come from the Golgi, and autophagosomes bring material from inside the cell. Remember the general rules from the Golgi lecture: a coat bends the membrane and chooses the cargo, Rab proteins mark which compartment is which, and SNARE proteins fuse the vesicle with its target. Today the coat is mostly clathrin, and the important Rabs are Rab5 on early endosomes and Rab7 on late endosomes. This is a simplified map; real cells have more routes.

title: Endocytosis, lysosomes and autophagy
section: Clathrin-mediated endocytosis, step by step
text:
Clathrin-mediated endocytosis, step by step


Adaptor proteins (AP2) grab short sorting signals in the cytosolic tails of receptors (for the LDL receptor: NPxY, a 4-amino-acid motif).
Clathrin binds the adaptors and forms a lattice that bends the membrane into a pit.
Dynamin, a GTPase, forms a collar around the neck and pinches the vesicle off. The coat comes off within seconds.
A pit takes about a minute; a cell makes thousands of coated vesicles per minute.


Clathrin-mediated endocytosis is the main way cells take up specific molecules. Follow the steps. First, adaptor proteins called AP2 sit on the inner face of the plasma membrane and bind short signals in the cytosolic tails of receptors. For the LDL receptor this signal is four amino acids, asparagine, proline, any amino acid, tyrosine, written NPxY. This is how cargo is chosen: a receptor with the signal is collected, one without it is not. Second, clathrin binds the adaptors. Clathrin molecules have three legs and link up into a cage of hexagons and pentagons, which forces the membrane to curve into a pit. Third, when the pit is deep, the GTPase dynamin assembles as a ring around its neck. When dynamin hydrolyses GTP, the ring tightens and twists, and the vesicle is cut free. Fourth, the clathrin coat is removed by an ATP-driven chaperone within seconds, and the naked vesicle fuses with an early endosome. A coated pit forms and closes in about a minute, and a cultured fibroblast makes a few thousand coated vesicles every minute.

title: Endocytosis, lysosomes and autophagy
section: How do we know? Coats in the electron microscope, and a paralysed fly
text:
How do we know? Coats in the electron microscope, and a paralysed fly



A clathrin-coated vesicle, thin-section EM: the bristly coat surrounds the membrane.


Structure of a clathrin cage (PDB 1XI4): legs of many three-legged clathrin molecules.


1964, Roth and Porter: mosquito eggs take up yolk protein through pits with a bristly coat on the cytosolic side.
1976, Anderson, Brown and Goldstein: LDL tagged with ferritin (iron core, dark in EM) sits in coated pits and appears in vesicles minutes later.
Dynamin: the fruit-fly mutant shibire is paralysed within seconds at 29 °C. Its nerve endings are full of pits stuck on necks: they cannot pinch off, so synaptic vesicles are not recycled. The gene encodes dynamin. Cooling the fly reverses it.



How do we know that pits, coats and dynamin do what the diagram claims? The first clue came from electron microscopy in 1964. Thomas Roth and Keith Porter studied mosquito eggs, which take up large amounts of yolk protein, and saw small pits in the membrane with a bristly coat on the cytosolic side. Twelve years later, Richard Anderson, Michael Brown and Joseph Goldstein attached ferritin, an iron-containing protein that is very dark in the electron microscope, to LDL. At low temperature the ferritin-LDL sat in coated pits; after warming for a few minutes it was inside vesicles. The left image shows a coated vesicle; the middle image is a model of the clathrin cage built from structural data. Dynamin was found through genetics. A fruit-fly mutant called shibire, Japanese for paralysed, collapses within seconds when warmed to 29 degrees. Its nerve endings fill with deep pits with long necks that cannot be cut, so synaptic vesicles are not recycled and the synapses run out. When the gene was cloned, it encoded dynamin. Cooling the flies lets the pits pinch off and the flies walk again: a temperature-sensitive switch for endocytosis.

title: Endocytosis, lysosomes and autophagy
section: Receptor-mediated uptake: the LDL receptor cycle
text:
Receptor-mediated uptake: the LDL receptor cycle


LDL: a particle of about 22 nm with ~1500 cholesterol esters inside and one apoB protein that the receptor binds.
The receptor enters pits with or without LDL; at the acidic pH of the endosome it lets go. LDL goes to the lysosome; the receptor recycles.
Feedback: a cell with plenty of cholesterol makes fewer receptors. Try it: the LDL receptor cycle.


Now the LDL receptor cycle, the classic example of receptor-mediated endocytosis. LDL, low-density lipoprotein, is a particle of about 22 nanometres. Its core holds about 1500 cholesterol molecules esterified to fatty acids; its surface is a single layer of phospholipid with one very large protein, apolipoprotein B, which the receptor recognises. Step one: the receptor in the plasma membrane binds LDL. Step two: the receptor’s NPxY signal brings it into a clathrin-coated pit. Step three: the vesicle delivers it to the sorting endosome, where the pH is about 6. At this pH the receptor changes shape and releases LDL. Step four: the empty receptor returns to the surface in a recycling vesicle. A round trip takes about ten minutes, and one receptor can make more than a hundred trips during its life. Step five: LDL travels on to the lysosome, where enzymes split the cholesterol esters and free cholesterol leaves for the ER and membranes. Step six: when the cell has enough cholesterol, it makes fewer receptors and less cholesterol of its own. The demo lets you change each step and see the effect on blood LDL.

title: Endocytosis, lysosomes and autophagy
section: How do we know? Patients’ cells revealed the receptor
text:
How do we know? Patients’ cells revealed the receptor


Brown and Goldstein grew skin fibroblasts from patients and gave them radioactive (¹²⁵I) LDL. Binding at 4 °C (no endocytosis), uptake and degradation at 37 °C.
Most FH cells could not bind LDL: no working receptor. One patient’s cells (“J.D.”) bound LDL but never took it in. His receptor had lost the tyrosine of NPxY: the signal that brings receptors into coated pits.
Schematic heights, not their data.


This is the experiment that revealed the receptor. Brown and Goldstein took small skin biopsies from healthy people and from patients with FH, grew the fibroblasts in culture and gave them LDL labelled with radioactive iodine. At 4 degrees, membranes do not bud, so the label measures only LDL bound to the surface. At 37 degrees they measured how much LDL got inside and how much was broken down to free iodotyrosine, which shows it reached the lysosome. Normal cells bound, took in and degraded LDL. Cells from most children with severe FH did none of these: they had no working receptor. But cells from one patient, known by his initials J.D., were different. They bound LDL normally but did not take it in. Electron microscopy showed his receptors spread over the surface instead of collected in coated pits. Years later, sequencing showed a single change in the receptor’s cytosolic tail: the tyrosine of the NPxY signal was replaced by cysteine. One amino acid in the tail decides whether the receptor enters coated pits. The bar heights here are schematic.

title: Endocytosis, lysosomes and autophagy
section: Endosomes mature and become more acidic
text:
Endosomes mature and become more acidic


The V-ATPase uses ATP to pump H⁺ into the lumen (the transporters lecture). The further along, the more pumps and the lower the pH.
Early endosome: sorting station, tubules for recycling, marked by Rab5. It matures into a late endosome (Rab7) with internal vesicles (a multivesicular body), which fuses with lysosomes.
Block the pump (bafilomycin) or neutralise the acid (chloroquine, ammonia): sorting and digestion stop.


The endocytic compartments form a series with falling pH. A vesicle from the surface has the neutral pH of the outside, 7.4. Within a few minutes it fuses with an early endosome, at about pH 6 to 6.5. The early endosome is the sorting station; it sends out thin tubules that carry membrane and receptors back to the surface. Over ten to twenty minutes the early endosome matures: it loses Rab5 and gains Rab7, moves towards the centre of the cell along microtubules, and buds parts of its own membrane inwards to form internal vesicles. This is a late endosome, also called a multivesicular body, at pH 5 to 5.5. It then fuses with lysosomes, at pH 4.5 to 5. The pH is set by the V-ATPase, the rotary proton pump you met in the transporters lecture, together with chloride channels that balance the charge. We know the acid matters because drugs that block the pump, such as bafilomycin, or weak bases that soak up the protons, such as chloroquine, stop receptors from releasing their cargo and stop lysosomal digestion.

title: Endocytosis, lysosomes and autophagy
section: Sorting: recycle or destroy?
text:
Sorting: recycle or destroy?


The same acid gives different results: it frees LDL from its receptor, frees iron from transferrin.
What goes back to the surface follows the membrane (tubules); what stays in the lumen goes to the lysosome.
Ubiquitin on a receptor’s tail sends it into internal vesicles and to the lysosome: this is how cells switch off growth-factor signalling.


Three receptors, three outcomes, all decided in the same early endosome. The LDL receptor lets go of LDL in acid. The receptor stays in the membrane and returns to the surface, while LDL, free in the lumen, goes on to the lysosome. The transferrin receptor carries iron into the cell. Transferrin is a blood protein that holds two iron ions. In the acidic endosome the iron is released and transported into the cytosol, but the empty transferrin, unusually, stays bound to its receptor at acid pH. Both return to the surface, where at pH 7.4 the empty transferrin falls off and can pick up more iron. The EGF receptor is a growth-factor receptor. After it binds EGF it is tagged with ubiquitin on its cytosolic tail. A protein machine called ESCRT recognises the ubiquitin and pushes the receptor into the small internal vesicles of the late endosome, so it can no longer signal and is destroyed in the lysosome. This is one way cells end a signal, and it returns in the signalling lectures. The rule: membrane with no tag recycles, lumen content and tagged membrane go to the lysosome.

title: Endocytosis, lysosomes and autophagy
section: How do we know? Follow labelled cargo in the electron microscope
text:
How do we know? Follow labelled cargo in the electron microscope









HeLa cell, 5 minutes after uptake. Two cargoes are labelled in two ways:

EGF receptors: antibody with a 10 nm gold bead (black dots, arrowheads);
transferrin: coupled to an enzyme (peroxidase) that makes a dark stain.

Both are in early endosomes (E); none yet in late endosomes (M), which are full of internal vesicles, or lysosomes (L).
Repeat at 15, 30, 60 min: EGF receptor moves on to M and L; transferrin goes back to the surface. Scale bar 500 nm.



How do we know which compartment a cargo visits, and when? This electron micrograph shows the method. The cells were given two labelled cargoes. The EGF receptors carry an antibody coupled to a gold particle of 10 nanometres, which is very dense to electrons and shows up as a sharp black dot; the arrowheads point to them. Transferrin was coupled to the enzyme horseradish peroxidase, which turns a chemical called DAB into a dark precipitate, so every compartment that contains transferrin is darkly stained. The cells were fixed five minutes after uptake. Both labels are in early endosomes, marked E, which are irregular and tubular. The late endosome, M, is round and full of small internal vesicles, and the lysosome, L, is dense; neither contains label yet. If you fix cells at later times, the EGF receptor gold appears in the late endosomes and then the lysosomes, while transferrin never gets there: it returns to the surface. Such pulse–chase experiments, a labelled pulse followed by a chase of time, built the map you saw at the start. Today they are often done with fluorescent tags in living cells.

title: Endocytosis, lysosomes and autophagy
section: Lysosomes: the cell’s digestive organelle
text:
Lysosomes: the cell’s digestive organelle


About 60 hydrolases that break down proteins, lipids, nucleic acids and sugars. They work best at pH 4.5–5 and poorly at pH 7.2: a safety lock if a lysosome leaks.
The membrane is protected by a thick layer of sugar-coated proteins on its inner face; transporters export amino acids, sugars and cholesterol for reuse.
Discovered by Christian de Duve by cell fractionation (Nobel Prize 1974).


The lysosome is where endocytosed material ends up. It is a membrane-bound organelle, usually a few hundred nanometres across, filled with about sixty different hydrolases, enzymes that split bonds with water: proteases, lipases, nucleases, phosphatases and glycosidases. Together they can break down almost any biological molecule. Two features keep the cell safe. First, the enzymes are acid hydrolases: they work best at the lysosome’s pH of 4.5 to 5 and are much less active at the cytosol’s pH of 7.2, so if a lysosome leaks a little, the cytosol is not digested. Second, the lysosomal membrane proteins are heavily glycosylated on the luminal side, and this sugar coat protects them from the proteases. The products of digestion are not wasted: transporters in the membrane export amino acids, sugars, nucleotides and cholesterol back to the cytosol. The lysosome was discovered in the 1950s by Christian de Duve, who separated rat liver cells by centrifugation and found a fraction with acid phosphatase activity that was hidden until the membranes were broken: a method you met in the cell-methods lecture. Lysosomes are also a signalling platform, as the autophagy slide will show.

title: Endocytosis, lysosomes and autophagy
section: Getting enzymes to the lysosome: the mannose-6-phosphate tag
text:
Getting enzymes to the lysosome: the mannose-6-phosphate tag


Lysosomal enzymes are made in the ER like secreted proteins. In the Golgi an enzyme adds phosphate to a mannose sugar on them: mannose-6-phosphate (M6P).
M6P receptors in the trans Golgi collect them into clathrin vesicles; in the acidic late endosome they let go, and the receptor returns.
M6P receptors also sit on the cell surface and catch enzymes from outside: the basis of enzyme replacement therapy.


How do new lysosomal enzymes find the lysosome? They begin like secreted proteins: they are made on ribosomes on the ER, enter the ER lumen and receive N-linked sugar chains. In the cis Golgi, an enzyme called GlcNAc phosphotransferase recognises a patch on the folded surface of lysosomal enzymes, and only on them, and adds a phosphate to one or more mannose sugars. This mannose-6-phosphate is the address label. In the trans Golgi network, mannose-6-phosphate receptors bind the label at neutral pH and are collected into clathrin-coated vesicles, using the same coat as at the plasma membrane but a different adaptor. The vesicles fuse with late endosomes. At pH about 5.5 the receptor releases its enzyme, the phosphate is removed, and the receptor returns to the Golgi for another load: the same logic as the LDL receptor. Some enzyme escapes into the secretory route and leaves the cell, but M6P receptors on the cell surface catch it and bring it in by endocytosis. In I-cell disease the phosphotransferase is missing: the enzymes are not tagged, are secreted into the blood, and the patient’s lysosomes fill with undigested material.

title: Endocytosis, lysosomes and autophagy
section: Big gulps: macropinocytosis and phagocytosis
text:
Big gulps: macropinocytosis and phagocytosis







A neutrophil (yellow) engulfing anthrax bacteria (orange), coloured scanning EM. Scale bar 5 µm.
