title: Quiz: actin, cell shape and migration
text:
Short questions to check your understanding of the lecture Actin: cell shape and migration. Try each on paper first, then open the hint or the answer. The tag after each question shows the learning outcome (ELO) it practises.

Q1. Which of the three filament systems (a) has no polarity, (b) binds GTP in its subunits, (c) is about 7 nm wide and binds ATP? Which one has no motor proteins? [ELO 6]






Hint





Think of the comparison table: subunit, width, polarity, motors.









Answer






Intermediate filaments have no polarity (and no motors). (b) Microtubules: the αβ-tubulin dimer binds GTP. (c) Actin filaments: 7 nm wide, actin binds ATP. Intermediate filaments are the only system without motor proteins; myosins move on actin, kinesins and dynein on microtubules.





Q2. Why are the two ends of an actin filament different? Name them and say which one grows faster. [ELO 6]






Hint





How are the subunits oriented in the filament?









Answer





All actin subunits join head-to-tail and point the same way, so the two ends expose different faces of the subunit: the filament is polar. The barbed (+) end grows much faster than the pointed (−) end (higher on-rate). In addition, the + end usually carries fresh ATP-actin, while the − end carries old ADP-actin.




Q3. The critical concentration is about 0.1 µM at the barbed end and about 0.6 µM at the pointed end. Predict what happens at each end of a filament at (a) 0.05 µM, (b) 0.3 µM, (c) 2 µM free G-actin. [ELO 6]






Hint





Above its critical concentration, an end grows; below it, it shrinks.









Answer






0.05 µM is below both: both ends shrink. (b) 0.3 µM is between them: the + end grows and the − end shrinks, so the filament treadmills (at this concentration it also gets a little longer overall). (c) 2 µM is above both: both ends grow, the + end much faster.





Q4. Why does a cell need nucleators such as Arp2/3 and formins, although it contains plenty of free actin? How do the filaments they make differ? [ELO 6]






Hint





What is the slow step in making a new filament?









Answer





Starting a new filament is slow: actin dimers and trimers are unstable and fall apart before they grow. Nucleators make the first seed, so the cell decides where and when filaments start. Arp2/3 binds the side of an existing filament and makes a branch at 70°, giving a branched mesh (lamellipodia). Formins stay on the growing + end and make long, unbranched filaments, which are bundled in filopodia and stress fibres.




Q5. Match each protein to its job: profilin, capping protein, cofilin, fascin. Jobs: (i) cuts old ADP filaments; (ii) packs filaments into tight parallel bundles; (iii) blocks the + end; (iv) delivers ATP-actin to free + ends. [ELO 6]






Hint





Two of them act on the ends or on free actin, one on old filaments, one between filaments.









Answer





Profilin → (iv); capping protein → (iii); cofilin → (i); fascin → (ii).




Q6. A fibroblast is injected with a form of Rac that is always bound to GTP. What actin structure appears? Which structure would you expect with active Rho, and with active Cdc42? [ELO 6] [ELO 3]






Hint





Each of the three GTPases switches on its own nucleator.









Answer





Active Rac → lamellipodia (via WAVE and Arp2/3, also called membrane ruffles). Active Rho → stress fibres and focal adhesions, with contraction (formin mDia and ROCK → myosin II). Active Cdc42 → filopodia (N-WASP/Arp2/3 and formins). A GTP-locked form cannot be switched off by a GAP, so the structure keeps forming.




Q7. You want to know whether a cell needs actin polymerisation to take up particles by phagocytosis. Which drug would you add, and what control would you include? Why can you not use fluorescent phalloidin to film actin in the living cell? [ELO 6] [ELO 1]






Hint





Which drugs block polymerisation? Does phalloidin cross the plasma membrane?









Answer





Add latrunculin (binds G-actin, so filaments cannot grow) or cytochalasin D (caps + ends) and measure uptake. Controls: cells with the solvent only (e.g. DMSO); a washout to show the effect is reversible; a check that the cells are still alive (e.g. another process that does not need actin still works). Phalloidin does not enter living cells (and it would freeze the filaments if it did), so it is used on fixed cells. For live cells, use GFP-actin or Lifeact-GFP.




Q8. Listeria moves through the cytosol of a host cell without any motor protein of its own. Explain how. [ELO 6] [ELO 9]






Hint





Which host protein complex does ActA switch on, and what does it build?









Answer





The bacterial surface protein ActA, at one pole only, mimics the cell’s WASP proteins and activates the host Arp2/3 complex. A branched actin network, the comet tail, forms behind the bacterium; the + ends grow against the bacterial surface and push it forward, just as a lamellipodium pushes the membrane. Cofilin and capping protein from the host keep the tail turning over. The bacterium uses this to push into the neighbouring cell.

title: Actin: cell shape and migration
section: About this lecture

title: Actin: cell shape and migration
section: The question: how does a cell crawl?
text:
The question: how does a cell crawl?

A fish keratocyte crawling on glass (time in min:s; the cell is about 40 µm wide). Its front edge is labelled with a fluorescent actin-binding protein (EGFP-VASP).

A fish skin cell (keratocyte) crawls about 10–20 µm per minute, about its own length every minute, and keeps its fan shape. White blood cells chasing bacteria are about as fast.
It has no legs, no cilia and no flagellum. The front edge is a thin sheet, about 0.2 µm thick. What pushes it, and how does the cell steer?


These are frames from a movie of a keratocyte, a skin cell from a fish, crawling on a glass surface. A fluorescent protein marks the front edge, where actin grows. In about three minutes the top cell crosses most of the picture. Fish keratocytes are a favourite model because they move fast and steadily and keep the same fan shape for a long time. Many cells in your body crawl: white blood cells crawl out of blood vessels towards an infection, fibroblasts crawl into a wound to close it, and nerve cells send growth cones along paths in the developing brain. Cancer cells crawl too, which is how a tumour spreads. A crawling cell has no legs and no flagellum. The front of the keratocyte is a very thin sheet, the lamellipodium, only a fraction of a micrometre thick, and this sheet advances steadily. By the end of the lecture you will see that the front is pushed by actin filaments growing against the membrane, that adhesions grip the surface, and that the motor protein myosin pulls the rear forward. We will build this up from a single filament.

title: Actin: cell shape and migration
section: Three filament systems
text:
Three filament systems








Actin and microtubules are polar, dynamic and carry motor proteins. Intermediate filaments are non-polar ropes that resist pulling.
All three are built from many small subunits held by non-covalent bonds: quick to build, quick to take apart.









Here is the whole cytoskeleton on one slide. Actin filaments are the thinnest, about seven nanometres wide, made of the globular protein actin, which binds ATP. Microtubules are hollow tubes, 25 nanometres wide, made of tubulin dimers that bind GTP. Intermediate filaments are about ten nanometres wide and built from long fibrous proteins that twist together like a rope; there are many kinds, such as keratins in skin and lamins in the nucleus. Actin filaments and microtubules have two different ends, so they are polar, and motor proteins walk along them in one direction: myosins on actin, kinesins and dynein on microtubules. Both are highly dynamic. Intermediate filaments have no polarity, no motors, and are much more stable; their job is mechanical strength. All three are polymers of small subunits held together by weak, non-covalent bonds, so the cell can build and dismantle them in seconds to minutes. The picture shows cultured cells stained for actin in red, microtubules in green and DNA in blue. Microtubules come in the next lecture; intermediate filaments in the one after.

title: Actin: cell shape and migration
section: G-actin and F-actin: a polar filament that splits ATP
text:
G-actin and F-actin: a polar filament that splits ATP








G-actin (globular) joins head-to-tail to form F-actin (filament), a two-stranded helix. One of the most abundant proteins in a cell.
All subunits point the same way: the filament has a fast-growing barbed (+) end and a slow pointed (−) end.
Soon after joining, each subunit hydrolyses its ATP. A young filament end carries an ATP cap; old parts hold ADP.



Atomic model of an actin filament, 13 subunits; one strand blue, the other white.


Actin is a 42-kilodalton globular protein, called G-actin when it is free. It has a deep cleft that holds one ATP or ADP molecule. G-actin subunits join head-to-tail to form a filament, F-actin, which looks like two strands twisted around each other. Because every subunit faces the same way, the two ends of the filament are different. The names barbed end and pointed end come from old electron micrographs: when myosin heads are bound along a filament, they look like arrowheads, and the barbed end is the feathered end of the arrow. Subunits join the barbed end much faster, so it is also called the plus end. Here is the important chemistry. Free actin binds ATP. A few seconds after a subunit has joined a filament, it hydrolyses its ATP to ADP and phosphate, and the phosphate leaves slowly, over minutes. ADP-actin binds its neighbours less tightly. So a growing filament has a fresh ATP region near the barbed end, and the older part is ADP-actin. This difference between young and old actin is how the cell knows which filaments to take apart.

title: Actin: cell shape and migration
section: The two ends have different critical concentrations
text:
The two ends have different critical concentrations


At each end, subunits join at a rate proportional to [G-actin] and leave at a constant rate. Where the two balance is the critical concentration (Cc).
Below Cc an end shrinks; above it the end grows. Because of ATP hydrolysis, Cc is lower at the barbed end (about 0.1 µM) than at the pointed end (about 0.6 µM).


Think of each filament end as a place where two reactions happen. Free actin joins with a rate equal to an on-rate constant times the G-actin concentration, and subunits leave with a constant off-rate. The net growth is the difference, a straight line against concentration. Where the line crosses zero, joining and leaving balance; that concentration is called the critical concentration. Below it, the end shrinks; above it, the end grows. You know this logic from chemical equilibrium: the critical concentration is like a dissociation constant. If the filament were made of ATP-actin only, both ends would have the same critical concentration, because the subunit is the same at both ends. But the barbed end usually carries ATP-actin and the pointed end old ADP-actin, which leaves more easily. Measured in the test tube, the critical concentration is about 0.1 micromolar at the barbed end and about 0.6 at the pointed end. That gives three zones. Below 0.1, both ends shrink. Above 0.6, both grow. In between, the barbed end grows while the pointed end shrinks. That middle zone is the topic of the next slide.

title: Actin: cell shape and migration
section: Treadmilling
text:
Treadmilling


Between the two critical concentrations, subunits join the + end and leave the − end at the same rate: the filament keeps its length and moves forward, while each subunit stays in place.
This needs a constant supply of energy: ATP hydrolysis. Try it: Demo: actin treadmilling


At one particular concentration between the two critical concentrations, about 0.2 micromolar in the test tube, the barbed end gains exactly as many subunits per second as the pointed end loses. The filament keeps the same length, but it moves through space, like the track of a tank or a treadmill. Look at the green subunit. It was labelled with a dye, and it stays at the same place while the filament moves past it to the right. Each subunit joins at the plus end, ages as it moves towards the minus end, and leaves from there, to be recharged with ATP and used again. This is a steady state, not equilibrium: it runs only because ATP is hydrolysed in the filament. A real lamellipodium works like this, but as a whole network rather than one filament, and much faster, because helper proteins speed up both joining at the front and loss at the back. In the demo you can move the concentration slider and watch a single filament grow, treadmill or shrink, and see the dyed subunits stand still.

title: Actin: cell shape and migration
section: Starting a filament: nucleators
text:
Starting a filament: nucleators


Making a new filament from scratch is slow: a pair of actin molecules falls apart before a third one arrives. So the cell decides where filaments start.
Arp2/3 complex binds the side of an existing filament and starts a branch at 70°. It is switched on by WASP/WAVE proteins at the membrane.
Formins ride on the growing barbed end and make long, unbranched filaments.


Once a filament exists, it grows fast. The hard part is starting one. Two actin molecules stick together only weakly and usually separate again before a third arrives; a trimer is the first stable seed. This step is so slow that a cell can keep a high concentration of free actin without filaments forming at random. Instead, the cell uses nucleators, which it places where it wants new filaments. The first is the Arp2/3 complex. Arp stands for actin-related protein: Arp2 and Arp3 look like actin and act as the first two subunits of a new filament. The complex sits on the side of an existing filament, the mother, and starts a daughter filament at an angle of about seventy degrees. Repeated branching makes a tree-like network. Arp2/3 is inactive until proteins of the WASP and WAVE family switch it on, and these sit at the plasma membrane. The second kind of nucleator is the formins. A formin forms a ring around the barbed end and stays attached while subunits are added, while it feeds in actin bound to profilin. Formins make long straight filaments, which cross-linkers gather into bundles.

title: Actin: cell shape and migration
section: Actin-binding proteins run the cycle
text:
Actin-binding proteins run the cycle


In a cell, free actin is tens of µM, far above both critical concentrations. Yet filaments do not grow everywhere: profilin lets actin join only free + ends, and capping protein blocks most + ends.
Cofilin takes old ADP filaments apart, so monomers come back for new growth.


The test-tube rules hold in the cell, but a set of actin-binding proteins changes the speeds. Profilin binds free actin. It helps actin swap its ADP for ATP, and the profilin–actin complex can join a free barbed end but not a pointed end, and it does not start new filaments. Capping protein binds barbed ends very tightly and stops growth there, so filaments stay short and only new, uncapped ends grow. Cofilin binds the sides of old, ADP-containing filaments, twists them and cuts them. Cutting makes new ends and speeds up disassembly, which returns subunits to the pool. So the ATP clock in the filament marks old actin for destruction. Finally, cross-linking proteins hold filaments together. Fascin packs them into tight parallel bundles, as in filopodia. Alpha-actinin makes looser bundles with room for myosin, as in stress fibres. Filamin joins filaments at wide angles into a mesh, as in the cortex. A cell contains a high concentration of unpolymerised actin, tens of micromolar, mostly bound to profilin and to another small protein, thymosin. That pool is ready to grow fast wherever the cell uncaps or creates new barbed ends.

title: Actin: cell shape and migration
section: Four actin structures in one cell
text:
Four actin structures in one cell





Electron micrograph of a cell edge: the lamellipodium’s dense mesh (left) and filopodia filled with bundles of parallel filaments.

Lamellipodium, filopodium, stress fibre, cortex: the same actin, different helper proteins.



With these building blocks a cell makes four main actin structures. At the front of a crawling cell is the lamellipodium, a thin sheet filled with a branched mesh made by Arp2/3; it pushes the leading edge. Filopodia are thin finger-like spikes that stick out from the edge. They contain a tight parallel bundle of long filaments made by formins and held together by fascin, with all barbed ends at the tip; filopodia explore the surroundings, like antennae. Stress fibres are thick bundles that cross the cell. They contain actin, the motor myosin II and alpha-actinin, and they end in focal adhesions, where the cell grips the surface. They can contract. Finally, the cortex is a thin mesh just under the whole plasma membrane. It gives the surface its stiffness and shape, and it is the layer that cuts the cell in two at cytokinesis. The electron micrograph on the right shows the real thing at the edge of a cultured cell: the dense mesh of the lamellipodium and the long bundles of filopodia growing out of it.

title: Actin: cell shape and migration
section: Rho, Rac and Cdc42: switches for actin
text:
Rho, Rac and Cdc42: switches for actin


Small GTPases of the Rho family are on with GTP and off with GDP. Signals turn them on through GEFs; GAPs turn them off.
Cdc42 → filopodia, Rac → lamellipodia, Rho → stress fibres and contraction (via myosin II). How do we know: injecting active forms into resting fibroblasts made each structure within minutes.


How does a cell decide where to build a lamellipodium or a stress fibre? The decision is made by three small GTPases of the Rho family: Cdc42, Rac and Rho. They work like the Ras switch you meet in the signalling lectures. Bound to GDP, they are off. A guanine nucleotide exchange factor, a GEF, activated by a signal from a receptor, swaps GDP for GTP and turns them on. A GTPase-activating protein, a GAP, helps them hydrolyse the GTP and turns them off. Each active GTPase switches on its own set of actin regulators. Cdc42 activates N-WASP, which activates Arp2/3, and formins: the result is filopodia. Rac activates the WAVE complex and Arp2/3: lamellipodia. Rho activates a formin called mDia, which makes long filaments, and a kinase called ROCK, which activates myosin II: stress fibres and contraction. This was found in a classic set of experiments around 1992 to 1995. Researchers starved fibroblasts so they had few actin structures, then microinjected active forms of each GTPase and stained the actin. Each GTPase produced its own structure within minutes. This is a simplified picture; in real cells the three also affect each other.

title: Actin: cell shape and migration
section: The crawling cycle: protrude, adhere, contract
text:
The crawling cycle: protrude, adhere, contract


At the front, active Rac builds a lamellipodium that pushes the membrane forward; new adhesions (integrins) grip the surface.
At the rear, Rho activates myosin II, which pulls the cell body forward, and old adhesions let go. (Myosin is the topic of the lecture on myosin and the mechanical cell.)


Now put the parts together. Cell crawling is a cycle of four steps that run at the same time in different parts of the cell. First, protrusion: at the front, Rac is active, and a lamellipodium pushes the membrane forward. Second, adhesion: the new front forms adhesions, where transmembrane proteins called integrins bind to proteins of the surface or the extracellular matrix, and link inside to the actin filaments. Third, contraction: myosin II, activated by Rho at the back and in the middle of the cell, pulls on actin filaments and drags the cell body forward. Fourth, release: adhesions at the rear come loose, so the rear can follow. The front and the rear must be different, so the cell is polarised: Rac and Cdc42 dominate at the front and Rho at the rear. If adhesion is too weak, the cell slips; if it is too strong, it cannot let go at the rear. That is why the fastest cells have medium adhesion. We look closer at the pushing step next, and at myosin in a later lecture.

title: Actin: cell shape and migration
section: How the lamellipodium pushes
text:
How the lamellipodium pushes


Front: Rac and WAVE switch on Arp2/3 at the membrane; new branches start there. Their + ends grow against the membrane and push it, a few nanometres at a time.
Capping protein stops ends that fall behind, so actin goes to the ends at the front. Back: cofilin takes the old network apart; profilin returns the monomers to the front.


Let us zoom into the lamellipodium. This picture is a snapshot from the model in the demo, drawn to scale: one micrometre of edge. At the membrane, Rac and the WAVE complex activate Arp2/3, so new branches start right behind the membrane. Their barbed ends grow towards the membrane. A single growing filament can push only with a small force; the membrane fluctuates a little, and each time a gap opens, another subunit slips in. Many filaments together push the whole edge forward. Filaments that point the wrong way, or fall behind, are capped by capping protein and stop. That is useful: by limiting the number of growing ends, the cell sends its actin to the ends that do the work. Behind the front, the network ages: its ATP is hydrolysed, cofilin binds and cuts the old filaments, and subunits are released. Profilin recharges them with ATP and they diffuse forward to be used again. So the whole lamellipodium treadmills, much like the single filament, but much faster. In the demo you can change the amounts of Arp2/3, capping protein and cofilin and measure how fast the edge moves.

title: Actin: cell shape and migration
section: How do we know? Seeing actin
text:
How do we know? Seeing actin



Mouse fibroblasts stained with fluorescent phalloidin: stress fibres and edges. Scale bar 10 µm.


Phalloidin, a toxin from the death cap mushroom, binds only F-actin. With a fluorescent dye attached, it stains filaments in fixed cells (it does not enter living cells).
Live imaging: express GFP-actin or Lifeact-GFP (a small actin-binding peptide) and film the cell.
Speckle microscopy: very little labelled actin makes single speckles in the network. Speckles stay put or flow backwards while the edge moves forward: the network treadmills.
FRAP (bleach and watch recovery, the membrane lecture) shows actin turns over in seconds to minutes.



How do we see actin? The standard method for fixed cells is phalloidin. It comes from the death cap mushroom, Amanita phalloides, and it binds tightly between subunits of actin filaments, but not to free actin. Coupled to a fluorescent dye, it stains all filaments in a fixed and permeabilised cell, as in this picture of mouse fibroblasts, where the bright lines are stress fibres. Phalloidin does not cross the membrane of a living cell, and it would freeze the filaments if it did. For living cells we express a fluorescent actin-binding probe. GFP-actin is built into filaments; Lifeact is a short peptide of seventeen amino acids that binds filaments and is fused to GFP. Watching live cells shows how fast actin structures change. A clever trick is speckle microscopy: if only a tiny fraction of the actin carries a dye, the network looks speckled, and each speckle marks a group of subunits. In a lamellipodium the speckles do not move forward with the edge; they stay still or flow backwards and disappear further back. That is direct evidence that the network grows at the front and is taken apart at the back. FRAP, from the membrane lecture, gives the turnover time.

title: Actin: cell shape and migration
section: How do we know? Drugs as tools
text:
How do we know? Drugs as tools









Drug (source)
Target
Effect on filaments




Latrunculin (sponge)
binds G-actin
no new growth; filaments fall apart


Cytochalasin D (fungus)
caps + ends
no growth at + ends


Jasplakinolide (sponge), phalloidin
binds F-actin
filaments cannot come apart




A powerful way to test whether a process needs actin is to block actin with a drug and see if the process stops. Several natural toxins act on actin, each at a different step. Latrunculin, from a Red Sea sponge, binds free G-actin one to one, so the free concentration falls below the critical concentration. Filaments stop growing and are taken apart. Cytochalasin D, from a fungus, binds barbed ends and blocks growth there, like capping protein. Jasplakinolide, from another sponge, and phalloidin stabilise filaments so they cannot come apart; jasplakinolide enters living cells, phalloidin does not. A surprise: both destroying and freezing actin stop a lamellipodium. Freezing works because the network can no longer be recycled, so the monomer pool runs out. This tells us that the turnover itself, not just the presence of filaments, is needed. In experiments, a lamellipodium stops within a minute of adding latrunculin or cytochalasin. Good experiments use a low dose, short times and a washout, because these drugs act on every actin structure in the cell. The demo lets you add latrunculin, cytochalasin and phalloidin to a single filament.

title: Actin: cell shape and migration
section: Why it matters: cancer spreads by crawling
text:
Why it matters: cancer spreads by crawling


Most cancer deaths are caused by metastasis: cells leave the primary tumour, invade the tissue, enter a vessel and grow elsewhere.
Invading cells use the actin machinery of this lecture: lamellipodia, invadopodia (actin-rich protrusions that digest the matrix), Rho/ROCK and myosin to squeeze through gaps. Many tumours make more Rac, Cdc42 or their activators.
Blocking migration in patients has been hard: actin is everywhere, and cells switch between crawling modes. Rho-kinase (ROCK) inhibitors are used for glaucoma; as anti-metastasis drugs they are still experimental.


A primary tumour in a well-defined place can often be removed by surgery. The real danger is metastasis, when cells spread and form new tumours in other organs; most cancer deaths are caused by it. Metastasis starts with cell migration. A cancer cell in an epithelium loosens its junctions to its neighbours, crosses the basement membrane, crawls through the connective tissue, squeezes into a blood or lymph vessel, and later squeezes out somewhere else. Every step uses the actin machinery from this lecture. Invasive cells form lamellipodia and invadopodia, small actin-rich protrusions driven by Arp2/3 and cortactin that deliver enzymes to digest the matrix. They also use Rho, ROCK and myosin II to push their nucleus through narrow gaps. Many tumours make too much of Rac, Cdc42 or the proteins that turn them on. Drugs against migration have been disappointing so far. Actin is needed in every cell, including the heart, so a general actin drug is too toxic, and cancer cells can switch between a lamellipodium-based and a contraction-based way of moving. ROCK inhibitors such as netarsudil are approved for glaucoma, but not for cancer. You meet tumour biology in the disease course, and drug development in the course on clinical trials.

title: Actin: cell shape and migration
section: Why it matters: Listeria hijacks the lamellipodium machine
text:
Why it matters: Listeria hijacks the lamellipodium machine









Listeria monocytogenes in infected tissue (electron micrograph).


The food-borne bacterium Listeria makes ActA at one end. ActA acts like WASP: it switches on host Arp2/3, and a comet tail of branched actin pushes the bacterium through the cytosol at several µm per minute.
It pushes into the next cell without leaving the cytosol, so it escapes antibodies. It is dangerous in pregnancy and for the immunocompromised.


Our last example shows how good a machine the lamellipodium is: a bacterium steals it. Listeria monocytogenes causes listeriosis, a food-borne infection that can cross the placenta and the blood–brain barrier. It is dangerous in pregnancy, for newborns, old people and people with a weak immune system. After entering a cell, Listeria breaks out of its vacuole into the cytosol. It makes a surface protein called ActA at one pole only. ActA mimics the cell’s own WASP proteins and switches on Arp2/3. The bacterium then sits at the front of its own little lamellipodium: a comet tail of branched actin forms behind it and pushes it through the cytosol at roughly the speed of a crawling cell. In the tail, the filaments stay still while the bacterium moves; it is treadmilling again. When the bacterium hits the plasma membrane, it pushes out a finger that is taken up by the neighbouring cell. Listeria then escapes from the double-membrane vacuole and starts again. It spreads from cell to cell without ever being outside, where antibodies could reach it. Famously, Listeria movement was rebuilt in a test tube with a handful of pure proteins: actin, Arp2/3, cofilin and capping protein, with ATP; profilin made it faster. Capping protein was essential. More in the course on microbial pathogenesis.

title: Actin: cell shape and migration
section: Summary
text:
Summary

The cytoskeleton has three filament systems: actin (7 nm, ATP, polar, myosins), microtubules (25 nm, GTP, polar, kinesin and dynein) and intermediate filaments (10 nm, non-polar, strength).
G-actin polymerises into polar F-actin and then hydrolyses ATP. The barbed (+) end has a lower critical concentration than the pointed (−) end; between the two, filaments treadmill.
The cell controls actin with nucleators (Arp2/3: branches; formins: long filaments) and actin-binding proteins (profilin, capping protein, cofilin, cross-linkers), switched by Cdc42, Rac and Rho.
Lamellipodia, filopodia, stress fibres and the cortex are built from the same actin. A cell crawls by protruding, adhering, contracting (myosin II) and releasing its rear.
Methods: phalloidin staining, live imaging, speckles and FRAP, and drugs (latrunculin, cytochalasin, jasplakinolide). Metastasis and Listeria depend on this machinery.

Read more (optional): Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell, 7th ed., ch. 16.
Image credits

Five take-home points. First, the cytoskeleton has three filament systems with different subunits, widths and jobs; actin and microtubules are polar and dynamic and carry motors, intermediate filaments give strength. Second, actin polymerisation follows simple rules: subunits join and leave at each end, ATP is hydrolysed after joining, and the two ends have different critical concentrations, which allows treadmilling. Third, the cell decides where and when filaments grow with nucleators, actin-binding proteins and the Rho-family switches. Fourth, the same actin builds four structures, and crawling is a cycle of protrusion, adhesion, contraction and release. Fifth, you can see actin with phalloidin and live probes, and block it with drugs that act at specific steps, and the same machinery drives cancer cell invasion and the spread of Listeria. Next lecture: microtubules and motor proteins.

title: Study questions: actin, cell shape and migration
text: Study questions in the style of the written exam. Write your answer first (a few sentences, or a labelled sketch where it helps), then compare with the model answer. Each question is tagged with its learning outcome (ELO). Questions tagged [VG] are of the kind used for the higher grade: predict, compare, explain an unexpected result or design an experiment.

title: Study questions: actin, cell shape and migration
section: G-level questions
text:
G-level questions
1. Compare actin filaments, microtubules and intermediate filaments. For each, give the subunit, the approximate width, whether it is polar, its motor proteins and one main job. [ELO 6]






Model answer















Actin filaments
Microtubules
Intermediate filaments




Subunit
actin (globular), binds ATP
αβ-tubulin dimer, binds GTP
fibrous proteins: keratins, vimentin, lamins …


Width
about 7 nm
about 25 nm (hollow tube)
about 10 nm


Polar?
yes (barbed + / pointed −)
yes (plus / minus)
no


Motors
myosins
kinesins, dynein
none


Main job
cell shape, crawling, cortex, contraction, cytokinesis
long-range transport, mitotic spindle, cilia
mechanical strength, nuclear lamina



All three are built from many subunits held by non-covalent bonds. Actin and microtubules are highly dynamic; intermediate filaments are much more stable.




2. Describe what happens to the nucleotide of an actin subunit from the moment it is free in the cytosol until it leaves a filament again. Why does this matter for the cell? [ELO 6]






Model answer





Free G-actin binds ATP (profilin helps exchange ADP for ATP). The ATP-actin joins a filament, mostly at the barbed (+) end. A few seconds later the subunit hydrolyses ATP to ADP + Pi; the Pi leaves slowly, over minutes. The older part of the filament therefore holds ADP-actin, which binds less tightly and is recognised by cofilin, which cuts and takes apart old filaments. The released ADP-actin exchanges its ADP for ATP again and can be reused. This matters because (1) the ATP clock marks old filaments for removal, so the cell turns its actin over; (2) hydrolysis makes the two ends different, which allows treadmilling; (3) the energy of ATP keeps the system out of equilibrium.




3. Explain the terms critical concentration and treadmilling. Sketch net growth against G-actin concentration for both ends of a filament and mark the three zones. [ELO 6]






Model answer





At each end, subunits join at a rate \(k_\text{on}[\text{G-actin}]\) and leave at a rate \(k_\text{off}\). The net growth is a straight line against concentration; it is zero at the critical concentration \(C_c = k_\text{off}/k_\text{on}\). Below \(C_c\) the end shrinks, above it grows. Because of ATP hydrolysis, \(C_c\) is lower at the barbed end (about 0.1 µM) than at the pointed end (about 0.6 µM). Sketch: two rising lines, the barbed one steeper, crossing zero at 0.1 and 0.6 µM. Zones: below 0.1 µM, both ends shrink; between 0.1 and 0.6 µM, the + end grows while the − end shrinks; above 0.6 µM, both grow. Treadmilling is the state in the middle zone where the + end gains as many subunits as the − end loses (about 0.2 µM in the test tube): the filament keeps its length but moves forward, and each subunit stays in place while it passes from the + end to the − end. It needs a constant supply of ATP.




4. What is the role of the Arp2/3 complex and of formins? Where in the cell would you find the filaments that each one makes? [ELO 6]






Model answer





Both are nucleators: they overcome the slow step of starting a filament (unstable actin dimers and trimers), so the cell decides where new filaments start. Arp2/3 (with the actin-like Arp2 and Arp3) binds the side of an existing filament and starts a branch at about 70°. It must be activated by WASP/WAVE proteins, which sit at the plasma membrane. Repeated branching makes the branched mesh of the lamellipodium (and of endocytic patches and Listeria comet tails). Formins form a ring around the barbed end and stay on it while it grows, feeding in profilin–actin. They make long, unbranched filaments, found in filopodia (bundled by fascin), stress fibres and the contractile ring of cytokinesis.




5. A cell contains tens of µM unpolymerised actin, far above the critical concentration. Explain why actin does not polymerise everywhere, and how the cell makes it grow fast in one place. [ELO 6]






Model answer






Nucleation is slow, so new filaments do not form spontaneously. (2) Most monomers are bound to profilin (and thymosin): profilin–actin cannot start filaments and cannot join pointed ends, only free barbed ends. (3) Capping protein blocks most barbed ends. So growth happens only where there are free barbed ends. The cell makes them locally: a signal activates Rac or Cdc42 at one part of the membrane, which activates WAVE/WASP → Arp2/3 (new branches) or formins. The large profilin–actin pool then adds rapidly to these ends. Behind, cofilin takes old ADP filaments apart and refills the pool.





6. Describe the four main actin structures in a crawling fibroblast. For each, say what the filaments look like and name one protein that builds or organises it. [ELO 6]






Model answer





Lamellipodium: a thin sheet at the leading edge with a branched mesh of short filaments, + ends towards the membrane; built by Arp2/3 (activated by Rac and WAVE), trimmed by capping protein, recycled by cofilin. Filopodia: thin finger-like protrusions with a tight parallel bundle of long filaments, + ends at the tip; formins and fascin. Stress fibres: thick contractile bundles across the cell, with myosin II and α-actinin, ending at focal adhesions; made under Rho (formin mDia, ROCK). Cortex: a thin mesh under the whole plasma membrane, cross-linked by filamin (and spectrin); gives the surface stiffness and forms the contractile ring at cytokinesis.




7. Explain how Rho-family GTPases work as switches, and which actin structure Cdc42, Rac and Rho each control. Describe the experiment that showed this. [ELO 6] [ELO 3]






Model answer





Rho-family GTPases are small G proteins: on with GTP, off with GDP. A GEF, activated by a signal (e.g. a growth-factor receptor), exchanges GDP for GTP; a GAP stimulates GTP hydrolysis and turns the switch off. Active Cdc42 → filopodia (N-WASP/Arp2/3, formins); active Rac → lamellipodia (WAVE → Arp2/3); active Rho → stress fibres and focal adhesions, and contraction (formin mDia; ROCK → myosin II). Experiment: fibroblasts were starved of serum so they had few actin structures. Active (GTP-locked) forms of each GTPase were microinjected, and the cells were fixed and stained with fluorescent phalloidin a few minutes later. Each GTPase gave its own structure.




8. Describe the steps by which a cell crawls across a surface. What is the job of actin polymerisation, of adhesions and of myosin II? [ELO 6]






Model answer






Protrusion: at the front, actin polymerisation in the lamellipodium (Rac, WAVE, Arp2/3) pushes the membrane forward; filopodia probe the surroundings. (2) Adhesion: new adhesions form at the front, where integrins bind the surface or extracellular matrix and link to actin inside; they give the cell grip. (3) Contraction: myosin II (activated by Rho/ROCK) pulls on actin filaments and drags the cell body forward. (4) Release: adhesions at the rear come apart, so the rear follows. Polymerisation pushes, adhesion transmits force to the surface, myosin pulls. The cell is polarised: Rac and Cdc42 at the front, Rho at the rear.





9. Name three drugs that act on actin, say what each binds, and what happens to the actin in a living cell. Which one is used to stain actin, and why only in fixed cells? [ELO 6] [ELO 1]






Model answer





Latrunculin binds G-actin (1:1) and lowers the free monomer concentration below the critical concentration: filaments are taken apart and do not regrow. Cytochalasin D binds barbed ends and blocks growth there (like capping protein): structures that need + end growth, such as lamellipodia, stop. Jasplakinolide (and phalloidin) bind F-actin and stabilise it: filaments cannot be taken apart, the monomer pool is used up, and dynamic structures stop as well. Phalloidin, coupled to a fluorescent dye, stains filaments in fixed and permeabilised cells; it does not cross the membrane of living cells (and would freeze actin if it did). For live cells one uses GFP-actin or Lifeact-GFP.

title: Study questions: actin, cell shape and migration
section: VG-style questions
text:
VG-style questions
10. [VG] A lamellipodium in a cultured cell stops advancing within a minute after (a) latrunculin and also after (b) jasplakinolide, although the two drugs have opposite effects on filaments. Explain both results. What does this tell you about how a lamellipodium works? [ELO 6]






Model answer






Latrunculin binds free G-actin, so the free concentration falls below the critical concentration of the barbed end. The barbed ends at the membrane cannot grow and cannot push; the network is taken apart. (b) Jasplakinolide stabilises filaments, so old filaments at the back of the lamellipodium can no longer be taken apart. The network keeps adding actin at the front but returns none, so the monomer pool runs out within a short time, and growth at the membrane stops too. Together: the lamellipodium is a treadmilling network, not a static structure. It needs both polymerisation at the front and disassembly at the back (cofilin), and the recycling of monomers between them. Blocking either half stops the edge.





11. [VG] In a test tube with pure proteins, beads coated with an Arp2/3 activator (like Listeria ActA) move by forming actin comet tails. Predict what happens to bead speed when you (a) leave out capping protein, (b) leave out cofilin, (c) double the Arp2/3 complex. Explain. [ELO 6]






Model answer






No capping protein: the beads stop (or move very slowly). New branches keep forming and no barbed end is ever capped, so the number of growing ends rises. All of them use monomers, and the free actin falls to near the critical concentration; growth spreads over too many ends and few of them push the bead. Capping protein “funnels” monomers to the few young ends at the bead surface. This was the observed result in the reconstitution experiments. (b) No cofilin: the beads slow down and stop after a while: filaments in the tail are not taken apart, actin accumulates in the tail and the monomer pool runs out. (c) More Arp2/3: more branches and more ends. At first more ends share the load and may push faster, but more ends also use more monomers; beyond an optimum the speed falls for the same reason as in (a). (The demo shows the same behaviour.)





12. [VG] Researchers suspect that a new kinase inhibitor reduces metastasis because it blocks cell migration. Design experiments in cultured cancer cells to test (a) whether the drug slows migration, and (b) whether it acts through Rac-driven lamellipodia or through Rho/ROCK-driven contraction. [ELO 6] [ELO 1] [ELO 9]






Model answer






Live imaging of migration with and without the drug (solvent control, several doses): a scratch (wound-healing) assay or single-cell tracking on a matrix-coated dish (speed, persistence), and a 3D invasion assay (cells in or through a collagen or Matrigel layer, e.g. a Transwell chamber). Check that the drug does not simply kill cells or stop division (viability, short times, or block division). (b) Phalloidin staining of fixed cells: loss of lamellipodia suggests the Rac pathway; loss of stress fibres suggests Rho/ROCK. Live imaging with Lifeact-GFP to measure protrusion of the leading edge. Pull-down assays for active (GTP-bound) Rac and Rho with and without the drug. Rescue: express a GTP-locked Rac (or Rho) and see whether migration is restored. Compare with known inhibitors (a ROCK inhibitor, an Arp2/3 inhibitor such as CK-666) as reference. A drug that acts on Rac should reduce edge protrusion and lamellipodia; one that acts on ROCK should reduce myosin activity (phospho-myosin light chain staining) and contraction.

title: Study questions: actin, cell shape and migration
section: Explore
text:
Explore
Demo: actin treadmilling. Two tabs. 1 · One filament: a single actin filament in a large pool of G-actin, seen from the side. Subunits join and leave one at a time, at random moments, with measured on- and off-rates for each end (the barbed end has a critical concentration of 0.12 µM, the pointed end 0.6 µM). Colours show the nucleotide: fresh ATP-actin (light yellow), ADP-Pi-actin (amber) and old ADP-actin (grey). A few subunits carry a green dye (speckles). The left graph gives the expected net growth at each end against free G-actin; the right graph follows the two ends over time. Add capping protein, cytochalasin D, phalloidin or latrunculin. 2 · Lamellipodium: a 1 µm piece of the leading edge seen from above. Arp2/3 makes branches next to the membrane, the growing ends push the membrane, capping protein stops ends, and cofilin takes old filaments apart. Change the amounts and watch the edge speed, or press Measure speed curve. Both tabs are stochastic models that are qualitatively right: the behaviour is right, the numbers are illustrative. Time starts at real time; you can speed it up. Live runs are random, so your numbers will differ a little from the solutions; the “expected” rates and the speed curve use fixed values and seeds.



E1. Tab 1. Press below both (0.05), then between (0.3), then above both (1.0). For each, read the expected net rate at the + and − ends and say whether the filament shrinks, treadmills or grows. Where are you on the left graph? [ELO 6]
E2. Tab 1. Press steady state (0.17) and set time to 10× real time. Watch for about 2 minutes. What happens to the length, to the two lines in the right graph, and to the green speckles? Where are the yellow (ATP) and the grey (ADP) subunits, and why? [ELO 6]
E3. [VG] Predict first. At 0.3 µM, what will happen if you add capping protein? And at 1.0 µM? Check, and explain. Why is it useful for a cell, which has tens of µM free actin, to cap most of its barbed ends? [ELO 6]
E4. Tab 1. Set G-actin to 1.0 µM and add latrunculin 1 µM, then 2 µM. Read the free G-actin and the net rates. Then set G-actin to 0.05 µM, latrunculin to 0, and tick phalloidin. Compare the two drugs: which one destroys filaments, which one protects them, and why? [ELO 6]
E5. [VG] Tab 2. Predict first: sketch how the edge speed will depend on the amount of capping protein, from 0 to 3× normal. Then choose vary: capping protein and press Measure speed curve. Explain the shape. Repeat for Arp2/3 and cofilin. Why does the edge stop when there is no capping protein, although capping protein itself blocks growth? [ELO 6]
E6. Tab 2. Press no Arp2/3 and watch for 20 s. Then press normal. What happens, and why? How does this explain why Listeria needs the host’s Arp2/3 complex, and what would a drug that blocks ActA do? [ELO 6] [ELO 9]






Solutions





E1. 0.05 µM: + end −0.82, − end −0.74 subunits/s: both ends shrink (below both critical concentrations, the red zone on the left), about 1.6 subunits/s in total; a 100-subunit filament is gone within about a minute. 0.3 µM: + end +2.08, − end −0.41: the + end grows and the − end shrinks: the filament treadmills (between the two critical concentrations) and also gets longer overall, +1.7 subunits/s (about 0.3 µm/min). 1.0 µM: + end +10.2, − end +0.50: both ends grow (above both). On the left graph the dots sit on the two lines at the chosen concentration; an end grows when its dot is above zero.
E2. At 0.17 µM the + end gains about 0.58 subunits/s and the − end loses about 0.58: the length stays about the same (it wanders up and down a little, because events are random). In the right graph both lines rise in parallel: the filament moves to the right, about 1.5 nm/s (0.1 µm/min). The green speckles stay where they are: the filament moves through space while each subunit stays put, joins at + and, minutes later, leaves at −. The yellow ATP subunits are only at the + end, because ATP is hydrolysed seconds after a subunit joins; behind them are amber ADP-Pi subunits and then grey ADP subunits towards the − end, because Pi leaves over minutes. The subunits that leave at the − end are the oldest ones.
E3. Capping blocks the + end completely (no joining, no loss). At 0.3 µM only the − end works, and 0.3 µM is below its critical concentration (0.6 µM): the filament shrinks from the − end at about 0.4 subunits/s. At 1.0 µM the − end is above its critical concentration and grows slowly, about +0.5 subunits/s; the filament grows only from the − end, 20 times slower than an uncapped + end would. In a cell, free actin is far above both critical concentrations, so every free + end would grow fast and use up the monomers. By capping most ends, the cell keeps a large pool of free actin ready and lets only the ends it chooses (new branches, formin-bound ends at the right place) grow. Cytochalasin D does the same as capping protein in this model.
E4. With 1.0 µM actin and 1 µM latrunculin, most monomers are bound: free actin is about 0.36 µM; the filament still treadmills (+2.8, −0.3). With 2 µM latrunculin, free actin falls to about 0.15 µM: + end +0.3, − end −0.6, so the filament shrinks overall (−0.3 subunits/s). More latrunculin pushes free actin below the + end critical concentration and both ends shrink. Phalloidin at 0.05 µM: the off-rates fall 50-fold, so both critical concentrations drop almost to zero; the filament now grows (+0.55 and +0.05) at a concentration where it shrank before (E1). Latrunculin destroys filaments indirectly by taking away the monomers; phalloidin protects them by gluing the subunits together so they cannot leave. That is why phalloidin is used as a stain for filaments (in fixed cells) and why it is poisonous.
E5. The capping curve rises and then falls: speed about 0 at 0×, 3.6 at 0.25×, 7 at 0.5×, about 10 µm/min at 1–1.5×, and 9.5 at 2× and 7 at 3×. With too little capping, branches keep forming and no end stops growing; the many growing ends use up the monomers (free G-actin falls to 0; nearly all actin is in the network) and none of them can grow and push. Capping protein funnels the monomers to the few young ends next to the membrane. With too much capping, ends are stopped before they reach the membrane, so few ends push (about 7 touch the membrane at 3×, against about 25 at 1×), and the edge slows. Arp2/3: about 0.7 µm/min at 0 (only a few filaments made without Arp2/3), about 10 at 0.5–1×, then falling to about 6 at 3× (too many ends use the monomers, as with too little capping). Cofilin: about 1.6 µm/min at 0, rising steadily to about 12.6 at 3×: without cofilin the old network is not taken apart, most actin is stuck in it, and the monomer pool is nearly empty; more cofilin recycles faster. (Real numbers vary by cell type; the shapes of the curves are the point.)
E6. Without Arp2/3 no new branches form. The existing ends are capped one by one within a few seconds, the network falls behind and is taken apart, and the edge stops (0–2 µm/min; free G-actin rises to the full 20 µM, but there are no ends to use it). With normal Arp2/3 the network restarts (there are a few filaments from other nucleators to branch from) and the edge returns to about 10 µm/min. Listeria has no motor of its own; its ActA protein switches on the host Arp2/3 complex at the bacterial surface, so the bacterium sits at the front of its own small lamellipodium (the comet tail). A drug that blocks ActA would stop the tail forming, so the bacterium could not move or spread to the next cell; it would stay in one cell, exposed to the immune system.

title: Taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: About this lecture
text:
About this lecture
Microscopy tells you where things are. This lecture is about the other half of cell biology: what things are, how many cells have them, and what happens if you change them.
After this lecture you can:

Say what cell culture gives you (primary cells, cell lines, organoids) and what it cannot tell you.
Explain how fractionation separates organelles, and how marker proteins show what is in each fraction.
Explain how antibodies are used to detect and pull out one protein (western blot, immunoprecipitation).
Read a flow cytometry dot plot and explain how cells are sorted.
Choose a perturbation (inhibitor, RNAi, CRISPR, overexpression) and the right controls to test whether a protein is needed for a process.

ELO 1: methods used to study cell biological processes.

In the microscopy lecture we looked at cells. Looking tells you where a protein is, but it does not tell you what the protein does. To answer that question, cell biologists do three kinds of things. They grow cells outside the body, so they have material to work with. They take cells apart, to find out which molecules belong to which compartment. And they change cells on purpose, by removing or adding a protein, and watch what happens. This lecture goes through these three steps. You have met some of the tools before: protein purification, SDS-PAGE and PCR from biochemistry. Here we use them on whole cells. Several of these methods also come back in the laboratory part of the course, so this lecture is also your preparation for the labs. At the end we see how the same methods are used to find new drugs and to make a living cancer therapy.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it
Taking cells apart and perturbing them

title: Taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: The question: one protein, four questions
text:
The question: one protein, four questions


You have found a new protein, X. Immunofluorescence shows it in the cytoplasm.
To understand it, you need four more answers:

Which compartment is it really in? (fractionation)
How much is there, and does the amount change? (western blot)
Which cells in a mixed population have it? (flow cytometry)
Is it needed for anything? (perturbation)

And for all of these you need cells to work on. (cell culture)






HeLa cells stained with antibodies: microtubules, mitochondria (HSP60), nucleoli (fibrillarin) and DNA.


Here is a typical situation. Someone has made an antibody against a new protein, X, and the image shows it somewhere in the cytoplasm. That is a start, but a fluorescence image has limits. Two compartments can look the same at two hundred nanometres resolution, so you cannot be sure which one X is in. An image is also hard to quantify: is there more X after a treatment, or is the staining just brighter? An image shows a few cells; you may want to know the fraction of cells in a whole blood sample that carry X. And above all, seeing X tells you nothing about what X does. Each of these questions has its own standard method, and those methods are the topic of this lecture. Keep protein X in mind; we come back to it in a worked example near the end.

title: Taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: Cell culture: primary cells and cell lines
text:
Cell culture: primary cells and cell lines



Cells are grown in a sterile dish or flask, in a medium with salts, glucose, amino acids and growth factors, at 37 °C.
Primary cells come straight from a tissue. They behave like the tissue, but divide only a limited number of times.
Cell lines divide without limit (they are immortal), usually because they come from a tumour or carry an immortalising gene. HeLa, from the tour of the cell, is the classic example.
Trade-off: cell lines are easy and reproducible; primary cells are closer to the body.







Living HeLa cells in a culture flask (phase contrast).





A sterile bench (biosafety cabinet) for cell culture work.


Cell culture means growing cells outside the body. The cells sit in a plastic dish or flask, covered by a liquid medium that gives them what the blood would: salts, glucose, amino acids, vitamins and growth factors, usually from serum. They are kept at body temperature in an incubator. All work is done on a sterile bench, because bacteria and fungi grow much faster than human cells. There are two main kinds of cultured cells. Primary cells are taken directly from a tissue, for example skin fibroblasts or blood cells. They are close to the real tissue but stop dividing after a limited number of divisions, so you must keep getting new ones. Cell lines have become immortal, either because they come from a tumour, like HeLa, or because an immortalising gene was added. They are cheap, grow fast and every lab can use the same line, which makes results comparable. The price is that a cell line has adapted to life on plastic and is often genetically abnormal.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it
Taking cells apart and perturbing them

title: Taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: Stem cells, 3D culture and organoids
text:
Stem cells, 3D culture and organoids



Cells on flat plastic lose much of their normal shape and behaviour.
3D culture: cells grow in a soft gel that mimics the extracellular matrix.
Organoids: stem cells in a gel organise themselves into a small, simple version of an organ, with several cell types in roughly the right places.
Made from adult stem cells (e.g. gut) or from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPS cells), which can be made from a patient’s skin or blood.
Use: study a patient’s own cells, and test drugs on them.







A small-intestine organoid. Green: E-cadherin at cell–cell contacts; red: the signalling protein AKT; blue: nuclei.


A cell spread flat on hard plastic is not in its natural situation. In a tissue, cells touch neighbours on all sides, sit on a soft extracellular matrix, and have a top and a bottom. One way closer to the body is 3D culture in a soft gel. Organoids take this a step further. If you put intestinal stem cells into such a gel with the right growth factors, they divide and organise themselves into a small hollow structure with crypts and villus-like regions and several cell types, like a tiny gut. Organoids can also be made from induced pluripotent stem cells, which are made by reprogramming ordinary adult cells, such as skin cells, back to a stem-cell state. This means you can grow organoids from a particular patient. A well-known use is cystic fibrosis: gut organoids from a patient swell when the chloride channel works, so you can test which drug works for that patient’s mutation. You will meet that channel in the ion channels lecture.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it
Taking cells apart and perturbing them

title: Taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: Is the culture what you think it is?
text:
Is the culture what you think it is?
Two classic problems, both easy to miss:








Problem
Why it matters
How labs check




Wrong cells (misidentified cell line)
Hundreds of published “cell lines” turned out to be another line, often HeLa. Results are then about the wrong tissue.
DNA fingerprint (STR profile) compared with a reference database


Hidden bacteria (Mycoplasma)
Tiny bacteria without a cell wall. Not visible in the microscope, not killed by common antibiotics; they change the cells’ metabolism and gene expression.
Regular PCR test of the culture



Lesson: a result from cultured cells is only as good as the cells. Good laboratory practice includes checking them.

Two problems have caused a lot of wrong results in cell biology, and both are invisible. The first is the wrong cells. Because HeLa grows so well, a few HeLa cells carried over into another culture can take it over within weeks. Many lines that were thought to come from, for example, breast or prostate tissue were later shown to be HeLa or another line. Today journals often ask for proof of identity, a DNA fingerprint based on short tandem repeats, which is compared with the database for that line. The second problem is Mycoplasma, a group of very small bacteria without a cell wall. Because they lack a wall, the usual penicillin-type antibiotics do not kill them, and because they are so small, the culture still looks clear. Yet they change how the cells behave. Labs therefore test their cultures regularly, usually with PCR. The general lesson fits the lab part of this course: you must be able to trust your material before you can trust your result.

Taking cells apart and perturbing them

title: Taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: Taking cells apart: homogenisation and centrifugation
text:
Taking cells apart: homogenisation and centrifugation


First break the cells gently (homogenisation), so organelles stay intact.
Then spin at increasing speed and time. Large, dense particles pellet first; small ones need stronger force.


To find out which compartment a protein belongs to, you can take the cell apart and separate its organelles. First the cells are broken open gently, for example by pushing them through a narrow gap, in a buffer that keeps the organelles intact. This is called homogenisation, and the result is a homogenate. Then comes differential centrifugation. A short, slow spin pellets the biggest and heaviest particles: nuclei and unbroken cells. The liquid on top, the supernatant, is spun again, faster and longer. Now mitochondria, lysosomes and peroxisomes form a pellet. A still stronger spin pellets small membrane pieces called microsomes, which are mostly bits of ER and Golgi that closed into little vesicles. After the strongest spin, what stays in the supernatant is the cytosol with its soluble proteins. The g-values and times in the figure are typical numbers; every lab adjusts them. This approach earned Albert Claude, Christian de Duve and George Palade a Nobel Prize in 1974; de Duve found lysosomes and peroxisomes this way.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it
Taking cells apart and perturbing them

title: Taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: Density gradients and marker proteins
text:
Density gradients and marker proteins








Differential spins give mixtures. For better separation, spin through a gradient (e.g. sucrose): each organelle stops where its density matches.
Which fraction holds which organelle? Use marker proteins known to sit in one organelle only. If protein X runs with the ER marker, X is probably in the ER.









Differential centrifugation is quick but crude: each pellet is a mixture. A cleaner separation uses a density gradient. A tube is filled with a sugar solution that is light at the top and dense at the bottom. The homogenate goes on top, and during a long spin in an ultracentrifuge each organelle moves down until it reaches the layer that has the same density as itself, and stops there. Afterwards the tube is emptied in small fractions from top to bottom. But the fractions are not labelled, so how do you know what is in each one? You run each fraction on a western blot, which comes in two slides, and stain for marker proteins: proteins that are known to live in only one organelle. In the figure, GM130 marks the Golgi, calnexin the ER, TOM20 mitochondria and catalase peroxisomes. Then you stain for your protein X. If X appears in the same fractions as calnexin, it is probably an ER protein. Real gradients overlap more than this clean figure shows.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it
Taking cells apart and perturbing them

title: Taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: Antibodies as tools
text:
Antibodies as tools


An antibody binds one small patch, the epitope, on one protein. That makes it a tag-free “probe” for a protein.
Immunoprecipitation (IP): antibody on beads pulls the target, and the proteins bound to it, out of a cell lysate.
The same antibody, with a fluorophore, gives the immunofluorescence images from the microscopy lecture.


Antibodies are the most used tool in cell biology, because they recognise one protein among thousands. An antibody of the IgG type has two identical binding sites, each of which fits a small patch on the target, the epitope, typically five to ten amino acids or a small surface. In immunofluorescence, which you saw in the microscopy lecture, the antibody carries a fluorophore so you can see where the target is. In immunoprecipitation, the antibody is attached to small beads. You mix the beads with a cell lysate, the target binds, you spin the beads down and wash away everything else. What remains is the target protein together with any proteins that were bound to it. That is how you find the partners of a protein. Everything depends on the antibody being specific. A bad antibody also binds other proteins, and then every result is wrong. A good control is to use cells where the target gene has been knocked out: the signal should disappear.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it
Taking cells apart and perturbing them

title: Taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: Western blot: which protein, how much
text:
Western blot: which protein, how much








Recap: SDS-PAGE separates proteins by size. Proteins are then transferred to a membrane, and one protein is found with an antibody.
Band position = size (check it!). Band strength = amount, compared between lanes.
Always include a loading control (a protein that should not change).









You know SDS-PAGE from biochemistry: proteins are coated with a negative detergent and pulled through a gel by an electric field, so small proteins move fastest. A western blot adds two steps. First the separated proteins are moved from the gel onto a thin membrane by a second electric current, where they stick. Then the membrane is incubated with a primary antibody against your protein, and a secondary antibody that binds the first one and carries an enzyme. The enzyme turns a substrate into light, and you see a band. The position of the band tells you the size, which is a good check that the antibody found the right protein. The strength of the band tells you roughly how much protein there is, compared between lanes. In lane three of the figure there is less protein X, for example after the gene was knocked down. To compare lanes fairly you also stain a loading control, a protein such as actin or tubulin whose amount should be the same everywhere, to show that the same amount of material was loaded.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it
Taking cells apart and perturbing them

title: Taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: Flow cytometry: measuring thousands of single cells
text:
Flow cytometry: measuring thousands of single cells








Cells pass a laser one at a time, thousands per second. Scatter gives size (forward) and granularity (side); fluorescence tells which labelled molecules each cell carries.
FACS (cell sorting): droplets with a wanted cell get a charge and are deflected into a tube.









A western blot measures the average of millions of cells ground up together. Often you want to know about single cells instead: what fraction of the cells carry protein X, and do they carry a lot or a little? Flow cytometry does this. Cells, labelled with fluorescent antibodies, are made into a suspension and pushed through a narrow stream, squeezed by sheath fluid so that they pass a laser one by one. For each cell, detectors record how much light is scattered forwards, which tells about size, how much is scattered sideways, which tells about internal granularity, and how much fluorescence comes out in each colour. A modern machine measures tens of thousands of cells per second and a dozen or more colours. A cell sorter, called FACS for fluorescence-activated cell sorting, goes one step further: the stream breaks into droplets, a droplet that contains a wanted cell gets an electric charge, and electric plates steer it into a collection tube. So you can collect, for example, only the cells that carry X, and keep them alive.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it
Taking cells apart and perturbing them

title: Taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: Reading a dot plot: gating
text:
Reading a dot plot: gating


Each dot is one cell. First gate on scatter to keep the cells you want (here lymphocytes) and drop debris.
Then plot two fluorescent markers: four quadrants, four kinds of cell. Report the percentage in each. Try it: the gating game.


The results of flow cytometry are shown as dot plots, where every dot is one cell. Analysis is done in steps called gating. In panel A, forward scatter is plotted against side scatter for a blood sample. Small, smooth lymphocytes form one cloud, granulocytes with many granules sit higher, and monocytes between. Debris and dead cells sit in the low corner. We draw a gate, a boundary, around the lymphocytes, and from now on look only at those cells. In panel B the same lymphocytes are plotted by two fluorescent antibodies: one against CD4 and one against CD8, two surface proteins that mark two kinds of T cell. The plot falls into four quadrants. Cells with only CD4 are helper T cells, cells with only CD8 are cytotoxic T cells, cells with neither are mostly B cells and NK cells here, and very few have both. The result is reported as percentages. In HIV infection, for instance, the CD4 percentage falls over time, and this is how it is measured in the clinic. These data are simulated, but typical.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it
Taking cells apart and perturbing them

title: Taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: Changing cells on purpose: four tools
text:
Changing cells on purpose: four tools

Each tool acts at a different step from gene to activity, and each has its own speed, strength and pitfalls.

So far we have described cells. Now we change them. You can interfere at each step from gene to working protein, and the figure arranges the four common tools along that path. CRISPR knockout cuts the gene itself, so the cell can never make the protein again; it is all-or-none and permanent, but it takes weeks to make a cell line, and a cell may adapt to the loss over that time. RNA interference destroys the messenger RNA with a short matching RNA; the protein drops, usually not to zero, for a few days. Overexpression adds extra copies of the gene, so the cell makes more protein than normal; this tests whether the protein is sufficient to cause an effect. Finally, small-molecule inhibitors, which are drugs, block the protein directly. They act within minutes, can be washed out, and you can vary the dose, but most inhibitors also hit other proteins, called off-targets. Because each tool has different weaknesses, a strong conclusion usually uses two different tools that give the same answer.
