Taking cells apart and perturbing them

title: Taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: CRISPR–Cas9: knocking out a gene
text:
CRISPR–Cas9: knocking out a gene


Cas9 cuts DNA where a guide RNA matches. The quick repair often adds or removes a few letters: the reading frame shifts, and no working protein is made.
A bacterial defence against viruses, turned into a tool by Emmanuelle Charpentier (partly at Umeå University) and Jennifer Doudna: Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2020.


CRISPR-Cas9 comes from bacteria, where it is an immune system against viruses: the bacterium stores short pieces of viral DNA and uses them to guide the Cas9 enzyme to cut the virus. Researchers turned this into a tool. Cas9 is given a guide RNA whose sequence matches the gene you want to target, and it cuts both DNA strands at that place. The cell cannot leave a broken chromosome, so it repairs it, usually by simply joining the ends again. This repair is fast but sloppy: it often adds or deletes a few base pairs. If the change is not a multiple of three, the reading frame shifts, the ribosome soon meets a stop codon, and no working protein is made. That is a knockout. You know reading frames and stop codons from molecular biology, so you can see why this works. Emmanuelle Charpentier did part of her key work on CRISPR at Umeå University, and she and Jennifer Doudna received the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. CRISPR is now also used in medicine, which you may meet in later courses.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it
Taking cells apart and perturbing them

title: Taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: How do we know? Necessary, sufficient, and controls
text:
How do we know? Necessary, sufficient, and controls


Necessary: remove X → the process stops (knockout, knockdown, inhibitor). Sufficient: add X → the process starts or increases (overexpression).
Controls: a non-targeting guide or RNA; rescue (put back X and the effect disappears); a second, independent tool.


This slide is the logic behind every experiment in this lecture. Imagine you observe that cells with more protein X divide faster. Three stories fit this observation. X may drive division. Dividing cells may simply make more X, so the arrow goes the other way. Or a third factor, such as a growth signal, may raise both, and X does nothing at all. Observation alone cannot tell these apart. You must change X and keep everything else the same. If removing X stops division, X is necessary. If adding X causes division, X is sufficient. Many proteins are necessary but not sufficient. Controls make the result believable. A control guide RNA or RNA that targets nothing shows that the treatment itself does no harm. A rescue experiment, where you put back a version of X that the tool cannot hit, should bring the process back; if it does, the effect really came from losing X and not from an off-target. And a second tool that acts in a different way, giving the same result, makes the conclusion much stronger.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it
Taking cells apart and perturbing them

title: Taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: Worked example: is protein X needed for cell division?
text:
Worked example: is protein X needed for cell division?








Step
Choice
Why




Cells
A human cell line that divides well (e.g. HeLa or RPE1)
Easy to grow, many divisions to measure


Perturbation 1
RNAi against X, and a non-targeting control RNA
Fast; partial loss is fine for a first test


Check
Western blot for X, with a loading control
Did X actually go down?


Readout
Count cells over 4 days; flow cytometry of DNA content (cell-cycle phase)
Do cells divide less? Where do they stop?


Perturbation 2
CRISPR knockout, plus a rescue with X put back
Independent tool; rules out off-targets


Location
Fractionation or immunofluorescence
Where does X act?



Conclusion only if both tools agree and the rescue works.

Let us put the methods together on protein X. Suppose we want to know whether X is needed for cell division. We pick a human cell line that divides well. As a first, quick test we use RNA interference against X, side by side with a control RNA that targets nothing. Before we look at the cells we check with a western blot that X really went down, with a loading control in every lane; a perturbation that did not work tells you nothing. The readout is the number of cells over a few days, and flow cytometry of DNA content, which tells us in which phase of the cell cycle the cells get stuck; you will understand that readout fully in the cell-cycle lectures. If division slows, we confirm with a second tool, a CRISPR knockout, and do a rescue by adding back X. Finally we ask where X is, by fractionation or imaging. Only when the independent tools agree and the rescue works do we write that X is needed for division. This is the kind of reasoning the VG exam questions ask for.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it
Taking cells apart and perturbing them

title: Taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: Single-cell omics: a census of cells
text:
Single-cell omics: a census of cells


Each cell is put in its own droplet with a barcode; all its mRNAs are sequenced and counted.
Cells with similar mRNA sit together on a map: cell types, and sometimes new ones.
Cell atlases (e.g. the Human Cell Atlas) aim to map every cell type in the body.


Flow cytometry measures a dozen proteins per cell. Single-cell RNA sequencing goes much wider: it measures thousands of messenger RNAs in each of thousands of cells. A tissue is broken into single cells, and each cell is captured in a tiny droplet together with a bead that carries a unique DNA barcode. Inside the droplet, the cell’s mRNAs are copied and tagged with that barcode, so after sequencing every read can be traced back to its cell. The result is a large table of cells by genes. A computer then places cells with similar expression close together on a map, and groups of cells appear: T cells, B cells, macrophages, epithelial cells, and sometimes a small group that nobody had described before. International projects such as the Human Cell Atlas use this to make a reference map of all cell types in the human body. One cell type found this way was the ionocyte in the airways, a rare cell with very high levels of the cystic fibrosis channel CFTR. For this course, the main idea is enough: the same principle as flow cytometry, many single cells, but measuring the whole transcriptome.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it
Taking cells apart and perturbing them

title: Taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: Why it matters: finding drugs in cultured cells
text:
Why it matters: finding drugs in cultured cells



High-content screening: thousands of compounds, each in its own well with cultured cells; an automated microscope images every well.
A computer scores each well: did cells stop dividing, die, change shape, move a protein?
Example: monastrol was found in such a screen for compounds that block mitosis. It inhibits the motor protein kinesin-5, which builds the mitotic spindle.
Hits from screens are the first step of drug development, long before animals or patients.







Preparing a 384-well plate for a high-throughput screen.


Everything in this lecture comes together in drug discovery. In a high-content screen, cultured cells are grown in plates with 384 or more small wells. Each well gets a different compound from a library of many thousands. After a day or two, the cells are fixed and stained, and an automated microscope takes images of every well. Software then measures many features per cell: number of cells, nucleus size, cell shape, where a fluorescent protein sits. Compounds that cause the change you are looking for are called hits. A classic example is monastrol. In a screen for compounds that arrest cells in mitosis, researchers found a small molecule that gave cells a single round spindle instead of the normal two-poled one. It turned out to inhibit kinesin-5, a motor protein that pushes the spindle poles apart; you will meet motor proteins in the cytoskeleton lectures. Kinesin-5 inhibitors were later tested as cancer drugs. A hit like this is only the first step; the later programme course on clinical trials and drug development covers the long road from hit to medicine.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it
Taking cells apart and perturbing them

title: Taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: Why it matters: CAR-T cells, a living drug
text:
Why it matters: CAR-T cells, a living drug


A patient’s own T cells are given a new receptor, a CAR, that recognises a protein on cancer cells (here CD19 on B-cell leukaemia).
Every step uses this lecture: cell culture to grow them, flow cytometry to check them.


The second example is a therapy that is itself a cultured cell. CAR-T therapy treats some leukaemias and lymphomas that come from B cells. Blood is taken from the patient and the T cells are isolated. A gene for a chimeric antigen receptor, a CAR, is added. The outside part of the CAR comes from an antibody and binds CD19, a protein on the surface of B cells; the inside part gives the T cell its “go” signal. The modified T cells are grown in culture for one to two weeks until there are enough of them. Before they are given back, they are checked by flow cytometry: what percentage carry the CAR, and are they the right kind of cells? Then they are infused into the same patient, where they find and kill the cancer B cells. So cell culture, antibodies and flow cytometry, three methods from this lecture, are part of making the medicine. You will learn how T cells recognise and kill their targets in the later immunology course.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it
Taking cells apart and perturbing them

title: Taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: Summary
text:
Summary

Cell culture gives material to work on: cell lines are easy and reproducible, primary cells and organoids are closer to the body. Check identity and contamination.
Fractionation (differential and density-gradient centrifugation) separates organelles; marker proteins show what is in each fraction.
Antibodies find one protein: western blot (size and amount), immunoprecipitation (partners), immunofluorescence (location).
Flow cytometry measures many single cells; gating picks populations; FACS sorts them.
Perturbations (inhibitor, RNAi, CRISPR, overexpression) test whether a protein is necessary or sufficient; controls and a second tool make the conclusion strong.

Read more (optional): Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell, 7th ed., ch. 8.
Image credits

To sum up. Cell culture is the basis: cell lines for convenience, primary cells and organoids for realism, and always a check that your cells are what you think. Fractionation separates organelles by size and density, and marker proteins tell you which fraction is which. Antibodies are the most used tool: in a western blot they report size and amount, in immunoprecipitation they pull out a protein and its partners, and in immunofluorescence they show where it is. Flow cytometry turns this into single-cell numbers, and a sorter can collect living cells of one kind. Finally, to learn what a protein does you must change it, with an inhibitor, RNA interference, CRISPR or overexpression, and think carefully about necessary versus sufficient and about controls. These methods return in every later lecture, in the “How do we know?” slides, and in the lab part of the course.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it
Taking cells apart and perturbing them

title: Quiz: taking cells apart and perturbing them
text:
Short questions to check that you can choose and read the methods from the lecture. Try each on paper first, then open the hint, and only then the answer.

Q1. [ELO 1] Give one advantage of a cell line and one advantage of primary cells.






Hint





Think about how long each kind divides, and how close each is to the tissue.









Answer





Cell line: divides without limit, is cheap and easy to grow, and the same line can be used in many labs, so results are reproducible. Primary cells: come directly from the tissue, so they behave more like cells in the body (normal genome, normal regulation).




Q2. [ELO 1] In differential centrifugation, which comes down first, nuclei or ribosomes? Why?






Hint





Larger and denser particles sediment at lower force.









Answer





Nuclei, already at a low speed (about 1,000 g), because they are large and dense. Ribosomes are very small and need a very strong, long spin (well over 100,000 g).




Q3. [ELO 1] After a density gradient, fraction 4 contains the protein calnexin. What does that tell you, and why?






Hint





Calnexin is a marker protein.









Answer





Fraction 4 contains ER membranes, because calnexin is a marker protein found only in the ER. A new protein that appears in the same fractions as calnexin is probably also in the ER.




Q4. [ELO 1] In a western blot, why do you also stain for a loading control such as actin?






Hint





What if one lane simply got more sample?









Answer





To show that the same amount of protein was loaded in every lane. Only then does a weaker band of your protein mean less of that protein, not just less sample.




Q5. [ELO 1] What does immunoprecipitation give you that a western blot on a whole lysate does not?






Hint





What else comes down with the target protein?









Answer





It pulls out the target protein together with the proteins bound to it, so you can find its binding partners (for example by running the pulled-down material on a western blot or by mass spectrometry).




Q6. [ELO 1] In a flow cytometry dot plot, what is one dot, and what is a gate?






Hint





Flow cytometry measures single cells.









Answer





One dot is one cell. A gate is a region you draw on a plot so that only the cells inside it (for example lymphocytes, not debris) are analysed in the next plot.




Q7. [ELO 1] Match each tool to what it acts on: CRISPR knockout, RNAi, small-molecule inhibitor. (gene / mRNA / protein)






Hint





Follow the path from gene to active protein.









Answer





CRISPR knockout → gene (DNA). RNAi → mRNA. Inhibitor → protein (its activity).




Q8. [ELO 1] Removing protein X stops cell migration. Is X necessary or sufficient for migration? What experiment would test the other?






Hint





Removing tests one; adding tests the other.









Answer





X is necessary. To test whether it is sufficient, overexpress X (for example in cells that do not normally migrate) and see whether migration starts or increases.

title: A tour of the cell
section: About this lecture
text:
About this lecture
This is the first lecture of the course. It gives you a map of the cell that every later lecture uses.
After this lecture you can:

Name the main compartments of an animal cell and say in one sentence what each one does.
Explain topology: which spaces are on the cytosol side of a membrane and which are on the lumen side.
Give the size and number of the things inside a cell (ions, proteins, ribosomes, organelles, cells) to within a factor of ten.
Choose a model system (yeast, a cell line such as HeLa, an organoid) for a question, and say what it cannot tell you.

ELO 1 (parts of the cell, methods) and ELO 5 (organelles compared; this lecture is the first look).

Welcome to Cell Biology. This first lecture is a guided tour. We will not go deep into any one organelle today; every organelle you see here gets its own lecture later. The aim is a mental map that you can hang the rest of the course on. Keep three ideas in mind. First, the cell is divided into compartments by membranes, and the chemistry inside each compartment is different. Second, every membrane has two sides, and knowing which side is which, the topology, explains a lot of later material on protein sorting and vesicle traffic. Third, sizes and numbers matter: a protein is about five nanometres, a cell is about fifteen micrometres, and a cell holds billions of protein molecules. At the end we look at how we study cells, using model systems, and at HeLa cells: the most used human cells in research, and a story about consent that every biomedical scientist should know. This lecture belongs to ELO 1 and is the first step towards ELO 5.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it

title: A tour of the cell
section: The course map: from molecules to cells
text:
The course map: from molecules to cells

You already think in molecules: DNA, proteins, enzymes, ΔG. This course moves you one level up: to compartments (where things are), machines (what moves and signals) and decisions (divide, move or die), and to disease when these go wrong.

Here is the whole course on one slide. On the left is what you bring from biochemistry, molecular biology and chemistry: molecules, reactions, equilibria and the central dogma. We will not teach these again. The course moves you up one level of organisation. The first blocks are about compartments: what a cell is made of and how we study it, then membranes and transport, then how proteins are made, folded and sent to the right organelle. The middle blocks are about signals and machines: how a cell senses its surroundings and how the cytoskeleton gives it shape and movement. Then come decisions: when to divide and when to die. The last block is disease, seen as cell biology going wrong. Each block is one or more expected learning outcomes, ELOs, and the ELO numbers on the tiles are the same numbers as on the exam. Every lecture also ends with a drug or a disease, so you see why the mechanism matters for medicine and drug development.

How the exam works

VG

How to use this site: every quiz and study question is tagged with its ELO, for example [ELO 1]. Practise each ELO separately, because the exam passes each one separately.

The written exam is built in a way that shapes how you should study. There is one section for each of the nine theory outcomes, and you must pass every section on its own, with at least sixty per cent correct. A very good result in signalling cannot make up for a weak result in cell death. This is why every quiz and study question on this site carries an ELO tag: you can check that you can handle each outcome. Each section also has one harder question that is marked G or VG; to get VG on the exam you need VG on at least five of these nine. The VG questions ask you to predict, compare, explain an unexpected result or design an experiment, so the study questions include that kind of question for every lecture. If you pass at least six ELOs but not all nine, you do not need to redo everything: you can take an oral exam on the ELOs you missed. The exact rules are in the course plan and on Canvas. That is all the administration for today.

title: A tour of the cell
section: The question: how does one small drop do everything at once?
text:
The question: how does one small drop do everything at once?


A cultured animal cell holds about 2 picolitres of water, and in it:

billions of protein molecules, many thousands of different kinds,
enzymes that make fats next to enzymes that burn them,
enzymes that digest proteins at pH 5, in a cell whose cytosol is pH 7.2,
DNA that must be copied once per division and never digested.

How does the cell keep incompatible chemistry apart, and still get every molecule to the place where it is needed?






Cultured endothelial cells. Blue: nucleus (DNA). Green: microtubules. Red: actin filaments.


Look at the image. These are cultured cells from a cow blood vessel, stained with three fluorescent dyes: blue for DNA in the nucleus, green for microtubules and red for actin filaments. Even with only three stains you can see order: the nucleus sits in the middle, microtubules spread out from near the nucleus, and actin lines the cell edge. Now the puzzle. Each cell is a tiny volume, about two picolitres, but inside it there are billions of protein molecules doing thousands of reactions at once. Some of these reactions would destroy each other if they were mixed. Digestive enzymes that work best at pH 5 would attack the cell’s own proteins. Fat synthesis and fat breakdown would cancel each other out. DNA must be kept safe and copied exactly once per cycle. The answer, which the rest of this lecture develops, has three parts: compartments separated by membranes, transport routes between the compartments, and a cytoskeleton that organises space. Keep this question in mind; we come back to it in the summary.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it

title: A tour of the cell
section: Recap: prokaryote and eukaryote
text:
Recap: prokaryote and eukaryote










Prokaryote (bacterium)
Eukaryote (animal cell)




DNA
in the cytosol (nucleoid)
inside a nucleus with a double membrane


Internal membranes
almost none
many: ER, Golgi, endosomes, lysosomes, mitochondria, …


Typical volume
~1 µm³
~1000–4000 µm³ (about 1000× larger)




This is a recap of what you met in microbiology. A bacterium such as E. coli is about two micrometres long. It has a plasma membrane, usually a cell wall, ribosomes and its DNA in a region called the nucleoid, but no membrane around the DNA and almost no internal membranes. A eukaryotic cell is about a thousand times larger in volume. That is the key point on this slide: a bigger cell has a problem. Its surface is small compared with its volume, and molecules must travel further. Eukaryotes solve this with internal membranes, which add a large membrane area for reactions and divide the volume into compartments with different chemistry. Notice the mitochondria on the right: they are about the size of a bacterium. That is not a coincidence. Mitochondria come from a bacterium that was taken up by an ancestral cell, and they still have their own DNA and ribosomes. We come back to this in the mitochondria lecture.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it

title: A tour of the cell
section: A map of the animal cell
text:
A map of the animal cell


This is the map we use in the whole course, and the colours are fixed: every later lecture uses the same colour for the same organelle. Purple is the nucleus, teal the endoplasmic reticulum, orange the Golgi apparatus, red the mitochondria, green the endosomes and lysosomes, blue the peroxisomes, grey the cytoskeleton, and brown the plasma membrane. Start in the centre. The nucleus holds the DNA, surrounded by the nuclear envelope, which is two membranes with pores through them. The outer nuclear membrane continues into the endoplasmic reticulum, the ER. The rough ER has ribosomes on its surface and makes membrane proteins and proteins for secretion; the smooth ER makes lipids and stores calcium. Proteins go from the ER to the Golgi, which modifies and sorts them, and then on to the plasma membrane in secretory vesicles, or to lysosomes. Material taken in from outside goes to endosomes and then to lysosomes for digestion. Mitochondria make most of the ATP. The centrosome organises the microtubules. Everything else, the fluid between the organelles, is the cytosol. The picture is a simplification: a real cell has hundreds of mitochondria and a much larger ER.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it

title: A tour of the cell
section: Explore a real HeLa cell
text:
Explore a real HeLa cell

One slice through a real HeLa cell (electron microscopy, 48 × 26 µm), with the organelles outlined in the same colours as the map. Open the cell explorer: zoom in, tap an organelle to read what it is, then try Find the organelle.

The map on the previous slide is a cartoon. This is one slice through a real HeLa cell, imaged with a focused-ion-beam scanning electron microscope by the OpenOrganelle project at Janelia; the coloured outlines come from their machine-learning segmentation, checked by us. Point out the purple nucleus with its dark chromatin, the red mitochondria scattered all around it, the teal ER everywhere, and the brown plasma membrane at the edges. Note the scale: the whole slice is about 48 micrometres wide, and there are about a hundred mitochondria in this one plane alone. Note also the strange patch of cytoplasm in the middle of the nucleus: a deep fold of the nucleus, cut across, which is a good reminder that a single section can mislead. Ask students to open the explorer after the lecture, zoom in on a mitochondrion and the Golgi, and play the “Find the organelle” quiz; we will come back to how this image was made in the microscopy lecture.

*Rough values for a liver cell. They change a lot between cell types: a pancreas cell that secretes enzymes is full of ER, a fat cell is mostly a lipid droplet.

This table is the text version of the map. Do not learn the percentages by heart; learn the pattern. About half of a typical cell is cytosol, and the cytosol is where proteins are made on free ribosomes and where much of metabolism happens, for example glycolysis. Each membrane-bound organelle has a special job, and each has its own lecture, shown in the right column. Notice that the amounts depend on what the cell does. A liver cell, which does a lot of metabolism, has many mitochondria, about a fifth of its volume. A pancreatic acinar cell, which secretes large amounts of digestive enzymes, is packed with rough ER. A plasma cell, which secretes antibodies, also has a lot of rough ER. So you can often guess what a cell does by looking at its organelles under an electron microscope, and the reverse is also true. Two jobs are worth noting now because they come back: mitochondria do not only make ATP, they also start one form of cell death; and the ER is the main calcium store of the cell, which matters for signalling.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it

title: A tour of the cell
section: Two sides of every membrane: topology
text:
Two sides of every membrane: topology


This is the most important idea of today, because it explains much of protein sorting and vesicle traffic later. Every membrane separates two spaces. Look at the colours. The light yellow space is the cytosol side: the cytosol itself and the inside of the nucleus, the nucleoplasm. These two are joined through nuclear pores, which are large open channels, so they count as one space. The light blue space is the lumen side: the inside of the ER, the gap between the two nuclear membranes, the Golgi, the vesicles, endosomes and lysosomes. The lumen side is, in topology, the same as the outside of the cell. Why? Because these compartments are connected to the outside by vesicles that bud from one membrane and fuse with another, without a molecule ever crossing a membrane. A protein secreted from the ER lumen reaches the outside without ever being in the cytosol. Mitochondria are the exception: their inner space, the matrix, is a third space of its own, a legacy of their bacterial origin. Peroxisomes, not shown here, also import their proteins from the cytosol.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it

title: A tour of the cell
section: Inside-out logic: a protein keeps its orientation
text:
Inside-out logic: a protein keeps its orientation


The part of a protein that is in the ER lumen ends up outside the cell.
This is why sugar chains (added in the ER and Golgi lumen) are found on the outer surface of the cell, and why receptors have their binding site outside.


Here is topology in action. A membrane protein is made in the ER membrane. One part of it faces the ER lumen, and in the lumen the cell adds sugar chains to it. The other part, the tail, faces the cytosol. Now follow it. A vesicle buds from the ER: the lumen side of the protein now faces the inside of the vesicle. The vesicle fuses with the Golgi: the lumen side faces the Golgi lumen. A new vesicle carries it to the plasma membrane and fuses: now the lumen side faces the outside of the cell. At no step does the protein flip, and at no step does any part of it cross a membrane. So the rule is simple: lumen side equals outside. This explains why all the sugar chains of the cell surface face outwards, and why a hormone receptor made in the ER has its hormone-binding part outside the cell and its signalling part in the cytosol. When we study receptors and protein sorting, you will use this rule again and again. It is also a common exam question.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it

title: A tour of the cell
section: The scale ladder: from ion to cell
text:
The scale ladder: from ion to cell

Each step on the axis is a factor of 10. A cell is about 50,000× wider than an ion and about 3000× wider than a protein.

Cell biology covers about five orders of magnitude in size, so the axis is logarithmic: each tick is ten times the one before. An ion such as potassium is about a third of a nanometre across. A typical protein is about five nanometres. A ribosome, a large machine made of RNA and about eighty proteins, is about twenty-five nanometres. Many viruses, such as influenza or SARS coronavirus 2, are about a hundred nanometres. A bacterium and a mitochondrion are about one micrometre wide. The nucleus is a few micrometres, and a whole animal cell is ten to twenty micrometres. The bars at the bottom link to the next lecture. A light microscope cannot separate two objects closer than about two hundred nanometres, so with light you can see cells, nuclei and mitochondria, but not single ribosomes or proteins, unless you label them with a fluorescent tag. An electron microscope sees down to about a nanometre in a thin section of a cell. Remember these sizes: they let you check whether an answer is reasonable.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it

section: Numbers worth knowing
text:

Rough values of the kind collected in BioNumbers (bionumbers.hms.harvard.edu) and Cell Biology by the Numbers (Milo and Phillips). Diffusion time: t \approx x^2 / 6D with D \approx 5–10\ \mu\text{m}^2/\text{s} for a protein in cytoplasm.

These are numbers to remember as orders of magnitude, not exact values. A cell holds about one to ten billion protein molecules. Spread over a volume of a few picolitres, that is a protein concentration of a few hundred milligrams per millilitre: the cytoplasm is crowded, more like a gel than like water. Now diffusion. For a molecule that moves randomly, the time to travel a distance x grows with x squared: t is roughly x squared divided by six times the diffusion coefficient. A protein in cytoplasm has a diffusion coefficient of about five to ten square micrometres per second, so it crosses a ten-micrometre cell in a few seconds. That is fast enough for most signals. But because of the x squared, diffusion becomes useless over long distances: to diffuse one metre, from your spinal cord to your foot along a nerve axon, would take hundreds of years. This is why cells have motor proteins that carry cargo along the cytoskeleton, which you meet in the cytoskeleton block. Small molecules such as glucose diffuse about ten to a hundred times faster than proteins.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it

title: A tour of the cell
section: How do we know? Electron microscopy revealed the compartments
text:
How do we know? Electron microscopy revealed the compartments



Light microscopy (from the 1600s) showed cells and nuclei, but nothing smaller than ~0.2 µm.
1940s–1950s: the electron microscope and thin sections showed the ER, ribosomes, Golgi stacks and the inner structure of mitochondria.
At the same time, cell fractionation (breaking cells and separating parts by centrifugation) showed what each part does, for example lysosomes full of digestive enzymes.
Nobel Prize 1974: Claude, de Duve and Palade.

Lesson: one method shows where; another shows what it does. You need both.






Transmission electron micrograph of a human B lymphocyte. Large nucleus with dark chromatin; mitochondria with folded inner membranes in the cytoplasm. Scale bar 500 nm.


How do we know that the map is true? Until the 1940s, the light microscope was the main tool, and it cannot resolve anything smaller than about two hundred nanometres. Cells and nuclei were visible, and mitochondria as tiny dots, but the ER and ribosomes were invisible. The electron microscope uses electrons instead of light, and electrons have a much shorter wavelength, so it resolves structures down to about a nanometre. When researchers learned to cut cells into very thin sections, they suddenly saw the membranes inside cells: the ER, ribosomes, the Golgi stacks and the folded inner membrane of mitochondria. In the image you see a human B lymphocyte: the large nucleus with dark, condensed chromatin, and mitochondria with their folded inner membrane. But a picture shows where things are, not what they do. At the same time, others broke cells open and separated their parts by centrifugation, then measured enzymes in each fraction. This is how lysosomes and peroxisomes were discovered. Combining the two methods won the Nobel Prize in 1974. Microscopy and fractionation are the topics of the next two lectures.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it

title: A tour of the cell
section: Model systems: choose the simplest system that can answer the question
text:
Model systems: choose the simplest system that can answer the question










System
Good for
Cannot tell you




Bacteria (E. coli)
fast genetics, basic machines
anything about organelles


Budding yeast (S. cerevisiae)
eukaryote; divides in ~90 min; easy genetics
how tissues and animals behave


Human cell lines (HeLa, HEK293, …)
human proteins; easy to image and perturb
normal behaviour: most are cancer cells grown on plastic


Organoids
3D tissue from stem cells, even from a patient
blood supply, immune system, whole body


Mice
whole organism
human biology exactly; slow, costly, ethics



Yeast genetics found the genes for the cell cycle (Nobel 2001), vesicle traffic (2013) and autophagy (2016).






Budding yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae (DIC microscopy). Small buds are daughter cells growing out of the mother cells.


No single system answers every question, so cell biologists choose a model system. The rule is to use the simplest system that still has the feature you want to study. Bacteria are fast and simple but have no organelles. Budding yeast, the yeast used for baking and brewing, is the simplest common eukaryote: it has a nucleus, ER, Golgi and mitochondria, it divides in about ninety minutes, and its genes are easy to delete. Because most of the core machinery is shared with human cells, yeast genetics found the genes that control the cell cycle, the genes for vesicle traffic and the genes for autophagy, and each of these won a Nobel Prize. In the image you see yeast cells with buds; each bud is a new daughter cell. Human cell lines give human proteins in a dish. Organoids add three-dimensional tissue structure. Mice give a whole body. Each step up is closer to a patient but slower, more expensive and harder to control. In a VG question you may be asked to choose a system and to say what it cannot show.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it

title: A tour of the cell
section: Cell lines: HeLa, the first human cells that never stopped dividing
text:
Cell lines: HeLa, the first human cells that never stopped dividing



Normal human cells divide only about 40–60 times in culture, then stop.
A cell line divides without limit. Most come from tumours.
HeLa (1951) came from the cervical tumour of Henrietta Lacks. It was the first human cell line.
HeLa cells carry human papillomavirus 18 (HPV-18). Viral proteins switch off two brakes on cell division (you meet them in the cell-cycle and cancer lectures).
HeLa is not a normal cell: around 76–80 chromosomes instead of 46, and the number varies. And HeLa grows so well that it has contaminated many other cell lines, so labs now check the identity of their cells with a DNA test.







Living HeLa cells. Blue: nucleus. Green: microtubules. Red: mitochondria. Scale bar 10 µm.


Most cells taken from a human body divide a limited number of times in a dish, about forty to sixty times, and then stop. A cell line is a population of cells that can divide without limit. Almost all human cell lines come from tumours, because cancer cells have lost the normal limits on division. The first human cell line came from Henrietta Lacks, a thirty-one-year-old African American woman treated for cervical cancer at Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore in 1951. Her cells, named HeLa from her name, grew faster than any human cells before them. We now know why. Her tumour was caused by human papillomavirus type 18, and viral proteins in HeLa cells switch off two key brakes on cell division, proteins called p53 and Rb, which you meet in the cell-cycle and cancer lectures. HeLa cells also have an abnormal genome, with about eighty chromosomes. In the image you see living HeLa cells with three fluorescent labels: nucleus, microtubules and mitochondria. Note the scale bar: these cells are about twenty to forty micrometres long when they spread on glass.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it

title: A tour of the cell
section: Organoids: tissue in a dish
text:
Organoids: tissue in a dish



An organoid is a small 3D structure that grows from stem cells in a gel, with the right growth factors.
The cells organise themselves: an intestinal organoid forms crypts and a lumen, with several cell types, like the real gut lining.
Organoids can be grown from one patient’s biopsy, so you can test drugs on that patient’s own cells.
Example: in cystic fibrosis, a patient’s intestinal organoids swell when a drug restores the faulty chloride channel (CFTR). The test helps choose a drug for that patient.







Intestinal organoid grown from Lgr5⁺ stem cells. The buds are crypt-like domains around a central lumen.


Cell lines grow as a flat layer on plastic, which is far from a real tissue. Organoids are a newer model, developed from about 2009. You take adult stem cells, for example from the base of an intestinal crypt, put them in a gel that mimics the material around cells in a tissue, and add the growth factors that the stem cells normally receive. The stem cells divide and organise themselves into a small three-dimensional structure with a central lumen and buds that look like crypts, with several cell types, much like the lining of the gut. The image shows such an intestinal organoid. Because organoids can be grown from a small biopsy, they can be made from one patient. A good example is cystic fibrosis, which is caused by a faulty chloride channel called CFTR. When a drug restores channel function in a patient’s intestinal organoids, chloride and water flow into the lumen and the organoids swell. The amount of swelling helps predict whether the drug will work in that patient. You meet ion channels in lecture six and cystic fibrosis again in the disease lectures.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it

title: A tour of the cell
section: Why it matters: HeLa cells changed medicine
text:
Why it matters: HeLa cells changed medicine


Polio vaccine: poliovirus grows in HeLa, so HeLa was mass-produced to test the Salk vaccine (1953–55).
HPV and cervical cancer: HPV-18 DNA in HeLa helped show that a virus causes cervical cancer (Nobel 2008), which led to the HPV vaccine.
Drug screening: cell lines like HeLa are the first test for thousands of drug candidates: does the compound kill cells, reach its target, change an organelle?


Here is why HeLa cells matter for medicine, and why we tie them back to the cell-line slide. Because HeLa cells were the first human cells that could be grown in large amounts, they became a tool for everything. In the early 1950s, poliovirus was found to grow in HeLa cells. A laboratory at the Tuskegee Institute mass-produced HeLa cells and sent them across the United States to test whether the Salk polio vaccine produced protective antibodies. In the 1980s, researchers found DNA from human papillomavirus type 18 in HeLa cells and in many other cervical cancers. This helped prove that a virus causes cervical cancer, work that won the Nobel Prize in 2008, and it led to the HPV vaccine that is now given to children, including in Sweden. HeLa cells have been used in more than a hundred thousand research papers. Today, cell lines are the first step of drug development: before any animal or human test, a drug candidate is tested on cells. You meet the later phases in the later programme course on clinical trials and drug development.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it

title: A tour of the cell
section: Why it matters: consent, then and now
text:
Why it matters: consent, then and now



In 1951 Henrietta Lacks was not asked whether her cells could be used. This was common practice at the time. She died the same year, aged 31.
Her family learned about HeLa decades later. Companies sold HeLa cells; the family received nothing.
2013: the HeLa genome was published without the family’s consent. It also says something about her relatives’ DNA. The US National Institutes of Health then agreed with the family on controlled access, with family members on the committee.
Today, in Sweden: research on human tissue needs ethical approval and, as a rule, informed consent. Samples in biobanks are protected by law.

Ask yourself: who should decide how cells from a patient are used, and who should benefit?






HeLa cells, DNA stained with the blue dye Hoechst 33258.


The science of HeLa cannot be separated from the person. Henrietta Lacks was a mother of five who was treated for cervical cancer in a segregated hospital ward in 1951. A sample of her tumour was taken during treatment and given to a research laboratory without her knowledge. This was common practice then, but that does not make it right, and her family did not learn about the cells for more than twenty years. When the HeLa genome sequence was published in 2013, it again happened without asking the family, even though a genome also reveals information about relatives. After discussions, the US National Institutes of Health agreed with the family that the data should be in controlled access, with family members helping to decide who can use it. In 2021 the World Health Organization honoured Henrietta Lacks, and in 2023 the family reached a settlement with a company that had sold HeLa cells. In Sweden today, research on human tissue needs approval from the Swedish Ethical Review Authority, informed consent is the rule, and biobank samples are protected by law. Treat this as a question for discussion, not a closed story.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it

title: A tour of the cell
section: Summary
text:
Summary

A eukaryotic cell is divided by membranes into compartments, each with its own chemistry and job: nucleus, ER, Golgi, endosomes and lysosomes, mitochondria, peroxisomes, and the cytosol between them.
Every membrane has two sides. The cytosol and nucleoplasm form one side; the lumen of the ER, Golgi, vesicles and lysosomes is topologically outside the cell. Mitochondria have a third space.
Sizes and numbers: protein ~5 nm, ribosome ~25 nm, cell 10–20 µm; 10⁹–10¹⁰ proteins per cell; diffusion is fast over a cell but useless over long distances.
We know this from microscopy (where) and fractionation (what), and we study cells in model systems (yeast, cell lines such as HeLa, organoids), each with its limits.

Read more (optional): Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell, 7th ed., ch. 1 and ch. 12 (first section).
Image credits

Let us return to the opening question: how does one small drop of cytoplasm do everything at once? The answer is compartments. Membranes divide the cell into spaces with different chemistry, such as the acidic lysosome and the calcium-rich ER, and vesicles carry material between the lumen-side compartments without crossing a membrane. Topology is the rule to remember: the lumen side equals the outside of the cell, and the cytosol side includes the nucleus. Sizes and numbers let you check your reasoning, and the diffusion numbers explain why a large cell needs a cytoskeleton and motors. Finally, every fact on today’s map came from methods: electron microscopy showed where structures are, fractionation showed what they do, and model systems let us test ideas. The next two lectures are about these methods: microscopy, and how to take cells apart and perturb them. If you want to read more, chapter one and the first section of chapter twelve of Molecular Biology of the Cell cover today’s material, but the slides and notes are enough for the exam.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it

title: Quiz: a tour of the cell
text:
Short questions to check that you can use the map of the cell from the lecture. Try each on paper first, then open the hint, and only then the answer.

Q1. [ELO 1] Name three structures that a eukaryotic animal cell has and a bacterium does not.






Hint





Think of everything that is surrounded by its own membrane inside the cell.









Answer





Any three of: a nucleus with a double membrane (nuclear envelope), endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, endosomes and lysosomes, mitochondria, peroxisomes, and a cytoskeleton with microtubules organised by a centrosome. A bacterium has a plasma membrane, ribosomes and DNA in a nucleoid, but almost no internal membranes.




Q2. [ELO 1] Which of these spaces are on the same side of a membrane as the outside of the cell: cytosol, ER lumen, nucleoplasm, lysosome lumen, Golgi lumen?






Hint





Which compartments exchange material with the outside by vesicles that bud and fuse? Which are joined by open pores?









Answer





The ER lumen, the Golgi lumen and the lysosome lumen are topologically equivalent to the outside of the cell: vesicles carry material between them and the outside without crossing a membrane. The cytosol and the nucleoplasm form the other side; they are joined through nuclear pores.




Q3. [ELO 1] Put these in order from smallest to largest, and give a typical size for each: ribosome, mitochondrion (width), protein, nucleus, potassium ion, virus such as influenza.






Hint





Each step on the scale ladder was roughly a factor of 3–10.









Answer





Potassium ion (~0.3 nm) < protein (~5 nm) < ribosome (~25 nm) < influenza virus (~100 nm) < mitochondrion (~1 µm wide) < nucleus (~5–10 µm).




Q4. [ELO 1] A protein diffuses across a 10 µm cell in a few seconds. About how long would it take to diffuse 100 µm? What does this tell you about very long cells such as nerve cells?






Hint





Diffusion time grows with the square of the distance: \(t \approx x^2 / 6D\).









Answer





Ten times the distance means \(10^2 = 100\) times the time: a few hundred seconds, that is several minutes. Over a metre, the time becomes hundreds of years. So long cells such as nerve cells cannot rely on diffusion; they carry cargo with motor proteins along the cytoskeleton.




Q5. [ELO 5] A cell type is packed with rough ER and Golgi. What does the cell probably spend most of its effort on? Give one example of such a cell.






Hint





What does the rough ER make, and where do those proteins go?









Answer





It probably secretes large amounts of protein. The rough ER makes proteins for secretion and the Golgi modifies and sorts them. Examples: a pancreatic acinar cell (digestive enzymes) or a plasma cell (antibodies).




Q6. [ELO 1] A membrane receptor has a sugar chain on one domain. On which side of the plasma membrane do you expect to find that domain, and why?






Hint





Sugar chains are added in the lumen of the ER and Golgi. Follow the protein from the ER to the plasma membrane.









Answer





On the outside of the cell. The sugar chain is added while that domain faces the ER and Golgi lumen. Vesicles bud and fuse without the protein flipping, so the lumen-facing side ends up facing the outside of the cell.




Q7. [ELO 1] Give one advantage and one limitation of using HeLa cells to study a human protein.






Hint





Think of what a cell line is, and where HeLa came from.









Answer





Advantage: human cells that divide without limit, are cheap and easy to grow, image and perturb, and are used in many labs, so results can be compared. Limitation: HeLa cells are cancer cells with an abnormal genome (around 76–80 chromosomes) and an HPV infection that disables normal cell-cycle brakes; they grow flat on plastic, so they may not behave like a normal cell in a tissue. (Also acceptable: contamination of other cell lines, or the ethical questions about consent.)




Q8. [ELO 1] Electron microscopy of thin sections first showed the ER and ribosomes. Why was another method also needed to understand what lysosomes do?






Hint





What does a picture tell you, and what does it not tell you?









Answer





A micrograph shows where a structure is and what it looks like, but not what it does. Cell fractionation (breaking cells and separating their parts by centrifugation, then measuring enzyme activities in each fraction) showed that one fraction held digestive enzymes that work at acidic pH: the lysosomes.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it

title: Glossary
text: Key terms used in the course. Definitions are short; follow the link for the full explanation. Add terms here as lectures are written.

title: Glossary
section: The cell and how we study it
text:
The cell and how we study it

A tour of the cell
See A tour of the cell.
Cytosol: the fluid part of the cell between the organelles, where free ribosomes make proteins and much of metabolism takes place.
Cytoplasm: everything inside the plasma membrane except the nucleus: the cytosol plus the organelles.
Organelle: a membrane-bound compartment inside a eukaryotic cell with its own job, such as the ER or a mitochondrion.
Lumen: the space inside a membrane-bound organelle, on the other side of its membrane from the cytosol.
Topology (membrane): which side of a membrane a space or a part of a protein lies on; the lumen of the ER, Golgi, vesicles and lysosomes is topologically equivalent to the outside of the cell.
Nuclear envelope: the two membranes around the nucleus, crossed by nuclear pores; the outer membrane continues into the ER.
Nuclear pore: a large protein channel in the nuclear envelope that joins the nucleoplasm to the cytosol.
Endoplasmic reticulum (ER): a network of membrane sheets and tubes that makes membrane and secreted proteins (rough ER) and lipids (smooth ER), and stores Ca²⁺.
Golgi apparatus: a stack of flattened membrane compartments that modifies proteins from the ER, for example by adding sugar chains, and sorts them to their destinations.
Lysosome: an acidic organelle (pH about 5) full of digestive enzymes that breaks down material taken up by the cell or from the cell itself.
Model system: a simpler organism or cell type (yeast, a cell line, an organoid) chosen because it answers a question more easily than a human body can.
Informed consent: a person’s voluntary agreement, after being told the purpose and risks, to let their tissue or data be used in research.
Cell fractionation: breaking cells open and separating their parts, usually by centrifugation, to find out what each part does.


Seeing cells: microscopy
See Seeing cells: microscopy.
Resolution: the smallest distance at which two points can still be seen as two separate points.
Magnification: how much larger the image is than the object; it adds no detail beyond the resolution limit.
Numerical aperture, NA: how wide a cone of light an objective collects; a higher NA gives better resolution.
Phase-contrast microscopy: turns small delays of light in dense cell parts into differences in brightness, so living unstained cells become visible.
Differential interference contrast, DIC: shows steep changes in optical path as light and shadow, so cells look three-dimensional.
Fluorophore: a molecule that absorbs light of one wavelength and emits light of a longer wavelength.
Stokes shift: the difference in wavelength between a fluorophore’s excitation peak and emission peak.
Dichroic mirror: a mirror that reflects light below a certain wavelength and lets longer wavelengths pass; it separates excitation light from emitted light.
Immunofluorescence: labelling a protein in fixed, permeabilised cells with antibodies coupled, directly or through a secondary antibody, to a fluorophore.
Green fluorescent protein, GFP: a jellyfish protein that forms its own fluorescent group, used as a genetic tag to see proteins in living cells.
Fusion protein: one protein chain made from two genes joined in the same reading frame, for example a protein of interest joined to GFP.
Confocal microscopy: fluorescence microscopy in which a pinhole blocks out-of-focus light, giving a sharp optical section of a thick sample.
Photobleaching: the permanent loss of fluorescence when a fluorophore is destroyed by repeated excitation.
Super-resolution microscopy: light-microscopy methods, such as STED and PALM/STORM, that resolve details below the ~200 nm limit.
Transmission electron microscopy, TEM: electrons pass through an ultrathin, heavy-metal-stained section, showing structures inside the cell at about 1–2 nm.
Scanning electron microscopy, SEM: images the 3D surface of a metal-coated sample by scanning it with a fine electron beam.
Cryo-electron microscopy, cryo-EM: electron microscopy of rapidly frozen samples in glass-like ice; averaging many images of one protein gives its 3D structure.


Taking cells apart and perturbing them
Cell line: a population of cells that has been made immortal and can be grown in culture without limit.
Primary cells: cells taken directly from a tissue, which divide only a limited number of times in culture.
Organoid: a small 3D structure grown from stem cells that contains several cell types of an organ, arranged roughly as in the tissue.
Mycoplasma: very small bacteria without a cell wall that often contaminate cell cultures unnoticed and change how the cells behave.
Differential centrifugation: separating cell components by spinning at increasing speeds, so larger and denser particles form a pellet first.
Density-gradient centrifugation: separating particles by spinning them through a solution that gets denser towards the bottom, so each stops at its own density.
Marker protein: a protein known to be found in only one organelle, used to identify that organelle in a fraction.
Epitope: the small part of a target molecule that an antibody binds.
Western blot: separates proteins by size, transfers them to a membrane and detects one protein with antibodies.
Immunoprecipitation: using an antibody on beads to pull a protein, and the proteins bound to it, out of a cell lysate.
Flow cytometry: measuring light scatter and fluorescence of single cells as they pass a laser one at a time.
Gating: choosing a region in a flow cytometry plot so that only one population of cells is analysed further.
RNA interference, RNAi: lowering the amount of a protein with a short double-stranded RNA that leads to the matching mRNA being cut.
Knockout: disabling a gene completely, for example by a CRISPR-Cas9 cut that causes a frameshift.

title: Glossary
section: Membranes and transport
text:
Membranes and transport

Membrane structure
See Membrane structure.
Amphipathic: describes a molecule with one part that likes water (polar) and one part that avoids water (hydrophobic).
Hydrophobic effect: the tendency of non-polar groups to gather together in water, driven mainly by the rise in entropy of the water molecules they release.
Lipid bilayer: two layers of lipid molecules with their tails facing inwards, forming the basic sealed structure of every cell membrane.
Membrane fluidity: how easily lipids and proteins move within the plane of a membrane, set by tail length, double bonds, cholesterol and temperature.
Flip-flop: movement of a lipid from one leaflet of the bilayer to the other, which is very rare without the help of enzymes.
Flippase: an ATP-driven enzyme that moves specific lipids, such as phosphatidylserine, from the outer to the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane.
Scramblase: a membrane protein that, when switched on, lets lipids move in both directions between leaflets without using energy, so their asymmetry is lost.
Lipid raft: a proposed small, short-lived membrane domain rich in sphingolipids and cholesterol that may gather certain proteins.
Integral membrane protein: a protein with parts embedded in the hydrophobic core of the bilayer, which can be released only with a detergent.
GPI anchor: a glycolipid attached to the end of a protein that holds the protein on the outer surface of the plasma membrane.
Hydropathy plot: a graph of average hydrophobicity along a protein sequence, used to predict transmembrane α-helices.
Detergent: a small amphipathic molecule with one tail that forms micelles and can dissolve membranes to extract membrane proteins.
FRAP: fluorescence recovery after photobleaching; a laser bleaches a small spot and you measure how fast fluorescent molecules diffuse back in.
Freeze-fracture electron microscopy: splitting a frozen membrane between its two leaflets, which shows the integral proteins as particles in a metal replica.
Glycocalyx: the coat of sugar chains on glycoproteins, glycolipids and proteoglycans that covers the outside of the cell.
Lipid nanoparticle (LNP): a small particle of ionisable lipid, helper phospholipid, cholesterol and PEG-lipid that carries RNA into cells.


Transporters and pumps
See Transporters and pumps.
Simple diffusion: movement of a molecule straight through the lipid bilayer, down its concentration gradient, without help from a protein.
Passive transport: movement of a solute down its (electro)chemical gradient (ΔG < 0); it needs no energy input but may need a transport protein as a path.
Active transport: movement of a solute against its (electro)chemical gradient (ΔG > 0), driven by ATP hydrolysis or by another gradient.
Electrochemical gradient: the combined driving force on an ion from its concentration difference and from the voltage across the membrane.
Transporter (carrier): a membrane protein that binds a specific solute and changes shape to move it across the membrane, one or a few molecules per cycle.
Alternating access: the mechanism by which a transporter’s binding site faces first one side of the membrane and then the other, never both at once.
Uniport: transport of a single kind of solute by a transporter, always down its gradient (e.g. GLUT1).
Symport: coupled transport of two different solutes in the same direction by one transporter (e.g. SGLT1: 2 Na⁺ + 1 glucose).
Antiport: coupled transport of two different solutes in opposite directions by one transporter (e.g. the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger).
Secondary active transport: uphill transport of a solute driven by the downhill flow of another ion, usually Na⁺ or H⁺, whose gradient was made by a pump.
Na⁺/K⁺ pump (Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase): a P-type pump in all animal cells that uses one ATP to move 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ into the cell.
P-type pump: an ATP-driven pump that phosphorylates itself on an aspartate during each transport cycle (e.g. the Na⁺/K⁺ pump and the Ca²⁺ pumps).
ABC transporter: a pump with two ATP-binding cassettes that uses ATP to move substrates across a membrane; in human cells mostly exporters of lipids, toxins and drugs.
P-glycoprotein (ABCB1): an ABC exporter that pumps many hydrophobic drugs out of cells, causing multidrug resistance in cancer and limiting drug uptake into the gut and brain.
Aquaporin: a water channel that lets water, but not ions or H⁺, cross the membrane rapidly by osmosis.
SGLT2 inhibitor (gliflozin): a drug that blocks the kidney Na⁺–glucose symporter SGLT2, so glucose leaves in the urine; used in type 2 diabetes, heart failure and kidney disease.


Ion channels and membrane potential
See Ion channels and membrane potential.
Ion channel: a membrane protein that forms a water-filled pore through which specific ions flow rapidly down their electrochemical gradient when the channel is open.
Selectivity filter: the narrowest part of a channel pore, whose lining atoms decide which ion can pass; in K⁺ channels it is lined by backbone carbonyl oxygens.
Gating: the switching of a channel between closed and open states in response to a signal such as voltage, a bound ligand or mechanical force.
Voltage sensor: a transmembrane helix carrying positive charges that moves when the membrane potential changes, and so opens or closes a voltage-gated channel.
Equilibrium (Nernst) potential: the membrane potential at which an ion’s concentration and electrical forces balance, so its net flow through open channels is zero.
Nernst equation: \(E = \frac{RT}{zF}\ln\frac{c_\text{out}}{c_\text{in}}\), which gives the equilibrium potential of an ion from its concentrations and charge.
Resting membrane potential: the steady voltage across the plasma membrane of an unstimulated cell, about −70 mV, set mainly by open K⁺ leak channels.
Depolarisation: a change of the membrane potential towards less negative values.
Action potential: a brief, all-or-none electrical signal in which voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open and then voltage-gated K⁺ channels restore the resting potential.
Refractory period: the short time after an action potential when inactivated Na⁺ channels cannot reopen, so a new action potential cannot start.
Patch clamp: a glass pipette sealed tightly onto a membrane records the tiny currents through single ion channels or a whole cell.
CFTR: an ATP- and phosphorylation-gated Cl⁻ channel in epithelial cells whose loss of function causes cystic fibrosis.
CFTR potentiator: a drug, such as ivacaftor, that increases the time a CFTR channel at the cell surface spends open.
CFTR corrector: a drug, such as elexacaftor or tezacaftor, that helps misfolded CFTR fold and leave the ER so that it reaches the plasma membrane.

title: Glossary
section: Protein handling and organelles
text:
Protein handling and organelles

Sorting proteins to the right compartment
See Sorting proteins to the right compartment.
Sorting signal: a part of a protein (a short amino-acid pattern or a surface patch) that a receptor reads to decide where the protein goes.
Signal peptide (ER): an N-terminal stretch of 15–30 amino acids with a hydrophobic core that sends a protein into the ER during translation and is then cut off.
Nuclear localisation signal (NLS): a short basic stretch of amino acids (e.g. PKKKRKV) that importins recognise to carry a protein into the nucleus.
Nuclear export signal (NES): a short leucine-rich stretch that exportins such as XPO1 recognise to carry a protein out of the nucleus.
Nuclear pore complex: a large protein channel (about 120 MDa) through the nuclear envelope, filled with FG repeats, that lets small molecules diffuse and larger ones pass with a carrier.
FG repeats: disordered, phenylalanine–glycine-rich chains of nucleoporins that fill the nuclear pore and act as a selective sieve.
Importin: a transport receptor that binds NLS cargo in the cytosol, carries it through the nuclear pore and releases it when Ran-GTP binds.
Ran: a small GTPase whose GTP form is made in the nucleus and destroyed in the cytosol; the resulting gradient makes nuclear transport one-way.
Gated transport: movement between the cytosol and the nucleus through nuclear pores, without crossing a membrane.
Mitochondrial presequence: an N-terminal, positively charged amphipathic helix that targets a protein to the mitochondrial matrix and is removed there.
TOM and TIM complexes: the protein translocators of the outer (TOM) and inner (TIM) mitochondrial membranes, through which proteins made in the cytosol are imported.
PTS1: a C-terminal tripeptide (typically -SKL) that the receptor PEX5 reads to import a folded protein into peroxisomes.
KDEL retrieval: return of ER-resident proteins with a C-terminal KDEL from the Golgi to the ER by the KDEL receptor.
Selinexor: a drug that blocks the exportin XPO1, trapping tumour-suppressor proteins in the nucleus; used in multiple myeloma.


The endoplasmic reticulum
See The endoplasmic reticulum.
Signal sequence: a stretch of about 15–30 amino acids at the N-terminus, with a hydrophobic core, that sends a protein into the ER and is then cut off.
Signal recognition particle (SRP): a protein–RNA complex that binds a signal sequence as it leaves the ribosome, pauses translation and brings the ribosome to the ER membrane.
Translocon (Sec61): the protein channel in the ER membrane through which a new chain enters the lumen; a lateral gate lets membrane segments out into the lipid.
Co-translational translocation: moving a protein into the ER while the ribosome is still making it.
Stop-transfer sequence: a hydrophobic segment that stops translocation of a chain already entering the ER and stays in the membrane.
Signal-anchor sequence: an uncleaved hydrophobic segment that starts translocation and stays as a membrane anchor; the positive charges next to it set its orientation.
Positive-inside rule: positively charged amino acids next to a membrane segment stay on the cytosolic side.
Protein disulfide isomerase (PDI): an ER enzyme that forms disulfide bonds in new proteins and rearranges wrong ones.
BiP: the main Hsp70 chaperone of the ER lumen; it binds unfolded chains and holds the UPR sensors inactive.
N-linked glycosylation: transfer of a 14-sugar block from dolichol to an asparagine in the sequence N-X-S/T, by oligosaccharyltransferase in the ER.
Calnexin cycle: repeated binding of a glycoprotein with one glucose to the lectin chaperone calnexin until it folds; UGGT re-adds the glucose to unfolded proteins.
ERAD (ER-associated degradation): return of misfolded ER proteins to the cytosol, where they are ubiquitinated and degraded by the proteasome.
Unfolded protein response (UPR): signalling from the ER sensors IRE1, PERK and ATF6 that raises folding capacity and lowers translation when unfolded proteins pile up, or triggers apoptosis.
Microsomes: small sealed vesicles of ER membrane formed when cells are broken; used to study translocation and topology.
Russell body: a swollen ER compartment filled with retained immunoglobulin in a plasma cell.


The Golgi and the secretory pathway
See The Golgi and the secretory pathway.
Secretory pathway: the route of proteins from the ER through the Golgi to the plasma membrane, secretory granules or lysosomes, always inside membrane compartments.
ERGIC: the ER–Golgi intermediate compartment, a set of tubules and vesicle clusters between the ER exit sites and the cis Golgi.
COPII: the coat that makes vesicles leaving the ER, switched on by the small GTPase Sar1.
COPI: the coat that makes vesicles carrying proteins back from the Golgi to the ER and between Golgi cisternae, switched on by ARF1.
Clathrin: a three-legged protein that forms basket-like coats on vesicles at the trans-Golgi network and the plasma membrane, linked to cargo by adaptors such as AP1 and AP2.
Rab GTPase: a small GTPase that marks the identity of a membrane and, in its GTP form, recruits tethers and other effectors.
Tether: a long coiled-coil protein or multi-subunit complex that catches an arriving vesicle before fusion.
SNARE: a membrane protein whose helices zip with partner SNAREs on the other membrane into a four-helix bundle that fuses the two bilayers.
NSF: an ATPase that pulls SNARE complexes apart after fusion so the SNAREs can be reused.
Trans-Golgi network (TGN): the tubular exit face of the Golgi, where cargo is sorted to the plasma membrane, secretory granules or endosomes.
Cisternal maturation: the model in which Golgi cisternae themselves move and change from cis to trans, carrying cargo with them.
Mannose-6-phosphate (M6P): a sugar tag added to lysosomal enzymes in the Golgi, which the M6P receptor uses to send them to the lysosomes.
Constitutive secretion: continuous, unregulated delivery of proteins and membrane to the cell surface, which happens in every cell.
Regulated secretion: storage of products in secretory granules that fuse with the plasma membrane only when a signal raises cytosolic Ca²⁺.
Brefeldin A: a fungal compound that blocks activation of ARF1, so COPI cannot form and the Golgi merges into the ER.


Endocytosis, lysosomes and autophagy
See Endocytosis, lysosomes and autophagy.
Endocytosis: uptake of material by folding in the plasma membrane and pinching off a vesicle.
Dynamin: a GTPase that forms a ring around the neck of a budding vesicle and pinches it off.
Receptor-mediated endocytosis: uptake of specific molecules bound to receptors that collect in clathrin-coated pits.
LDL (low-density lipoprotein): a particle of about 22 nm that carries cholesterol esters in the blood and is recognised through its apoB protein.
Endosome: a membrane compartment that receives endocytosed material and sorts it for recycling or degradation; it becomes more acidic as it matures.
Macropinocytosis: unselective, actin-driven uptake of large gulps of extracellular fluid.
Phagocytosis: receptor-triggered, actin-driven engulfment of large particles such as bacteria or dead cells by specialised cells.
Autophagy: delivery of parts of the cell’s own cytosol and organelles to lysosomes inside a double-membrane autophagosome.
mTORC1: a kinase on the lysosome surface that senses nutrients, drives growth and blocks autophagy when nutrients are plentiful.
PCSK9: a liver protein that binds the LDL receptor and sends it to the lysosome instead of recycling; the target of cholesterol-lowering antibodies.
Familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH): an inherited disease with high blood LDL from birth, usually caused by faulty LDL receptors.
Endosomal escape: release of a drug, such as RNA from a lipid nanoparticle, from the endosome into the cytosol before it reaches the lysosome.


Protein life and death
See Protein life and death.
Chaperone: a protein that binds exposed hydrophobic parts of unfolded chains to prevent wrong contacts and help them fold, without carrying information about the final shape.
Hsp70: the main cytosolic chaperone, which binds and releases short hydrophobic stretches of a chain in an ATP-driven cycle.
Chaperonin: a barrel-shaped chaperone (GroEL/GroES in bacteria, TRiC in the human cytosol) that encloses a protein so it can fold alone.
Amyloid: an ordered, very stable protein aggregate in which β-strands from many chains stack across a long fibril (cross-β) and seed further growth.
Protein kinase: an enzyme that moves a phosphate from ATP onto a serine, threonine or tyrosine of a protein; a protein phosphatase removes it.
Acetylation: addition of an acetyl group to a lysine, which removes its positive charge (for example on histones).
Ubiquitin: a small protein of 76 amino acids attached to lysines of other proteins as a signal; Lys48-linked chains mark proteins for the proteasome.
E3 ubiquitin ligase: the enzyme that recognises a specific substrate and transfers ubiquitin from an E2 onto it; about 600 kinds in humans give the system its specificity.
Degron: a feature of a protein, such as a phosphorylated motif or an exposed hydrophobic stretch, that an E3 ligase recognises as a signal for destruction.
Proteasome: a large protease complex in the cytosol and nucleus; its 19S cap unfolds ubiquitinated proteins and its 20S core cuts them into short peptides.
Protein half-life: the time for half of a protein’s molecules to be destroyed (t½ = ln 2 / k_d).
Cycloheximide chase: blocking protein synthesis with cycloheximide and following the decay of a protein over time to measure its half-life.
Pulse-chase: labelling newly made proteins briefly, then following the labelled group over time.
PROTAC: a two-headed drug that links a target protein to an E3 ligase so that the target is ubiquitinated and destroyed.
Molecular glue: a small molecule, such as lenalidomide bound to cereblon, that makes an E3 ligase recognise and destroy new substrate proteins.


Organelles compared: keeping the cell in balance
See Organelles compared: keeping the cell in balance.
Nuclear lamina: a mesh of lamin filaments under the inner nuclear membrane that gives the nucleus its shape and anchors chromatin.
Lamin: an intermediate-filament protein (A- or B-type) that forms the nuclear lamina.
Peroxisome: a single-membrane organelle that imports folded enzymes, carries out oxidations that make H₂O₂, and shortens very-long-chain fatty acids.
Catalase: a peroxisomal enzyme that breaks down hydrogen peroxide to water and oxygen.
Lipid droplet: an organelle that stores neutral fat in a core covered by a single layer of phospholipids.
Contact site: a place where two organelle membranes are held 10–30 nm apart by tether proteins without fusing, so lipids and ions can pass between them.
Store-operated Ca²⁺ entry: refilling of the ER Ca²⁺ store, in which STIM in the ER opens ORAI channels in the plasma membrane.
SERCA: the ATP-driven pump that moves Ca²⁺ from the cytosol into the ER.
V-type H⁺-ATPase: the proton pump that acidifies the lumen of the Golgi, endosomes and lysosomes.
AMPK: a kinase that senses a low energy charge (high AMP) and switches on fuel use and switches off synthesis.
Homeostasis: keeping a variable near a set point by negative feedback.
Stereology: estimating volume fractions from sections by counting how many grid points fall on each structure.
Progerin: a shortened lamin A that keeps its farnesyl lipid and causes Hutchinson–Gilford progeria.
Lonafarnib: a farnesyltransferase inhibitor, the first approved drug for progeria.
Zellweger syndrome: an inherited disease in which a defect in a PEX gene blocks protein import into peroxisomes.

title: Glossary
section: Cell signalling
text:
Cell signalling

Principles of cell communication
See Principles of cell communication.
Endocrine signalling: a hormone travels in the blood to target cells throughout the body.
Paracrine signalling: a local mediator acts on nearby cells and is quickly removed.
Autocrine signalling: a cell responds to a signal that it releases itself.
Contact-dependent signalling: a membrane-bound signal acts only on cells that touch the sending cell.
Nuclear receptor: an intracellular receptor for a small fat-soluble hormone that acts as a transcription factor.
Dissociation constant (K_d): the free ligand concentration at which half the receptors are occupied; a low K_d means high affinity.
Dose–response curve: a plot of response against log drug concentration, giving E_max and EC₅₀.
EC₅₀: the concentration of a drug that gives half of its maximal response; a measure of potency.
IC₅₀: the inhibitor concentration that removes half of a response, at a stated agonist concentration.
Efficacy: how strongly a drug activates a receptor once bound.
Agonist: a drug that binds a receptor and activates it.
Partial agonist: a drug that binds a receptor but activates it only part-way, even at full occupancy.
Antagonist: a drug that binds a receptor without activating it and blocks the agonist; competitive antagonists shift the curve right, non-competitive ones lower the maximum.
Spare receptors: receptors beyond those needed for a maximal response, which make EC₅₀ lower than K_d.
Desensitisation: a fall in response to a signal that stays on, for example by receptor phosphorylation, arrestin binding or receptor endocytosis.


G-protein-coupled receptors and second messengers
See G-protein-coupled receptors and second messengers.
G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR): a cell-surface receptor made of one protein chain that crosses the membrane seven times and activates a trimeric G protein.
Trimeric G protein: a membrane-bound switch of three subunits (Gα, Gβ, Gγ) that is on when Gα holds GTP and off when it holds GDP.
GEF (guanine nucleotide exchange factor): a protein that makes a GTPase release GDP so that GTP can bind; an active GPCR is the GEF for its G protein.
Gs / Gi / Gq: the main Gα families: Gs stimulates and Gi inhibits adenylyl cyclase; Gq activates phospholipase C-β.
Second messenger: a small molecule or ion made or released inside the cell in response to a signal, such as cAMP, IP₃, DAG or Ca²⁺.
Adenylyl cyclase: a plasma-membrane enzyme that turns ATP into cyclic AMP (cAMP).
Phosphodiesterase (PDE): an enzyme that breaks down cAMP (or cGMP) and so ends the signal.
Protein kinase A (PKA): a kinase whose catalytic subunits are released when cAMP binds its regulatory subunits.
Phospholipase C-β: a Gq-activated enzyme that cuts the membrane lipid PIP₂ into IP₃ and DAG.
IP₃ receptor: a Ca²⁺ channel in the ER membrane that opens when IP₃ binds.
Protein kinase C (PKC): a kinase activated at the membrane by DAG together with Ca²⁺.
Calmodulin: a small Ca²⁺-binding protein that, with four Ca²⁺ bound, wraps around and activates target proteins.
Arrestin: a protein that binds phosphorylated active GPCRs, blocks G-protein coupling and links the receptor to clathrin for endocytosis.
Cholera toxin: a bacterial enzyme that ADP-ribosylates Gαs so it cannot hydrolyse GTP, keeping cAMP high in gut cells.


Enzyme-coupled receptors: kinase cascades
See Enzyme-coupled receptors: kinase cascades.
Receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK): a single-pass receptor whose cytosolic kinase domain phosphorylates tyrosines when ligand binding brings two receptor chains together.
Autophosphorylation: phosphorylation of a kinase by a second molecule of the same kinase, as in an RTK dimer where each chain phosphorylates the other.
SH2 domain: a protein domain of about 100 amino acids that binds a phosphorylated tyrosine together with the next few amino acids.
Adaptor protein: a protein without enzyme activity that links two other proteins, such as Grb2 linking an active RTK to SOS.
Ras: a small membrane-anchored GTPase that is active with GTP and links RTKs to the MAP kinase cascade.
GAP (GTPase-activating protein): a protein that switches a GTPase off by speeding up hydrolysis of its bound GTP.
MAP kinase cascade: a chain of three kinases (here RAF → MEK → ERK), each phosphorylating and activating the next.
Ultrasensitivity: a switch-like response in which the output goes from off to on over a small change in input (Hill coefficient above 1).
PI3K: a lipid kinase that turns PIP₂ into PIP₃ in the plasma membrane, recruiting proteins such as Akt.
Akt (protein kinase B): a kinase recruited to PIP₃ by its PH domain that promotes cell survival and growth.
JAK–STAT pathway: a pathway in which receptor-bound JAK kinases phosphorylate STATs, which pair up and act directly as transcription factors.
Phospho-specific antibody: an antibody that binds a protein only when a particular site is phosphorylated, so it reports the active form.
Gatekeeper mutation: a mutation that puts a larger amino acid at the entrance of a kinase’s ATP pocket, keeping an inhibitor out but letting ATP in.
Imatinib: the first targeted cancer drug; it blocks the ATP pocket of the BCR-ABL kinase in chronic myeloid leukaemia.


Signalling that shapes tissues and decides fates
See Signalling that shapes tissues and decides fates.
β-catenin: transcriptional coactivator that is destroyed continually unless Wnt signalling blocks the destruction complex.
Destruction complex: protein complex (APC, Axin, GSK3) that phosphorylates β-catenin and marks it for destruction by the proteasome.
Primary cilium: single non-moving cell projection that acts as a signalling antenna, where Hedgehog signalling takes place.
Patched: Hedgehog receptor that keeps Smoothened inactive until Hedgehog binds it.
Smoothened: membrane protein that activates Gli when it moves into the primary cilium; the target of vismodegib.
SMAD: transcription factor phosphorylated by TGF-β-family receptor kinases, which then enters the nucleus with SMAD4.
Notch: receptor for the membrane-bound signal Delta; it is cut, and its released intracellular domain activates genes with CSL.
