γ-secretase: protease that cuts proteins inside the membrane, including Notch and the amyloid precursor protein.
Lateral inhibition: feedback in which a cell signalling via Delta stops its neighbours from taking the same fate, giving a salt-and-pepper pattern.
Morphogen: a signal that forms a concentration gradient and gives different cell fates at different concentrations.
NF-κB: inflammatory transcription factor held in the cytosol by IκB until IκB is phosphorylated and destroyed by the proteasome.
Reporter gene: a gene for luciferase or GFP placed after binding sites for a transcription factor, so that light measures pathway activity.
Tamoxifen: drug that binds the oestrogen receptor but blocks coactivator binding, used in ER-positive breast cancer.
Competence: a cell’s readiness to respond to a signal in a particular way, set by its open chromatin and partner transcription factors.

title: Glossary
section: Cytoskeleton
text:
Cytoskeleton

Actin: cell shape and migration
See Actin: cell shape and migration.
G-actin: the free, globular actin monomer, which binds ATP or ADP.
F-actin: the filament made of G-actin subunits, a polar two-stranded helix about 7 nm wide.
Barbed end (+ end): the fast-growing end of an actin filament, with the lower critical concentration.
Pointed end (− end): the slow-growing end of an actin filament, where old ADP subunits leave.
Critical concentration: the free monomer concentration at which subunits join and leave a filament end equally fast.
Treadmilling: a steady state in which a filament gains subunits at its + end as fast as it loses them at its − end, so it keeps its length and moves.
Arp2/3 complex: a nucleator that binds the side of an actin filament and starts a branch at about 70°, building branched networks.
Formin: a nucleator that stays on the growing barbed end and makes long, unbranched actin filaments.
Profilin: a protein that binds actin monomers, recharges them with ATP and lets them join only free barbed ends.
Cofilin: a protein that binds old ADP-actin filaments, cuts them and speeds their disassembly.
Capping protein: a protein that binds barbed ends tightly and stops growth there.
Lamellipodium: the thin sheet at the front of a crawling cell, filled with a branched actin network that pushes the membrane.
Filopodium: a thin, finger-like protrusion containing a tight bundle of parallel actin filaments.
Stress fibre: a contractile bundle of actin and myosin II that ends in focal adhesions.
Rho GTPases (Rho, Rac, Cdc42): small GTP-binding switches that turn on stress fibres, lamellipodia and filopodia respectively.
Phalloidin: a mushroom toxin that binds and stabilises F-actin; with a fluorescent dye it stains actin in fixed cells.
Latrunculin: a sponge toxin that binds G-actin and so makes actin filaments disassemble.


Microtubules and motor proteins
See Microtubules and motor proteins.
Tubulin: the αβ protein dimer, 8 nm long, that builds microtubules; both subunits bind GTP.
Protofilament: a head-to-tail row of tubulin dimers; 13 of them form a microtubule.
Plus end / minus end: the fast-growing end of a microtubule (β-tubulin exposed) and the slow, usually anchored end (α-tubulin exposed).
GTP cap: the GTP-tubulin at a growing microtubule end that keeps it straight and stable.
Dynamic instability: random switching of a microtubule end between slow growth and fast shrinkage.
Catastrophe: the switch from growth to rapid shrinkage when the GTP cap is lost.
Rescue: the switch from shrinkage back to growth.
Centrosome: the main microtubule-organising centre of animal cells: two centrioles in pericentriolar material.
γ-tubulin ring complex: a ring that templates new microtubules and caps their minus ends.
EB1: a protein that binds only growing plus ends; fused to GFP it shows them as moving comets.
Kinesin: a family of motor proteins that mostly walk towards the plus end, 8 nm and one ATP per step.
Dynein: a large motor that walks towards the minus end; it also bends cilia (axonemal dynein).
Axonal transport: motor-driven transport along an axon, out to the tip (anterograde, kinesin) or back to the cell body (retrograde, dynein).
Axoneme: the 9 + 2 microtubule core of a motile cilium or flagellum.


Myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell
See Myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell.
Myosin: a motor protein that uses ATP to walk along actin filaments; the tail decides whether it pulls (myosin II) or carries cargo (myosin V).
Cross-bridge cycle: the repeating cycle in which a myosin head binds actin, makes a power stroke, releases when ATP binds, and is re-cocked by ATP hydrolysis.
Power stroke: the swing of the myosin lever arm, triggered by phosphate release, that moves an actin filament 5–10 nm.
Rigor: the state in which myosin heads stay locked to actin because no ATP is bound; it causes rigor mortis.
Sarcomere: the repeating contractile unit of striated muscle, from one Z-disc to the next, about 2–3 µm long.
Sliding-filament model: muscle shortens because thick and thin filaments slide past each other while keeping their length.
Length–tension curve: the dependence of a muscle’s active force on sarcomere length, set by how much the thick and thin filaments overlap.
Tropomyosin: a rod-shaped protein along the actin filament that covers the myosin-binding sites in resting muscle.
Troponin: a protein complex on tropomyosin that binds Ca²⁺ and then moves tropomyosin so myosin can bind actin.
Contractile ring: a ring of actin and non-muscle myosin II that pinches a dividing cell in two.
Intermediate filament: a 10 nm rope-like, non-polar filament (keratins, vimentin, desmin, neurofilaments, lamins) that gives cells mechanical strength.
Desmosome: a cell–cell junction that anchors intermediate filaments and links the networks of neighbouring cells.
Hemidesmosome: a junction that anchors a cell’s intermediate filaments to the basal lamina.
TIRF microscopy: fluorescence microscopy that lights only a layer about 100 nm thick above the glass, for sharp images of the cell bottom and single molecules.
Traction-force microscopy: a method that calculates the forces a cell exerts from how far beads move in the soft gel the cell grows on.
Mavacamten: a cardiac myosin inhibitor that parks myosin heads, used to treat hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

title: Study questions: endocytosis, lysosomes and autophagy
text: Study questions in the style of the written exam. Write your answer first (a few sentences, or a labelled sketch where it helps), then compare with the model answer. Each question is tagged with its learning outcome (ELO). Questions tagged [VG] are of the kind used for the higher grade: predict, compare, explain an unexpected result or design an experiment.

title: Study questions: endocytosis, lysosomes and autophagy
section: G-level questions
text:
G-level questions
1. Describe clathrin-mediated endocytosis in four steps. Name the protein that chooses the cargo and the protein that cuts the vesicle free. [ELO 4]






Model answer






Adaptor proteins (AP2) on the inner face of the plasma membrane bind short sorting signals in the cytosolic tails of receptors (for example NPxY in the LDL receptor). This is how cargo is chosen. (2) Clathrin, a three-legged protein, binds the adaptors and assembles into a curved lattice that bends the membrane into a coated pit. (3) Dynamin, a GTPase, forms a ring around the neck of the pit and, using GTP, pinches off the coated vesicle (about 100 nm). (4) The clathrin coat is removed (by an ATP-using chaperone), and the uncoated vesicle fuses with an early endosome. The whole process takes about a minute.





2. Describe the LDL receptor cycle, from LDL in the blood to cholesterol in the cell. Explain why one receptor can take in many LDL particles. [ELO 4] [ELO 5]






Model answer





The LDL receptor in the plasma membrane binds apoB on an LDL particle. Its NPxY tail signal brings it into a clathrin-coated pit; dynamin pinches off the vesicle, which loses its coat and fuses with the early (sorting) endosome. The endosome is acidified by the V-ATPase to about pH 6; at this pH the receptor changes shape and releases LDL. The empty receptor is carried back to the surface in recycling tubules and vesicles, while LDL stays in the lumen, moves on through the late endosome to the lysosome, and is digested: cholesterol esters are split and free cholesterol leaves the lysosome for the ER and membranes. Because the receptor is not degraded with its cargo but recycles (a round trip of about 10 minutes, over 100 trips in its life), one receptor brings in many LDL particles.




3. Name the compartments of the endocytic pathway in order, with their approximate pH. Which protein sets the pH, and why does the pH matter? Give two examples. [ELO 5]






Model answer





Endocytic vesicle (about 7.4, like the outside) → early endosome (6.0–6.5) → late endosome / multivesicular body (5.0–5.5) → lysosome (4.5–5). The V-ATPase, an ATP-driven proton pump, pumps H⁺ into the lumen (chloride channels balance the charge). The pH matters because (1) acid makes receptors release their cargo: LDL from the LDL receptor, iron from transferrin, lysosomal enzymes from the M6P receptor; so receptors can recycle; and (2) the lysosomal acid hydrolases work best at pH 4.5–5, so digestion needs the acid (and they are nearly inactive if they leak into the cytosol at pH 7.2).




4. In the early endosome, the LDL receptor, the transferrin receptor and the EGF receptor meet different fates. Describe what happens to each receptor and its ligand. [ELO 4] [ELO 5]






Model answer





LDL receptor: acid releases LDL; the receptor recycles to the surface; LDL goes to the lysosome and is digested. Transferrin receptor: acid releases iron, which is transported to the cytosol; the empty transferrin stays bound to the receptor and both recycle; at pH 7.4 at the surface transferrin is released. EGF receptor: after binding EGF it is tagged with ubiquitin; the ESCRT machinery sorts it into the internal vesicles of the late endosome (multivesicular body), so it stops signalling, and it is destroyed in the lysosome together with EGF. This switches off the growth signal.




5. How do newly made lysosomal enzymes reach the lysosome? Explain what goes wrong in I-cell disease. [ELO 4]






Model answer





Lysosomal enzymes are made on the ER and glycosylated like secreted proteins. In the cis Golgi an enzyme (GlcNAc phosphotransferase) recognises a patch on the folded lysosomal enzyme and adds a phosphate to mannose: the mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) tag. In the trans Golgi network, M6P receptors bind the tag at neutral pH and collect the enzymes into clathrin-coated vesicles, which fuse with late endosomes. At pH about 5.5 the enzyme lets go, the phosphate is removed, and the receptor returns to the Golgi. The endosome matures into or fuses with the lysosome. Enzymes that escape to the cell surface can be caught by M6P receptors there and endocytosed. In I-cell disease the phosphotransferase is defective, so no tag is added: the enzymes follow the default route and are secreted into the blood, and the lysosomes, lacking enzymes, fill with undigested material (“inclusions”).




6. Compare clathrin-mediated endocytosis, macropinocytosis and phagocytosis: size, what is taken up, what drives it and which cells use it. [ELO 4] [ELO 5]






Model answer















Clathrin-mediated
Macropinocytosis
Phagocytosis




Vesicle size
~0.1 µm
0.2–5 µm
> 0.5 µm (as big as the particle)


What
specific cargo bound to receptors with tail signals
extracellular fluid and what is dissolved in it, unselective
particles: bacteria, dead cells, debris


Driven by
clathrin coat, adaptors, dynamin
actin-driven membrane ruffles that close
actin-driven pseudopods, triggered by receptors (Fc, complement, “eat-me” phosphatidylserine)


Cells
all cells
most cells; very active in macrophages and some cancer cells
specialised phagocytes: macrophages, neutrophils



All three deliver their content to endosomes or lysosomes for digestion.




7. Describe autophagy from start to finish, and explain how it is controlled by nutrients. [ELO 5]






Model answer





A flat double-membrane cup, the phagophore, forms in the cytosol (partly from ER membrane) and grows around a portion of cytosol or a specific target (damaged mitochondrion, protein aggregate, bacterium). It closes into an autophagosome with two membranes, which fuses with a lysosome. The acid hydrolases digest the inner membrane and the contents, and amino acids, lipids and sugars are exported back to the cytosol for reuse. The kinase mTORC1, on the lysosome surface, senses amino acids and growth signals: when nutrients are plentiful it is active and blocks autophagy; in starvation (or with rapamycin) it is inactive and autophagy is switched on, so the cell can recycle its own material to survive.




8. Explain how statins and PCSK9 inhibitors lower blood LDL. Name the molecular target of each and the effect on the LDL receptor. [ELO 4] [ELO 9]






Model answer





Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis in the ER of liver cells. Cholesterol in the ER falls, the transcription factor SREBP2 is activated and more LDL receptors are made. More receptors at the liver cell surface take more LDL out of the blood (about 30–50 % lower LDL). PCSK9 is a secreted protein that binds the LDL receptor at the surface; in the acidic endosome it stays bound and prevents recycling, so the receptor is sent to the lysosome and destroyed. PCSK9 inhibitors (antibodies such as evolocumab and alirocumab, which bind PCSK9 in the blood; or inclisiran, an siRNA that destroys PCSK9 mRNA) let the receptors recycle more times, so more receptors are at the surface (about 50–60 % lower LDL, also on top of statins).




9. What is a lysosomal storage disease? Explain how enzyme replacement therapy reaches the lysosome, and why it does not help the brain. [ELO 5] [ELO 9]






Model answer





An inherited disease in which one lysosomal enzyme (or transporter) is missing or defective, so its substrate cannot be broken down and accumulates in lysosomes, which swell and disturb the cell (about 70 diseases, together about 1 in 5000 births; for example Gaucher, Fabry, Pompe, Tay–Sachs). In enzyme replacement therapy the missing enzyme is made in cultured cells and infused into the blood. It carries mannose-6-phosphate (or exposed mannose), so it binds M6P receptors on the surface of target cells (or the mannose receptor of macrophages in Gaucher disease), is taken in by receptor-mediated endocytosis, and reaches the lysosome through endosomes. The enzyme is a large protein that does not cross the blood–brain barrier, so it cannot reach brain cells, and forms of the diseases that affect the brain are not helped.

title: Study questions: endocytosis, lysosomes and autophagy
section: VG-style questions
text:
VG-style questions
10. [VG] Two patients have familial hypercholesterolaemia. Cells from patient A do not bind radioactive LDL at 4 °C. Cells from patient B bind LDL normally at 4 °C, but at 37 °C they take in and degrade almost none. Explain each result at the level of the LDL receptor, and describe what you would see in the electron microscope with ferritin-labelled LDL. Suggest where in the receptor the mutation of patient B lies. [ELO 4] [ELO 9]






Model answer





At 4 °C membranes do not bud, so binding measures receptors on the surface. Patient A has no working receptor at the surface: either none is made, it is misfolded and kept in the ER, or its LDL-binding part is defective. No LDL binds, so none is taken in or degraded. Patient B has receptors that reach the surface and bind LDL, so the binding domain is normal, but they are not internalised. In the EM, ferritin-LDL on normal cells collects in coated pits and appears in vesicles and endosomes a few minutes after warming; on patient B’s cells it is spread evenly over the surface, outside coated pits, and stays outside. The mutation is most likely in the cytosolic tail, in the internalisation signal (NPxY) that the AP2 adaptor binds; this is the classic “J.D.” patient, whose tyrosine of NPxY is replaced by cysteine. Without the signal, the adaptors cannot collect the receptor into pits, although clathrin endocytosis of other receptors (for example the transferrin receptor) works normally, which could be checked as a control.




11. [VG] Cells are treated with bafilomycin, which blocks the V-ATPase. Predict what happens over the next hours to (a) the number of LDL receptors at the cell surface, (b) LDL degradation, and (c) uptake of iron through transferrin. Explain each prediction. [ELO 5]






Model answer





Without the V-ATPase, endosomes and lysosomes are no longer acidified; their pH rises towards that of the cytosol. (a) The LDL receptor needs acid to release LDL. Receptors that still hold LDL are not sorted normally into the recycling route; they are trapped in endosomes or sent on with their ligand, so fewer receptors return to the surface and the number at the surface falls (some FH mutations do the same: receptors that cannot release LDL are degraded). (b) LDL degradation stops, because the lysosomal acid hydrolases need low pH; LDL that reaches lysosomes accumulates undigested. (c) Iron uptake falls, because iron is released from transferrin only at acid pH; transferrin and its receptor may still cycle, but they bring back the iron instead of leaving it in the cell. (In the demo, an endosome pH of 6.5 or above makes the surface receptors collapse to a few per cent and blood LDL rise five-fold.)




12. [VG] An mRNA medicine in a lipid nanoparticle works poorly. A chemist proposes to replace the ionisable lipid (pKa 6.4) with a lipid that is always positively charged. Predict the effects on (a) binding of the RNA in the particle, (b) escape from the endosome, (c) behaviour in the blood and toxicity, and (d) overall delivery. What would you suggest instead? [ELO 5] [ELO 2]






Model answer






The RNA would still be bound well, because the positive lipid pairs with the negative RNA. (b) Escape from the endosome would be at least as good, because the lipid is positive from the start and can pair with negative lipids of the endosome membrane. (c) In the blood (pH 7.4) a permanently positive particle sticks to negatively charged blood proteins and cell surfaces, is cleared quickly and is more toxic (it disturbs membranes everywhere, not only in endosomes). (d) Fewer particles reach the target cells, so overall delivery falls even though escape per particle is higher. The point of an ionisable lipid is that its charge switches with pH: at pKa about 6.2–6.5, only a few per cent is charged in blood but most is charged in the late endosome (pH 5–5.5). Better suggestions: tune the pKa within that range, use a lipid that disrupts membranes better when charged, or target the particle to cells with better uptake; in any case measure both escape and toxicity. (The demo’s second tab shows this trade-off.)

title: Study questions: endocytosis, lysosomes and autophagy
section: Explore
text:
Explore
Tab 1, LDL receptor cycle. On the left is a liver cell at real time: LDL receptors (dark Y shapes) sit on the surface facing the blood, bind LDL (yellow), gather in clathrin-coated pits, and are pinched off in coated vesicles to the sorting endosome. If the endosome is acid enough, LDL lets go and moves on to the lysosome, and the empty receptor recycles to the surface. A receptor that carries PCSK9 (pink), that still holds its LDL, or by chance (1 trip in 200) is sent to the lysosome instead, and new receptors come from the Golgi. Use 10× or 60× to see more trips, and Skip ahead 6 hours to let the cell settle after a change. On the right, the same model is used to calculate what happens in the body over weeks: the LDL in the blood and the receptors at the liver cell surface, compared with the same person without drugs. Tab 2, LNP escape shows 100 lipid nanoparticles in one endosome that acidifies, and calculates how much RNA reaches the cytosol for each pKa of the ionisable lipid. Both tabs are a qualitative compartment model with round numbers: the behaviour is right, the exact numbers are not patient data. The cell view is random, so its counts differ from run to run; the solutions use the calculated values.



E1. Choose Healthy and watch the cell at real time for a minute, then at 60× for a few minutes. Describe the route of one receptor and one LDL particle. Where do they part, and why? What do the readouts say about how long a receptor lives and how many trips it makes? [ELO 4]
E2. Predict first. Raise the PCSK9 level to 3× (or choose PCSK9 gain of function). What will happen to the receptor lifetime, the receptors at the surface and the blood LDL? Check. Then tick PCSK9 antibody. Explain the result with the words recycling and lysosome. [ELO 4] [ELO 9]
E3. Choose FH: one faulty LDLR gene. Read the blood LDL. Tick statin, then also PCSK9 antibody. How much does each step lower LDL? Then choose FH: two faulty LDLR genes and repeat. Why do the drugs work so much less well in this patient? [ELO 4] [ELO 9]
E4. [VG] Predict first. Choose Healthy and raise the endosome pH step by step from 6.0 to 7.0 (as if the V-ATPase were partly blocked). At which pH does blood LDL start to rise, and why does it rise so steeply? Why does the cell lose its receptors, although nothing is wrong with the receptor itself? [ELO 5]
E5. [VG] Open the LNP escape tab. With the lowest endosome pH at 5.5, move the pKa from 5 to 9 and read the two curves. Which pKa gives the most RNA in the cytosol, and how much? Explain why a lower and a higher pKa are both worse. Then choose V-ATPase blocked: what happens, and what does it tell you about how LNPs escape? [ELO 5] [ELO 2]






Solutions





E1. A receptor at the surface binds an LDL particle, drifts until it is caught in a clathrin-coated pit (on average after about 7 minutes at the surface), and the pit is pinched off as a coated vesicle within about 40 seconds. The coat comes off, and the vesicle delivers the receptor and its LDL to the sorting endosome. There, at pH 6.0, 99.7 % of the LDL lets go of the receptor. The LDL stays in the endosome lumen and is passed on to the lysosome, where it slowly fades (digested); the empty receptor leaves the endosome after a few minutes and returns to the surface. They part in the endosome because the acid makes the receptor release LDL, and only the receptor, which is in the membrane, is taken into the recycling vesicles. The readouts say a receptor lives about 11 hours and makes about 60 round trips (the real number is of the same order: more than a hundred). Only about 1 trip in 60 ends in the lysosome, by chance or because the receptor carried PCSK9.
E2. With PCSK9 at 3× (gain of function), more receptors pick up PCSK9 at the surface and are destroyed in the lysosome after a single trip. The receptor lifetime falls from about 11 to about 5 hours (about 27 trips), the receptors at the surface fall to about 46 % of healthy, and blood LDL rises from 2.6 to about 4.9 mmol/L within two to three weeks: an FH-like level, as in families with gain-of-function PCSK9 mutations. With the antibody, 95 % of PCSK9 is caught in the blood before it can bind, so receptors are no longer sent to the lysosome; they keep recycling (lifetime about 24 hours, over 120 trips). Receptors at the surface rise to about 214 % and LDL falls to about 1.3 mmol/L (−73 %). The antibody does not touch the receptor or LDL itself: it only stops receptors being sent to the lysosome.
E3. One faulty gene: about half the receptors (49 %), LDL about 4.6 mmol/L. With a statin: receptors rise to about 77 % and LDL falls to about 3.2 mmol/L (−30 %). With statin + PCSK9 antibody: receptors about 240 %, LDL about 1.2 mmol/L (−74 %). Both drugs need working receptors: the statin makes the one working gene produce more receptors, and the antibody lets each receptor make more trips. The statin effect is limited partly because the same switch (SREBP2) that makes more receptors also makes more PCSK9 (1.5× in the model), which the antibody removes. With two faulty genes almost no working receptors are made (2 %): LDL is about 16 mmol/L. A statin lowers it only to about 15.5 (−5 %) and statin + antibody to about 12.4 (−24 %, from 2 % to 8 % of the normal receptors). There is (almost) nothing for the drugs to increase or save. Real patients with no working receptors respond little to statins or PCSK9 inhibitors and need other treatment, such as removing LDL from the blood (apheresis) or drugs that act without the receptor.
E4. Up to about pH 6.1 almost nothing happens. From about pH 6.2 LDL starts to rise: at 6.2 only 96.9 % of the LDL lets go, receptors fall to about 45 % and LDL nearly doubles (about 4.9 mmol/L). At 6.3, 91 % lets go, receptors are about 19 % and LDL about 8.5; at 6.5 only half lets go, receptors are about 4 % and LDL about 14.5 mmol/L, close to two faulty genes. It is steep because a receptor that still holds its LDL is sent to the lysosome on every trip, and a receptor makes about 60 trips in its life: a 3 % failure to let go per trip already more than doubles the chance of being destroyed per trip (from about 1.7 % to about 3.7 %, so the lifetime falls from about 60 to about 27 trips). Small changes per trip add up over many trips. The receptor itself is normal; it is lost because the endosome is not acid enough for it to let go of LDL, and a loaded receptor is not recycled (the same happens with FH mutations in the part of the receptor that releases LDL). In the real cell the lysosome would also stop digesting LDL.
E5. The most RNA in the cytosol is reached at a pKa of about 6.2, about 1.9 % of the dose (at pKa 6.4, about 1.7 %; approved LNPs use pKa about 6.2–6.7). With a low pKa (5.0–5.5) the lipid is hardly charged even in the late endosome (at pKa 5 and pH 5.5 only about 24 %), so it cannot disturb the endosome membrane before the contents reach the lysosome: escape is below 1 %. With a high pKa (7–9) the lipid is already charged in the blood (at pKa 7, about 28 % at pH 7.4), so escape per particle is higher (4–6 %), but most particles stick to blood proteins and cells and are removed before they reach the target cells (11 % reach the cells at pKa 7, 1 % at pKa 9); overall only 0.1–0.5 % of the dose arrives in the cytosol. With the V-ATPase blocked (lowest pH 7.2) the lipid stays mostly uncharged in the endosome and escape falls to about 0.1 % at pKa 6.4. The escape depends on acidification: the lipid becomes positive only when the endosome pH falls below its pKa. Even at best, about 97 % of the particles end in the lysosome, which is why better endosomal escape is a major goal of RNA medicine.

title: The endoplasmic reticulum: making, folding and checking proteins
section: About this lecture

title: The endoplasmic reticulum: making, folding and checking proteins
section: The question: why is this cell full of membrane?
text:
The question: why is this cell full of membrane?



Pancreatic acinar cell (mammal), transmission electron micrograph; scale bar 500 nm. Centre: the nucleus, with gaps in its envelope (nuclear pores). Top right and left edge: stacked sheets of rough ER, lined with ribosomes.


This cell makes digestive enzymes and secretes them into the gut, all day.
Its cytoplasm is packed with flat membrane sheets covered in ribosomes: the rough ER.
Each enzyme is made by a ribosome in the cytosol, but must end up outside the cell, folded, with its disulfide bonds.
A receptor in the plasma membrane must also face the right way: its binding site outside, its signalling tail inside.

How does a protein get into the ER, fold correctly, and how does the cell catch the ones that fail?


This electron micrograph shows part of a pancreatic acinar cell. On the left is the nucleus; you can see gaps in its envelope, the nuclear pores. The rest of the picture is filled with parallel membranes, each lined with small black dots. The dots are ribosomes, and the membranes are the rough ER. Cells that secrete a lot of protein, such as pancreatic cells, plasma cells that make antibodies, and liver cells that make serum proteins, are full of rough ER. Here is the puzzle. Ribosomes sit in the cytosol, so every protein starts there. Yet a digestive enzyme must end up outside the cell, and it must be folded and stable outside, which for most secreted proteins means disulfide bonds. Membrane proteins have an extra problem: they must sit in the membrane facing the right way. A hormone receptor with its binding site inside the cell would be useless. Today we answer three questions: how does a chain get in, how does it fold, and how is it checked.

title: The endoplasmic reticulum: making, folding and checking proteins
section: The ER: one membrane, one lumen
text:
The ER: one membrane, one lumen


The ER is a single network of membrane: sheets (rough ER, with ribosomes) and tubules (smooth ER). The outer nuclear membrane is part of it.
Inside is one continuous space, the lumen. In topology it is like the outside of the cell (cell tour).
In a liver cell the ER is about half of all membrane in the cell.


The ER is not a set of separate bags. It is one continuous membrane system that spreads from the nuclear envelope through the whole cytoplasm. Where it carries ribosomes it forms flat sheets: the rough ER. Where it has no ribosomes it forms a network of thin tubules: the smooth ER. The two kinds are connected, and the space inside, the lumen, is one continuous compartment. Even the space between the two membranes of the nuclear envelope belongs to it, because the outer nuclear membrane is part of the ER. Remember the topology rule from the cell tour: the lumen of the ER is equivalent to the outside of the cell, because vesicles can carry material from the lumen to the outside without crossing a membrane. In a liver cell, the ER membrane makes up about half of all the membrane in the cell, and the lumen is about a tenth of the cell’s volume. This large size reflects how much work the ER does. Its chemistry is also different from the cytosol: it is oxidizing, rich in calcium and full of chaperones.

title: The endoplasmic reticulum: making, folding and checking proteins
section: The signal sequence: a ticket into the ER
text:
The signal sequence: a ticket into the ER


Most ER proteins start with an N-terminal signal sequence: a few positive charges, then a hydrophobic core, then a cut site.
The pattern is the signal, not an exact sequence. Put one in front of a cytosolic protein and it enters the ER.
Signal peptidase in the ER membrane cuts it off: the mature protein is shorter.


How does the cell know which proteins belong in the ER? The answer is a signal sequence, a stretch of about fifteen to thirty amino acids at the N-terminus. It has three parts: a few positive charges, a core of six to fifteen hydrophobic amino acids, and a polar region with small amino acids that marks where it will be cut. The example is the real start of human preproinsulin. The first twenty-four amino acids form the signal sequence, coloured here by region. After the cut, the chain becomes proinsulin, and later insulin. Signal sequences of different proteins share almost no exact sequence. What matters is the pattern, above all the hydrophobic core. Experiments show this clearly: put a signal sequence in front of a protein that normally stays in the cytosol, such as globin, and it is taken into the ER. Remove the signal from a secreted protein and it stays in the cytosol. Signal peptidase, an enzyme with its active site in the lumen, cuts the signal sequence off while the protein is still being made.

title: The endoplasmic reticulum: making, folding and checking proteins
section: SRP brings the ribosome to the ER
text:
SRP brings the ribosome to the ER


SRP (signal recognition particle: six proteins + an RNA) binds the signal as it leaves the ribosome and pauses translation.
SRP docks on the SRP receptor in the ER membrane; the ribosome is handed to the translocon.
GTP hydrolysis releases SRP for another round. The chain is threaded in while it is made: co-translational translocation.


All protein synthesis starts on free ribosomes in the cytosol. When a signal sequence comes out of the exit tunnel of the ribosome, it is grabbed by the signal recognition particle, SRP. SRP is a complex of six proteins and a long RNA. One of its proteins has a pocket lined with flexible methionine side chains that holds hydrophobic signals of many shapes. SRP also slows down translation, so the chain does not grow too long, or fold, before it reaches the ER. Then SRP, carrying the ribosome, binds the SRP receptor in the ER membrane, right next to the translocon. Both SRP and its receptor are GTPases. When they meet, the ribosome is handed to the translocon, the GTPs are hydrolysed, and SRP and its receptor separate, ready for another ribosome. Translation now continues, and the chain goes straight from the ribosome into the channel as it is made. This is co-translational translocation. Because many ribosomes can read one mRNA, the ER surface becomes covered in ribosomes: this is why rough ER looks rough.

title: The endoplasmic reticulum: making, folding and checking proteins
section: The translocon: a channel with a plug and a side gate
text:
The translocon: a channel with a plug and a side gate



SecY translocon of the archaeon Methanococcus jannaschii (PDB 1RHZ), side view; cytosol on top. Human Sec61 has the same fold.


Sec61 complex: a pore in the membrane. A short plug helix keeps it closed when no chain is inside, so ions do not leak.
The chain goes through as an unfolded string: one chain at a time.
A lateral gate in the wall opens sideways into the lipid. A hydrophobic segment can slip out and stay in the membrane: this is how membrane proteins are made.
Some proteins enter after translation: tail-anchored proteins, whose only hydrophobic segment is at the C-terminus (another route, the GET pathway).



The translocon is a protein channel called the Sec61 complex. The picture shows the related channel from an archaeon, seen from the side, with the cytosol on top. The channel is shaped like an hourglass. In the middle there is a ring of hydrophobic side chains that seals tightly around the passing chain, and a short helix, the plug, closes the pore when no chain is inside. This matters because the ER is a calcium store, and an open hole would let calcium and other ions leak out. The chain passes through unfolded, like a thread through the eye of a needle. The most important feature is a seam in the wall, the lateral gate. It can open sideways towards the lipid bilayer. When a hydrophobic segment of about twenty amino acids sits in the channel, it can slip out through this gate and stay in the membrane as a transmembrane helix. That is how all multipass membrane proteins of the secretory pathway are made. A small group of proteins, called tail-anchored proteins, have their only membrane segment at the very end. They are inserted after translation, by a separate pathway.

title: The endoplasmic reticulum: making, folding and checking proteins
section: How do we know? Microsomes and protease
text:
How do we know? Microsomes and protease


Milstein (1972): antibody light chain made in a test tube without ER is about 20 amino acids longer: the uncut signal.
Blobel: with microsomes (ER vesicles) the chain is cut and protected from protease, unless detergent opens the membrane. Nobel Prize 1999 for the signal hypothesis.
The same test shows topology: parts on the cytosolic side are digested, parts in the lumen are protected.


How did we learn all this? With a test tube system. You can make protein from mRNA in a cell-free extract that contains ribosomes but no membranes. In 1972 César Milstein and colleagues did this with the mRNA for an antibody light chain. The product was about twenty amino acids longer than the light chain secreted by cells. Günter Blobel and colleagues then added microsomes: small sealed vesicles of ER membrane that form when cells are broken up. Now the chain was the normal, shorter size, so the signal had been cut off. Next they added a protease to the outside. The protein survived, because it was inside the vesicle and proteases cannot cross membranes. Only when they also added detergent, which dissolves the membrane, was the protein digested. This showed that the chain had crossed the membrane while it was being made. Blobel received the Nobel Prize in 1999 for the signal hypothesis. The same experiment is still used to find the topology of membrane proteins: whatever faces the cytosol is cut, whatever faces the lumen is protected.

title: The endoplasmic reticulum: making, folding and checking proteins
section: Membrane proteins: which way round?
text:
Membrane proteins: which way round?


Type I: cleaved signal sequence, then a stop-transfer: N-terminus in the lumen, C-terminus in the cytosol.
Types II and III: no cleaved signal. The first hydrophobic segment is a signal-anchor. Positive charges stay on the cytosolic side and decide which end goes in.


Now we can make membrane proteins. A type I protein, such as the LDL receptor, has a normal signal sequence. The chain after it is threaded into the lumen. Later a second hydrophobic segment arrives in the channel. It cannot be pushed through: it leaves the translocon sideways and stays in the membrane. This is a stop-transfer sequence. Everything after it stays in the cytosol. So the N-terminus is in the lumen and the C-terminus in the cytosol. Types II and III have no cleaved signal. Their first hydrophobic segment both brings them to the ER, through SRP, and stays as the membrane anchor: a signal-anchor. Which way it inserts depends mainly on charges. Positive amino acids, lysine and arginine, nearly always stay on the cytosolic side: the positive-inside rule. With the charges before the segment, the N-terminus stays in the cytosol: type II, such as the transferrin receptor. With the charges after it, the N-terminus is pulled into the lumen: type III, such as the cytochrome P450 enzymes in the liver ER.

title: The endoplasmic reticulum: making, folding and checking proteins
section: Multipass proteins, and the side that faces out
text:
Multipass proteins, and the side that faces out


After the first segment, hydrophobic segments act as start-transfer and stop-transfer in turn. The same kind of helix plays either role: it depends on where the chain is when it arrives.
The orientation is fixed in the ER. Vesicles carry it to the cell surface without flipping it: the lumen side becomes the outside (cell tour). Sugars are added only in the lumen, so they always end up outside. Try it: Demo: topology builder


Many membrane proteins cross the membrane several times: GLUT1 twelve times, receptors coupled to G proteins seven times. The rule is a simple extension. The first hydrophobic segment starts translocation. The next one stops it and stays in the membrane. The next one starts it again, and so on. A hydrophobic helix does not carry a label that says start or stop. Its role depends on where the chain is when the helix arrives in the translocon: if the chain is going into the lumen, the helix stops it; if the chain is in the cytosol, the helix starts a new loop into the lumen. A useful consequence: with an odd number of segments, the two ends are on opposite sides; with an even number, on the same side. This is a simplified rule: in real proteins charges and loop lengths matter too. Once made, the orientation never changes. Vesicles bud and fuse, and the part in the ER lumen ends up outside the cell. That is why sugar chains, which are added in the lumen, always face outwards. The topology builder lets you test this.

title: The endoplasmic reticulum: making, folding and checking proteins
section: Folding in the ER: BiP and disulfide bonds
text:
Folding in the ER: BiP and disulfide bonds


The lumen is crowded with chaperones. BiP (an Hsp70) binds exposed hydrophobic stretches and lets go again, using ATP.
Disulfide bonds (S–S) form only in the oxidizing ER lumen. PDI makes them and breaks wrong ones, until the right pairs are found.


A chain entering the lumen is unfolded, and unfolded chains expose hydrophobic stretches that make them stick to each other and aggregate. The ER lumen is full of chaperones that prevent this. The main one is BiP, a member of the Hsp70 family. BiP binds a hydrophobic stretch, holds it for a moment using the energy of ATP, and lets it go again. Many cycles of binding and release give the chain time to fold without aggregating. BiP also sits at the translocon and helps pull the chain in. The second job is disulfide bonds, covalent links between two cysteines. They form only in an oxidizing environment. The ER lumen is oxidizing, while the cytosol is reducing, kept so by glutathione. This is why disulfide bonds are typical of secreted and cell-surface proteins, which must survive outside the cell. Protein disulfide isomerase, PDI, transfers disulfide bonds to the new chain, and it can also break a wrong pair and try again. An antibody, for example, has more than ten disulfide bonds that must be paired correctly.

title: The endoplasmic reticulum: making, folding and checking proteins
section: N-glycosylation: a sugar block added in one step
text:
N-glycosylation: a sugar block added in one step


Oligosaccharyltransferase (OST), next to the translocon, moves a ready-made block of 14 sugars from the lipid dolichol to an asparagine in the sequence N-X-S/T (X is not proline).
It happens co-translationally, on most proteins that enter the ER. The sugars are later trimmed in the ER and rebuilt in the Golgi.
Tunicamycin, an antibiotic, blocks the first step: proteins misfold. A standard way to stress the ER in the lab.


Most proteins that enter the ER get sugar chains attached to asparagines, which is called N-linked glycosylation. The process is unusual. The sugar chain is not built on the protein one sugar at a time. Instead, a block of fourteen sugars is first built on a lipid carrier in the ER membrane, called dolichol. The block has two N-acetylglucosamines, nine mannoses and three glucoses. The enzyme oligosaccharyltransferase, OST, sits right next to the translocon. As the chain comes into the lumen, OST looks for the sequence asparagine, any amino acid except proline, then serine or threonine, and moves the whole block onto the asparagine in one step. The symbols in the figure follow the international colour code for sugars, which you will see in papers. The block is then trimmed in the ER and rebuilt in the Golgi, as the Golgi lecture shows. The antibiotic tunicamycin blocks the first step of building the block. Cells treated with it make proteins without N-glycans, many of which misfold. It is a standard tool to trigger ER stress.

title: The endoplasmic reticulum: making, folding and checking proteins
section: The calnexin cycle: sugars as a folding tag
text:
The calnexin cycle: sugars as a folding tag


Glucosidases remove two glucoses. With one glucose left, the protein binds calnexin, a lectin chaperone in the ER membrane.
When the last glucose is removed, it is released. If it is still unfolded, UGGT puts a glucose back: another round.
Slow mannose trimming works as a timer: a protein that never folds is sent to degradation.


The sugar chain has a second job: it is a label that tells the ER how folding is going. Right after the block is added, two enzymes called glucosidases remove two of the three glucoses. A protein with one glucose left is bound by calnexin, a chaperone in the ER membrane that recognises this sugar. Its soluble partner in the lumen is calreticulin. While bound, the protein is protected and is helped by a PDI-like enzyme to make its disulfide bonds. Then the last glucose is removed and the protein is released. Now comes the check. An enzyme called UGGT looks at the released protein. If it still has exposed hydrophobic patches, UGGT adds one glucose back, and the protein binds calnexin again for another round. A folded protein is ignored by UGGT and moves on to the exit sites of the ER. Meanwhile, a slow mannosidase trims mannoses from the sugar chain. This works as a timer: after many failed rounds, the trimmed sugar chain marks the protein for destruction. The protein is not kept forever.

title: The endoplasmic reticulum: making, folding and checking proteins
section: Quality control and ERAD
text:
Quality control and ERAD





Myeloma cells in pleural fluid. Red arrows: plasma cells filled with Russell bodies, ER swollen with antibody that cannot leave. White arrow: a nearly normal plasma cell.


Only folded and assembled proteins leave the ER. Unfolded ones are held by chaperones.
ERAD (ER-associated degradation): the protein is pulled back into the cytosol through the Hrd1 complex, ubiquitinated, extracted by p97 (ATP) and destroyed by the proteasome.


The ER lets only correctly folded and correctly assembled proteins move on. An antibody heavy chain, for example, stays in the ER, bound to BiP, until it has paired with a light chain. Proteins that cannot fold must not pile up, so they are removed by ER-associated degradation, ERAD. But the destroying machine, the proteasome, is in the cytosol, not in the ER. So the misfolded protein is pulled back across the membrane, the opposite way. This happens through a membrane complex built around Hrd1. Hrd1 forms a channel and is also a ubiquitin ligase: it attaches a chain of ubiquitin to the protein as it comes out. An ATP-driven machine called p97 pulls the protein out of the membrane, and the proteasome degrades it. You meet ubiquitin and the proteasome in more detail in the lecture on protein life and death. The picture on the right shows what happens when export fails: plasma cells from a myeloma patient with Russell bodies, ER compartments swollen with antibody that could not leave.

title: The endoplasmic reticulum: making, folding and checking proteins
section: When the ER is overloaded: the unfolded protein response
text:
When the ER is overloaded: the unfolded protein response


Three sensors, IRE1, PERK, ATF6, are held quiet by BiP. Unfolded proteins pull BiP away and the sensors switch on.
The cell makes more chaperones and ERAD machinery, translates less, and grows more ER. If the stress lasts, the UPR triggers apoptosis (CHOP).
Plasma cells and β cells live with high ER load; ER stress contributes to diabetes and to many neurodegenerative diseases.


What if more unfolded protein arrives than the ER can handle? Three sensors in the ER membrane notice. Each has a part in the lumen and a part in the cytosol. At rest, BiP sits on their lumenal parts. When unfolded proteins pile up, they take BiP away, and the sensors become active. IRE1 is a kinase and an RNA-cutting enzyme. It cuts an intron out of the mRNA for XBP1 in the cytosol, an unusual way to splice, and the spliced mRNA makes an active transcription factor. PERK phosphorylates the translation factor eIF2α, which slows down almost all translation, so less new protein enters the ER. ATF6 travels to the Golgi, where proteases cut it free from the membrane, and its fragment becomes a transcription factor. Together they make more chaperones, more ERAD machinery and more ER membrane. If balance cannot be restored, prolonged signalling, partly through the transcription factor CHOP, triggers apoptosis, which the apoptosis lecture explains. Insulin-making β cells in the pancreas work at the edge of this balance, and ER stress is one reason they fail in diabetes.

title: The endoplasmic reticulum: making, folding and checking proteins
section: The smooth ER: lipids, drugs and calcium
text:
The smooth ER: lipids, drugs and calcium


Lipids: most phospholipids and cholesterol are made here, on the cytosolic side; steroid hormones in adrenal and gonad cells. Statins block HMG-CoA reductase, an ER enzyme.
Drug metabolism: cytochrome P450 enzymes (type III, as shown earlier) in the liver smooth ER oxidise drugs so they can be excreted.
Ca²⁺ store: SERCA pumps keep ER Ca²⁺ high; IP₃ receptors release it as a signal. In muscle: the sarcoplasmic reticulum.


The smooth ER has no ribosomes and does different work. First, lipids. Most membrane phospholipids and cholesterol are made by enzymes facing the cytosol, so new lipids appear in the cytosolic half of the bilayer. Proteins called scramblases move half of them to the lumenal half, so the membrane grows evenly. The rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis, HMG-CoA reductase, is an ER membrane protein, and statins block it. Cells that make steroid hormones, in the adrenal gland, testis and ovary, are full of smooth ER. Second, drug metabolism. In liver cells, cytochrome P450 enzymes, anchored in the ER membrane with a type III topology, add oxygen to drugs and toxins and make them easier to excrete. When a person takes certain drugs for a long time, the smooth ER of the liver grows. Third, calcium. SERCA pumps use ATP to keep the free calcium in the lumen thousands of times higher than in the cytosol. Channels such as the IP3 receptor release it as a signal, as the signalling lectures show. In muscle this specialised ER is called the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

title: The endoplasmic reticulum: making, folding and checking proteins
section: Why it matters: diseases of ER quality control
text:
Why it matters: diseases of ER quality control



Cystic fibrosis, ΔF508: CFTR loses one phenylalanine in its first ATP-binding domain. It misfolds, is held by the calnexin cycle and destroyed by ERAD. Little reaches the surface, although it could still partly work. Correctors (elexacaftor, tezacaftor) help it fold and leave the ER (ion-channel lecture).
α1-antitrypsin deficiency (Z variant, Glu342Lys): the liver’s protease inhibitor folds slowly and forms polymers in the ER. Liver: the polymers damage hepatocytes (cirrhosis). Lungs: too little reaches the blood, so neutrophil elastase destroys lung tissue (emphysema; smoking makes it much worse). Discovered in Sweden (Laurell and Eriksson, Malmö, 1963).
Both are trafficking diseases: the protein is made but stuck in the ER. Disease mechanisms in depth: Sjukdomslära.



Liver biopsy, α1-antitrypsin deficiency, PAS stain after diastase. Pink globules: α1-antitrypsin trapped in the ER of hepatocytes.


Here the ER’s strict checking becomes a problem. In cystic fibrosis, the most common mutation, called delta F508, removes one phenylalanine from the first ATP-binding domain of the CFTR chloride channel. The protein folds badly. The calnexin cycle and other chaperones hold it, and ERAD destroys almost all of it, although the few molecules that escape can still work partly as channels. A classic experiment showed this: growing the cells at a lower temperature lets some ΔF508 CFTR fold and reach the surface. Today, corrector drugs such as elexacaftor and tezacaftor bind CFTR and help it fold and pass quality control, combined with a potentiator that opens the channel; you met these in the ion-channel lecture. The second disease was discovered in Malmö in 1963. Alpha-1-antitrypsin is made in the liver and released into the blood, where it inhibits elastase from white blood cells. The Z variant folds slowly and links into long polymers inside the ER. The liver cells are damaged, which can cause cirrhosis, and the lungs, without enough inhibitor, are slowly digested by elastase, which causes emphysema. The pink globules in this biopsy are the trapped protein.

title: The endoplasmic reticulum: making, folding and checking proteins
section: Why it matters: antibody drugs and their sugars
text:
Why it matters: antibody drugs and their sugars



Most therapeutic antibodies (e.g. trastuzumab, adalimumab) are made in CHO cells (Chinese hamster ovary) in large bioreactors. Their ER folds them, adds 16 disulfide bonds per IgG and assembles two heavy and two light chains.
Each heavy chain carries one N-glycan (Asn297), added in the ER and finished in the Golgi. It changes how the antibody works: without core fucose, it binds killer-cell receptors much better (stronger killing). Obinutuzumab is made fucose-poor on purpose.
The cell line matters: cetuximab, made in mouse cells, carries a non-human sugar (α-gal) that causes allergic reactions in some patients.
So the glycan pattern is a quality attribute that regulators require (Kliniska prövningar och läkemedelsutveckling).



Structure of an IgG1 antibody: two heavy chains (blue, yellow) and two light chains (green, pink).


Antibodies are the largest class of protein drugs, and almost all are made by living cells, most often Chinese hamster ovary cells grown in steel bioreactors of thousands of litres. Why use mammalian cells and not bacteria? Because the antibody needs an ER: it has sixteen disulfide bonds in its most common form, two heavy and two light chains must be assembled, and each heavy chain carries an N-linked sugar chain at asparagine 297 in its constant part. Bacteria have no ER that can do all of this. The sugar chain is not decoration. It shapes the constant part of the antibody and changes how it binds to receptors on immune cells. Antibodies that lack one sugar, the core fucose, bind a receptor on natural killer cells much more strongly and kill target cells better. Obinutuzumab, used for some leukaemias and lymphomas, is made in cells engineered to add less fucose. The host cell also matters: cetuximab, made in a mouse cell line, carries a sugar humans do not make, and some patients who already have antibodies against it react with anaphylaxis. Manufacturers must therefore control the glycan pattern batch by batch, as you will meet again in the drug development course.

title: The endoplasmic reticulum: making, folding and checking proteins
section: Summary
text:
Summary

Proteins with an ER signal sequence are caught by SRP and threaded through the Sec61 translocon while they are made (co-translational translocation).
Topology is set in the ER: a stop-transfer stops translocation, a signal-anchor starts it, positive charges stay in the cytosol. The lumen side becomes the outside of the cell.
In the lumen, BiP prevents aggregation, PDI makes disulfide bonds, OST adds N-glycans; the calnexin cycle uses the glucose on the glycan as a folding tag.
Quality control keeps unfolded proteins in the ER; ERAD returns them to the cytosol for the proteasome; the UPR adjusts the ER to its load, or kills the cell.
The smooth ER makes lipids, metabolises drugs (P450) and stores Ca²⁺. Misfolding in the ER causes cystic fibrosis and α1-antitrypsin deficiency; the ER of CHO cells makes antibody drugs.

Read more (optional): Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell, 7th ed., ch. 12.
Image credits

Five take-home points. First, entry: a hydrophobic signal is recognised by SRP, which brings the ribosome to the translocon, and the chain enters the ER while it is being made. Second, topology: hydrophobic segments act as start or stop signals depending on where the chain is, positive charges stay in the cytosol, and the side facing the ER lumen ends up facing the outside of the cell. Third, folding: the ER lumen is a special folding environment with chaperones, an oxidizing chemistry for disulfide bonds, and N-glycans that serve both as part of the protein and as a tag in the calnexin cycle. Fourth, checking: unfolded proteins are held back and eventually destroyed by ERAD, and when the load is too high the unfolded protein response restores balance or triggers cell death. Fifth, the smooth ER makes lipids, breaks down drugs and stores calcium. Next, the Golgi lecture follows the proteins that pass the check on their way to the cell surface.

title: Quiz: the endoplasmic reticulum
text:
Short questions to check your understanding of the lecture The endoplasmic reticulum: making, folding and checking proteins. Try each on paper first, then open the hint or the answer. The tag after each question shows the learning outcome (ELO) it practises.

Q1. A ribosome is making a protein with an N-terminal signal sequence. Put these events in order: (a) translation continues and the chain enters the lumen; (b) SRP binds the signal sequence; (c) signal peptidase cuts off the signal; (d) SRP binds the SRP receptor; (e) the signal sequence comes out of the ribosome. [ELO 4]






Hint





SRP cannot bind what is still inside the ribosome’s exit tunnel.









Answer





e → b → d → a → c. The signal comes out of the ribosome, SRP binds it and pauses translation, SRP docks on its receptor next to the translocon, the ribosome is handed to the translocon and translation continues with the chain going into the lumen. Signal peptidase cuts the signal off while the rest of the chain is still being made.




Q2. You make a secreted protein in a test tube from its mRNA, without and with microsomes (ER vesicles). Without microsomes the product is 2 kDa larger. Why? [ELO 4, ELO 1]






Hint





What is missing when there is no ER membrane?









Answer





Without microsomes there is no signal peptidase, so the signal sequence stays on: about 20 amino acids, about 2 kDa. With microsomes, the chain enters the vesicle and the signal is cut off. This was the first evidence for the signal sequence (Milstein, 1972).




Q3. A single-pass membrane protein has no cleavable signal sequence. Its only hydrophobic segment has lysines and arginines on its C-terminal side. Which way does it insert? What type is it? [ELO 4]






Hint





Positive charges stay on the cytosolic side.









Answer





The positive charges after the segment stay in the cytosol, so the C-terminal part is cytosolic and the N-terminus goes into the lumen. It is a type III protein (a signal-anchor with N in the lumen), like the cytochrome P450 enzymes of the liver ER.




Q4. A receptor crosses the membrane 7 times and its N-terminus is outside the cell. Where is its C-terminus? Where on the protein do you expect its N-glycans? [ELO 4, ELO 5]






Hint





Each crossing switches the side. Where are sugars added?









Answer





An odd number of crossings puts the two ends on opposite sides: the C-terminus is in the cytosol. N-glycans are added only in the ER lumen, which becomes the outside of the cell, so they are on the N-terminal part or the outside loops, never on the cytosolic loops or the C-terminal tail.




Q5. Why do disulfide bonds form in the ER lumen but hardly ever in the cytosol? Name the enzyme that helps. [ELO 4, ELO 5]






Hint





A disulfide bond is an oxidised pair of cysteines.









Answer





The ER lumen is oxidizing; the cytosol is reducing (much glutathione in its reduced form), which keeps cysteines as free –SH. PDI (protein disulfide isomerase) makes disulfide bonds in new chains and also breaks wrong pairs so that the correct pairs can form.




Q6. What does the glucose on an N-glycan tell the ER, and what does UGGT do? [ELO 4]






Hint





Calnexin binds glycoproteins with exactly one glucose.









Answer





A single glucose means “hold me”: calnexin (and calreticulin) bind the protein and help it fold. When the last glucose is removed the protein is released. UGGT checks it: if it is still unfolded (exposed hydrophobic patches), UGGT adds one glucose back, so the protein binds calnexin again. Folded proteins are not re-glucosylated and can leave the ER.




Q7. A misfolded protein in the ER lumen is destroyed by the proteasome, which is in the cytosol. How does it get there? [ELO 4]






Hint





ERAD runs translocation in reverse.









Answer





By ERAD: the protein is recognised (trimmed mannoses, exposed hydrophobic parts), pulled back across the ER membrane through the Hrd1 complex, ubiquitinated on the cytosolic side (Hrd1 is a ubiquitin ligase), extracted by the ATPase p97 and degraded by the proteasome.




Q8. Name the three sensors of the unfolded protein response and one thing each does. Why is reducing translation useful? [ELO 4, ELO 5]






Hint





Think of the ER as a factory with too many unfinished products.









Answer





IRE1 splices the XBP1 mRNA, making the transcription factor XBP1 (more chaperones, ERAD and ER membrane). PERK phosphorylates eIF2α, which slows down almost all translation. ATF6 moves to the Golgi, is cut, and its fragment is a transcription factor for chaperone genes. Less translation means less new protein enters the ER while its folding capacity grows, so the backlog can clear. If it cannot, the UPR triggers apoptosis.

title: Study questions: signalling that shapes tissues and decides fates
text: Study questions in the style of the written exam. Write your answer first (a few sentences, or a labelled sketch where it helps), then compare with the model answer. Each question is tagged with its learning outcome (ELO). Questions tagged [VG] are of the kind used for the higher grade: predict, compare, explain an unexpected result or design an experiment.

title: Study questions: signalling that shapes tissues and decides fates
section: G-level questions
text:
G-level questions
1. In all the pathways of this lecture, the transcription factor is already present in the cell before the signal arrives. Explain why this is so, and list the five ways in which a signal can free such a factor, with one pathway for each. [ELO 3]






Model answer





A factor that is already made can be activated quickly and reversibly, without waiting for transcription and translation of the factor itself; it only has to be kept inactive until the signal comes. Five ways:

Stop destroying it: β-catenin in Wnt signalling (no longer phosphorylated by the destruction complex and degraded).
Cut it out of the membrane: the Notch intracellular domain, released by ADAM and γ-secretase.
Phosphorylate it: SMAD2/3 phosphorylated by the TGF-β type I receptor.
Stop converting it into a repressor: Gli in Hedgehog signalling.
The signal binds the factor directly: nuclear receptors for steroid hormones.

NF-κB is a variant of the first: the signal destroys its inhibitor IκB rather than stabilising the factor.




2. Draw and explain the Wnt/β-catenin pathway with and without Wnt. Include the destruction complex, the proteasome and TCF. [ELO 3]






Model answer





Without Wnt: β-catenin is made but held by the destruction complex (scaffolds Axin and APC, kinases GSK3 and CK1). It is phosphorylated, recognised by a ubiquitin ligase, ubiquitylated and degraded by the proteasome within minutes. In the nucleus, TCF sits on Wnt target genes together with a repressor: genes off.
With Wnt: Wnt binds Frizzled and its co-receptor (LRP5/6); the cytoplasmic protein Dishevelled is recruited and the destruction complex is pulled to the receptor and blocked. β-catenin accumulates, enters the nucleus, displaces the repressor and binds TCF as a coactivator: target genes on (e.g. MYC, cyclin D1: division; AXIN2: negative feedback). In the adult, Wnt keeps stem cells in intestinal crypts dividing.




3. Describe Hedgehog signalling, including the role of the primary cilium. What is the role of Patched, Smoothened and Gli? [ELO 3]






Model answer





The primary cilium is a single, non-moving projection on most cells that acts as a signalling antenna. Without Hedgehog, the receptor Patched sits in the cilium and keeps Smoothened out and inactive; the transcription factor Gli is partly cut (by the proteasome) into a short repressor that keeps target genes off. With Hedgehog, Hedgehog binds Patched, which leaves the cilium; Smoothened moves into the cilium and becomes active; Gli is no longer cut and the full-length protein enters the nucleus as an activator. Targets include Patched itself (negative feedback) and Gli1. The logic is a double negative: Hedgehog ⊣ Patched ⊣ Smoothened.




4. Explain how a Notch signal reaches the nucleus. Why does Notch signalling need direct cell–cell contact? [ELO 3]






Model answer





The ligand (Delta or Jagged) is a transmembrane protein on the sending cell, so only a cell that touches the receiving cell can signal; Notch also needs the pulling force made when the sending cell endocytoses Delta. Steps: (1) Delta binds Notch; (2) the pull exposes a site that an ADAM protease cuts outside the membrane; (3) γ-secretase cuts Notch inside the membrane; (4) the Notch intracellular domain enters the nucleus and binds CSL, turning it from a repressor into an activator; (5) target genes such as the Hes repressors are switched on. Each receptor is used once; there is no amplification step.




5. What is lateral inhibition? Explain how it can turn a sheet of almost identical cells into a regular pattern. [ELO 3]






Model answer





Lateral inhibition is a feedback between neighbouring cells through Delta–Notch: Delta on one cell activates Notch in its neighbours, and active Notch (via Hes repressors) lowers Delta and the “differentiate” genes in that same neighbour. If cell A has slightly more Delta than its neighbour B, B receives more Notch signal and makes less Delta, so A receives less Notch signal and makes more Delta. This double-negative loop amplifies small random differences until A is Delta-high (e.g. hair cell or neuron) and B is Notch-high (supporting cell or epidermis). In a sheet, the result is a salt-and-pepper pattern: single Delta-high cells, each surrounded by Notch-high cells, with no two Delta-high cells touching.




6. Describe TGF-β signalling from receptor to gene, and explain why the same TGF-β signal can have different effects in different cell types. [ELO 3]






Model answer





The TGF-β dimer brings together type II and type I receptors, which are serine/threonine kinases. Type II phosphorylates type I; type I phosphorylates SMAD2/3. Phosphorylated SMAD2/3 binds SMAD4, the complex enters the nucleus and binds DNA. SMADs bind DNA weakly and act together with other transcription factors that differ between cell types, and the chromatin that is open also differs. So the target genes depend on the cell: in epithelial cells TGF-β stops division (p15, p21), in fibroblasts it increases matrix production. The pathway is switched off by phosphatases and by SMAD7, which is itself a target gene (negative feedback).




7. Describe how NF-κB is activated by an inflammatory signal such as TNF-α, and how the response is switched off again. [ELO 3] [ELO 4]






Model answer





At rest, IκB binds NF-κB in the cytosol and covers its nuclear localisation signal. TNF-α (or IL-1, or bacterial LPS) acts through its receptor on the kinase complex IKK, which phosphorylates IκB. Phosphorylated IκB is recognised by a ubiquitin ligase, gets a polyubiquitin chain and is destroyed by the proteasome. Free NF-κB enters the nucleus within minutes and switches on cytokines, adhesion molecules and anti-apoptosis genes. Switch-off: one target gene is IκB; the new IκB binds NF-κB, takes it out of the nucleus and ends the response (negative feedback).




8. Compare signalling by a steroid hormone through a nuclear receptor with signalling by a hormone through a GPCR. Give at least four differences. [ELO 3]






Model answer














Nuclear receptor (e.g. cortisol)
GPCR (e.g. adrenaline)




Hormone
small, hydrophobic; crosses the membrane
usually polar; stays outside


Receptor location
inside the cell (cytosol or nucleus)
plasma membrane


Relay
none: the receptor is the transcription factor
G protein, second messengers, kinases


Amplification
little
large (enzyme cascade)


Output
changes transcription
changes activity of existing proteins (and sometimes genes)


Speed and duration
hours, long-lasting
seconds, short

title: Study questions: signalling that shapes tissues and decides fates
section: VG-style questions
text:
VG-style questions
9. [VG] A biotech company develops a γ-secretase inhibitor to treat Alzheimer’s disease (γ-secretase makes the amyloid-β peptide from its precursor protein). Predict, from what you know about Notch, which side effects may appear in tissues that keep renewing in the adult, such as the gut lining and the skin. Explain the mechanism. How could the company test this early, in cells? [ELO 3] [ELO 9]






Model answer





γ-secretase also makes the Notch intracellular domain, so the drug will block Notch signalling in every tissue it reaches. In adult tissues that renew, Notch decides between fates of newly made cells. In the gut, blocking Notch makes progenitor cells take the secretory fate: too many goblet cells (mucus) and too few absorptive cells, which gives diarrhoea and poor absorption. In the skin, Notch is needed for normal differentiation of keratinocytes; loss of Notch disturbs it and can promote skin tumours. Immune cell development (T cells need Notch) may also suffer. (In a real phase III trial, the γ-secretase inhibitor semagacestat worsened cognition and increased skin cancers, and the trial was stopped.) Early test: cells with a Notch reporter gene (CSL binding sites driving luciferase) plus a source of Delta: measure how strongly each candidate blocks Notch at the dose that blocks amyloid-β. Search for compounds that spare Notch.




10. [VG] Researchers make two kinds of mouse with intestinal tumours. In mouse A the tumour cells have lost APC; in mouse B the tumour cells have an activating mutation in β-catenin that removes its phosphorylation sites. They test a drug that activates GSK3 (helps the destruction complex). Predict the effect in each mouse, and explain. Then predict the effect of a drug that blocks the binding of β-catenin to TCF. [ELO 3] [ELO 9]






Model answer





GSK3 activator: in mouse A, the destruction complex lacks its scaffold APC, so GSK3 cannot effectively reach β-catenin; the drug likely has little effect. In mouse B, β-catenin has no phosphorylation sites, so whatever GSK3 does, β-catenin cannot be marked for destruction: no effect. (In neither case does more kinase activity help, because the fault is in the complex or in the substrate.) Blocking β-catenin–TCF binding acts downstream of both mutations, at the last step before the genes: it should switch off Wnt target genes in both mice. General rule: a drug works only if it acts at or below the faulty step; this is the same reason vismodegib (Smoothened) works when Patched is lost but not when Gli is changed.




11. [VG] You suspect that a new gene, X, is a Notch target in the developing inner ear and that it is needed for supporting cells. Design experiments to show (a) that Notch signalling switches X on, and (b) that X is needed for the supporting-cell fate. Include controls. [ELO 3] [ELO 1]






Model answer





(a) Notch switches X on. (1) Look where X is expressed (in situ hybridisation or immunostaining): it should be in supporting cells (Notch-high), not hair cells. (2) Treat inner-ear explants with a γ-secretase inhibitor (control: solvent only): X expression should fall within hours, and Hes genes (known targets, positive control) too. (3) Express an active Notch intracellular domain in cells that normally lack X: X should appear. (4) Put the X enhancer in front of luciferase in a reporter assay; it should respond to the Notch tail, and mutating the CSL binding sites should abolish the response.
(b) X is needed. Knock out X (CRISPR, or a conditional knockout only in the inner ear; control: littermates without the deletion) and count hair cells and supporting cells with markers. If X is needed for the supporting-cell fate, supporting cells should be fewer and hair cells may increase, as in a Notch loss. Rescue: re-expressing X should restore the normal pattern.

title: Study questions: signalling that shapes tissues and decides fates
section: Explore
text:
Explore
A sheet of 288 hexagonal cells, each making Delta (the signal) and Notch (the receptor). Delta on a cell activates Notch in its six neighbours; active Notch switches off Delta in the same cell. The model is Collier et al. (1996): two differential equations per cell (an ODE system on a grid), with Collier’s parameter values. The cells start almost equal, with small random differences, and keep a little random noise in how much Delta they make. Colours change smoothly: dark green = Delta high (future hair cell or neuron), cream = Notch on (supporting cell). Use Colour cells by to switch to Notch activity. Tap a cell to follow it (A, orange) and its right-hand neighbour (B, dashed) in the graph.
The demo opens at real time: in a tissue the pattern takes about a day, so nothing visible happens. Choose a time-lapse speed (1 s = 1 h is a good start). Time scale and noise are illustrative; in the model, fates never lock in (real cells commit after a while). Restart gives a new random start; Reset all restores the defaults. Because of the noise, your numbers will differ a little from the solutions.



E1. Set the clock to 1 s = 1 h and watch the sheet. When do the first clearly dark cells appear? What fraction of cells ends up Delta-high, and do any two Delta-high cells touch? Follow cells A and B in the graph: how do two neighbours that start equal end up? Press Restart two or three times: what changes and what stays the same? [ELO 3]
E2. Predict first. What will happen if every cell is exactly the same and there is no noise? Set noise to 0 %, press Restart and watch for 30 hours of tissue time. Then, while it runs, set noise back to 5 %. Explain both results. [ELO 3]
E3. Lower the feedback strength (how strongly Notch switches off Delta) to 30 and press Restart. Watch for 2–3 days of tissue time. Then try 50, 300 and 3000 (Restart each time). Describe what changes. Why does lateral inhibition need a strong feedback? [ELO 3]
E4. [VG] Predict first. Tick Notch knockout in a patch of cells and press Restart. What will the cells inside the patch become? What about the normal cells that border the patch? Check, using both colour modes. Relate the result to the fly experiments on the “How do we know?” slide. [ELO 3]
E5. [VG] Predict first. Let a pattern form (defaults), then set the γ-secretase inhibitor to 100 %. What happens, and why? Reset, let a pattern form again, and set the inhibitor to 50 % instead. Explain the difference. How does the 100 % result relate to the inner-ear experiment in the lecture, and what does the model leave out that matters for a real treatment? [ELO 3] [ELO 9]






Solutions





E1. For the first 10–12 hours the sheet looks uniform: the tiny differences are growing, but too little to see. Dark cells appear at about 12–16 h, and the pattern is complete after about 20–25 h: about 30 % of cells (roughly one in three) are Delta-high, and no two Delta-high cells touch (the readout shows 0 %). In the graph, A and B start at the same Delta level (about 0.07); then one of them rises to about 1 while the other falls to almost 0. Which one wins depends only on the random start. After Restart the positions of the dark cells change, but the rules stay: about 30 % dark cells, none touching, each surrounded by light cells. On a hexagonal sheet, “no two neighbours both high” allows at most one cell in three to be high, so the pattern packs the dark cells almost as tightly as possible. This is what lateral inhibition predicts: the pattern is reproducible, the choice of individual cells is not.
E2. With no noise, all cells are exactly equal and stay equal: no pattern after 30 h (or ever). The uniform state is a balance in which each cell receives exactly as much Delta as it sends, but it is unstable, like a pencil standing on its tip: nothing pushes it over unless something breaks the symmetry. When noise is turned back on, small differences appear and are amplified; dark cells appear after about 15 h and the pattern is complete about 25 h later. Real cells always differ a little (gene-expression noise, cell size, the time since division), so lateral inhibition does not need a pre-made pattern: it creates one from noise.
E3. At 30 the sheet stays uniform for days: the feedback is too weak to amplify differences, so each cell settles at the same middle level of Delta and Notch (no decision). At 50 a pattern forms, but slowly (first dark cells after about 30 h). At 300 and 3000 it forms faster (complete after about 20 h and about 10 h) and looks the same: about 30 % dark cells, none touching. A small difference must be amplified around the loop: more Delta in A → more Notch in B → less Delta in B → less Notch in A → more Delta in A. If each step is weak, the difference shrinks on each round instead of growing, and the cells return to the uniform state. Only when the gain around the loop is large enough do differences grow (the threshold in this model lies between about 30 and 50).
E4. Inside the patch, all cells become Delta-high (dark), and they touch each other: without Notch they cannot be inhibited, so they all take the “default” fate (in the fly: neural). Their Notch activity is 0. The normal cells bordering the patch all become Notch-high (light): each receives Delta from Delta-high knockout neighbours and is strongly inhibited (in our run, all 18 border cells were light). Further away, the normal salt-and-pepper pattern forms. This is the result of the fly mosaic experiments: a Notch-negative patch becomes all neural (and in a whole embryo without Notch, too many neurons and almost no skin form), and the effect is cell-autonomous: the knockout cells still send Delta normally, they just cannot receive the signal.
E5. At 100 % inhibitor no Notch tail can be released, so no cell receives a Notch signal. Every cell, including the light ones, raises its Delta: within about 10 h all cells are Delta-high (all would become hair cells or neurons). This matches the experiment in which a γ-secretase inhibitor turned supporting cells into extra hair cells in the mouse inner ear. At 50 %, the result is different: the pattern fades (after 20 h only a few dark cells are left) and the cells drift to an intermediate, undecided level. Halving Notch cleavage weakens the feedback loop, as in E3, so the differences are no longer amplified and are lost. In the model, fates are never locked and every cell can switch back. Left out: real cells commit; after some time, hair cells and supporting cells no longer change fate. In adult ears few supporting cells can still convert, so a drug can only make a limited number of new hair cells, and a cell that converts is lost as a supporting cell. A real treatment also has to reach the inner ear and must not block Notch in the rest of the body (see question 9).

title: The Golgi and the secretory pathway
section: About this lecture
