title: The Golgi and the secretory pathway
section: The question: how does a cell export its proteins?
text:
The question: how does a cell export its proteins?







Pancreatic acinar cells, transmission EM. Nucleus (left), stacks of rough ER (thin parallel lines) and dark zymogen granules (right). Scale bar 500 nm.


Acinar cells of the pancreas make digestive enzymes for the gut: several grams of protein a day in a human.
The enzymes are made on the rough ER, but they leave the cell from granules at the other end of the cell.
They are never free in the cytosol: they cross no membrane after the ER.
And they wait in granules until a meal signal says “now”.

How does a protein travel from ER to outside without crossing a membrane? And how does it know where to go?


This electron micrograph shows acinar cells from the pancreas. These cells make digestive enzymes: proteases, lipases and amylase, several grams of protein per day in a human. You can see the nucleus on the left, the rough ER as many thin parallel membranes filling the cell, and on the right the round, dark zymogen granules, which are packets of stored enzyme. The enzymes are made by ribosomes on the ER and enter the ER lumen during synthesis, as you saw in the ER lecture. They leave the cell when a granule fuses with the plasma membrane facing the gland duct. In between they never touch the cytosol, and this matters, because a protease loose in the cytosol would digest the cell. They also do not leave at once: they are stored until a hormone or nerve signal after a meal triggers release. So we have three questions. How does a protein move between compartments without crossing a membrane? How is it sorted to the right place? And how is release controlled in time?
crumbs: The Golgi and the secretory pathway

title: The Golgi and the secretory pathway
section: The secretory pathway: a map
text:
The secretory pathway: a map


Anterograde (forward): ER → ERGIC (ER–Golgi intermediate compartment) → cis, medial, trans Golgi → trans-Golgi network (TGN) → plasma membrane, granules or lysosomes. Retrograde (back): COPI vesicles return escaped ER proteins.
The lumen of every compartment is topologically outside the cell: what faces the lumen will face the outside after fusion.


Here is the whole route on one map. A protein that leaves the ER first reaches the ER–Golgi intermediate compartment, called the ERGIC, a set of tubules and vesicle clusters close to the Golgi. From there it enters the Golgi apparatus at its cis face, the side facing the ER, and passes through the stack of flattened cisternae, cis, medial and trans, to the trans-Golgi network, the TGN. The TGN is the sorting station: it sends cargo to the plasma membrane, into secretory granules, or to endosomes and lysosomes. Each step uses a membrane carrier, a vesicle or a tubule, which buds from one compartment and fuses with the next. Traffic also goes backwards: retrograde carriers bring back ER proteins that leaked out. One idea to keep in mind: the inside of every compartment on this map is topologically equivalent to the outside of the cell. A protein in the ER lumen, or the part of a membrane protein facing the lumen, ends up outside the cell or on the outer face of the plasma membrane. That is why sugars on your glycoproteins face outwards.
crumbs: The Golgi and the secretory pathway

title: The Golgi and the secretory pathway
section: How do we know? Pulse-chase showed the route
text:
How do we know? Pulse-chase showed the route


Pulse: give pancreas slices radioactive amino acid (³H-leucine) for 3 minutes. Chase: wash it away, add unlabelled amino acid. Only the proteins made during the pulse are labelled.
Fix samples over time, EM autoradiography shows where the label is: rough ER (3 min) → Golgi (about 7–20 min) → condensing vacuoles (about 37 min) → zymogen granules (about 2 h).
George Palade, Nobel Prize 1974 (with Albert Claude and Christian de Duve).


How do we know that proteins take this route? George Palade and James Jamieson answered it in the 1960s with a pulse-chase experiment, a method you will meet again and again. They incubated slices of guinea-pig pancreas with a radioactive amino acid, tritium-labelled leucine, for only three minutes. That is the pulse: every protein made in those three minutes carries the label. Then came the chase: they washed out the label and added a large excess of ordinary leucine, so proteins made afterwards are not labelled. The labelled cohort is like a group of runners with red shirts in a marathon: you can follow them. At different times they fixed the tissue, cut thin sections, coated them with photographic emulsion and looked in the electron microscope. Silver grains appear where the radioactivity is. At three minutes the label was over the rough ER; after about ten minutes over the Golgi; after about forty minutes over condensing vacuoles at the trans side; and after two hours over zymogen granules. The order of compartments in time gave the route. The demo for this lecture is a modern version of this experiment.
crumbs: The Golgi and the secretory pathway

title: The Golgi and the secretory pathway
section: One transport step: bud, move, tether, fuse
text:
One transport step: bud, move, tether, fuse


A coat bends the donor membrane and collects cargo → a vesicle (about 50–100 nm) pinches off → the coat falls off.
Rab on the vesicle and tethers on the target catch it; SNAREs on both membranes zip together and fuse the bilayers.
The lumen stays lumen and the cytosolic side stays cytosolic: cargo never crosses a membrane.


Every step on the map uses the same four-part cycle. First, budding: coat proteins assemble on the cytosolic face of the donor membrane. They bend it into a bud and, at the same time, gather the right cargo into it. The bud pinches off as a vesicle, typically 50 to 100 nanometres across. Second, the coat comes off, because a fusion machine cannot reach a coated membrane. Third, the vesicle moves, often along microtubules, and is caught at the right target membrane. Two kinds of proteins do this: a Rab GTPase on the vesicle, which acts as an address label, and tethering proteins on the target, which grab vesicles that carry the right Rab. Fourth, SNARE proteins on the vesicle and on the target wind together and pull the two bilayers so close that they fuse. Look at the topology. Soluble cargo inside the vesicle enters the lumen of the target. A membrane protein keeps its orientation: the part that faced the lumen still faces the lumen. Nothing crosses a membrane, which answers the first question from the acinar cell.
crumbs: The Golgi and the secretory pathway

title: The Golgi and the secretory pathway
section: Three coats for three kinds of route
text:
Three coats for three kinds of route


Cells use three main coats, and each marks a different route. COPII, for coat protein complex two, makes vesicles that leave the ER; it is the exit coat. COPI, coat protein complex one, works at the ERGIC and the Golgi and makes vesicles that mostly travel backwards: from the Golgi to the ER and between Golgi cisternae. Clathrin forms a basket-like cage of three-legged units called triskelions. It works at two places: at the trans-Golgi network, where it makes vesicles going to endosomes and lysosomes, and at the plasma membrane, where it makes vesicles for endocytosis, the topic of the endocytosis lecture. Clathrin does not bind cargo itself: adaptor proteins sit between the cage and the membrane, AP1 at the TGN and AP2 at the plasma membrane, and the adaptors bind the cargo. Notice that there is no special coat on this map for the route from the TGN to the plasma membrane. Those constitutive carriers are larger tubules and vesicles whose coat proteins are still poorly understood. Learn the three coats with their routes; that is enough for this course.
crumbs: The Golgi and the secretory pathway

title: The Golgi and the secretory pathway
section: How a coat forms and chooses its cargo
text:
How a coat forms and chooses its cargo


A small GTPase is the switch: Sar1 (COPII) or ARF1 (COPI, clathrin at the TGN). A GEF in the donor membrane loads GTP → the GTPase puts an amphipathic helix into the membrane and recruits the coat.
The inner coat binds sorting signals on cargo: e.g. a di-acidic motif (DxE) in a cytosolic tail for COPII. Soluble cargo is collected by cargo receptors.
GTP hydrolysis releases the coat, so it can be used again.


How does a coat know where and when to assemble? The answer is a small GTPase, a protein that is active with GTP bound and inactive with GDP, like the Ras switch you will meet in signalling. For the COPII coat the switch is Sar1. Its exchange factor, a GEF, sits only in the ER membrane, so Sar1 is turned on only there. Sar1 with GTP pushes an amphipathic helix into the cytosolic leaflet, which starts to bend it, and recruits the inner coat proteins. The inner coat has binding sites for sorting signals: short amino-acid motifs in the cytosolic tails of membrane cargo. For example, the viral glycoprotein VSVG, which you will see again as a tracer, carries a di-acidic signal, aspartate–x–glutamate. Soluble cargo in the lumen cannot touch the coat, so it binds transmembrane cargo receptors, which bind the coat. Then the outer coat forms a cage and the bud closes. After the vesicle leaves, GTP is hydrolysed, the GTPase leaves the membrane and the coat falls apart. COPI works the same way with ARF1 as its switch. Remember ARF1: the drug brefeldin A blocks its GEF.
crumbs: The Golgi and the secretory pathway

title: The Golgi and the secretory pathway
section: Address labels and hooks: Rab GTPases and tethers
text:
Address labels and hooks: Rab GTPases and tethers


Rabs: about 60 small GTPases in human cells; each membrane carries its own set (e.g. Rab1 ER→Golgi, Rab27 secretory granules). Rab-GTP sits in the membrane, Rab-GDP is extracted into the cytosol.
Tethers bind Rab-GTP and catch the vesicle from up to ~200 nm away: long coiled-coil proteins (golgins) or multi-subunit complexes (e.g. the exocyst at the plasma membrane).
Rabs and tethers give specificity; SNAREs give fusion (and some more specificity).


A cell has many membranes and many vesicles, so how does a vesicle find the right target? Part of the answer is Rab proteins, another family of small GTPases, with about sixty members in human cells. Each compartment carries a characteristic set of Rabs, so Rabs work like address labels or membrane identity cards. For example, Rab1 works between the ER and the Golgi, Rab5 on early endosomes, and Rab27 on secretory granules. In the GTP form, a Rab is anchored to the membrane by a lipid tail and binds effector proteins. In the GDP form, a protein called GDI pulls it out of the membrane into the cytosol, ready to be used again. The most important effectors are tethers. Some are long, thin coiled-coil proteins, the golgins, that stick out from the Golgi like fishing lines up to a few hundred nanometres long and catch passing vesicles. Others are large complexes of several subunits, such as the exocyst, which catches secretory vesicles at the plasma membrane. Tethering brings the vesicle close, but the membranes are not yet fused. That is the job of the SNAREs.
crumbs: The Golgi and the secretory pathway

title: The Golgi and the secretory pathway
section: SNAREs zip two membranes together
text:
SNAREs zip two membranes together


A v-SNARE on the vesicle (e.g. VAMP/synaptobrevin) and t-SNAREs on the target (e.g. syntaxin, SNAP-25) form a bundle of four α-helices.
The helices zip from the far end towards the membranes, pulling the bilayers together until they fuse. About 35 SNAREs in human cells; different pairs at different membranes.
After fusion, the ATPase NSF (with α-SNAP) uses ATP to pull the SNAREs apart so they can be reused.


SNAREs are the fusion machine. A SNARE is a membrane protein with a long helical segment, the SNARE motif, that sticks out into the cytosol. The vesicle carries a v-SNARE, v for vesicle, such as VAMP, also called synaptobrevin. The target membrane carries t-SNAREs, t for target, such as syntaxin and SNAP-25. When the vesicle comes close, four SNARE motifs, one from the vesicle and three from the target, wind around each other into a very stable bundle of four helices. Assembly starts at the end far from the membranes and zips towards them, like a zipper that pulls two pieces of cloth together. The energy released by zipping overcomes the repulsion between the two water-covered bilayers, and the lipids of the two membranes merge: fusion. Afterwards both SNAREs sit in the same membrane in a relaxed complex, which is useless. The ATPase NSF, with its adaptor α-SNAP, spends ATP to pull the bundle apart so that the SNAREs can work again. Human cells have about 35 SNAREs, and only certain combinations work together, which adds a second layer of specificity on top of the Rabs.
crumbs: The Golgi and the secretory pathway

title: The Golgi and the secretory pathway
section: How do we know? Yeast mutants and a test-tube assay
text:
How do we know? Yeast mutants and a test-tube assay


Genetics (Randy Schekman): yeast temperature-sensitive sec mutants grow at 25 °C; at 37 °C they stop secreting, and membranes pile up where the block is: ER, Golgi or vesicles. Double mutants gave the order of the steps.
Biochemistry (James Rothman): transport between Golgi membranes in a test tube needs ATP and cytosol → purified NSF, SNAP and then the SNAREs.
Physiology (Thomas Südhof): synaptotagmin is the Ca²⁺ sensor that times fusion at synapses. Nobel Prize 2013 to all three.


Three approaches found the machinery, and they shared the Nobel Prize in 2013. Randy Schekman used yeast genetics. Yeast secretes enzymes into its cell wall, so a mutant that cannot secrete is lethal. Schekman searched for temperature-sensitive mutants: they grow normally at 25 degrees, but at 37 degrees the mutant protein fails. When shifted to 37 degrees, these sec mutants, for secretion, stopped secreting, and the electron microscope showed where traffic was blocked: some filled with ER, some with Golgi-like stacks, others with thousands of small vesicles. By combining two mutations, he found which block comes first and so ordered the steps. Many sec genes turned out to code for coat proteins, a Rab and SNAREs. James Rothman used biochemistry. He mixed Golgi membranes from two kinds of mutant cells in a test tube and measured transport between them. Transport needed ATP and cytosol, so he purified the active cytosolic proteins: NSF, then SNAP, and finally the SNAREs. Thomas Südhof asked how fusion is timed at nerve terminals, and found that synaptotagmin binds calcium and triggers SNARE-driven fusion within a millisecond.
crumbs: The Golgi and the secretory pathway

title: The Golgi and the secretory pathway
section: The Golgi apparatus: a stack with two faces
text:
The Golgi apparatus: a stack with two faces







Golgi apparatus in a human cell, transmission EM: the stack of cisternae, the cis face and the trans-Golgi network (TGN) with tubules (arrows). Scale bar 100 nm.


A stack of 4–8 flat cisternae, each about 1 µm wide; mammalian cells link many stacks into one Golgi ribbon next to the nucleus.
Polarised: the cis face receives from the ER; the trans face and the TGN ship out.
Each cisterna has its own enzymes, in the order the cargo needs them, like an assembly line.
Found by Camillo Golgi in 1898 with a silver stain; its existence was doubted until EM in the 1950s.



Here is the Golgi apparatus itself, in a thin section of a human cell seen by transmission electron microscopy. Look for the curved stack of flat, membrane-bounded sacs, the cisternae, lying close together like a pile of plates. The side at the bottom, labelled cis, faces the ER and receives cargo. The trans side at the top continues into the trans-Golgi network, a mesh of tubules and buds; the white arrows point to tubules leaving the stack. In mammalian cells, many such stacks are connected side by side into a ribbon next to the nucleus, near the centrosome. The Golgi is polarised: each cisterna contains a different set of processing enzymes, arranged in the order in which they act on the cargo, from early trimming enzymes in cis to late enzymes in trans. Camillo Golgi saw this structure in nerve cells in 1898 with a silver stain, and for decades many people thought it was an artefact of the staining. Only electron microscopy settled that it is real.
crumbs: The Golgi and the secretory pathway

title: The Golgi and the secretory pathway
section: What the Golgi does: rebuilding sugars and cutting proteins
text:
What the Golgi does: rebuilding sugars and cutting proteins


N-linked glycans made in the ER are trimmed (mannose removed) and rebuilt (GlcNAc, galactose, sialic acid added): a complex glycan. Each step is done by a different enzyme in a different cisterna.
O-linked glycosylation on Ser/Thr (mucins), proteoglycans, sulfation; lysosomal enzymes get a mannose-6-phosphate tag (cis Golgi).
Proteolytic cleavage in the TGN and granules: proinsulin → insulin. Lab test for Golgi arrival: the glycan becomes resistant to the enzyme Endo H.


What happens to a protein while it passes through the Golgi? Mostly, its sugars change. In the ER lecture you saw that proteins get a large N-linked glycan, a block of fourteen sugars on asparagine, and that the ER trims it during quality control. In the Golgi this tree is cut down and rebuilt. In the cis Golgi, mannosidases remove more mannose. In the medial Golgi, the first N-acetylglucosamine is added and more mannose is removed. In the trans Golgi, galactose and finally sialic acid are added, which gives the branched complex glycans on most cell-surface and secreted proteins. Each enzyme sits in its own cisterna, so the order of the stack gives the order of the reactions. The Golgi also adds O-linked sugars to serine and threonine, for example on the mucins that make mucus, builds the long sugar chains of proteoglycans, and marks lysosomal enzymes with mannose-6-phosphate. Late in the pathway, proteases cut some proteins into their active form, for example proinsulin into insulin. A useful lab trick: once the glycan has passed the medial Golgi, the enzyme Endo H can no longer cut it, so Endo H resistance tells you that a protein has reached the Golgi.
crumbs: The Golgi and the secretory pathway

title: The Golgi and the secretory pathway
section: Moving through the stack: cisternal maturation
text:
Moving through the stack: cisternal maturation


The cisternae themselves move forward and mature: a new cis cisterna forms from ERGIC carriers, becomes medial, then trans, then breaks up in the TGN. Cargo rides along.
COPI vesicles carry Golgi enzymes backwards to younger cisternae, and escaped ER proteins back to the ER (KDEL signal + KDEL receptor).
Evidence: large cargo (procollagen rods, about 300 nm) crosses the stack without vesicles; in live yeast, one cisterna changes from cis to trans markers within minutes.


How does cargo cross the stack? For years there were two models. In the first, the cisternae stay put and cargo hops forward from one to the next in vesicles. In the second, cisternal maturation, the cisternae themselves move: a new cis cisterna forms by fusion of carriers from the ERGIC, then it matures into a medial and a trans cisterna, and finally breaks up into carriers at the TGN. The cargo stays inside and rides along. To keep each cisterna’s enzymes in place, COPI vesicles carry them backwards to the next younger cisterna. Two observations favour maturation. Procollagen forms rigid rods about 300 nanometres long, too big for a 60-nanometre COPI vesicle, yet it crosses the stack. And in live yeast cells, where cisternae are separate, a single cisterna labelled with a cis marker was seen to lose it and gain a trans marker within a few minutes. COPI also works at the start of the route. ER-resident proteins that escape, such as chaperones, carry a KDEL signal at their C-terminus. The KDEL receptor in the ERGIC and cis Golgi binds them and returns them to the ER in COPI vesicles. Today most researchers think maturation is the main mechanism, with some vesicle traffic as well.
crumbs: The Golgi and the secretory pathway

title: The Golgi and the secretory pathway
section: Sorting at the trans-Golgi network: three exits
text:
Sorting at the trans-Golgi network: three exits


To lysosomes: enzymes with mannose-6-phosphate bind the M6P receptor; clathrin + adaptor (AP1) vesicles take them to endosomes, where the acid pH releases them (the endocytosis lecture follows them on).
Regulated secretion: hormones aggregate in the TGN and bud as secretory granules that wait for a signal.
Constitutive secretion: everything without a special signal goes straight to the surface (the default). In epithelia there are separate apical and basolateral routes.


The trans-Golgi network is the main sorting station. Three exits leave it. First, lysosomal enzymes. In the cis Golgi they received a special tag, mannose-6-phosphate. In the TGN, the mannose-6-phosphate receptor, a membrane protein, binds them on the lumen side and is collected into clathrin-coated vesicles with the adaptor AP1. These vesicles fuse with endosomes. The endosome is more acidic, so the enzyme lets go of the receptor and moves on to the lysosome, while the receptor returns to the TGN. The endocytosis lecture follows this route further. Second, regulated secretion. In cells that store products, such as endocrine cells, hormones such as insulin clump together in the mildly acidic, calcium-rich TGN and are packed into dense secretory granules. Third, everything else goes to the plasma membrane in a steady stream. This is the default: a protein without a sorting signal is secreted. That has a clinical consequence. In I-cell disease, the enzyme that adds mannose-6-phosphate is missing, so lysosomal enzymes take the default route and are secreted into the blood, while the lysosomes fill with undigested material.
crumbs: The Golgi and the secretory pathway

title: The Golgi and the secretory pathway
section: Constitutive and regulated secretion
text:
Constitutive and regulated secretion













Close-up of the acinar cell from the start of the lecture: rough ER (parallel lines) and dark, stored zymogen granules (right). TEM.


Constitutive: in every cell, all the time: collagen, albumin, antibodies, new plasma membrane proteins and lipids.
Regulated: in endocrine, exocrine and nerve cells: granules mature (acidify, concentrate, cut prohormones), wait docked near the membrane, and fuse when cytosolic Ca²⁺ rises. Synaptotagmin senses the Ca²⁺.


Every cell secretes constitutively. Vesicles from the TGN fuse with the plasma membrane at a steady rate, carrying secreted proteins such as collagen from fibroblasts, albumin from liver cells and antibodies from plasma cells, as well as new membrane proteins and lipids for the plasma membrane. Constitutive secretion is not controlled at the fusion step: what is made is shipped. Regulated secretion exists only in specialised cells: endocrine cells such as β cells, exocrine cells such as the pancreatic acinar cells in the micrograph, a close-up of the cell you saw at the start, mast cells and neurons. Their secretory granules mature after budding: they become more acidic, their content is concentrated up to two hundred times, and prohormones are cut into active hormones. Then they wait, some of them docked at the plasma membrane with partly assembled SNARE complexes. When the cell is stimulated, calcium enters the cytosol, through calcium channels in the plasma membrane or from the ER. Synaptotagmin on the granule binds calcium and triggers the final zipping of the SNAREs, and the granule fuses within milliseconds in a neuron, or seconds in an endocrine cell. Synaptic vesicles are a special case: small vesicles recycled locally in the nerve terminal.
crumbs: The Golgi and the secretory pathway

title: The Golgi and the secretory pathway
section: How do we know? Watching cargo move in living cells
text:
How do we know? Watching cargo move in living cells


Synchronise a wave of cargo: VSVG-GFP ts045 misfolds and stays in the ER at 40 °C and leaves when cooled to 32 °C. RUSH: cargo is held in the ER on a streptavidin hook; adding biotin releases it.
Blocks stop the wave at one station: 15 °C (cargo collects in the ERGIC), 20 °C (in the TGN), brefeldin A (blocks ARF1 activation: no COPI, the Golgi merges into the ER). Try it: the pulse-chase demo.


Palade’s autoradiographs were snapshots of fixed cells. Today we watch living cells. The trick is to start a synchronised wave of fluorescent cargo. The classic tracer is VSVG, the glycoprotein of vesicular stomatitis virus, in a temperature-sensitive mutant form called ts045, fused to GFP. At 40 degrees the protein misfolds and the ER keeps it. Cool the cells to 32 degrees, it folds, and the whole wave leaves the ER together: within about ten minutes it fills the Golgi, and within an hour it reaches the surface. A newer method, RUSH, works for any protein and at body temperature. The cargo is fused to a streptavidin-binding peptide, and an ER-resident hook protein carries streptavidin. The cargo sticks to the hook until you add biotin, which binds streptavidin much more tightly and releases the cargo. Blocks then stop the wave at chosen places. At 15 degrees cargo collects in the ERGIC, at 20 degrees in the TGN; warming again releases a sharp wave. Brefeldin A, a fungal compound, blocks the GEF that activates ARF1. Without COPI, the Golgi forms tubules that fuse with the ER within minutes. Try all of these in the demo.
crumbs: The Golgi and the secretory pathway

title: The Golgi and the secretory pathway
section: Why it matters: botulinum toxin cuts SNAREs
text:
Why it matters: botulinum toxin cuts SNAREs













Botulinum neurotoxin A (PDB 3BTA). Red: α-helices, cyan: β-strands.


Botulinum toxins (from Clostridium botulinum) enter motor nerve terminals; their protease chain cuts SNAP-25, VAMP or syntaxin. Vesicles dock but cannot fuse → no acetylcholine → flaccid paralysis. Among the most toxic substances known (about 1 ng/kg).
Tetanus toxin cuts VAMP in inhibitory neurons of the spinal cord → spastic paralysis.
Botox injections: tiny doses for dystonia, spasticity, chronic migraine, excessive sweating, wrinkles. The effect lasts about 3–4 months, until the nerve terminal recovers.


This is the SNARE zipper from earlier, now as a drug target. Botulinum toxins are made by the bacterium Clostridium botulinum, which grows without oxygen, for example in badly canned food. The toxin has two chains. The heavy chain binds receptors on motor nerve terminals and helps the light chain enter the cytosol. The light chain is a zinc protease that cuts one SNARE: type A, the form in Botox, cuts SNAP-25; type B cuts VAMP; type C cuts syntaxin. Synaptic vesicles still dock, but the zipper cannot close, so acetylcholine is not released and the muscle does not contract. The result is a flaccid paralysis that can stop breathing. About a nanogram per kilogram of body weight is enough to kill, which makes these toxins among the most poisonous substances known. Tetanus toxin cuts the same SNARE as type B, but travels backwards along the axon to the spinal cord and blocks inhibitory neurons, so muscles cramp instead. In medicine, tiny local injections of botulinum toxin weaken overactive muscles in dystonia and spasticity and are used for chronic migraine and excessive sweating. The effect wears off after about three to four months, as the nerve terminal recovers.
crumbs: The Golgi and the secretory pathway

title: The Golgi and the secretory pathway
section: Why it matters: insulin secretion and type 2 diabetes
text:
Why it matters: insulin secretion and type 2 diabetes













Rat pancreas, immunostained for insulin (brown): an islet of Langerhans among acinar tissue.


A β cell stores about 10 000 granules. Glucose → more ATP → KATP channels close → depolarisation → Ca²⁺ channels open → granules fuse: a fast first phase (docked granules) and a slower second phase.
Type 2 diabetes: the first phase is lost early; β cells are overloaded (ER stress) and release more unprocessed proinsulin.
Drugs act on this pathway: sulfonylureas close KATP; GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide) strengthen glucose-triggered granule exocytosis. More in Sjukdomslära.


The β cells of the pancreatic islets, the brown cells in this stained section, are regulated-secretion specialists. Each stores about ten thousand insulin granules. Insulin is made as proinsulin in the ER, and it is cut into insulin and C-peptide inside maturing granules. Release is tied to blood glucose. Glucose enters the β cell and is metabolised, which raises ATP. ATP closes ATP-sensitive potassium channels, the membrane depolarises, voltage-gated calcium channels open, and calcium triggers granule fusion through synaptotagmin and SNAREs, as on the previous slides. When glucose rises suddenly, a first phase of release lasting a few minutes comes from granules already docked at the membrane; then a second, slower phase follows as new granules are brought up. In type 2 diabetes, the first phase is one of the earliest things to disappear. The β cells also make more proinsulin than they can process, so more unprocessed proinsulin appears in the blood. Several drugs act here. Sulfonylureas close the potassium channel directly. GLP-1 receptor agonists such as semaglutide raise cyclic AMP in β cells and strengthen glucose-triggered exocytosis. You will meet these drugs again in Sjukdomslära and in drug development.
crumbs: The Golgi and the secretory pathway

title: The Golgi and the secretory pathway
section: Summary
text:
Summary

Secretory proteins travel ER → ERGIC → Golgi (cis → trans) → TGN → surface, granules or lysosomes, always inside membranes; pulse-chase and live imaging of a synchronised cargo wave showed the route.
Each step uses a carrier: a coat (COPII out of the ER, COPI back and within the Golgi, clathrin at the TGN and plasma membrane), switched on by a small GTPase, bends the membrane and selects cargo by its sorting signals.
Rab GTPases and tethers find the right target; SNAREs zip the membranes together and fuse them; NSF takes them apart again.
The Golgi rebuilds glycans in cisternae that mature from cis to trans; COPI brings enzymes and escaped ER proteins (KDEL) back. The TGN sorts: M6P → lysosomes, granules → regulated secretion, the rest → constitutive secretion.
Regulated secretion fuses stored granules when Ca²⁺ rises; botulinum toxin blocks fusion by cutting SNAREs, and the loss of first-phase insulin secretion is an early sign of type 2 diabetes.

Read more (optional): Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell, 7th ed., ch. 13.
Image credits

Five take-home points. First, the route: secretory proteins move from the ER through the ERGIC and the Golgi stack to the trans-Golgi network, and from there to the plasma membrane, into secretory granules or to the lysosomes, without ever crossing a membrane; pulse-chase experiments and live imaging of synchronised cargo showed this. Second, budding: coats bend the membrane and pick the cargo, and each coat belongs to a route; a small GTPase switch decides where a coat forms. Third, targeting and fusion: Rab GTPases and tethers recognise the right membrane, SNAREs fuse the two bilayers, and NSF recycles the SNAREs. Fourth, the Golgi: it rebuilds sugar chains in an ordered stack whose cisternae mature from cis to trans, COPI retrieves enzymes and ER proteins, and the TGN sorts cargo by its signals, with constitutive secretion as the default. Fifth, regulated secretion waits for a calcium signal, and medicine meets this machinery in botulinum toxin and in type 2 diabetes. The endocytosis lecture takes the reverse direction, into the cell, and follows the mannose-6-phosphate route on to the lysosomes.
crumbs: The Golgi and the secretory pathway

title: Quiz: the Golgi and the secretory pathway
text:
Short questions to check your understanding of the lecture The Golgi and the secretory pathway. Try each on paper first, then open the hint or the answer. The tag after each question shows the learning outcome (ELO) it practises.

Q1. Put these compartments in the order a newly made antibody passes through on its way out of a plasma cell: cis Golgi, ER, trans-Golgi network, ERGIC, medial Golgi, plasma membrane. [ELO 4]






Hint





Start where the protein is made, and remember the station between the ER and the Golgi.









Answer





ER → ERGIC → cis Golgi → medial Golgi → trans-Golgi network → plasma membrane. The antibody is made on ribosomes on the rough ER, leaves the ER in COPII vesicles, passes the ERGIC, crosses the Golgi stack from cis to trans and leaves the TGN in a carrier that fuses with the plasma membrane (constitutive secretion).




Q2. Which coat would you find on (a) a vesicle leaving the ER, (b) a vesicle taking an escaped ER chaperone back from the Golgi to the ER, (c) a vesicle taking a lysosomal enzyme from the TGN towards the endosomes? [ELO 4]






Hint





One coat for the exit from the ER, one for going backwards, one that works at the TGN and the plasma membrane.









Answer






COPII. (b) COPI (the chaperone’s KDEL signal binds the KDEL receptor, which is packed into COPI vesicles). (c) Clathrin, with the adaptor AP1, which binds the mannose-6-phosphate receptor carrying the enzyme.





Q3. A soluble protein in the ER lumen cannot touch the COPII coat, which sits on the cytosolic side of the membrane. How can it still be collected into a COPII vesicle? [ELO 4]






Hint





Think of a protein that spans the membrane and can bind on both sides.









Answer





It binds a transmembrane cargo receptor. The receptor binds the soluble cargo in the lumen and, with its cytosolic tail, binds the inner coat (a sorting signal). So the coat collects the receptor, and the receptor brings the cargo. (Some soluble proteins also enter vesicles at low concentration by “bulk flow”, without a receptor.)




Q4. What are the jobs of (a) a Rab GTPase, (b) a tether, (c) a SNARE, in the arrival of a vesicle at its target membrane? [ELO 4]






Hint





Address label, hook, fusion machine.









Answer






A Rab in its GTP form marks the identity of a membrane or vesicle and recruits effector proteins: an address label. (b) A tether (a long coiled-coil golgin or a multi-subunit complex such as the exocyst) binds the Rab and catches the vesicle at a distance, bringing it close. (c) SNAREs on the vesicle (v-SNARE) and target (t-SNAREs) wind into a four-helix bundle that pulls the membranes together and fuses them.





Q5. A cell biologist asks whether a glycoprotein has reached the Golgi yet. She treats a cell extract with the enzyme Endo H and runs an SDS gel. What result means “still in the ER”, and what means “has passed the medial Golgi”? [ELO 1, 4]






Hint





Endo H cuts N-linked glycans of the high-mannose type, before the medial Golgi enzymes have rebuilt them.









Answer





If Endo H removes the glycans, the protein runs faster (smaller) on the gel: the glycans are still high-mannose, so the protein is in the ER (or the cis Golgi). If the band does not move after Endo H, the glycans have been trimmed and rebuilt by medial Golgi enzymes (Endo H-resistant): the protein has reached at least the medial Golgi.




Q6. In I-cell disease, the enzyme that adds mannose-6-phosphate to lysosomal enzymes is missing. Where do the lysosomal enzymes end up, and why? [ELO 4, 9]






Hint





What happens in the TGN to a protein with no sorting signal?









Answer





Without mannose-6-phosphate, the enzymes are not bound by the M6P receptor in the TGN and are not packed into clathrin/AP1 vesicles to the endosomes. They follow the default route, constitutive secretion, and leave the cell: high enzyme levels are found in the blood, while the lysosomes lack enzymes and fill with undigested material (“inclusion cells”).




Q7. Brefeldin A blocks the GEF that activates ARF1. Why does this make the Golgi disappear into the ER within minutes? [ELO 4, 5]






Hint





Which coat needs ARF1, and which direction does that coat carry membrane?









Answer





Without active ARF1, COPI coats fall off and cannot form again on Golgi membranes. The uncoated Golgi membranes grow long tubules that fuse with the ER (this return route does not need COPI), so Golgi lipids and enzymes flow into the ER. Cargo leaving the ER in COPII vesicles cannot build a separate Golgi again, so it stays in the merged ER–Golgi. The lesson: the Golgi exists only as a steady state of traffic in and out. When brefeldin A is washed out, the Golgi re-forms.




Q8. Botulinum toxin type A cuts SNAP-25 in motor nerve terminals. Synaptic vesicles still reach the membrane and dock. Why can they not release acetylcholine, and what does the patient experience? [ELO 4, 9]






Hint





Docking is done by Rabs and tethers. What does the four-helix bundle do?









Answer





SNAP-25 provides two of the four helices of the SNARE bundle. Cut SNAP-25 cannot complete the zipper, so the vesicle membrane and plasma membrane are not pulled together and do not fuse. Docking (Rab, tethers) still works, but no acetylcholine is released, the muscle gets no signal, and the patient has a flaccid (limp) paralysis, which can stop breathing.
crumbs: The Golgi and the secretory pathway

title: Study questions: G-protein-coupled receptors and second messengers
text: Study questions in the style of the written exam. Write your answer first (a few sentences, or a labelled sketch where it helps), then compare with the model answer. Each question is tagged with its learning outcome (ELO). Questions tagged [VG] are of the kind used for the higher grade: predict, compare, explain an unexpected result or design an experiment.

title: Study questions: G-protein-coupled receptors and second messengers
section: G-level questions
text:
G-level questions
1. Describe the structure of a G-protein-coupled receptor and explain how binding of a hormone outside the cell activates a G protein inside. [ELO 3]






Model answer





A GPCR is one polypeptide that crosses the membrane as seven α-helices (N-terminus outside, C-terminus inside); the helices form a bundle. Small ligands bind in a pocket between the helices, reached from outside. Agonist binding stabilises an active arrangement in which helix 6 moves outwards and a cavity opens on the cytosolic face. The C-terminal helix of Gα inserts there, which opens Gα’s nucleotide site: GDP leaves and GTP binds. The receptor is thus a GEF for the G protein. Gα–GTP separates from Gβγ and from the receptor, which can then activate another G protein.




2. Explain why the trimeric G protein is called a switch with a built-in timer. What do RGS proteins do? [ELO 3]






Model answer





Gα is on with GTP and off with GDP. With GTP it leaves βγ, and both halves bind and regulate target proteins. Gα is itself a slow GTPase: after seconds to minutes (for Gs, on average 10–20 s) it hydrolyses GTP to GDP + Pᵢ, switches off and rebinds βγ. The time until hydrolysis is the timer, and it sets how long each activation lasts. RGS proteins (regulators of G-protein signalling) are GTPase-activating proteins: they speed up hydrolysis, making the signal shorter.




3. Compare Gs, Gi and Gq: the enzyme each acts on, the second messenger(s) that change, and one example receptor. [ELO 3]






Model answer





Gs stimulates adenylyl cyclase → cAMP rises (e.g. β-adrenergic receptor for adrenaline, GLP-1 receptor). Gi inhibits adenylyl cyclase → cAMP falls; its βγ also opens K⁺ channels (e.g. μ-opioid receptor, α₂-adrenergic receptor). Gq activates phospholipase C-β → IP₃ and DAG, and IP₃ releases Ca²⁺ from the ER (e.g. α₁-adrenergic receptor, M3 muscarinic acetylcholine receptor).




4. Describe the cAMP pathway from adenylyl cyclase to a change in gene expression. [ELO 3]






Model answer





Active Gαs binds and activates adenylyl cyclase in the plasma membrane, which converts ATP to cAMP. cAMP binds the regulatory subunits of PKA (two cAMP per R, four in total); the R subunits release the two catalytic subunits, which are active Ser/Thr kinases. They phosphorylate cytosolic targets within seconds (enzymes of glycogen metabolism, ion channels such as CFTR). Some C subunits enter the nucleus and phosphorylate the transcription factor CREB, which then activates transcription of target genes over minutes to hours. Phosphodiesterases turn cAMP into AMP and end the signal.




5. Explain how a Gq-coupled receptor raises cytosolic Ca²⁺ and activates protein kinase C. [ELO 3]






Model answer





Gαq–GTP activates phospholipase C-β, which cleaves the membrane lipid PIP₂ into IP₃ and DAG. IP₃ is water-soluble, diffuses to the ER and opens the IP₃ receptor, a Ca²⁺ channel; Ca²⁺ flows down its large gradient from the ER lumen into the cytosol, which rises from about 100 nM to about 1 µM. PKC binds Ca²⁺, moves to the plasma membrane and is fully activated when it also binds DAG there. Ca²⁺ also binds calmodulin, which activates other targets (CaM-kinases, myosin light-chain kinase).




6. Explain, with an example, how a GPCR cascade amplifies a signal. Which step does not amplify, and why? [ELO 3]






Model answer





Gain comes from steps where one active molecule catalyses the activation or production of many. One hormone-bound receptor activates G proteins one after another; each Gαs activates an adenylyl cyclase, which makes many cAMP per second; each PKA catalytic subunit phosphorylates many target proteins; in the liver, PKA → phosphorylase kinase → glycogen phosphorylase, each an enzyme, so a few hormone molecules release millions of glucose molecules. The step from cAMP to PKA is binding, not catalysis: four cAMP release two catalytic subunits, so there is no gain at that step.




7. Describe desensitisation of a GPCR by GRK and arrestin, and what happens to the receptor afterwards. [ELO 3]






Model answer





A G-protein-coupled receptor kinase (GRK) recognises the active receptor and phosphorylates Ser/Thr on its cytosolic tail. Arrestin binds the phosphorylated receptor on its cytosolic face and blocks G-protein binding: the receptor is desensitised although the hormone is still bound. Arrestin also binds clathrin and its adaptor, so the receptor is internalised by clathrin-mediated endocytosis. In the endosome the ligand dissociates and the receptor is dephosphorylated and recycled to the surface (resensitisation), or it is sent to the lysosome and degraded, which lowers the number of receptors (down-regulation). This contributes to drug tolerance.




8. Describe one method to follow a second messenger in a living cell. What would you see when you add a Gq-activating hormone? [ELO 1] [ELO 3]






Model answer





Ca²⁺ imaging: load cells with a Ca²⁺-sensitive dye such as fura-2, or express a genetically encoded indicator such as GCaMP (GFP fused to calmodulin), and record fluorescence over time in a fluorescence microscope. Binding of Ca²⁺ changes the brightness (or the excitation ratio for fura-2). After adding a Gq-activating hormone, the fluorescence rises within seconds as IP₃ releases Ca²⁺ from the ER, often as a spike or repeated oscillations, and falls back as pumps remove Ca²⁺. (Alternative: a FRET sensor for cAMP, CFP–Epac–YFP; cAMP binding opens the sensor, FRET falls and the CFP/YFP emission ratio rises.)




9. Explain how cholera toxin and pertussis toxin both raise cAMP, although they act on different G proteins. [ELO 3] [ELO 9]






Model answer





Both toxins transfer ADP-ribose from NAD⁺ to a Gα subunit. Cholera toxin modifies Gαs so that it can no longer hydrolyse GTP: once activated, Gs stays on and adenylyl cyclase is stimulated continuously. Pertussis toxin modifies Gαi so that its receptors can no longer activate it: Gi stays off, and the inhibitory brake on adenylyl cyclase is lost. In both cases cAMP rises. In the gut, high cAMP keeps CFTR open, causing secretory diarrhoea (cholera).

title: Study questions: G-protein-coupled receptors and second messengers
section: VG-style questions
text:
VG-style questions
10. [VG] A patient takes theophylline, a phosphodiesterase inhibitor. (a) Predict how the cAMP response of a cell to a short adrenaline pulse changes in height and duration, and explain why. (b) Would theophylline have any effect in a cell with no adrenaline at all? (c) Explain why a PDE inhibitor and a β-blocker have opposite effects on the same pathway, although they act at very different steps. [ELO 3] [ELO 9]






Model answer






cAMP level is set by a balance between synthesis (adenylyl cyclase) and breakdown (PDE). With less PDE activity, the same cyclase activity builds up more cAMP, so the peak is higher; and after the pulse, when Gα has switched off the cyclase, cAMP is removed more slowly, so the response lasts longer. (b) Yes: there is always some basal cyclase activity, so resting cAMP also rises (and with it basal PKA activity). (c) Both change the amount of cAMP. The β-blocker reduces the input (fewer active receptors, less Gs, less cAMP made), the PDE inhibitor reduces the output (less cAMP destroyed). Any step in a cascade can be a drug target, and the effect on the end product depends on whether the drug acts on an “on” or an “off” step.





11. [VG] You suspect that a new compound is an agonist at a Gs-coupled receptor and want to show that its effect needs the receptor, Gs and cAMP. Design experiments using a cell line, a cAMP FRET sensor and tools from this lecture. Include controls. [ELO 1] [ELO 3]






Model answer





Express a cAMP FRET sensor (CFP–Epac–YFP) in a cell line that expresses the receptor, and image the CFP/YFP ratio before and after adding the compound; a rise in the ratio means a rise in cAMP. Make a dose–response curve (EC₅₀). Receptor: add a specific competitive antagonist of the receptor: the response should be reduced and shifted to higher compound concentrations; and test a cell line without the receptor (or with the receptor gene knocked out by CRISPR, then re-expressed as a rescue). Gs: compare with a known Gs agonist; in cells lacking Gαs (knock-out) the response should disappear; cholera toxin pre-treatment maximally activates Gs and should occlude a further response. cAMP-specific: a PDE inhibitor should make the response larger and longer; forskolin, which activates adenylyl cyclase directly, is a positive control for the sensor. Controls: vehicle alone, untransfected cells, and a check that the compound does not change CFP or YFP fluorescence by itself.

title: Study questions: G-protein-coupled receptors and second messengers
section: Explore
text:
Explore
The demo follows one Gs-coupled pathway in a liver-like cell: a hormone pulse (you choose the dose and how long it lasts) → active receptors → active Gαs → cAMP → active PKA, and, through two lumped enzyme steps, glucose release. The whole 10-minute run is recalculated when you move a slider, so you see the consequence at once. Grey curves show a normal cell given the same pulse. Drag along the plots, or press Play (time runs at 1× real time; you can choose faster), to see the cell schematic at that moment. The table counts molecules per cell at each step and the gain from one step to the next.
This is a simple model (a few differential equations) with illustrative numbers: qualitatively right, not a fit to data. Binding is treated as fast, there is only one receptor type and one PDE, and the steps from PKA to glucose are lumped.



E1. Choose Normal cell, 1 min pulse. Read the peak values of active receptors, active Gαs, cAMP and active PKA. In the table, find the gain per step. Which step amplifies most, and which step has a gain below 1? Explain both with the mechanism. How many extra glucose molecules are released per hormone molecule bound? [ELO 3]
E2. Still in the normal cell, find (by dragging the cursor) how long after the end of the pulse cAMP is half-way back to rest. Now predict, then test: (a) Slow GTPase; (b) the PDE inhibitor; (c) Fast GTPase. For each, how do the height and the duration of the cAMP signal change, and why? [ELO 3]
E3. Predict first. Choose Cholera toxin. What happens to Gαs, cAMP and PKA after the hormone has gone? Then set the dose to 0.1 × K_d, and then the duration to 5 s. Does it matter how much hormone the cell got? Explain using the G-protein cycle. [ELO 3] [ELO 9]
E4. Choose β-blocker, then β-blocker + 10 × more hormone. Compare the peaks with the normal cell. Now switch the β-blocker off and find the hormone dose that, without blocker, gives the same response as the blocker preset. What does this tell you about how a competitive antagonist works? [ELO 3] [ELO 9]
E5. [VG] Choose Long exposure (5 min). Read active receptors, cAMP and PKA at the start (about 60 s) and at the end of the pulse (320 s). Then set the arrestin slider to 0 and to 0.030 /s. (a) Explain the shapes with GRK and arrestin. (b) Active receptors fall much more than PKA activity does. Why? (c) Use the result to explain why patients who take an opioid every day need higher doses over time. [ELO 3] [ELO 9]






Solutions





E1. Peaks: active receptors about 82 % (8 200 of 10 000), active Gαs about 69 % (69 000), cAMP about 4.6 µM (5.6 million molecules), active PKA about 84 % (about 810 000 free C subunits). Gains: receptor → Gαs × 8, Gαs → cAMP × 81 (the largest: adenylyl cyclase is an enzyme that keeps making cAMP while switched on, and PDE removes it at a finite rate), cAMP → PKA × 0.15 (below 1: binding, not catalysis; four cAMP free two C subunits, and most cAMP is free in the cytosol), PKA → glucose × 30 per second (enzymes again). The receptor step amplifies because an active receptor is a GEF that activates one G protein after another. Over the 10 minutes the cell releases about 2 billion extra glucose molecules, about 220 000 per hormone molecule bound.
E2. Normal cell: the pulse ends at 80 s; cAMP is half-way back after about 24 s (t ≈ 104 s). (a) Slow GTPase (0.01 /s): each Gα stays active longer, so more Gα is on at the same time: cAMP peaks higher (6.2 µM) and is half-way back only after about 73 s; even resting cAMP is higher (0.74 µM instead of 0.26 µM), because spontaneously activated Gα also lasts longer. (b) PDE inhibitor: cAMP made at the same rate is removed more slowly: the peak is much higher (12.8 µM) and the return slower (about 38 s); resting cAMP also rises (0.79 µM). PKA, which is already almost saturated, rises less (98 %). (c) Fast GTPase (1 /s): each Gα is on for under a second, so few are active at once (11 %); cAMP peaks at only 0.8 µM, PKA at 14 %, and the signal ends within about 8 s of the pulse. Fast off-switches give short, weak signals; slow ones give large, long signals that no longer follow the hormone closely.
E3. With cholera toxin, Gαs that is switched on cannot switch off. During the pulse Gαs goes to about 100 %; after the pulse it stays at 100 %, cAMP stays at about 6.8 µM and PKA at about 92 % to the end of the run. With dose 0.1 × K_d the cell still ends at Gαs 76 %, cAMP 5.2 µM, PKA 87 % after 10 minutes; with a 5-second pulse Gαs reaches 72 %. Even with the dose at its lowest the end result is similar; and with no hormone at all, spontaneous activation alone would bring Gαs to about half in 10 minutes. The reason: the off-step (GTP hydrolysis) is gone, so every activation, by the hormone or by the slow spontaneous GDP–GTP exchange, adds up and is never undone. The amount of hormone only changes how fast the cell gets there. In the gut this means CFTR stays open for as long as the toxin-modified Gαs lasts.
E4. With the β-blocker (100 × K_B) and the normal dose, only about 9 % of receptors are active, cAMP peaks at 1.5 µM and PKA at 37 %. With 10 × more hormone the response recovers to 47 % receptors, cAMP 3.9 µM, PKA 79 %. Without the blocker, a dose of 0.1 × K_d gives the same response as the blocker preset (and 1 × K_d the same as blocker + 10 × hormone). A competitive antagonist does not lower the maximum; it competes for the same site, so it shifts the dose–response curve to the right by the factor (1 + [B]/K_B), here about 100. Enough agonist can overcome it. (In a patient on β-blockers, the same adrenaline surge has a smaller effect on the heart.)
E5. (a) Default arrestin (0.010 /s): at 60 s about 66 % of receptors are active (28 % already desensitised) and cAMP is at its peak (4.6 µM, PKA 84 %); by the end of the pulse (320 s) 79 % of the receptors are desensitised, only 19 % are active, cAMP has fallen to 2.7 µM and PKA to 64 %, although the hormone is still there. GRK phosphorylates only active receptors, and arrestin then blocks their coupling to Gs, so the more a receptor is used, the more it is switched off. With arrestin at 0, cAMP stays at a plateau (5.0 µM, PKA 86 %) for the whole pulse; with 0.030 /s it falls further (cAMP 1.3 µM, PKA 29 % at 320 s). After the pulse, receptors recover only slowly (still 45 % desensitised at 600 s with the default), as they are dephosphorylated and recycled from endosomes. (b) Amplification and saturation: with the default settings there are more active G proteins and more cAMP than PKA needs, so PKA is near its maximum. Losing receptors first removes this reserve; PKA falls only when cAMP drops below the range where PKA is saturated. (c) With daily opioid use, μ-opioid receptors are repeatedly activated, phosphorylated by GRK, bound by arrestin and internalised (some degraded). Fewer working receptors remain, so the same dose gives a smaller Gi signal: tolerance. A higher dose is needed for the same effect. (Other adaptations in the cell also contribute.)

title: Cell Biology
text: A first-cycle course (3MB001, 15 ECTS, Umeå University) in modern molecular cell biology. We follow molecules, signals and decisions through the cell: how membranes and organelles work, how proteins reach their place, how cells communicate, move, divide and die, and what happens when these processes go wrong. Every lecture ends with a drug or a disease that depends on it.

title: Study questions: ion channels and membrane potential
text:
Study questions in the style of the written exam. Write your answer first (a few sentences, or a labelled sketch where it helps), then compare with the model answer. Each question is tagged with its learning outcome (ELO). Questions tagged [VG] are of the kind used for the higher grade: predict, compare, explain an unexpected result or design an experiment.
Useful values (37 °C): \(RT/F \approx 26.7\) mV, or \(61.5\) mV per tenfold gradient for a singly charged ion.

title: Study questions: ion channels and membrane potential
section: G-level questions
text:
G-level questions
1. Compare ion channels and transporters with respect to (a) rate, (b) how the solute crosses, (c) whether they can move a solute against its gradient. [ELO 2]






Model answer






Rate: channels pass up to about 10⁸ ions per second; transporters move about 10²–10⁴ molecules per second. (b) A channel is a water-filled pore; when open, ions stream through without the protein changing shape for each ion. A transporter binds the solute, changes shape (alternating access) and releases it on the other side; it is never open to both sides at once. (c) Channels only allow passive flow down the electrochemical gradient. Transporters can be active: coupled to ATP hydrolysis (pumps) or to the downhill flow of another solute, they can move a solute uphill.





2. Describe the structure of the K⁺ channel selectivity filter and explain how it lets K⁺ through but keeps Na⁺ out. [ELO 2]






Model answer





Four identical subunits surround a central pore. Near the outer end the pore narrows into the selectivity filter, about 1.2 nm long, lined by the backbone carbonyl oxygens of a conserved sequence (TVGYG). In water, each ion is surrounded by water oxygens; to enter the narrow filter it must lose this water, which costs energy. The carbonyl oxygens are held rigidly at the distance at which they replace the water around a K⁺ ion, so the energy is paid back. Na⁺ is smaller; the oxygens are too far away to replace its water, so dehydration is not compensated and Na⁺ does not enter. The structure was solved by X-ray crystallography (MacKinnon, KcsA, 1998).




3. Name the three main ways a channel can be gated. For each, give one example and say what opens it. [ELO 2]






Model answer





Voltage-gated: e.g. the voltage-gated Na⁺ channel of nerve and muscle; a helix with positive charges (the voltage sensor) moves outwards when the membrane depolarises and opens the gate. Ligand-gated: e.g. the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor at the nerve–muscle junction; binding of two acetylcholine molecules opens a cation pore. Mechanically gated: e.g. Piezo channels; tension in the membrane flattens the channel’s blades and opens the pore (Piezo2 in touch, Piezo1 in sensing blood flow).




4. Derive the Nernst equation from the Gibbs energy for moving one mole of an ion with charge \(z\) from outside to inside a cell. [ELO 2]






Model answer





Chemical part: \(\Delta G = \Delta G^\circ + RT\ln Q\) with \(\Delta G^\circ = 0\) (same ion on both sides) and \(Q = c_\text{in}/c_\text{out}\), so \(RT\ln(c_\text{in}/c_\text{out})\). Electrical part: moving \(z\) moles of charge through the membrane potential \(V = V_\text{in} - V_\text{out}\) costs \(zFV\). Total: \(\Delta G = RT\ln(c_\text{in}/c_\text{out}) + zFV\). At equilibrium there is no net flow, so \(\Delta G = 0\), which gives \[E = \frac{RT}{zF}\ln\frac{c_\text{out}}{c_\text{in}}.\]




5. Calculate the equilibrium potentials for K⁺ (inside 140 mM, outside 5 mM) and Cl⁻ (inside 10 mM, outside 110 mM) at 37 °C. Explain the sign of each. [ELO 2]






Model answer





\(E_\text{K} = 26.7 \times \ln(5/140) = 26.7 \times (-3.33) \approx\) −89 mV. K⁺ is higher inside and tends to leave; the inside must be negative to hold the positive ion back.
\(E_\text{Cl} = \frac{26.7}{-1} \times \ln(110/10) = -26.7 \times 2.40 \approx\) −64 mV. Cl⁻ is higher outside and tends to enter; because it is negative, a negative inside repels it, so equilibrium is reached at a negative potential.




6. Explain how the resting membrane potential arises. Include the roles of the Na⁺/K⁺ pump, K⁺ leak channels and large intracellular anions. [ELO 2]






Model answer





The Na⁺/K⁺ pump uses ATP to move 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in, building high K⁺ inside and high Na⁺ outside (it also contributes a few mV directly, because it is electrogenic). The resting membrane has many open K⁺ leak channels and few open Na⁺ channels. K⁺ flows out down its concentration gradient; the large anions inside (proteins, phosphates, organic molecules) cannot follow. Each K⁺ that leaves adds a positive charge outside and leaves a negative charge inside, building a thin layer of charge at the membrane. The voltage grows until the electrical pull balances the concentration push, close to \(E_\text{K}\). The small Na⁺ leak makes it a bit less negative (about −70 mV): the resting potential is a permeability-weighted average (Goldman). Very few ions need to move (fewer than 1 in 10 000 of the K⁺ ions), so concentrations hardly change.




7. Describe the four phases of an action potential and which channels cause each. [ELO 2]






Model answer






A stimulus depolarises the membrane to threshold (about −55 mV). 2. Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open; Na⁺ rushes in, depolarising the membrane further and opening more Na⁺ channels (positive feedback); the voltage rises towards \(E_\text{Na}\) (peak about +35 mV). 3. Na⁺ channels inactivate and slower voltage-gated K⁺ channels open; K⁺ flows out and the voltage falls. 4. Undershoot towards \(E_\text{K}\) while K⁺ channels are still open; inactivated Na⁺ channels cannot yet reopen (refractory period), so the spike travels in one direction. The whole spike lasts about 1–2 ms and moves very few ions; the pump restores the gradients over time.





8. Describe the patch-clamp method. What is a gigaseal, and what does a single-channel recording show? [ELO 1] [ELO 2]






Model answer





A glass pipette with a tip about 1 µm wide, filled with salt solution and containing an electrode, is pressed against a cell, and gentle suction is applied. The membrane seals to the glass with a resistance above 1 GΩ (gigaseal), so no current leaks around the tip and the only current measured flows through channels in the membrane patch under the pipette. An amplifier holds the voltage constant (clamp) and measures the current. In the cell-attached configuration the cell stays intact. A single-channel recording shows the current jumping in square steps of a few pA between closed and fully open; open and closed times are random, and gating signals change the open probability. Developed by Neher and Sakmann (Nobel Prize 1991).




9. Explain how CFTR in airway epithelial cells keeps the airway surface wet, and why mucus becomes thick in cystic fibrosis. [ELO 2] [ELO 9]






Model answer





CFTR is a Cl⁻ channel in the apical membrane, opened by PKA phosphorylation and ATP binding. When open, Cl⁻ flows out into the airway lumen. Na⁺ follows between the cells (attracted by the negative charge), and water follows the salt by osmosis. This keeps a liquid layer under the mucus deep enough for the cilia to beat and move the mucus out of the lungs. In cystic fibrosis CFTR is missing or does not open, so little Cl⁻ and water are secreted; the liquid layer becomes thin, mucus becomes thick and sticky, cilia cannot clear it, and bacteria cause chronic infections.

title: Study questions: ion channels and membrane potential
section: VG-style questions
text:
VG-style questions
10. [VG] A patient’s blood K⁺ rises from 5 mM to 10 mM (intracellular K⁺ stays at 140 mM). (a) Calculate the new \(E_\text{K}\). (b) Predict what happens to the resting potential of heart muscle cells and explain why. (c) Explain why this can be dangerous, using what you know about voltage-gated Na⁺ channels. [ELO 2]






Model answer






\(E_\text{K} = 26.7 \times \ln(10/140) = 26.7 \times (-2.64) \approx\) −70 mV (instead of −89 mV).
The resting membrane is mostly permeable to K⁺, so the resting potential follows \(E_\text{K}\): it becomes less negative (depolarised), roughly 15–20 mV.
A sustained depolarisation brings the membrane closer to threshold, so cells can fire too easily at first, but it also inactivates voltage-gated Na⁺ channels, which cannot recover while the membrane stays depolarised. With fewer available Na⁺ channels, action potentials become smaller and conduct more slowly, and the heart’s rhythm can fail (arrhythmia, in severe cases cardiac arrest). This is why blood K⁺ is monitored closely in kidney failure and when K⁺ is given intravenously.





11. [VG] In the sweat gland duct, CFTR reabsorbs Cl⁻ from sweat into the cell, while in the airways it secretes Cl⁻ out of the cell. (a) How can the same channel move Cl⁻ in opposite directions? (b) Explain why people with cystic fibrosis have salty sweat. [ELO 2] [ELO 9]






Model answer






A channel only lets ions flow down their electrochemical gradient; it has no direction of its own. The direction depends on the Cl⁻ concentrations and the membrane potential in each tissue. In airway cells, transporters load Cl⁻ into the cell above its equilibrium, so when CFTR opens, Cl⁻ flows out into the lumen. In the sweat duct, the sweat starts out with a high NaCl concentration (similar to plasma), so Cl⁻ flows from the lumen into the duct cells (with Na⁺ through Na⁺ channels) and is returned to the blood.
Without working CFTR in the duct, Cl⁻ (and therefore Na⁺) cannot be reabsorbed, so the sweat reaching the skin stays salty. The sweat test measures this: Cl⁻ ≥ 60 mmol/L indicates cystic fibrosis.





12. [VG] A new compound blocks pain in an animal model. You suspect it blocks voltage-gated Na⁺ channels, like lidocaine. Design patch-clamp experiments to test (a) whether it blocks Na⁺ channels, (b) whether it acts from the inside or the outside of the membrane, and (c) whether, like lidocaine, it blocks more strongly when channels open often. [ELO 1] [ELO 2]






Model answer






Whole-cell recording from cells expressing the Na⁺ channel (e.g. cultured sensory neurons or a cell line expressing it). Depolarise with voltage steps and measure the inward Na⁺ current before and after adding the compound; a dose–response curve gives the IC₅₀. Controls: vehicle alone; a known blocker (tetrodotoxin or lidocaine); test other channels (e.g. K⁺ currents) to check specificity.
Use excised patches: in an inside-out patch, add the compound to the bath, which now faces the cytosolic side; in an outside-out patch, the bath faces the extracellular side. Block from one side only shows the site of action. A permanently charged version of the compound, which cannot cross the membrane, is a useful extra test.
Apply trains of depolarising pulses at low (e.g. 0.1 Hz) and high frequency (e.g. 10 Hz). If block builds up from pulse to pulse at high frequency (use-dependent block), the compound binds preferentially to open or inactivated channels, as lidocaine does. This property would let it block busy pain fibres more than normal nerves.

title: Study questions: ion channels and membrane potential
section: Explore
text:
Explore
The voltage scale shows each ion’s Nernst potential as a coloured line (K⁺ violet, Na⁺ blue, Cl⁻ green) and the membrane potential \(V_m\) from the Goldman equation as the orange marker. Change the inside and outside concentrations of each ion, and how many of its channels are open (its permeability, relative to K⁺ at rest, on a log scale). The table gives each ion’s \(E\), the driving force \(V_m - E\) and the direction of its net flow; the box below shows the calculation with your numbers (exact equations, 37 °C, \(RT/F = 26.7\) mV). Start from the presets. An optional particle view (tick the box) shows single ions crossing open channels; how often they cross in each direction follows the same equations.



E1. Choose Resting cell. Check \(E_\text{K}\), \(E_\text{Na}\), \(E_\text{Cl}\) and \(V_m\) against the lecture. For each ion, read the driving force \(V_m - E\) and the direction of net flow. Which ion is pushed hardest? Why does the membrane potential not change, although ions keep flowing? [ELO 2]
E2. Predict first. Blood K⁺ rises from 5 to 8 mM (High outside K⁺). Which way do \(E_\text{K}\) and \(V_m\) move, and by how much? Then try 10 mM and 3 mM outside. Why does \(V_m\) change less than \(E_\text{K}\)? [ELO 2]
E3. Choose Na⁺ channels open (action-potential peak). Where is \(V_m\) now? Why does it not reach \(E_\text{Na}\)? How many more Na⁺ channels must open (try the slider) to get within 5 mV of \(E_\text{Na}\)? Then choose Lidocaine + the same stimulus. What happens, and what does this mean for a pain fibre? [ELO 2]
E4. [VG] Choose Epithelial cell, CFTR closed (inside Cl⁻ is 50 mM here), then CFTR open. How do \(E_\text{Cl}\) and \(V_m\) change, and in which direction does Cl⁻ flow? Now predict what opening the same number of Cl⁻ channels would do in a cell with only 10 mM Cl⁻ inside (go to Resting cell and set the Cl⁻ open channels to 3). Explain the difference with one rule. [ELO 2]
E5. Tick the particle view and choose Resting cell. Compare how many K⁺ ions cross out and in per second, and how many Na⁺ ions come in (average over 10 s; the counts are random). How do the numbers show that the net charge flow is zero at \(V_m\)? Then choose Na⁺ channels open: what changes? [ELO 2]






Solutions





E1. \(E_\text{K} = -89\) mV, \(E_\text{Na} = +67\) mV, \(E_\text{Cl} = -64\) mV and \(V_m = -70\) mV, as in the lecture. Driving forces: K⁺ \(+19\) mV (net flow out), Na⁺ \(-136\) mV (net flow in), Cl⁻ \(-6\) mV (almost at equilibrium; a tiny net flow out). Na⁺ is pushed hardest, but few Na⁺ channels are open, so its flow is small. At \(V_m\) the positive charge that leaves as K⁺ equals the positive charge that enters as Na⁺ (plus the little Cl⁻ that leaves): the net current is zero, so the voltage stays put. This is exactly how the Goldman equation is defined. The ions themselves keep leaking, and the Na⁺/K⁺ pump keeps the gradients.
E2. With 8 mM outside, \(E_\text{K}\) rises from −89 to −76.5 mV and \(V_m\) from −70 to −63.5 mV: the cell is depolarised by about 6 mV. With 10 mM: \(E_\text{K}\) −70.5 mV, \(V_m\) −59.9 mV. With 3 mM (hypokalaemia): \(E_\text{K}\) −102.7 mV, \(V_m\) −75.2 mV (hyperpolarised). \(V_m\) moves less than \(E_\text{K}\) because it is a weighted average: the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ channels, whose \(E\) did not change, still pull on it. In heart muscle, a depolarised resting potential inactivates part of the Na⁺ channels and disturbs the rhythm, which is why high blood K⁺ is dangerous.
E3. \(V_m\) is about +36 mV (the lecture’s action-potential peak), well above 0 but not at \(E_\text{Na}\) (+67 mV), because the K⁺ (and Cl⁻) channels are still open and pull towards their own \(E\). Na⁺ channels must outnumber K⁺ channels much more: at 30 (relative units) \(V_m\) is +57 mV, at 100 it is +63 mV. With lidocaine the voltage stays at −70 mV: the Na⁺ channels are told to open, but their pores are blocked, so only the resting leak remains and there is no action potential. A pain fibre then sends no signal to the brain. (In real cells lidocaine blocks part of the channels and binds best to channels that open often; the demo blocks all of them.)
E4. CFTR closed: \(E_\text{Cl} = -21\) mV, \(V_m = -61.6\) mV. CFTR open: $V_m = $ −28.8 mV, close to \(E_\text{Cl}\); Cl⁻ flows out of the cell (the table: net flow out), and K⁺ out flow increases too. In an airway cell, this Cl⁻ leaves through the apical membrane into the airway, Na⁺ follows between the cells and water follows by osmosis. With only 10 mM Cl⁻ inside, \(E_\text{Cl} = -64\) mV, and opening the same channels moves \(V_m\) only from −70 to −65.8 mV. The rule: opening channels for an ion moves \(V_m\) towards that ion’s \(E\); how far and in which direction depends on where \(E\) lies, which is set by the concentrations. Without CFTR (cystic fibrosis) the Cl⁻ secretion and the water that follows it are lost.
E5. At rest about 6 K⁺ ions cross out and 3 cross in per second (net about 3 out), about 3 Na⁺ come in and almost none go out, and Cl⁻ crosses about equally in both directions (the rates are scaled to be watchable). The net K⁺ outflow equals the net Na⁺ inflow (plus a small Cl⁻ outflow): no net charge flows. Note that K⁺ crosses in both directions: equilibrium is not “no movement” but “equal movement both ways”. With Na⁺ channels open, many Na⁺ ions flood in, and the K⁺ outflow rises to match them, because \(V_m\) is now far above \(E_\text{K}\); the counts are scaled down so that you can still follow them.

title: Enzyme-coupled receptors: kinase cascades
section: About this lecture

title: Enzyme-coupled receptors: kinase cascades
section: The question: who decides when a cell divides?
text:
The question: who decides when a cell divides?


Cells in your body divide only when neighbours send growth factors. Take the growth factor away, and a normal cell stops.
Many cancer cells divide without the signal. Often the cause is a single changed amino acid in one kinase, or in Ras.
How does a signal outside become a decision inside? Why can one point mutation take over that decision? And can a drug take it back?


Cells in a tissue do not divide on their own initiative. A skin cell divides when a wound releases growth factors; a blood stem cell divides when cytokines call for more blood cells. In a cell culture dish, you add serum, which contains growth factors, and the cells divide; take the serum away and they stop in the first gap phase of the cell cycle. So the decision to divide is made outside the cell, by other cells. The signal must cross the membrane and travel to the nucleus, where genes for cell division are turned on. Look at the cell on the right. In many cancers, the decision is taken without any growth factor. When the genes of such tumours were sequenced, the cause was often one changed amino acid: glycine 12 of Ras, or valine 600 of the kinase BRAF. Today we follow the chain from receptor to nucleus and find out why such small changes take over the decision. We end with drugs that block the stuck switch.

title: Enzyme-coupled receptors: kinase cascades
section: Recap: two kinds of molecular switch
text:
Recap: two kinds of molecular switch


Phosphorylation: a kinase puts a phosphate from ATP on a Ser, Thr or Tyr; a phosphatase takes it off. The negative charge changes the protein’s shape or creates a binding site.
GTP binding: a GTPase is ON with GTP and OFF with GDP. A GEF swaps GDP for GTP; a GAP speeds up GTP hydrolysis.

Recap from the lecture on principles of cell communication; today both switches are wired together.

This is a recap from the lecture on principles of cell communication, because everything today is built from these two switches. The first switch is phosphorylation. A protein kinase takes the last phosphate of ATP and puts it on the hydroxyl group of a serine, threonine or tyrosine side chain. The phosphate carries two negative charges. It can change the shape of the protein, for example opening the active site of an enzyme, or it can create a binding site for another protein. A phosphatase removes the phosphate again. The second switch is a GTP-binding protein. With GTP bound, it has an active shape; when it hydrolyses GTP to GDP, it switches off. On its own, it does both steps slowly. A guanine nucleotide exchange factor, GEF, pulls out GDP so that GTP, which is more abundant in the cytosol, can bind. A GTPase-activating protein, GAP, speeds up hydrolysis. You met trimeric G proteins in the GPCR lecture. Today we meet a small, single-chain GTPase called Ras.

title: Enzyme-coupled receptors: kinase cascades
section: Enzyme-coupled receptors: three kinds
text:
Enzyme-coupled receptors: three kinds


Receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs): about 58 in humans. Growth factors (EGF, PDGF, FGF), insulin. Our main topic.
Kinase-associated receptors: no kinase of their own; a JAK kinase is bound to them. Most cytokines.
Receptor serine/threonine kinases: TGF-β family, in the lecture on signalling that shapes tissues.


Enzyme-coupled receptors are single-pass membrane proteins: each chain crosses the membrane once. That is very different from a GPCR, which crosses seven times. A single helix cannot easily transmit a change of shape from outside to inside. So these receptors use a different trick, as the bottom line says: the ligand brings two receptor chains together, and the enzyme domains inside then act on each other. There are three main kinds. Receptor tyrosine kinases carry the kinase domain inside the receptor itself. Humans have about 58 of them, including the receptors for epidermal growth factor, EGF, for platelet-derived growth factor, for fibroblast growth factors, and for insulin. Kinase-associated receptors, such as the receptors for interferons, interleukin-6 and erythropoietin, have no kinase domain; a separate tyrosine kinase called JAK sits on their tail. A third group, the receptor serine/threonine kinases for TGF-beta, phosphorylate serines and threonines; you meet them in the lecture on signalling that shapes tissues. Today we focus on the first two.

title: Enzyme-coupled receptors: kinase cascades
section: RTK activation: dimerisation and autophosphorylation
text:
RTK activation: dimerisation and autophosphorylation


One ligand brings two receptor chains together (a dimer).
The two kinase domains phosphorylate each other (trans-autophosphorylation): first in their activation loops, which turns the kinases fully on, then on tyrosines in the tails.
Simplified: the insulin receptor is already a dimer; insulin changes its shape. The EGF receptor forms an asymmetric dimer: one kinase activates the other.


Here is the key mechanism. In the membrane, receptor chains move around freely, mostly apart, and their kinase domains are nearly inactive. The ligand, for example EGF, binds the outside and stabilises a dimer of two receptor chains. Now the two kinase domains inside are close together. Each has a little activity, enough to phosphorylate the other on a tyrosine in its activation loop, a flexible part that blocks the active site. Phosphorylation moves the loop away, and the kinase becomes fully active. The active kinases then phosphorylate several more tyrosines on each other’s tails. This is called trans-autophosphorylation: the receptor phosphorylates itself, but each chain phosphorylates the other. Two details for honesty. The insulin receptor is already a covalent dimer, and insulin rearranges it. And in the EGF receptor, structures show an asymmetric dimer, where one kinase domain acts as an activator for the other. The principle is the same: bringing kinases together switches them on.

title: Enzyme-coupled receptors: kinase cascades
section: Phosphotyrosines are docking sites: SH2 domains
text:
Phosphotyrosines are docking sites: SH2 domains


An SH2 domain (about 100 amino acids) binds a phosphotyrosine plus the next few amino acids. Each docking site therefore attracts particular proteins.
Grb2 (an adaptor) brings SOS to the membrane → Ras. PI3K → lipid signals. PLCγ → IP₃ and Ca²⁺ (as in the GPCR lecture).
One active receptor builds a signalling complex that starts several pathways at once.


What do the phosphorylated tails do? They are not switches on the receptor itself. They are landing pads. Many signalling proteins carry a small domain of about one hundred amino acids called the SH2 domain, for Src homology 2, first found in the Src kinase. An SH2 domain has a deep pocket that binds a phosphorylated tyrosine, and a groove next to it that reads the three or so amino acids that follow the tyrosine. Because the neighbouring sequence differs between sites, each phosphotyrosine attracts a different set of SH2 proteins. Three important ones are shown. Grb2 is an adaptor, a protein with no enzyme activity that links two others; it holds the protein SOS, and brings it to the membrane, where we meet it on the next slide. PI3K, a lipid kinase, starts the survival pathway. PLC gamma makes IP3 and DAG, the same second messengers you saw in the GPCR lecture. So one active receptor assembles a whole complex and starts several pathways in parallel. Other proteins use a PTB domain, which also binds phosphotyrosine.

title: Enzyme-coupled receptors: kinase cascades
section: Ras: a GTPase switch at the membrane
text:
Ras: a GTPase switch at the membrane





Human H-Ras (PDB 121P): a small GTPase, about 21 kDa.


Grb2 brings SOS (a GEF) to the membrane, where Ras sits on a lipid anchor. SOS swaps GDP for GTP: Ras ON.
Ras-GTP binds and activates the kinase RAF. A GAP (e.g. neurofibromin, NF1) makes Ras hydrolyse its GTP: Ras OFF.


Ras is the link between the receptor and the kinase cascade. It is a small GTPase of about 21 kilodaltons, a single domain, shown on the right. A lipid group attached to its end anchors it to the inner face of the plasma membrane. In a resting cell, almost all Ras carries GDP and is off. When the receptor is active, Grb2 binds a phosphotyrosine with its SH2 domain and brings SOS from the cytosol to the membrane, right next to Ras. SOS is a guanine nucleotide exchange factor: it opens Ras so that GDP falls out, and GTP, which is about ten times more abundant in the cytosol, binds instead.
