Ras-GTP changes the shape of two loops, called switch regions, and now binds RAF. Ras switches itself off by hydrolysing GTP, but alone this is very slow. A GAP, for example neurofibromin, puts an arginine into the active site of Ras and speeds hydrolysis about a hundred thousand times. Now look at the red box: in cancer, mutations at glycine 12 leave no room for that arginine, so Ras stays on.

title: Enzyme-coupled receptors: kinase cascades
section: The MAP kinase cascade: Ras → RAF → MEK → ERK
text:
The MAP kinase cascade: Ras → RAF → MEK → ERK









RAF phosphorylates MEK on two serines. MEK phosphorylates ERK on a Thr and a Tyr. ERK is active only when both are phosphorylated.
Active ERK phosphorylates hundreds of proteins in the cytosol and enters the nucleus.
In the nucleus it activates transcription factors → immediate early genes (FOS, MYC) within minutes → cyclin D → the cell passes the start of the cell cycle.
General name: MAP kinase cascade (mitogen-activated protein kinase). The same three-kinase design is used for stress signals (JNK, p38).



Now the cascade. Ras-GTP pulls RAF to the membrane and helps it form an active dimer. RAF is a serine/threonine kinase. Its substrate is another kinase, MEK, which it phosphorylates on two serines. MEK is unusual: it is a dual-specificity kinase that phosphorylates its only known substrate, ERK, on a threonine and a tyrosine, two residues apart. ERK needs both phosphates to be active. ERK is the end of the chain. It phosphorylates hundreds of targets. Some are in the cytosol, including the upstream proteins, as we will see. A large fraction of active ERK moves into the nucleus and phosphorylates transcription factors. Within minutes, immediate early genes such as FOS and MYC are transcribed. Their products turn on later genes, among them cyclin D, which you will meet in the cell-cycle lectures as the protein that lets a cell pass the restriction point. The general name for this design is a MAP kinase cascade. Mitogen means a signal that causes division. Cells use the same three-level design for other signals, for example the JNK and p38 pathways that respond to stress.

title: Enzyme-coupled receptors: kinase cascades
section: Why three kinases? Amplification and a switch
text:
Why three kinases? Amplification and a switch


Amplification: each active kinase phosphorylates many molecules of the next. A few thousand active receptors can switch on hundreds of thousands of ERK molecules.
Switch-like (ultrasensitive): each level needs two phosphorylations, by enzymes near saturation, so each level is steeper than the one above. ERK goes from off to on over a small change in growth factor. Try it: Demo: kinase cascade.


Why not let the receptor phosphorylate ERK directly? A cascade does two things. First, it amplifies. Each active RAF molecule phosphorylates many MEK molecules before it is switched off, and each active MEK phosphorylates many ERK. There is also much more MEK and ERK in the cell than RAF. So a small number of active receptors can switch on a large part of the cell’s ERK. Second, a cascade makes a switch. Look at the plot, made with the demo model. The receptor follows a simple binding curve: from 10 to 90 percent bound takes an 81-fold change in growth factor, a Hill coefficient of 1, as you know from dose–response. ERK rises much more steeply, and at about ten times less growth factor. Two features cause this. MEK and ERK each need two phosphorylations, which roughly squares the response; and the kinases and phosphatases work close to saturation, which sharpens it more. The effect compounds level by level. James Ferrell and colleagues measured a Hill coefficient of about five for MAP kinase in frog egg extracts. So the cell makes a clear decision: divide or not, rather than a little bit.

title: Enzyme-coupled receptors: kinase cascades
section: PI3K–Akt–mTOR: survive and grow
text:
PI3K–Akt–mTOR: survive and grow


PI3K docks on the receptor and phosphorylates a membrane lipid: PIP₂ → PIP₃. PTEN reverses this.
Akt binds PIP₃ with its PH domain, is phosphorylated and activated, then leaves the membrane.
Akt blocks death proteins (BAD; the apoptosis lecture), activates mTORC1 (protein synthesis, cell growth) and, after insulin, sends GLUT4 to the cell surface.


The second pathway starts at the same receptors. PI3K, phosphoinositide 3-kinase, has a regulatory subunit with SH2 domains, so it docks on phosphotyrosines; Ras-GTP can also activate it. PI3K is a lipid kinase. It adds a phosphate to the inositol ring of the membrane lipid PIP2, making PIP3. PIP3 is a second messenger that stays in the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane. Proteins with a PH domain, short for pleckstrin homology, bind it. One of them is the kinase Akt, also called protein kinase B. At the membrane, Akt is phosphorylated by two other kinases, PDK1 and mTORC2, and becomes active. Akt has several jobs. It phosphorylates and inactivates BAD, a protein that promotes apoptosis; you will meet BAD in the apoptosis lecture. Through the proteins TSC and Rheb it activates mTORC1, the complex that drives protein synthesis and cell growth. And in muscle and fat cells, after insulin, it sends vesicles with the glucose transporter GLUT4 to the cell surface; you met GLUT transporters in the transport lecture. The phosphatase PTEN removes the phosphate from PIP3 and is a tumour suppressor.

title: Enzyme-coupled receptors: kinase cascades
section: JAK–STAT: from receptor to gene in four steps
text:
JAK–STAT: from receptor to gene in four steps


Cytokine receptors have JAK kinases bound to their tails. The ligand brings two JAKs together; they phosphorylate each other and the receptor.
STAT docks with its SH2 domain, is phosphorylated, and two STATs bind each other.
The STAT dimer is the transcription factor: no second messenger, no cascade. Interferons, IL-6, EPO; much more in Immunologi.


The JAK–STAT pathway is the shortest route from the cell surface to the genes. Receptors for many cytokines, such as interferons and interleukin-6, and for hormones like erythropoietin and growth hormone, have no kinase domain. Instead, a tyrosine kinase of the JAK family is bound to each receptor tail. Step one: the cytokine brings two receptor chains together, the two JAKs phosphorylate each other and then tyrosines on the receptor. The logic is the same as for an RTK, but with the kinase borrowed. Step two: a STAT protein, short for signal transducer and activator of transcription, docks on a phosphotyrosine with its SH2 domain, and JAK phosphorylates one tyrosine on the STAT. Step three: the phosphorylated STAT lets go of the receptor and binds another phosphorylated STAT, each SH2 domain grabbing the other’s phosphotyrosine. Step four: the dimer enters the nucleus and binds DNA. A mutation that keeps JAK2 on, V617F, causes polycythaemia vera, too many red blood cells; the JAK inhibitor ruxolitinib treats it. You will meet cytokine signalling again in Immunologi.

title: Enzyme-coupled receptors: kinase cascades
section: Switching off, and negative feedback
text:
Switching off, and negative feedback


Every step has an off switch: receptor endocytosis and degradation (the endocytosis lecture), GAPs for Ras, phosphatases for the kinases and for PIP₃.
Negative feedback: active ERK phosphorylates SOS and RAF, which weakens the signal upstream, and it turns on genes for ERK phosphatases. Result: a peak, then a lower plateau.
Feedback makes the response robust, but it also matters for drugs: block one step, and the brake upstream is released.


A signal is only useful if it can end. Each step has its own off switch. The active receptor is taken into the cell by endocytosis; part of it is degraded in lysosomes, which you will see in the endocytosis lecture. GAPs switch Ras off. Phosphatases remove the phosphates from ERK and MEK; some, called dual-specificity phosphatases or DUSPs, are made in response to ERK activity itself. PTEN removes the phosphate from PIP3. On top of this, the pathway brakes itself. Active ERK phosphorylates SOS and RAF, which makes them less active. This is negative feedback, a general principle from the lecture on principles of cell communication. The plot on the right, from the demo model, shows what feedback does to the time course: a peak after a few minutes, then a lower, steady level, as seen in real cells after adding EGF. Feedback makes a pathway more robust to changes in protein amounts. But it has a consequence for drugs that we will return to: when a drug lowers ERK, it also lowers the brake, and the upstream steps become more active.

title: Enzyme-coupled receptors: kinase cascades
section: Cross-talk: pathways form a network
text:
Cross-talk: pathways form a network


One receptor starts several pathways; one pathway is fed by several receptors.
The branches activate (Ras → PI3K; ERK → mTORC1) and inhibit each other (Akt → RAF). GPCR signals (PKA) feed in too.
The cell integrates all of this into one decision. Our slides show single lines through a network of hundreds of proteins.


So far we have drawn clean, separate lines. Real pathways are a network. One receptor, such as the EGF receptor, starts the MAP kinase, PI3K and PLC gamma pathways at the same time. Ras activates not only RAF but also PI3K. ERK and Akt both feed into mTORC1, so growth signals and division signals are coordinated. There is also inhibition between branches: Akt phosphorylates RAF and can weaken it. And signals from other receptor classes feed in. Protein kinase A, downstream of GPCRs and cyclic AMP, inhibits RAF in some cells and activates the MAP kinase pathway in others, such as neurons. This is called cross-talk. What the cell decides, divide, grow, survive or differentiate, depends on the combination of all inputs, and on how long ERK stays active, not only on whether it is on. For example, in a classic nerve-cell line, a short ERK pulse after EGF makes the cells divide, while a long ERK signal after nerve growth factor makes them grow neurites. Our slides, and the demo, simplify the network to a few lines; keep that in mind when you predict a drug effect.

title: Enzyme-coupled receptors: kinase cascades
section: How do we know? Phospho-specific antibodies
text:
How do we know? Phospho-specific antibodies


An antibody raised against a phosphorylated peptide binds the protein only when that site is phosphorylated: it reports activity, not just amount.
Western blot with anti-phospho-ERK and anti-total-ERK on cells at different times after EGF: P-ERK peaks at 5–10 min. Loading control: actin.
Add an inhibitor: the steps below it lose their phosphates, the steps above do not. This orders the pathway.


How do we know which kinase is active, and in which order they work? The key tool is the phospho-specific antibody. You immunise an animal with a short peptide that carries a phosphate on the tyrosine or threonine of interest, and then select the antibodies that bind the phosphorylated peptide but not the unphosphorylated one. Such an antibody recognises, for example, ERK only when both threonine 202 and tyrosine 204 are phosphorylated, which is the active form. You met the western blot in the cell-methods lecture. Here, cells are starved of growth factor, then EGF is added, and samples are taken at different times. The blot is stained with anti-phospho-EGFR, anti-phospho-ERK, an antibody against total ERK, and a loading control. The figure is a schematic, with the typical result: receptor phosphorylation within a minute or two, phospho-ERK peaking at five to ten minutes, then declining, while the total amount of ERK stays the same. In the last lane a MEK inhibitor removes phospho-ERK but not phospho-EGFR. That tells you MEK sits between the receptor and ERK. The same antibodies are used in flow cytometry and on tumour samples.

title: Enzyme-coupled receptors: kinase cascades
section: Why it matters: cancer breaks these switches
text:
Why it matters: cancer breaks these switches





Breast cancer stained for HER2 (brown, cell membranes), score 3+: the gene is amplified.


RAS genes are mutated in about one cancer in five; BRAF V600E in about half of melanomas; HER2 is amplified in about 15–20 % of breast cancers.
Trastuzumab (1998), an antibody against the outside of HER2, blocks signalling and marks the cells for immune attack. EGFR inhibitors (erlotinib, osimertinib) block the ATP pocket in lung cancers with EGFR mutations.


Now the medical side, which you will meet again in Sjukdomslära and in the cancer lecture. Many cancers have a broken switch in exactly these pathways. Mutated RAS genes are found in about one human cancer in five: in most pancreatic cancers, about four in ten colon cancers and a third of lung adenocarcinomas. About half of melanomas carry a BRAF mutation, mostly V600E. In about fifteen to twenty percent of breast cancers the HER2 gene is amplified: the cells make so many HER2 receptors that they dimerise and signal without any ligand. The photograph shows such a tumour stained with an anti-HER2 antibody; the brown outlines are cell membranes full of HER2. Trastuzumab, approved in 1998, is a monoclonal antibody against the extracellular part of HER2. It reduces signalling and marks the cancer cells for immune cells. HER2 testing decides who gets it: the drug only helps when the target is there. Small-molecule EGFR inhibitors, such as erlotinib and osimertinib, bind the ATP pocket inside the kinase. They work in lung cancers that carry activating EGFR mutations. Other drugs on the figure act on MEK, PI3K and mTOR.

title: Enzyme-coupled receptors: kinase cascades
section: Why it matters: imatinib, the first targeted cancer drug
text:
Why it matters: imatinib, the first targeted cancer drug









Chromosomes 9 and 22 from a CML patient; arrows: the swapped pieces.





CML blood: far too many white cells.


CML: chromosomes 9 and 22 swap pieces; the fusion gene makes BCR-ABL, a tyrosine kinase that is always on.
Imatinib (approved 2001) sits in the ATP pocket of ABL. About 8 in 10 patients are alive after 10 years.


The story that started targeted cancer therapy is chronic myeloid leukaemia. In 1960 two researchers in Philadelphia found an unusually small chromosome in the white blood cells of these patients, the Philadelphia chromosome shown on the upper right. In 1973 Janet Rowley showed that it comes from an exchange of pieces between chromosomes 9 and 22. The joint creates a fusion gene: the front of a gene called BCR joined to most of the tyrosine kinase ABL. The BCR part makes the protein form oligomers, which, like a dimerised receptor, keeps the kinase permanently active. The result is too many white blood cells, as in the blood smear. In the 1990s, chemists and the physician Brian Druker developed imatinib, a small molecule that fits the ATP pocket of ABL in its inactive shape. Without ATP, the kinase cannot phosphorylate its substrates. Imatinib was approved in 2001, and a disease that used to kill most patients within a few years became a chronic condition: about eight in ten patients are alive ten years later. It also works on the kinase KIT in gastrointestinal stromal tumours.

title: Enzyme-coupled receptors: kinase cascades
section: Why it matters: BRAF V600E and vemurafenib
text:
Why it matters: BRAF V600E and vemurafenib



Melanoma on the skin. About half carry a BRAF mutation.


BRAF V600E is active without Ras and escapes the ERK feedback. Melanoma cells depend on it.
Vemurafenib (2011) blocks V600E-BRAF: most tumours shrink, but often regrow within months.
In cells without the mutation, the same drug can activate RAF dimers (“paradoxical activation”): some patients get new skin tumours.
BRAF + MEK inhibitor together (dabrafenib + trametinib) work longer and cause fewer side effects.
In colon cancer with the same mutation, vemurafenib alone hardly works: the ERK brake is released and EGFR turns the pathway back on.



BRAF V600E is the clearest example of a cancer that depends on one stuck kinase. Valine 600 sits in the activation loop of BRAF. Replacing it with glutamate, which is negatively charged, mimics the phosphorylation that normally activates the loop. The mutant kinase is active as a single molecule, without Ras, and it ignores the negative feedback from ERK. Vemurafenib, approved in 2011, binds V600E-BRAF in its ATP pocket. Most patients’ tumours shrink within weeks, a dramatic result for a disease that used to have few options. But the tumours often grow back within months. And there was a surprise. In normal cells with Ras activity, vemurafenib binds one RAF in a dimer and makes the partner more active; some patients developed new, mostly benign skin tumours. Adding a MEK inhibitor blocks both problems, and the combination of dabrafenib and trametinib works longer. The biggest surprise came in colon cancers with the same mutation: vemurafenib alone hardly worked. The reason was negative feedback, as we will see on the next slide. You can test this in the demo.

title: Enzyme-coupled receptors: kinase cascades
section: How resistance appears
text:
How resistance appears





EGFR kinase domain; the ATP pocket lies between the two lobes, under the P-loop.


Gatekeeper mutation: a bigger amino acid at the entrance of the ATP pocket keeps the drug out, but not ATP (EGFR T790M, BCR-ABL T315I).
Bypass and feedback relief: another route turns ERK back on. Answer: next-generation drugs and combinations (Kliniska prövningar och läkemedelsutveckling).


Targeted drugs select for resistant cells, just as antibiotics select for resistant bacteria, which you know from microbiology. A tumour has billions of cells; if one carries a resistance mutation, it survives and grows. There are three common routes. First, the target changes. The gatekeeper residue is an amino acid at the back of the ATP pocket. When a small threonine is replaced by a bigger methionine or isoleucine, ATP still binds, but the drug no longer fits. In lung cancer, EGFR T790M appears in about half of patients who relapse on gefitinib or erlotinib; osimertinib was designed to bind it. In CML, T315I in BCR-ABL resists imatinib; ponatinib still binds. Second, bypass: another receptor such as MET is amplified, or a mutation further down, in NRAS or MEK, turns the pathway back on. Third, feedback relief: in BRAF V600E colon cancer, the drug lowers ERK, the feedback brake is released, and EGFR drives RAF dimers that the drug blocks poorly. Adding the EGFR antibody cetuximab works. Designing such combinations is part of drug development, which you study in Kliniska prövningar och läkemedelsutveckling.

title: Enzyme-coupled receptors: kinase cascades
section: Summary
text:
Summary

Enzyme-coupled receptors are single-pass. The ligand brings two chains together; the kinases phosphorylate each other, and phosphotyrosines become docking sites for SH2 proteins.
Ras is a GTPase switch: SOS (GEF) turns it on, a GAP turns it off. Ras-GTP starts the RAF → MEK → ERK cascade; ERK turns on genes for division.
A three-kinase cascade amplifies and makes a switch-like response. PI3K–Akt–mTOR drives survival and growth; JAK–STAT goes straight to the genes. The pathways cross-talk.
Signals are switched off by GAPs, phosphatases, endocytosis and negative feedback. Phospho-specific antibodies show which step is active.
Cancers break these switches (HER2, EGFR, KRAS, BRAF V600E, BCR-ABL). Targeted drugs (trastuzumab, imatinib, vemurafenib) block them; resistance comes from gatekeeper mutations, bypass and feedback relief.

Read more (optional): Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell, 7th ed., ch. 15.
Image credits

Five take-home points. First, enzyme-coupled receptors cross the membrane only once, so they signal by being brought together: the ligand makes a dimer, the kinase domains phosphorylate each other, and the phosphotyrosines become docking sites read by SH2 domains. Second, Ras links the receptor to the cascade. It is on with GTP, switched on by the exchange factor SOS and off by a GAP; mutations that stop the GAP from working keep it on. Third, a chain of kinases amplifies the signal and makes a switch-like response, which helps a cell make a clear decision. Two other pathways start at the same receptors: PI3K–Akt–mTOR for survival and growth, and JAK–STAT for cytokines. They form a network. Fourth, every step has an off switch, and the pathway brakes itself through negative feedback; we know the order of the steps from phospho-specific antibodies and inhibitors. Fifth, these pathways are where many cancers start, and where targeted drugs act. Tumours escape those drugs in predictable ways. In the next lecture we see signals that shape tissues and decide cell fates.

title: Quiz: enzyme-coupled receptors and kinase cascades
text:
Short questions to check your understanding of the lecture Enzyme-coupled receptors: kinase cascades. Try each on paper first, then open the hint or the answer. The tag after each question shows the learning outcome (ELO) it practises.

Q1. An RTK has a single transmembrane helix. How, then, does binding of a growth factor outside switch on the kinase inside? [ELO 3]






Hint





Think about what the ligand does to two receptor chains, not to one.









Answer





The growth factor brings two receptor chains together (dimerisation). The two kinase domains are then close enough to phosphorylate each other (trans-autophosphorylation), first in their activation loops, which makes them fully active, then on tyrosines in their tails. A single helix does not need to transmit a shape change.




Q2. What does an SH2 domain bind, and why do different SH2 proteins bind different phosphotyrosines on the same receptor? [ELO 3]






Hint





The pocket reads the phosphate; what does the groove next to it read?









Answer





An SH2 domain binds a phosphorylated tyrosine together with the few amino acids that follow it. The pocket binds the phosphotyrosine; the neighbouring groove reads the next (about three) amino acids. Because each phosphotyrosine on the receptor has a different neighbouring sequence, each one attracts particular SH2 proteins (e.g. Grb2, PI3K, PLCγ).




Q3. Fill in: Ras is active when it binds ______. The ______ SOS switches it on by ______. A ______ switches it off by ______. [ELO 3]






Hint





GEF, GAP, GTP, GDP.









Answer





Ras is active when it binds GTP. The GEF (guanine nucleotide exchange factor) SOS switches it on by letting GDP out so that GTP can bind. A GAP (GTPase-activating protein, e.g. neurofibromin) switches it off by speeding up hydrolysis of the bound GTP to GDP.




Q4. Put in order, from the receptor to the nucleus: ERK, Grb2–SOS, MEK, Ras, RAF. Which of them are kinases? [ELO 3]






Hint





Two of the five have no kinase activity.









Answer





Receptor → Grb2–SOS → Ras → RAF → MEK → ERK → nucleus. RAF, MEK and ERK are kinases (the MAP kinase kinase kinase, MAP kinase kinase and MAP kinase). Grb2 is an adaptor, SOS is a GEF and Ras is a GTPase.




Q5. PI3K adds a phosphate to a membrane lipid. Why does that activate Akt, which is a cytosolic kinase? And what does the phosphatase PTEN do? [ELO 3]






Hint





Akt has a PH domain.









Answer





PI3K turns PIP₂ into PIP₃ in the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane. Akt’s PH domain binds PIP₃, so Akt is brought to the membrane, where other kinases (PDK1, mTORC2) phosphorylate and activate it. PTEN removes the phosphate again (PIP₃ → PIP₂) and so switches the pathway off; losing PTEN keeps Akt on, which is why PTEN is a tumour suppressor.




Q6. Why does a three-kinase cascade give a more switch-like (steeper) response than the receptor itself? Name two reasons. [ELO 3]






Hint





How many phosphates do MEK and ERK need? And how busy are the kinases and phosphatases?









Answer






MEK and ERK each need two phosphorylations to be active, which roughly squares the response at low input. (2) The kinases and phosphatases work near saturation, so a small change in kinase activity tips the balance strongly (zero-order ultrasensitivity). (3) The steepness compounds from level to level. Together, the response of ERK can have a Hill coefficient of 4–5, compared with 1 for simple receptor binding.





Q7. Cells are treated with EGF, and a western blot is stained with an antibody against phospho-ERK and one against total ERK. Phospho-ERK peaks at 5 min and falls by 30 min; total ERK stays the same. Give two reasons why phospho-ERK falls although EGF is still there. [ELO 1] [ELO 3]






Hint





Think about the off switches, and about what active ERK does upstream.









Answer





Negative feedback: active ERK phosphorylates SOS and RAF and makes them less active, and it turns on genes for ERK phosphatases (DUSPs). Receptor endocytosis: active EGF receptors are taken into the cell and partly degraded in lysosomes. GAPs also return Ras to the GDP form. Total ERK is unchanged, so the fall is in activity, not in amount.




Q8. A patient’s chronic myeloid leukaemia responds well to imatinib for several years, then comes back. Sequencing shows BCR-ABL with the mutation T315I. Explain what has happened. [ELO 3] [ELO 9]






Hint





Where does imatinib bind, and what is a gatekeeper residue?









Answer





Imatinib binds the ATP pocket of the ABL kinase. T315 is the gatekeeper residue at the entrance of that pocket. Replacing the small threonine with the bigger isoleucine keeps imatinib out, but ATP can still bind, so BCR-ABL is active again. Among the billions of leukaemia cells, a cell with this mutation survived the drug and grew out (selection, as for antibiotic resistance). A different inhibitor that still binds T315I (ponatinib) can be used.

title: Study questions: membrane structure
text: Study questions in the style of the written exam. Write your answer first (a few sentences, or a labelled sketch where it helps), then compare with the model answer. Each question is tagged with its learning outcome (ELO). Questions tagged [VG] are of the kind used for the higher grade: predict, compare, explain an unexpected result or design an experiment.

title: Study questions: membrane structure
section: G-level questions
text:
G-level questions
1. Explain, using \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\), why phospholipids in water form a bilayer by themselves. Why does a bilayer form closed compartments rather than flat sheets with edges? [ELO 2]






Model answer





Phospholipids are amphipathic: a polar head and two hydrophobic tails. Water cannot hydrogen-bond to a hydrocarbon tail, so the water molecules around a tail are held in an ordered cage, which lowers the entropy of the water. When the tails come together inside a bilayer, this water is released and its entropy rises (\(\Delta S > 0\)). \(\Delta H\) is small, so \(-T\Delta S\) dominates and \(\Delta G < 0\): assembly is spontaneous. This is the hydrophobic effect. At the edge of a flat sheet the tails would be exposed to water again, which is unfavourable, so a bilayer closes on itself into a sealed compartment (and small tears reseal).




2. Name the three main classes of membrane lipid. For each, give one example and one feature of its structure that matters for the membrane. [ELO 2]






Model answer






Glycerophospholipids, e.g. phosphatidylcholine (PC) or phosphatidylserine (PS): glycerol backbone with two fatty-acid tails (often one unsaturated, kinked) and a phosphate-linked head; PS carries a net negative charge.
Sphingolipids, e.g. sphingomyelin or glycolipids: sphingosine backbone; long, saturated tails that pack tightly; glycolipids carry sugars and sit only in the outer leaflet.
Sterols: cholesterol, a small, rigid ring structure with an OH head; it regulates fluidity and makes the membrane less leaky. It is abundant in the plasma membrane (about one per phospholipid).





3. Describe the movements a phospholipid molecule makes in a bilayer, and explain why one of them is very rare. [ELO 2]






Model answer





A lipid diffuses laterally within its leaflet (it swaps places with a neighbour about 10⁷ times per second and moves about 2 µm per second), it rotates about its long axis, and its tails flex. Flip-flop, moving to the other leaflet, is very rare (about once a month for a phospholipid on its own), because the polar, often charged head group would have to pass through the hydrophobic core of about 3 nm, which costs a lot of energy. Cells use enzymes (flippases, scramblases) when lipids must move between leaflets.




4. List four factors that change membrane fluidity and say in which direction each one acts. How do bacteria respond when the temperature falls? [ELO 2]






Model answer






Shorter tails: less contact between tails, more fluid.
More cis double bonds (unsaturation): kinks prevent tight packing, more fluid.
Higher temperature: more fluid (below a transition temperature a pure bilayer becomes a gel).
Cholesterol: at 37 °C less fluid (stiffens tails near the heads); at low temperature it prevents the gel state. It acts as a buffer.

When the temperature falls, bacteria make more unsaturated (and shorter) fatty acids, so their membrane stays fluid enough for membrane proteins to work.




5. What is meant by lipid asymmetry in the plasma membrane? Explain how cells maintain it, and give two situations where it is lost on purpose. [ELO 2]






Model answer





The two leaflets have different lipids: the outer leaflet is rich in PC, sphingomyelin and glycolipids, the inner leaflet in PS, PE and PI. Asymmetry is set up when lipids are made (on the cytosolic face of the ER) and moved, and maintained because flip-flop is slow and flippases (P-type ATPases) use ATP to move PS and PE back to the inner leaflet. It is lost when scramblases are switched on, which move lipids both ways without energy: (1) in apoptosis, caspases switch the flippase off and a scramblase on, so PS on the surface acts as an “eat me” signal for phagocytes; (2) in activated platelets, Ca²⁺ switches on a scramblase, and the exposed PS forms a surface on which clotting factors assemble.




6. Draw a bilayer and show the main ways in which proteins can be associated with a membrane. Say how each kind can be removed from the membrane in the laboratory. [ELO 2]






Model answer





Sketch should show:

Integral, single-pass: one α-helix crossing the bilayer.
Integral, multi-pass: several α-helices (e.g. seven), or a β-barrel (in outer membranes of bacteria, mitochondria and chloroplasts).
Lipid-anchored: on the cytosolic side through a covalently attached fatty acid (myristoyl, palmitoyl) or prenyl group; on the outside through a GPI anchor.
Peripheral: bound non-covalently to head groups or to the exposed part of an integral protein.

Removal: integral (and in practice lipid-anchored) proteins need a detergent that dissolves the bilayer (GPI-anchored proteins can also be cut off by a phospholipase). Peripheral proteins come off with high salt or a change in pH, which break non-covalent contacts while the membrane stays intact.




7. Why do the parts of membrane proteins that cross the bilayer form either α-helices or β-barrels? About how many amino acids does a transmembrane α-helix need, and why? [ELO 2]






Model answer





Every peptide bond has polar C=O and N–H groups. In water these bond to water, but inside the bilayer there is no water, so they must bond to each other. In an α-helix each backbone group bonds to another within the same helix, and the side chains point outwards, where hydrophobic side chains contact the lipid tails. A single β-strand cannot satisfy its backbone, but in a β-barrel each strand bonds to its two neighbours and the sheet closes on itself. A helix rises 0.15 nm per residue, so about 20 hydrophobic amino acids (20 × 0.15 nm = 3 nm) span the hydrophobic core of about 3 nm.




8. Explain how a hydropathy plot is made and how you read it. Give one limitation. [ELO 2]






Model answer





Each amino acid has a hydropathy score (e.g. Kyte–Doolittle: Ile +4.5, Arg −4.5). A window of about 19 residues slides along the sequence; the average score of the window is plotted at its central position. A broad peak of about 20 residues above a threshold (about +1.6 for this window) predicts a transmembrane α-helix; the number of peaks predicts the number of crossings (e.g. seven for a G-protein-coupled receptor). Limitations: it misses β-barrels (short strands alternating polar and non-polar); helices with polar residues (e.g. lining a pore) can fall below the threshold; an ER signal sequence gives a peak too; and it does not show which side of the membrane each loop is on. Predictions must be tested.




9. Describe the Frye–Edidin cell-fusion experiment and FRAP. What does each show about membrane proteins? [ELO 1] [ELO 2]






Model answer





Frye–Edidin (1970): a mouse cell and a human cell were fused (with a virus) into one hybrid cell. Mouse surface proteins were labelled with a green-fluorescent antibody and human proteins with a red one. At first each colour covered half the cell; after about 40 min at 37 °C the colours were completely mixed, but not at low temperature, and not prevented by blocking protein synthesis or ATP production. So membrane proteins diffuse laterally in a fluid bilayer.
FRAP: a fluorescent membrane protein (e.g. a GFP fusion) is bleached in a small spot with a strong laser; fluorescence recovers as unbleached molecules diffuse in. The rate of recovery gives the diffusion coefficient; the part that does not recover is the immobile fraction, held by the cytoskeleton or other proteins. FRAP measures mobility in living cells and shows that many proteins move more slowly than lipids.




10. Explain the principle of freeze-fracture electron microscopy and what it showed about the structure of membranes. [ELO 1] [ELO 2]






Model answer





Cells are frozen rapidly and cracked with a cold knife. The fracture runs between the two leaflets of the bilayer, where only weak contacts hold the tail ends together, exposing the inner faces of each half (the P face, cytosolic half, and the E face, outer half). The faces are shadowed with platinum from an angle, the biological material is removed, and the metal replica is examined in a TEM. Pure lipid bilayers give smooth faces, but cell membranes show many intramembrane particles (about 8–10 nm); their number rises with the protein content of the membrane, so they are integral proteins that cross the bilayer. This supported the fluid mosaic model (proteins embedded in a lipid bilayer), rather than a model in which proteins only coat the surface.




11. What is the glycocalyx? Use the ABO blood groups to explain how a small difference in the glycocalyx can matter clinically. [ELO 2]






Model answer





The glycocalyx is the coat of carbohydrate on the outside of the plasma membrane: sugar chains on glycoproteins, glycolipids and proteoglycans. Sugars are added in the ER and Golgi lumen, so they always face the outside. It protects the cell, holds water and takes part in cell recognition. On red blood cells, a sugar chain ends in the H antigen (galactose with fucose). One gene encodes a Golgi glycosyltransferase: the A form adds N-acetylgalactosamine, the B form adds galactose, the O form is inactive (H only). People make antibodies against the A or B sugar they lack (a type A person has anti-B). If a type A patient receives type B blood, the anti-B antibodies bind the donor red cells and destroy them (a haemolytic transfusion reaction). One sugar at the tip of a chain decides compatibility.

title: Study questions: membrane structure
section: VG-style questions
text:
VG-style questions
12. [VG] An E. coli culture is moved from 37 °C to 15 °C. (a) Predict what happens to the fatty-acid composition of its membrane over the next hours, and explain why this is needed. (b) A mutant cannot make unsaturated fatty acids unless they are added to the medium. Predict how the mutant behaves at 15 °C without added fatty acids, and design an experiment that tests your explanation using one method from the lecture. [ELO 2]






Model answer






At lower temperature the bilayer becomes less fluid and may approach a gel state. Membrane proteins (transporters, enzymes of the respiratory chain) need a fluid membrane to change shape and diffuse, and a gel membrane can also become leaky at phase boundaries. The bacteria respond by making a higher proportion of unsaturated (cis-kinked) and somewhat shorter fatty acids, restoring fluidity (homeoviscous adaptation). E. coli has no cholesterol, so it cannot use a sterol buffer.
The mutant cannot raise unsaturation, so its membrane becomes too ordered at 15 °C: expect slow or no growth, poor transport of nutrients and possibly leakiness; adding an unsaturated fatty acid (e.g. oleic acid) to the medium should rescue growth.

Experiment: measure membrane fluidity directly with FRAP. Label membranes with a fluorescent lipid probe (or express a GFP-tagged membrane protein), bleach a spot and measure recovery at 15 °C in wild-type cells, in the mutant without oleic acid and in the mutant with oleic acid. Prediction: slower recovery (smaller diffusion coefficient) in the mutant without oleic acid, restored by oleic acid, and the growth defect should track the fluidity. Fatty-acid analysis (gas chromatography of extracted lipids) would confirm the composition. Controls: same probe concentration, same temperature, and bleaching settings kept constant.




13. [VG] A lab expresses a new protein X fused to GFP in cultured epithelial cells grown as a sealed layer. X–GFP is found only on the apical surface. (a) Explain how X could stay apical even though the membrane is fluid. (b) The lab adds a drug that opens tight junctions, and after one hour X–GFP is on the basolateral surface too. A FRAP experiment before the drug shows full, fast recovery of a bleached spot on the apical surface. Explain both results together. (c) Suggest one experiment that tests whether X is held in place by the cortical cytoskeleton instead. [ELO 2]






Model answer






The tight junction forms a ring around each cell near its apical end. Besides sealing the space between cells, it acts as a fence: integral membrane proteins (and outer-leaflet lipids) cannot diffuse past it. If X is delivered to the apical membrane, it stays in the apical domain even though it diffuses freely within that domain.
The FRAP result shows that X is mobile within the apical membrane: it is not anchored, it diffuses. So the only thing keeping it apical was the fence. When the drug opens the tight junctions, the fence is lost and X diffuses into the basolateral membrane. Both results fit “free diffusion inside a fenced domain”.
Disrupt actin with a drug such as latrunculin or cytochalasin (with tight junctions intact) and repeat FRAP: if X were held by the cortical cytoskeleton, its immobile fraction would fall or its diffusion would speed up after actin disruption. Since X already recovers fully and fast, the prediction is little change. Controls: confirm actin is disrupted (phalloidin staining) and that the junctions stay closed (e.g. electrical resistance across the cell layer).





14. [VG] Compare liposomal doxorubicin (Doxil) and an mRNA lipid nanoparticle. For each, explain how the lipid composition serves its task, and explain why Doxil reduces damage to the heart. Why is the EPR effect not a full explanation of how Doxil works in patients? [ELO 2] [ELO 9]






Model answer





Doxil must keep a small drug inside for days and release it slowly. It is a liposome (aqueous core, one bilayer) of saturated phospholipid plus cholesterol, so the bilayer is rigid and not leaky; doxorubicin is loaded into the core with a gradient and crystallises there. A PEG coat hides the liposome from phagocytes, so it circulates for days. mRNA LNP must carry a large, negative RNA and release it into the cytosol. Its ionisable lipid is positive at low pH (binds RNA during manufacture; disrupts the acidic endosome membrane so RNA escapes) but nearly neutral at pH 7.4 (less toxic in blood). DSPC and cholesterol give structure, and a small amount of PEG-lipid controls particle size and stops aggregation; it is shed in the body, so the particle can be taken up (patisiran binds ApoE and enters liver cells through the LDL receptor).
Heart: free doxorubicin is a small molecule that leaves the blood everywhere, including through heart capillaries, and the high peak level damages heart muscle. Heart capillaries have a continuous, tight endothelium, so 90 nm liposomes stay in the blood there, and the free-drug peak is low, so cardiotoxicity falls.
EPR caveat: the enhanced permeability and retention effect (leaky tumour vessels, poor lymph drainage) was shown mainly in fast-growing mouse tumours. Human tumours vary a lot in leakiness, and in trials Doxil gave similar survival to free doxorubicin. So its main proven benefit is a different side-effect profile (less heart damage, but hand–foot syndrome in skin), not a much larger dose in the tumour.

title: Study questions: membrane structure
section: Explore
text:
Explore
A patch of plasma membrane seen from above, 15 µm across, with thousands of fluorescent molecules (green) that take random steps: 2D diffusion. Click or tap to bleach a spot 1.5 µm in radius, as the laser does in FRAP. Bleached molecules turn dark grey but keep moving. The graph shows the fraction of the molecules in the spot that are bright. The orange dashed curve is fitted to your data (the exact recovery curve for a circular spot); the readout gives the plateau, the mobile fraction, the half-time \(t_{1/2}\) and the diffusion coefficient \(D = 0.224\,w^2/t_{1/2}\) (\(w\) = spot radius). The fit says provisional until the curve is long enough to trust. Time runs in slow or fast motion (shown under the image). The fluidity sliders change how fast the molecules move by a qualitative rule (the shape is right, the numbers are illustrative). The second mode, Cell fusion, repeats the Frye–Edidin experiment. Each bleach is a new random experiment, so your numbers will differ from the solutions by about 10–20 %.



E1. Choose lipid and bleach a spot. Wait until the fit is no longer provisional, then read the mobile fraction, \(t_{1/2}\) and \(D\). Repeat with a small protein. How many times more slowly does the protein diffuse? Does this agree with the lecture? [ELO 2]
E2. Choose lipid, press Follow one molecule and watch its track for about 1 s of simulated time (the clock under the image). How far is it from where it started? Try a few molecules. Does the track look like a straight path? Compare with “about 2 µm in 1 s” from the lecture. [ELO 2]
E3. Predict first, then check. Choose small protein and set immobile (anchored) to 30 %: these molecules are held in place, as if bound to the cytoskeleton. Sketch the recovery curve you expect. Then bleach and compare. Does the half-time change? [ELO 2]
E4. [VG] Use the line under the fluidity sliders, which gives the fluidity factor and \(D\). (a) At 37 °C with the default membrane, compare cholesterol 0 % and 50 %. (b) Now set double bonds to 0 (saturated tails) and compare cholesterol 0 %, 30 % and 50 % again. (c) What do (a) and (b) together tell you about the role of cholesterol? (d) Predict the effect of cooling the default membrane to 10 °C, then check. Bleach a spot in one of these membranes to see the effect on the curve. [ELO 2]
E5. Switch to Cell fusion (Frye–Edidin): a mouse cell (green surface proteins) fused with a human cell (red). Press Default membrane, then Reset, set the speed to 240× real time (40 min then take 10 s), and read the percentage of red molecules in the left half at 40 min (37 °C). Then set the temperature to 4 °C, press Reset and read it again at 40 min. What would 50 % mean? How does this explain the 1970 experiment? [ELO 2]






Solutions





E1. For the lipid the curve rises to about 100 % within a few seconds: mobile fraction about 100 %, \(t_{1/2}\) about 0.5 s, \(D\) about 1 µm²/s (single experiments give roughly 0.8–1.1). The small protein recovers to the same level but much more slowly: \(t_{1/2}\) about 5 s, \(D\) about 0.1 µm²/s, ten times slower (the large protein: about 0.02 µm²/s, 50 times slower). This fits the lecture: proteins diffuse 10–100 times more slowly than lipids, because they are larger and, in real cells, crowded among other proteins and slowed by the cortical cytoskeleton. (The plateau ends a few per cent below 100 % in a long run: the bleach destroyed about 3 % of all the fluorescent molecules in the patch, so a little fluorescence is lost for good. Real FRAP has the same effect.)
E2. After 1 s a lipid is typically about 2 µm from its start (\(\sqrt{4Dt} = \sqrt{4 \times 1 \times 1} = 2\) µm), but single molecules vary a lot: about half end up closer than 1.6 µm, and some go 3 µm or more. The track is a tangle, not a line: each step goes in a random direction. That is why distance grows only with the square root of time: in 4 s the typical distance is about 4 µm, not 8 µm.
E3. Expected: the curve rises with the same speed as before but levels off at about 70 %, because the 30 % anchored molecules that were bleached stay in the spot and never recover. A run gives a plateau of about 67–75 % (mobile fraction about 70 %) and \(t_{1/2}\) about 5 s, the same as without anchored molecules: the mobile molecules diffuse just as before. So the height of the plateau tells you the mobile fraction, and the speed of recovery tells you \(D\). To test whether the cytoskeleton holds the immobile fraction, repeat FRAP after disrupting actin (for example with latrunculin): the plateau should rise.
E4. (a) Default membrane (18-carbon tails with one double bond) at 37 °C: without cholesterol the fluidity is about 1.6× the default, with 50 % cholesterol about 0.6×. Here cholesterol makes the membrane less fluid: its rigid rings stiffen the tails. (b) With saturated tails the membrane without cholesterol is a gel: fluidity about 0.03× (\(D\) for a lipid about 0.03 µm²/s, recovery very slow). With 30 % or 50 % cholesterol it is about 0.3×, ten times more fluid. (c) Cholesterol is a fluidity buffer: it makes a fluid membrane stiffer and less leaky, but stops a membrane that would freeze from becoming a gel, by getting in the way of the packed tails. (d) At 10 °C the default membrane drops to about 0.15× (lipid \(D\) about 0.15 µm²/s): cold slows diffusion and pushes the tails towards the gel state. This is why cells in the cold make more unsaturated (kinked) tails. Shorter tails (14 carbons) also raise the fluidity (about 1.3×), longer ones (22) lower it (about 0.4×).
E5. At 37 °C, about 56 % of the molecules in the left half are red after 40 min (mixing about 90 % complete); at 4 °C, about 85 % (only about 30 % mixed). 50 % red in each half would mean complete mixing. The proteins mix by diffusion in the fluid membrane, which needs no energy and no new proteins but is much slower in the cold, when the membrane is less fluid. Frye and Edidin saw exactly this: mixing in about 40 min at 37 °C, almost none in the cold, and no effect of drugs that block protein synthesis or ATP production. (The fused cell is drawn as a flat disc; its real surface is a sphere, so the times are illustrative.)

title: Moving molecules across membranes: transporters and pumps
section: About this lecture

title: Moving molecules across membranes: transporters and pumps
section: The question: how does sugar get from your gut into your blood?
text:
The question: how does sugar get from your gut into your blood?







Small intestine (rat), stained section. The finger-like villi are covered by one layer of epithelial cells.


After a meal, the gut takes up hundreds of grams of glucose a day.
Glucose is polar: it barely crosses a lipid bilayer.
It must cross two membranes: into the epithelial cell from the gut, and out again on the blood side.
Between meals the cell still takes up glucose when the gut has less glucose than the blood: uphill.
And every one of your cells keeps Na⁺ low and K⁺ high inside, the opposite of the blood. A resting cell spends about a quarter of its ATP on this.

How, and why?


Look at the picture. This is a section through the small intestine of a rat, stained with dyes. The finger-like folds are villi, and each villus is covered by a single layer of epithelial cells. Everything you absorb from food must pass through these cells: in through the membrane facing the gut, and out through the membrane facing the blood. Glucose is a polar molecule with many hydroxyl groups, so it hardly enters a lipid bilayer at all. Still, your gut absorbs it very efficiently, even towards the end of digestion when there is less glucose in the gut than in the blood. That means the cell can move glucose uphill, against its gradient. At the same time, every cell in your body keeps sodium low and potassium high inside, the reverse of the blood, and spends a large part of its ATP to do so. By the end of the lecture you will see that these two puzzles have the same answer: the sodium gradient made by one pump drives the uptake of glucose.

title: Moving molecules across membranes: transporters and pumps
section: What crosses a pure lipid bilayer?
text:
What crosses a pure lipid bilayer?


The middle of the bilayer is hydrophobic. A molecule must leave water and dissolve in oil to cross.
Small and hydrophobic (O₂, CO₂, steroid hormones, many drugs): fast. Small polar (water, urea): slower. Glucose: very slow. Ions: practically never, because they carry a charge and a shell of water.
So a cell needs membrane transport proteins: they make up about 15–30 % of the membrane proteins in a cell.


Imagine an artificial membrane made only of lipid, with no proteins, and ask what gets through. The answer depends on two things: size and how well the molecule dissolves in oil. Small hydrophobic molecules such as oxygen, carbon dioxide and nitrogen cross very fast, and so do steroid hormones and many drugs. This is why most drugs taken as tablets are designed to be fairly small and fairly lipophilic. Small uncharged polar molecules such as water, urea and glycerol also cross, more slowly. Larger polar molecules such as glucose cross very slowly, far too slowly for a cell’s needs. Ions almost never cross: a sodium ion carries a charge and holds a shell of water molecules, and pulling it into the oily core costs a great deal of energy. A pure bilayer lets water through about a billion times faster than sodium or potassium. So the bilayer is a barrier, and the cell controls traffic with proteins. In a typical cell, roughly 15 to 30 percent of membrane proteins are transport proteins, which shows how important this job is.

title: Moving molecules across membranes: transporters and pumps
section: Inside is not like outside
text:
Inside is not like outside









Ion
Inside a mammalian cell (cytosol)
Outside (blood, tissue fluid)
Ratio




Na⁺
about 12 mM
about 145 mM
~10× higher outside


K⁺
about 140 mM
about 5 mM
~30× higher inside


Ca²⁺
about 0.0001 mM (100 nM)
about 2 mM
~10 000× higher outside


Cl⁻
about 5–15 mM
about 110 mM
~10× higher outside


H⁺
pH about 7.2
pH 7.4





Inside, the extra positive charge of K⁺ is balanced by negatively charged proteins, nucleic acids and metabolites that cannot leave.
These differences are not equilibrium. Ions leak all the time, and pumps work all the time to restore them. Stop the pumps and the gradients run down.
Gradients store energy, like water behind a dam. Cells use them to drive transport and to send electrical signals (the ion-channels lecture).


This table is worth learning, because almost everything in the next two lectures follows from it. Typical values for a mammalian cell: sodium is about 12 millimolar inside and 145 outside. Potassium is the reverse: about 140 inside and 5 outside. Free calcium in the cytosol is extremely low, about 100 nanomolar, ten thousand times lower than outside. Chloride is low inside. The cytosol is slightly more acidic than blood. Inside the cell, the positive charge of potassium is balanced mostly by large negatively charged molecules, proteins, nucleic acids and phosphorylated metabolites, which cannot leave. The key word is steady state, not equilibrium. Ions leak slowly across the membrane all the time, down their gradients, and pumps keep putting them back. If you poison the pumps, for example by blocking ATP production, the gradients slowly disappear and the cell swells and dies. Why keep these gradients? Because a gradient is stored energy. Today we see how cells spend the sodium gradient to move other molecules. In the ion-channels lecture you will see how the same gradients create the membrane potential and nerve signals.

title: Moving molecules across membranes: transporters and pumps
section: Recap: ΔG decides the direction
text:
Recap: ΔG decides the direction

For an uncharged solute moving from outside to inside, at 37 °C:
\Delta G = RT \ln\frac{c_\text{in}}{c_\text{out}} \qquad (RT \approx 2.6\ \text{kJ/mol})

Passive transport: down the gradient, \Delta G < 0. A 10-fold gradient is worth about 5.9 kJ/mol.
Active transport: up the gradient, \Delta G > 0, so it must be coupled to a reaction with a larger negative ΔG. ATP hydrolysis in a cell gives about −50 kJ/mol.
For an ion, the membrane voltage adds an electrical term: the electrochemical gradient (the ion-channels lecture).


This is a recap from chemistry, applied to a membrane. Moving one mole of an uncharged solute from outside to inside changes free energy by RT times the natural log of the inside concentration over the outside concentration. If the inside is lower, the log is negative, ΔG is negative, and the movement can happen by itself, provided there is a path. That is passive transport, also called facilitated diffusion when a protein provides the path. If the inside is higher, ΔG is positive: the cell must pay. At body temperature RT is about 2.6 kilojoules per mole, so each tenfold difference in concentration is worth about 5.9 kilojoules per mole. Hydrolysis of ATP under cell conditions releases about 50 kilojoules per mole, enough to pump against large gradients. A pump couples the two reactions in one protein, so the total ΔG is negative. For ions there is one more term: the voltage across the membrane pushes or pulls charges. The sum is the electrochemical gradient, and we leave the electrical part to the ion-channels lecture, where it gives the Nernst equation.

title: Moving molecules across membranes: transporters and pumps
section: Two kinds of transport protein: transporters and channels
text:
Two kinds of transport protein: transporters and channels

A channel is a gated hole: fast, but only downhill. A transporter (also called a carrier) binds its solute and changes shape: slower, but it can be coupled to energy and move things uphill.

Membrane transport proteins come in two kinds. A channel forms a water-filled pore. When it is open, ions flow through it in single file, down their electrochemical gradient, at rates up to a hundred million ions per second. A channel cannot push anything uphill, because the pore is open to both sides at the same time. Channels open and close in response to signals, called gating, and they are the topic of the next lecture. A transporter works differently. It binds its solute at a specific site, like an enzyme binds its substrate, and then changes shape so that the site faces the other side. Each cycle moves one or a few molecules, so transporters are much slower, about a hundred to ten thousand molecules per second. But because each cycle is a defined series of shape changes, it can be linked to another event, such as ATP hydrolysis or the movement of a sodium ion. That is how transporters do active transport. Remember the rule: channels are fast and passive; transporters are slow, specific, saturable, and can be active.

title: Moving molecules across membranes: transporters and pumps
section: How a transporter works: alternating access
text:
How a transporter works: alternating access








The binding site faces out, then in, never both at once.
One cycle can run in either direction. With no energy input, net flow goes down the gradient (passive).
Example: GLUT1, the glucose uniporter of red blood cells and the blood–brain barrier.







Human GLUT1 (PDB 4PYP), side view. Its 12 membrane helices form two halves (blue, red) around the sugar site.


How does a transporter move a molecule without ever making a hole in the membrane? The answer is alternating access. In step one the transporter is open to the outside, and its binding site is empty. A glucose molecule binds. The protein then closes behind it, so for a moment the glucose is trapped inside the protein, closed to both sides. Then the protein opens to the inside and the glucose leaves into the cytosol. Finally the empty transporter flips back. Nothing in this cycle has a preferred direction, so if glucose is higher inside, the same cycle runs the other way. Net flow is always down the gradient. This is passive transport, but much faster and more specific than diffusion through lipid. The structure on the right is the real protein, GLUT1, solved by X-ray crystallography in 2014. It has twelve helices crossing the membrane, arranged as two bundles, and the sugar binds between them. The two halves rock against each other like a seesaw to open one side and close the other. GLUT1 supplies glucose to red blood cells and to the brain.

title: Moving molecules across membranes: transporters and pumps
section: How do we know? Uptake assays show that transporters saturate
text:
How do we know? Uptake assays show that transporters saturate


Diffusion through lipid rises linearly with concentration. Transport by a protein reaches a maximum (Vmax): all binding sites are busy. Km = concentration at half-maximal rate. Try it: the uptake assay.
Transporters are specific: GLUT1 takes D-glucose, not its mirror image L-glucose. They can be competed by similar molecules and blocked by inhibitors.


How do we know that a protein is involved at all? Here is the classic experiment, and you can do it in a teaching lab. Cells, for example red blood cells, are given glucose labelled with a radioactive atom such as tritium, or with a fluorescent tag. After a short time, say thirty seconds, uptake is stopped by washing with ice-cold buffer, and the label inside the cells is measured. Repeat at many concentrations and plot the initial rate against concentration. If glucose simply diffused through lipid, the rate would rise in a straight line. Instead the curve bends and reaches a plateau. You know this shape from enzyme kinetics: it is the Michaelis–Menten curve. The plateau, Vmax, is reached when all transporter molecules are busy. Km is the concentration that gives half of Vmax, a measure of affinity. Two more results point to a protein. The transporter is stereospecific: it moves D-glucose, the natural form, but hardly L-glucose, which has the same size and polarity. And similar sugars compete for uptake, just as competitive inhibitors do for an enzyme.

title: Moving molecules across membranes: transporters and pumps
section: Three ways to couple: uniport, symport, antiport
text:
Three ways to couple: uniport, symport, antiport


Uniport: one solute, passive (GLUT).
Symport (co-transport): two solutes cross in the same direction. Example: SGLT1 carries 2 Na⁺ + 1 glucose into gut cells.
Antiport (exchange): two solutes cross in opposite directions. Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger: 3 Na⁺ in, 1 Ca²⁺ out. Na⁺/H⁺ exchanger: 1 Na⁺ in, 1 H⁺ out (controls cytosolic pH).


Transporters are classified by how many solutes they move and in which direction. A uniporter moves one kind of molecule, like GLUT. It can only move it downhill. A symporter binds two different solutes and moves them together, in the same direction. The transporter only completes its cycle when both are bound, so the two movements are tightly coupled. In SGLT1, two sodium ions and one glucose molecule enter together. An antiporter, or exchanger, moves two solutes in opposite directions: it takes one in and carries the other out in the same cycle. The sodium–calcium exchanger lets three sodium ions in and pushes one calcium ion out; it is important in heart muscle. The sodium–proton exchanger lets one sodium in and pushes one proton out, which protects the cytosol from becoming acidic. The important point: in symport and antiport, one solute can go downhill and pay for the other going uphill. Notice that in all three examples, sodium enters the cell. That is not a coincidence, as the next slide shows.

title: Moving molecules across membranes: transporters and pumps
section: Secondary active transport: the Na⁺ gradient is a battery
text:
Secondary active transport: the Na⁺ gradient is a battery


Primary active transport uses ATP directly (a pump). Secondary active transport uses a gradient that a pump made.
Na⁺ flowing in releases energy: about −13 kJ/mol (concentration plus voltage). With 2 Na⁺ per glucose, SGLT1 can in theory concentrate glucose more than 10 000-fold.
Animal cells use Na⁺; bacteria, plants and fungi mostly use an H⁺ gradient.


Now we can solve the opening puzzle. The sodium–potassium pump, on the left, spends ATP to push sodium out. That keeps sodium about ten times higher outside than inside. In addition, the inside of the cell is electrically negative, which pulls positive sodium ions inwards. So sodium entering the cell is strongly downhill: about minus thirteen kilojoules per mole, about half from the concentration difference and half from the voltage. A symporter or antiporter can use this downhill flow to drive a second solute uphill. This is secondary active transport: no ATP is used by the transporter itself, but the energy came from ATP spent earlier by the pump. Think of the pump as charging a battery and the other transporters as devices running on it. Because SGLT1 couples two sodium ions to each glucose, it has twice that energy available and can, in theory, concentrate glucose more than ten thousand times. If you poison the pump, the battery runs down and glucose uptake stops too. Bacteria and plants do the same with a proton gradient instead of sodium.

title: Moving molecules across membranes: transporters and pumps
section: Primary active transport: the Na⁺/K⁺ pump
text:
Primary active transport: the Na⁺/K⁺ pump


A P-type ATPase: it phosphorylates itself on an aspartate, and this switches its shape from inward-open to outward-open.
3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in per ATP. It uses about a quarter of a resting cell’s ATP, and much more in nerve cells.
Found in every animal cell. Discovered by Jens Skou in crab nerves in 1957 (Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1997).


Here is the battery charger. The sodium–potassium pump, also called the sodium–potassium ATPase, is a P-type pump: P for phosphorylation. Follow the cycle. In state one, the binding sites face the cytosol, where sodium is relatively low, but the sites have a high affinity for sodium, so three sodium ions bind. That triggers the pump to transfer the phosphate of ATP to one of its own aspartate residues. The phosphorylated pump changes shape: the sites now face the outside, and their affinity for sodium drops, so the three sodium ions are released, even though sodium outside is high. In this shape the sites bind two potassium ions from the outside. Potassium binding triggers removal of the phosphate, the pump flips back, and potassium is released into the cytosol. Each cycle uses one ATP. Because three positive charges go out and only two come in, the pump also makes a small electrical current: it is electrogenic. This single protein uses roughly a quarter of the ATP of a resting cell, and in the brain a much larger share. Jens Skou found it in crab nerves in 1957.

title: Moving molecules across membranes: transporters and pumps
section: How do we know? Rebuild the pump, and block it
text:
How do we know? Rebuild the pump, and block it


Reconstitution: purify the pump, put it into liposomes (artificial lipid vesicles), add ATP: Na⁺ and K⁺ move in a 3 : 2 ratio. No other protein is needed.
Inhibitors: ouabain (an arrow poison) and digoxin block the pump only from the outside. Resealed red-cell membranes (“ghosts”) showed that ATP and Na⁺ must be inside, K⁺ outside.


Two classic approaches prove that one protein does all of this. The first is reconstitution. You dissolve membranes with a mild detergent, purify the pump protein, and mix it with lipids. When the detergent is removed, the lipids form closed vesicles, liposomes, with pumps in their membranes. The pumps insert in both orientations, but only those whose ATP-binding part faces the outside can use ATP added to the outside. Those pumps move sodium into the liposome and potassium out, three to two. Since the liposome contains nothing but lipid and pump, the pump alone is sufficient. The second approach uses inhibitors. Ouabain, a plant toxin once used on arrow tips, binds the pump and stops it. Researchers made red blood cell ghosts: they let the cells swell until the haemoglobin leaked out, then resealed the empty membranes with chosen solutions inside. Ouabain worked only when it was outside; the pump needed ATP and sodium inside and potassium outside. That told us the pump’s orientation in the membrane. Digoxin, a heart drug from the foxglove plant, binds the same site.

title: Moving molecules across membranes: transporters and pumps
section: Other pumps: Ca²⁺ pumps, V-type and F-type
text:
Other pumps: Ca²⁺ pumps, V-type and F-type


Ca²⁺ pumps (P-type) keep cytosolic Ca²⁺ at about 100 nM: out of the cell (PMCA) and into the ER (SERCA). A brief rise in Ca²⁺ is a signal (the signalling lectures).
V-type H⁺ pump acidifies lysosomes (pH 4.5–5), endosomes and secretory vesicles (the lysosome lecture).
F-type ATP synthase looks like a V-type pump but runs backwards: H⁺ flowing down its gradient makes ATP (the mitochondria lecture).


The sodium–potassium pump is not alone. Calcium pumps are also P-type pumps, with the same phosphorylation cycle. One kind in the plasma membrane pushes calcium out of the cell. Another, SERCA, pumps calcium into the endoplasmic reticulum, so the ER lumen holds thousands of times more calcium than the cytosol. Because cytosolic calcium is kept so low, opening a calcium channel for a moment makes a large relative rise, which the cell uses as a signal for muscle contraction, secretion and much more. A second family, the V-type pumps, are large rotating machines that pump protons into lysosomes, endosomes and secretory vesicles. That makes the lysosome acidic, around pH 4.5 to 5, which its digestive enzymes need. A third family, the F-type ATPases, is built like the V-type but works in reverse. In the inner membrane of mitochondria, protons flow back into the matrix through the ATP synthase, and this flow turns a rotor that makes ATP from ADP and phosphate. Any pump can in principle run backwards if the gradient is steep enough. You meet both again in the organelle lectures.

title: Moving molecules across membranes: transporters and pumps
section: ABC transporters: ATP-powered exporters
text:
ABC transporters: ATP-powered exporters


Two membrane halves plus two ATP-binding cassettes (hence “ABC”). ATP binding brings the cassettes together and flips the transporter to face outward; hydrolysis resets it.
The largest transporter family: humans have about 48 ABC genes. In our cells most are exporters: lipids, bile salts, toxins and drugs.
P-glycoprotein (ABCB1) pumps many different hydrophobic drugs out of cells. The CFTR chloride channel is an unusual member (the ion-channels lecture).


The third big family of ATP-driven pumps is the ABC transporters, named after their ATP-binding cassettes. Each ABC transporter has two halves that cross the membrane, and two cassettes in the cytosol that bind ATP. Follow the cartoon. In the inward-facing state the cassettes are apart and a cavity opens towards the cytosol and the inner half of the membrane. A hydrophobic molecule, often coming from inside the membrane itself, enters the cavity. Two ATP molecules then bind between the cassettes and glue them together. This pulls the membrane halves into an outward-facing shape, and the substrate is released outside. Hydrolysis of ATP lets the cassettes separate, and the transporter resets. Bacteria use ABC transporters to import nutrients, but in human cells nearly all of them export. They move lipids between membrane leaflets, bile salts out of liver cells, and toxins and drugs out of cells. One of them, P-glycoprotein, is famous for having a large, greasy binding cavity that accepts many unrelated drugs. We come back to it at the end. CFTR, the protein defective in cystic fibrosis, belongs to this family but works as a channel.

title: Moving molecules across membranes: transporters and pumps
section: Transcellular transport: from gut to blood
text:
Transcellular transport: from gut to blood




Apical (gut side): SGLT1 brings glucose in, uphill. Basolateral (blood side): GLUT2 lets it out, downhill; the Na⁺/K⁺ pump removes the Na⁺.
Tight junctions seal the gaps between cells and keep apical and basolateral proteins apart.



Microvilli on a human gut epithelial cell (TEM). Scale bar 100 nm. They enlarge the apical surface many times.


Now we put the pieces together in an epithelium. An epithelial cell is polarised: its apical membrane faces the gut and its basolateral membrane faces the blood, and the two membranes carry different proteins. The apical side is folded into thousands of microvilli, shown in the electron micrograph, which increase the surface area. In the apical membrane, SGLT1 couples glucose entry to sodium entry, so glucose builds up inside the cell even when the gut contains little. In the basolateral membrane, GLUT2, a uniporter, lets glucose leave down its gradient into the blood. The sodium that came in with the glucose is pumped out on the basolateral side by the sodium–potassium pump, which keeps the battery charged. Tight junctions seal the spaces between neighbouring cells, so glucose cannot leak back, and they act as a fence that keeps apical and basolateral proteins in their own membrane. The same design works in the proximal tubule of the kidney, which takes back glucose, amino acids and salt from the urine. Oral rehydration solution, sugar and salt in water, uses SGLT1 to save the lives of children with severe diarrhoea.

title: Moving molecules across membranes: transporters and pumps
section: Water: aquaporins
text:
Water: aquaporins



Aquaporin seen from outside the cell: four subunits, each with its own water pore (space-filling model, PDB 1FQY).


Water crosses lipid slowly. Kidney, red cells and glands need it fast.
Aquaporins are water channels: about a billion water molecules per second per pore, in single file.
They exclude ions, even H⁺, so they do not destroy gradients.
Water always moves passively, by osmosis: towards the side with more dissolved particles. Cells move water by moving solutes.
AQP2 in the kidney collecting duct is inserted into the membrane when the hormone vasopressin signals; this concentrates the urine. Peter Agre, Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2003.



One last passenger: water. Water does cross a lipid bilayer, but slowly. Cells that move a lot of water, such as kidney tubule cells, red blood cells and gland cells, add channels for it: aquaporins. Peter Agre found the first one in red blood cells. His team put its RNA into frog eggs, which normally take up very little water; in a dilute solution the eggs with aquaporin swelled and burst within minutes. Each aquaporin has four subunits, and each subunit has its own narrow pore, as you see in this view from outside the cell. Water passes in single file at up to a billion molecules per second. A clever feature of the pore stops protons, which could otherwise hop along a chain of water molecules; so aquaporins carry water without letting the proton gradient leak. Note that no pump moves water. Water always follows solutes by osmosis, so cells move water by moving salt first. In the kidney, the hormone vasopressin makes collecting-duct cells insert aquaporin 2 into their apical membrane, which lets water return to the blood and concentrates the urine. You meet this in the course on organs and tissues.

title: Moving molecules across membranes: transporters and pumps
section: Why it matters: SGLT2 inhibitors in diabetes and heart failure
text:
Why it matters: SGLT2 inhibitors in diabetes and heart failure


The kidneys filter about 180 g of glucose a day; SGLT2 in the proximal tubule takes back about 90 %, SGLT1 the rest. Above a blood glucose of about 10 mM the transporters saturate and glucose appears in urine.
Gliflozins (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) block SGLT2: glucose and some Na⁺ leave in the urine, and blood glucose falls in type 2 diabetes.
In large trials they also reduced heart failure and slowed kidney disease, even in people without diabetes. Exactly why is still studied.


Here the symporter from the gut slide becomes a drug target. The kidneys filter your blood plasma, about 180 litres a day, and with it about 180 grams of glucose. The proximal tubule takes nearly all of it back. The first part of the tubule uses SGLT2, a sodium–glucose symporter with one sodium per glucose, which takes about ninety percent; SGLT1 further along takes the rest. Basolateral GLUT2 lets glucose return to the blood, as in the gut. Remember saturation: when blood glucose is above about ten millimolar, the transporters are full and glucose spills into the urine. That is why untreated diabetes gives sweet urine. Gliflozins block SGLT2. The story started with phlorizin, a natural compound from apple tree bark known since the nineteenth century to cause glucose in the urine. A person on a gliflozin loses tens of grams of glucose a day in the urine, and blood glucose falls. Surprisingly, large clinical trials showed that these drugs also protect the heart and kidneys, even in people without diabetes. The mechanism is still debated. You meet trials like these in the course on clinical trials and drug development.

title: Moving molecules across membranes: transporters and pumps
section: Why it matters: pumps as drug targets and drug barriers
text:
Why it matters: pumps as drug targets and drug barriers



Digoxin (from foxglove) blocks the Na⁺/K⁺ pump in heart muscle. Less Na⁺ gradient → the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger removes less Ca²⁺ → more Ca²⁺ → stronger contraction. Used in heart failure and atrial fibrillation; the safe dose range is narrow.
P-glycoprotein (ABCB1) pumps chemotherapy drugs out of cancer cells: multidrug resistance. In the gut, liver, kidney and blood–brain barrier it pumps drugs back out, which limits oral absorption and keeps many drugs out of the brain.
A tablet must cross the gut epithelium: by diffusion through lipid (small, lipophilic drugs) or on a transporter, while escaping P-glycoprotein. More in drug development (Kliniska prövningar och läkemedelsutveckling).



P-glycoprotein (mouse, PDB 3G5U). Lines: outer (blue) and inner (red) face of the membrane.


Foxglove, Digitalis. Its leaves contain digitalis glycosides.


Two more examples of transport and medicine. Foxglove extracts were used for heart failure as early as 1785, by William Withering in England. The active compounds are digitalis glycosides, such as digoxin; digoxin itself is mostly made from a related species, the woolly foxglove. They bind the sodium–potassium pump from outside, as ouabain does. In heart muscle a partly blocked pump lets sodium rise a little inside. The smaller sodium gradient means the sodium–calcium exchanger removes less calcium, more calcium is stored in the sarcoplasmic reticulum, and each beat is stronger. The difference between a helpful and a toxic dose is small, so levels are monitored. The second example is P-glycoprotein, the ABC exporter from earlier. Cancer cells that make a lot of it pump out many unrelated chemotherapy drugs, which is called multidrug resistance. In healthy tissue it sits on the gut side of intestinal cells and in brain capillaries, where it pumps drugs back out. The diarrhoea drug loperamide, an opioid, does not reach the brain because P-glycoprotein removes it. Drug developers test early whether a candidate is a P-glycoprotein substrate.

title: Moving molecules across membranes: transporters and pumps
section: Summary
text:
Summary

A lipid bilayer lets small hydrophobic molecules through but blocks ions and most polar molecules; transport proteins give them a path.
Passive transport goes down the gradient (ΔG < 0); active transport goes up and must be coupled to ATP or to another gradient. Cells keep large, non-equilibrium gradients of Na⁺, K⁺ and Ca²⁺.
Channels are fast pores, always passive. Transporters bind their solute, work by alternating access, saturate like enzymes, and can be uniporters, symporters or antiporters.
Pumps use ATP directly: P-type (Na⁺/K⁺ pump, 3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in; Ca²⁺ pumps), V-type (acidify organelles), ABC (export, including drugs); the F-type ATP synthase runs in reverse. The Na⁺ gradient drives secondary active transport.
Epithelia move solutes across the cell with different transporters on the apical and basolateral sides; drugs such as gliflozins and digoxin act on transporters, and P-glycoprotein pumps drugs away.

Read more (optional): Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell, 7th ed., ch. 11.
Image credits

Five take-home points. First, the bilayer is a barrier to ions and polar molecules; only small hydrophobic molecules, and water slowly, cross on their own. Second, ΔG tells you whether transport can be passive, and cells keep large gradients of sodium, potassium and calcium that are not at equilibrium; they cost energy to maintain and are a store of energy to use. Third, transporters and channels are different machines: channels are fast and only passive, transporters bind their solute, alternate between outward-open and inward-open shapes, saturate like enzymes and can couple two solutes. Fourth, primary active transport uses ATP directly in P-type, V-type and ABC pumps, while secondary active transport spends the sodium gradient made by the sodium–potassium pump. Fifth, an epithelium combines these proteins on two sides of a cell to move glucose from gut to blood, and many drugs act on transporters or are limited by them. Next lecture: ion channels, where the same gradients produce the membrane potential.

title: Quiz: moving molecules across membranes
text:
Short questions to check your understanding of the lecture Moving molecules across membranes: transporters and pumps. Try each on paper first, then open the hint or the answer. The tag after each question shows the learning outcome (ELO) it practises.

Q1. Rank these by how fast they cross a pure lipid bilayer (no proteins), fastest first: glucose, O₂, Na⁺, water. [ELO 2]






Hint





Two things matter: size, and how well the molecule dissolves in the oily middle of the bilayer. A charge is the biggest obstacle.









Answer





O₂ > water > glucose > Na⁺. O₂ is small and hydrophobic and crosses fast. Water is small and uncharged, so it crosses, but more slowly. Glucose is larger and polar and crosses very slowly. Na⁺ is charged and surrounded by water molecules, so it practically does not cross (about 10⁹ times slower than water).
