Q2. Na⁺ is about 12 mM inside a cell and 145 mM outside. K⁺ is about 140 mM inside and 5 mM outside. If you block all ATP production in a cell, what happens to these concentrations over time, and why? [ELO 2]






Hint





Are the gradients at equilibrium, or are they kept up by work?









Answer





The gradients run down: Na⁺ slowly rises inside and K⁺ falls. The gradients are a steady state, not an equilibrium: ions leak through the membrane all the time, and the Na⁺/K⁺ pump uses ATP to put them back. Without ATP the pump stops, but the leak continues.




Q3. Using \(\Delta G = RT\ln(c_\text{in}/c_\text{out})\) with \(RT \approx 2.6\) kJ/mol, estimate ΔG for moving glucose into a cell when glucose is 5 mM outside and 0.5 mM inside. Is this passive or active transport? [ELO 2]






Hint





\(\ln(0.1) \approx -2.3\).









Answer





\(\Delta G \approx 2.6 \times \ln(0.5/5) = 2.6 \times (-2.3) \approx -6\) kJ/mol. ΔG is negative, so glucose moves downhill: passive transport, for example by a GLUT uniporter. No energy input is needed.




Q4. You measure the initial rate of uptake of a radiolabelled amino acid into cells at many concentrations. The rate rises and then levels off at high concentration. What does this tell you about how the amino acid enters, and what do Vmax and Km mean here? [ELO 2]






Hint





Compare with Michaelis–Menten kinetics of an enzyme. What would simple diffusion through lipid look like?









Answer





Saturation means a transporter with a limited number of binding sites carries the amino acid; diffusion through lipid would rise linearly without a maximum. Vmax is the rate when all transporters are busy (it depends on how many transporters there are). Km is the concentration that gives half of Vmax; a low Km means high affinity.




Q5. Classify each as uniport, symport or antiport, and as passive, primary active or secondary active: (a) GLUT1; (b) SGLT1; (c) the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger; (d) the Na⁺/K⁺ pump. [ELO 2]






Hint





Does the protein use ATP itself? Does it move one solute or two, and in which directions?









Answer






GLUT1: uniport, passive. (b) SGLT1: symport (2 Na⁺ + 1 glucose, both inwards), secondary active. (c) Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger: antiport (Na⁺ in, Ca²⁺ out), secondary active. (d) Na⁺/K⁺ pump: antiport (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in), primary active: it hydrolyses ATP itself (P-type pump).





Q6. Why is the Na⁺/K⁺ pump called a P-type pump, and how many ions does it move per ATP? [ELO 2]






Hint





Where does the phosphate of ATP go during the cycle?









Answer





During its cycle the pump phosphorylates itself on an aspartate; this switches it from the inward-open to the outward-open shape. P stands for phosphorylation. Per ATP it moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in. One net positive charge leaves per cycle, so the pump is electrogenic.




Q7. In a gut epithelial cell, which transporter sits in the apical membrane and which in the basolateral membrane to absorb glucose? Why must they be in different membranes? [ELO 2]






Hint





One brings glucose into the cell uphill; the other lets it out downhill. What would happen if both were on the same side?









Answer





Apical: SGLT1 (Na⁺–glucose symporter), which takes glucose into the cell even against its gradient. Basolateral: GLUT2 (uniporter), which lets glucose leave down its gradient into the blood, plus the Na⁺/K⁺ pump to remove the Na⁺. If both transporters were on the same side, glucose would just go in and out on that side, and there would be no net movement across the cell. Tight junctions keep the two sets of proteins apart and seal the gaps between cells.




Q8. Gliflozins block SGLT2. What happens to glucose in the urine of a patient taking one, and why does this lower blood glucose? [ELO 2] [ELO 9]






Hint





Where in the body is SGLT2, and what does it normally do with filtered glucose?









Answer





SGLT2 in the proximal tubule of the kidney normally takes back about 90 % of the glucose filtered from the blood. When it is blocked, much of that glucose (tens of grams a day) stays in the tubule and leaves in the urine. The body loses glucose, so blood glucose falls. Some Na⁺ is lost too, because SGLT2 is a Na⁺–glucose symporter.

title: Study questions: seeing cells (microscopy)
text: Study questions in the style of the written exam. Write your answer first (a few sentences, or a labelled sketch where it helps), then compare with the model answer. Each question is tagged with its learning outcome (ELO). Questions tagged [VG] are of the kind used for the higher grade: predict, compare, explain an unexpected result or design an experiment.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it

title: Study questions: seeing cells (microscopy)
section: G-level questions
text:
G-level questions
1. Explain the difference between magnification and resolution. Why can a light microscope not separate two objects that are 50 nm apart, however much it magnifies? [ELO 1]






Model answer





Magnification is how much bigger the image is than the object. Resolution is the smallest distance at which two points can still be seen as two. Light is a wave, so a lens turns each point of the sample into a small blur spot. When two points are closer than about \(0.61\,\lambda/\mathrm{NA}\), their blur spots merge into one. With visible light (about 500 nm) and the best objectives (NA about 1.4) this limit is about 200 nm. Two objects 50 nm apart give one blob, and magnifying the blob more adds no detail.




2. Describe how a phase-contrast microscope and a DIC microscope make living, unstained cells visible. Why is staining with dyes usually not an option for living cells? [ELO 1]






Model answer





Unstained cells absorb almost no light, but dense structures (nucleus, membranes) have a higher refractive index and slow light down (phase shift). Phase contrast converts these phase shifts into differences in brightness. DIC uses polarised light to turn gradients in optical path into light and shadow, so edges look three-dimensional. Most dyes for bright-field microscopy need the cells to be fixed and often sectioned, and many dyes are toxic, so stained cells are dead.




3. Draw and label the light path in an epifluorescence microscope with a filter cube for a green fluorophore. State what each filter and the dichroic mirror does. [ELO 1]






Model answer





Lamp → excitation filter (passes only blue light that excites the fluorophore) → dichroic mirror (reflects blue light down through the objective onto the sample) → fluorophore absorbs blue and emits green → green light goes back up through the objective → passes through the dichroic mirror (it transmits longer wavelengths) → emission filter (passes green, blocks stray blue) → camera or eye. The design works because of the Stokes shift: emitted light has a longer wavelength than the excitation light.




4. Describe the steps of indirect immunofluorescence to show where tubulin is in cultured cells. Why do we use a secondary antibody? [ELO 1] [ELO 6]






Model answer






Fix the cells (e.g. formaldehyde) so proteins are cross-linked and stay in place. 2. Permeabilise the membranes with a mild detergent so antibodies can enter. 3. Block free binding sites (e.g. with serum proteins) to reduce background. 4. Add the primary antibody against tubulin (e.g. made in mouse), wash. 5. Add a fluorescent secondary antibody against mouse antibodies, wash. 6. Often add a DNA dye (DAPI), mount and image. The secondary antibody amplifies the signal (several secondaries bind each primary), and one labelled secondary can be used with many different primaries from the same species.





5. What is GFP, why was it so useful for cell biology, and how is a GFP fusion protein made? [ELO 1] [ELO 6]






Model answer





GFP is the green fluorescent protein from the jellyfish Aequorea victoria. Its chain of 238 amino acids folds into a barrel and forms its fluorescent group by itself (it needs only oxygen), so the gene works in any cell. To make a fusion protein you join the coding sequence of the protein of interest to the GFP coding sequence in the same reading frame, without a stop codon between them, and introduce the DNA into cells. The cell makes one chain, protein–GFP, so you can see where the protein is in a living cell and follow it over time. Mutants of GFP and proteins from corals give other colours, so several proteins can be followed at once.




6. Explain how a confocal microscope gives sharper images of thick samples than a wide-field fluorescence microscope. What is the cost? [ELO 1]






Model answer





In wide-field fluorescence the whole depth of the sample is lit, so out-of-focus light adds haze. A confocal microscope focuses a laser spot in the sample and places a pinhole in front of the detector at the point where light from the focal plane is focused. Light from other depths is out of focus at the pinhole and mostly blocked. The spot is scanned to build the image. This gives a thin optical section (about 0.5–1 µm), and a stack of sections gives a 3D image. Costs: it is slower (point by point), and the sample receives more light, so there is more photobleaching and phototoxicity.




7. Name two problems you meet when you film living fluorescent cells for many hours, and one way to reduce each. [ELO 1]






Model answer





Photobleaching: fluorophores are destroyed by repeated excitation, so the signal fades. Phototoxicity: excited fluorophores make reactive oxygen species that damage the cell, so it may behave abnormally or die. Both are reduced by using less light (lower intensity, shorter exposures, fewer time points, a more sensitive camera) and gentler methods such as spinning-disk confocal or light-sheet microscopy, which light less of the sample. The cells must also be kept at 37 °C with the right CO₂ and medium.




8. Compare TEM and SEM: how is the image made, what does each show, and why can neither be used on living cells? [ELO 1]






Model answer





TEM: electrons pass through an ultrathin section (about 50–100 nm) stained with heavy metals; areas that scatter electrons look dark. It shows internal structure (membranes, organelles, ribosomes) at about 1–2 nm. SEM: a fine beam scans a metal-coated sample, and electrons knocked out of the surface are detected. It shows the 3D surface at a few nm. Both work in a vacuum, so samples are fixed and dried (and for TEM embedded and cut), which kills the cells.




9. What is single-particle cryo-EM? Explain why averaging many images is needed and what the result is. [ELO 1]






Model answer





A purified protein or complex is frozen so quickly that water forms glass-like ice, keeping the molecules in their native, hydrated shape without stain. Only a low electron dose can be used, so each image of a single molecule is very noisy. A computer finds tens of thousands to millions of particle images, sorts them by viewing angle and averages them, so noise cancels and the signal remains. The 2D views are combined into a 3D density map, often at better than 0.3 nm, into which an atomic model is built.

title: Study questions: seeing cells (microscopy)
section: VG-style questions
text:
VG-style questions
10. [VG] A research group makes a GFP fusion of a newly discovered protein, P. In living cells, P–GFP is spread evenly through the cytosol. But immunofluorescence with an antibody against P in fixed cells shows P on mitochondria. Give two possible explanations, and propose an experiment to decide between them. [ELO 1]






Model answer





Possible explanations:

The GFP tag disturbs targeting. If P has a mitochondrial targeting signal at its N-terminus and GFP was fused there, the signal may be hidden; or the fusion is overexpressed so much that the import machinery is saturated and the excess stays in the cytosol.
The antibody is not specific. It may bind another, mitochondrial protein, so the immunofluorescence result is wrong.
(Also acceptable) Fixation artefact: soluble proteins can be extracted or moved during fixation and permeabilisation.

Experiments: put GFP at the other end of P and express it at low level (e.g. from the gene’s own promoter, or by tagging the endogenous gene with CRISPR); check if it then goes to mitochondria (co-stain with a mitochondrial marker). Test the antibody on cells lacking P (knockout or knockdown): if mitochondria are still stained, the antibody is not specific. Biochemistry can add independent evidence: fractionate cells and test which fraction contains P on a western blot (next lecture).




11. [VG] You want to know (a) how often vesicles carrying a GFP-tagged cargo move along microtubules in living cells, and (b) whether the cargo sits inside the vesicle or on its outer membrane. Design an imaging approach for each part, and explain why one method cannot answer both. [ELO 1] [ELO 6]






Model answer






Live-cell fluorescence imaging of the GFP-cargo, ideally with microtubules labelled in a second colour (e.g. a red fluorescent tubulin fusion), using a fast, gentle method (spinning-disk confocal or light-sheet) and short exposures to limit bleaching and phototoxicity. Track vesicles over time and count runs along microtubules. Control: a drug that depolymerises microtubules should stop the directed runs.
A vesicle is about 50–100 nm across, below the 200 nm light limit, so inside versus outside cannot be decided with ordinary light microscopy. Use immuno-electron microscopy: fix cells, label the cargo (anti-GFP antibody with gold particles) on thin sections, and see whether the gold is in the lumen or on the cytosolic face of the vesicle membrane. Cryo-electron tomography or super-resolution would also help.

One method cannot do both because live imaging needs light microscopy (low resolution, living cells), while the nanometre question needs EM (high resolution, but dead or frozen cells). Combining them on the same cells is called correlative light and electron microscopy (CLEM).




12. [VG] Explain why the SARS-CoV-2 spike in the mRNA COVID-19 vaccines carries two extra prolines (the “2P” spike), and why cryo-EM was a good method to check this design quickly. [ELO 1]






Model answer





The spike is a fusion protein: it starts in a compact prefusion shape and, when it fuses the viral and cell membranes, S1 is lost and S2 refolds into a long postfusion rod. Many protective (neutralising) antibodies recognise the prefusion shape, but a spike made on its own can flip to the postfusion form. Two prolines, which are stiff, placed at a hinge in S2 block this refolding and keep the prefusion shape, so the immune system sees the right target. The idea came from structures of related coronavirus spikes (MERS, SARS). Cryo-EM was ideal because the spike is a large, flexible, glycosylated membrane-protein trimer that is hard to crystallise; cryo-EM needs only a small amount of purified protein, no crystals, and keeps it in a near-native state. In early 2020 a cryo-EM structure confirmed within weeks that the SARS-CoV-2 2P spike holds the prefusion shape.

title: Study questions: seeing cells (microscopy)
section: Explore
text:
Explore
Two glowing points (for example two fluorescent molecules) seen through a microscope. The lens turns each point into a blur spot with faint rings (an Airy pattern); the camera sees the sum of the two spots. The graph below the image shows the brightness along the line through both points: the dashed curves are the two single spots, the solid curve is what the camera records. Change the distance \(d\) between the points (slider, or drag on the image), the wavelength \(\lambda\) and the numerical aperture NA, or switch to electrons. The readout gives the Rayleigh limit \(0.61\,\lambda/\mathrm{NA}\) and the depth of the dip between the two peaks.



E1. Start with green light (520 nm) and the oil objective (NA 1.4), \(d = 300\) nm. Move the points slowly together. At what distance does the readout say you reach the Rayleigh limit? Check it with the formula. How deep is the dip there, and at about what distance does the dip disappear completely? [ELO 1]
E2. Set \(d = 250\) nm. Try the three objectives: dry 10× (NA 0.25), dry 40× (NA 0.65) and oil 100× (NA 1.4). Which of them separate the two points? What is the limit for each? [ELO 1]
E3. [VG] Predict first, then check. Keep \(d = 250\) nm and NA 1.4. Will the two points be resolved in red light (650 nm)? In blue light (450 nm)? Then explain why a light microscope cannot be improved much further by choosing a shorter wavelength or a better lens. [ELO 1]
E4. [VG] Switch to Electrons (TEM). The wavelength is about 100 000 times shorter than green light. What is the limit with a 10 mrad aperture, and why is it much larger than the wavelength? Why do electron micrographs of cells still show only about 1–2 nm detail? [ELO 1]






Solutions





E1. The limit is \(0.61 \times 520 / 1.4 \approx 227\) nm. At that distance the first dark ring of one spot falls on the centre of the other, and the solid curve has a dip of about 26 % between the two peaks: just enough to see two spots. Closer, the dip becomes shallower and disappears at about 175 nm (about \(0.47\,\lambda/\mathrm{NA}\), the Sparrow limit); below that the camera records one blob, and no magnification can split it again.
E2. The limits are about 1270 nm (NA 0.25), 490 nm (NA 0.65) and 227 nm (NA 1.4). Only the oil objective separates points 250 nm apart. A lens with a higher NA collects light from a wider cone, which makes the blur spot smaller.
E3. Red light: limit \(0.61 \times 650 / 1.4 \approx 283\) nm, larger than 250 nm, so not resolved (a faint dip only). Blue light: \(0.61 \times 450 / 1.4 \approx 196\) nm, so resolved. Shorter wavelengths help, but visible light stops at about 400 nm (shorter UV light damages cells and is absorbed by glass). NA \(= n \sin\theta\) cannot exceed the refractive index of the oil and glass (about 1.5), because \(\sin\theta \le 1\). So the limit for a light microscope stays near 200 nm. Super-resolution methods get around it by making neighbouring molecules glow at different times, not by a better lens.
E4. \(0.61 \times 0.0037 / 0.01 \approx 0.23\) nm. The limit is about 60 times the wavelength because electron lenses have large errors (aberrations), so only electrons travelling at a very small angle can be used: the NA is about 0.01 instead of 1.4. In cells, the sample sets the limit: the section is fixed, stained with heavy metals and about 50–100 nm thick, and the stain grains and the overlapping material in the section blur the detail to about 1–2 nm. Purified proteins imaged frozen (cryo-EM) get much closer to the lens limit.

title: Microtubules and motor proteins
section: About this lecture

title: Microtubules and motor proteins
section: The question: how does a one-metre cell feed its far end?
text:
The question: how does a one-metre cell feed its far end?


A motor neuron that moves your big toe has its cell body in the spinal cord and its synapse in the foot: one cell, about 1 m long.
Almost all proteins, membranes and mitochondria are made in the cell body.
The tour of the cell lecture showed that diffusion is fast across a cell (seconds) but hopeless over a metre: the time grows with distance squared.
Yet new material reaches the synapse within days. What carries it, and along what?


Here is the puzzle for today. Think of the nerve cell that makes your big toe move. Its cell body sits in the spinal cord in your lower back, and its axon runs all the way down the leg to a muscle in the foot. That is one single cell, about a metre long, yet only about ten micrometres thick. The nucleus, the rough ER and the Golgi are all in the cell body, so nearly every new protein, every new piece of membrane and many mitochondria start there. They are needed at the far end, at the synapse. In the tour of the cell you saw that diffusion is fine across a normal cell: a protein crosses ten micrometres in a few seconds. But diffusion time grows with the square of the distance. A hundred thousand times further means ten billion times longer: hundreds to thousands of years for one metre. Real neurons deliver new synaptic vesicle proteins in a few days. So there must be an active transport system with tracks and engines. The tracks are microtubules, and the engines are motor proteins. By the end of the lecture you can calculate how long the trip takes.

title: Microtubules and motor proteins
section: The building block: tubulin makes a polar, hollow tube
text:
The building block: tubulin makes a polar, hollow tube








αβ-tubulin dimers stack head to tail into protofilaments; 13 protofilaments close into a hollow tube 25 nm wide.
Every dimer points the same way, so the tube is polar: a fast-growing plus end (β exposed) and a slower minus end (α exposed).
Both subunits bind GTP. Only the GTP on β is hydrolysed to GDP, shortly after the dimer is added.







Tubulin dimer (PDB 1JFF): β (red) on top, α (gold) below.


The building block of a microtubule is a dimer of two similar proteins, alpha-tubulin and beta-tubulin, each about fifty kilodaltons. The dimer is eight nanometres long. On the right is the real atomic structure, solved by electron crystallography: beta on top in red, alpha below in gold, each with its nucleotide. Dimers join head to tail into a protofilament, and thirteen protofilaments sit side by side and close into a hollow tube twenty-five nanometres across. That makes the microtubule the stiffest and widest of the three filament systems: a good track. Because all dimers point the same way, the two ends are different. The plus end, where beta-tubulin is exposed, grows and shrinks fast; the minus end is slower and, in cells, is usually capped and anchored. Remember the polarity: motors read it to know which way to walk. Both tubulins bind GTP. The GTP in alpha is buried and stays. The GTP in beta is hydrolysed to GDP soon after the dimer is built in, and that single chemical detail is the key to the next slide.

title: Microtubules and motor proteins
section: Dynamic instability: the GTP cap
text:
Dynamic instability: the GTP cap


New dimers carry GTP. Hydrolysis lags behind growth, so a growing end has a GTP cap that holds it straight.
GDP-tubulin in the lattice is strained: it wants to curve. If the cap is lost, the protofilaments peel apart and the tube shrinks fast: a catastrophe. Regaining a cap stops the shrinking: a rescue.
Each microtubule switches at random. A typical microtubule lasts about 10 min in an interphase cell and less than a minute in mitosis.


Here is the most surprising property of microtubules. In 1984 Tim Mitchison and Marc Kirschner found that in one solution, with the same free tubulin, some microtubules grow while others shrink, and each one switches between the two states now and then. They called this dynamic instability. The explanation is the GTP on beta-tubulin. A dimer arrives carrying GTP and is built into the end. Its GTP is hydrolysed a little later. As long as dimers arrive faster than GTP is hydrolysed, the end carries a cap of GTP-tubulin, which keeps the protofilaments straight and stuck together. Behind the cap is GDP-tubulin, which would rather be curved. It is held straight only by its neighbours, like a loaded spring. If, by chance, the cap is lost, the protofilaments curl outward and fall apart, and the microtubule shrinks very fast. That switch is a catastrophe. Sometimes a shrinking microtubule regains a cap and starts growing again: a rescue. On the right is the life of one microtubule: slow growth, sudden catastrophe, fast shrinkage, rescue. The cell pays GTP for this, and gets tracks that it can rebuild within minutes.

title: Microtubules and motor proteins
section: How do we know? EB1 comets and kymographs
text:
How do we know? EB1 comets and kymographs







Human U2OS cell expressing EB1-GFP: each bright dash is the growing plus end of one microtubule (one frame of a time-lapse movie).


EB1 binds only the growing end (it reads the GTP cap). Fused to GFP, it makes each growing end a moving comet.
Track the comets: their speed is the growth rate (about 10–20 µm/min in a cell); a comet that vanishes marks a pause or a catastrophe.
A kymograph stacks the same line through the image at each time point: a growing end draws a sloped line, a catastrophe a sharp turn back.
In a test tube, purified tubulin shows the same switching: it needs no other protein. Try it: Demo: dynamic instability.



How can we watch single microtubule ends in a living cell? The best trick uses a protein called EB1, an end-binding protein. EB1 recognises the special structure of tubulin near the growing end, so it sits only on growing plus ends and falls off a few seconds after a dimer is built in. If you fuse EB1 to green fluorescent protein and express it in cells, every growing end lights up as a short moving comet, like in this human cell. The comets start near the centrosome and race outward. From a movie you can measure the speed of each comet, which is the growth rate, and you see comets disappear when a microtubule stops or has a catastrophe; shrinking ends are invisible with EB1. A common way to analyse such movies is a kymograph: take one line in the image, along a microtubule, and stack that line for every time point. Growth then draws a sloped line, and a catastrophe appears as a sharp turn. The original evidence came from purified tubulin in a test tube, which shows that dynamic instability is a property of tubulin itself. You can build your own kymograph in the demo.

title: Microtubules and motor proteins
section: Where microtubules start: the centrosome
text:
Where microtubules start: the centrosome













Electron micrograph of a centriole cut across (mouse embryo): nine triplet microtubules, about 0.2 µm across.


Starting a tube from free tubulin is slow. Cells start microtubules on γ-tubulin ring complexes, which act as a template and cap the minus end.
In animal cells most rings sit in the centrosome: a pair of centrioles in a cloud of pericentriolar material. Minus ends stay there; plus ends grow outward.
The centrosome is copied once per cell cycle; the two copies become the spindle poles (the mitosis lecture).


A microtubule can in principle start anywhere, but starting a new tube from free dimers is slow, because several dimers must come together in the right shape before growth becomes favourable. Cells solve this with a third tubulin, gamma-tubulin. Gamma-tubulin and some partner proteins form a ring that looks like the end of a microtubule. Dimers bind to the ring and grow into a tube with thirteen protofilaments. The ring also caps the minus end, so the minus end neither grows nor shrinks. In animal cells most of these rings are packed into the centrosome, the main microtubule-organising centre, close to the nucleus. The centrosome has a pair of centrioles at its core, surrounded by a cloud of protein called pericentriolar material, which holds the rings. The electron micrograph shows a centriole cut across: nine triplets of microtubules in a ring. Remember that structure, because a cilium grows from the same kind of barrel. Before a cell divides, the centrosome is duplicated, and the two centrosomes become the two poles of the mitotic spindle, which you meet in the mitosis lecture.

title: Microtubules and motor proteins
section: Different cells, different arrays
text:
Different cells, different arrays













Mouse fibroblasts stained for tubulin (confocal): radial arrays around the nucleus.


Fibroblast: a radial aster; minus ends at the centrosome, plus ends at the cell edge.
Neuron: in the axon every plus end points away from the cell body; dendrites have mixed directions. The arrays are made without a centrosome.
Epithelium: bundles run from apical to basal, minus ends near the apical surface. They deliver cargo to the right side of a polarised cell.


The rules are the same in every cell, but the arrangement differs, and it decides where motors can take things. In a fibroblast or most cells in culture, the centrosome sits next to the nucleus and microtubules radiate out like the spokes of a wheel. You can see it in the fluorescence image of mouse fibroblasts stained with an antibody against tubulin. Minus ends are in the middle and plus ends at the cell edge, so a plus-end motor carries cargo outward and a minus-end motor carries it inward. In a neuron, the axon has a uniform array: every microtubule has its plus end towards the axon tip. These microtubules are not attached to the centrosome; they are nucleated along the axon and cut and moved into place. Dendrites in mammals have mixed directions, which helps the cell send some cargo only to dendrites. In an epithelial cell, such as those lining your gut, microtubules run from top to bottom, with minus ends anchored near the apical surface. That lets the cell send membrane proteins to the apical or basolateral side, which matters for the transport epithelia you met in the transport lecture.

title: Microtubules and motor proteins
section: Microtubule-associated proteins tune the tracks
text:
Microtubule-associated proteins tune the tracks


Stabilisers such as tau (axon) bind along the lattice, reduce catastrophes and bundle microtubules.
Plus-end trackers such as EB1 ride on growing ends and recruit other proteins to them.
Destabilisers (kinesin-13, stathmin) and severing enzymes (katanin, spastin) make microtubules short and dynamic.
Cells change this balance quickly: in mitosis catastrophes become much more frequent, so microtubules get shorter and turn over faster.


Pure tubulin already shows dynamic instability, but in cells dozens of microtubule-associated proteins, MAPs for short, tune it. We group them by what they do. Stabilisers bind along the side of the microtubule. Tau in the axon and MAP2 in dendrites are the classic examples; they make catastrophes rarer and hold microtubules at a set distance from each other. Tau comes back at the end of this lecture, in Alzheimer’s disease. Plus-end tracking proteins, such as EB1 from the previous slide, ride on growing ends and recruit other proteins there, for example to capture the end at the cell cortex or at a chromosome. Destabilisers do the opposite: kinesin-13 is a kinesin that does not walk but pulls dimers off the ends, and stathmin holds free tubulin dimers away from the ends. Severing enzymes such as katanin and spastin use ATP to cut a microtubule in two, which makes new ends. The cell changes this balance by phosphorylating MAPs. When a cell enters mitosis, catastrophes become much more frequent, the long interphase array breaks down and many short, fast microtubules build the spindle.

title: Microtubules and motor proteins
section: Two motor families walk in opposite directions
text:
Two motor families walk in opposite directions










Kinesin (most kinds)
Cytoplasmic dynein




Direction
towards the plus end (outward)
towards the minus end (inward)


Size
two heads, ~80 nm long; ~45 kinesin genes in humans
very large (~1.4 MDa); one main form does most transport


Typical cargo
vesicles, mitochondria, mRNA particles
endosomes, Golgi membranes, viruses on their way to the nucleus




Two families of motor proteins walk on microtubules. Both convert the energy of ATP hydrolysis into steps, and both bind cargo with their tails. They differ in direction. Kinesins, with a few exceptions, walk towards the plus end, which in most cells means outward, from the centre to the periphery or down the axon. Humans have about forty-five kinesin genes, so different kinesins carry different cargo. Cytoplasmic dynein walks towards the minus end, inward. It is a much bigger machine: each motor head is a ring of six ATPase domains, and the whole complex is about one and a half megadaltons. Dynein needs a partner complex called dynactin and a cargo adaptor to move cargo over long distances. Unlike kinesins, there is essentially one cytoplasmic dynein that does nearly all minus-end transport. Many viruses, such as herpes viruses, hijack dynein to reach the nucleus, a topic of the pathogenesis course. A cargo often carries both kinds of motor, and the cell decides which one wins. The third motor family, myosin, walks on actin; it is the topic of the lecture on myosin and intermediate filaments.

title: Microtubules and motor proteins
section: How kinesin walks: one ATP per 8-nm step
text:
How kinesin walks: one ATP per 8-nm step


Kinesin walks hand over hand: the two heads take turns leading, and one head is always bound.
ATP binding to the front head swings the rear head forward by 16 nm; the cargo moves 8 nm, one tubulin dimer.
One ATP per step, ~100 steps per second: about 1 µm/s. It stalls against a force of about 6 pN.


How does a protein walk? Kinesin has two identical heads, each of which binds the microtubule and ATP. The cycle works like this. Imagine both heads are bound, the rear one holding ADP. ATP binds to the front head. That makes a short segment called the neck linker zip onto the front head and point forward, which throws the rear head ahead, past its partner, by sixteen nanometres. The swinging head finds the next binding site, releases its ADP and binds firmly. Meanwhile the old front head, now at the rear, hydrolyses its ATP and is ready to let go. The heads take turns, like your feet when you walk, and because one head is always attached, a single kinesin can take about a hundred steps before it falls off. We call that processive. Each step moves the cargo by eight nanometres, exactly one tubulin dimer, and uses exactly one ATP. At about a hundred steps per second, kinesin moves about one micrometre per second. It keeps going against a load of up to about six piconewtons, which is plenty to drag a vesicle through cytoplasm.

title: Microtubules and motor proteins
section: How do we know? Watching one motor at a time
text:
How do we know? Watching one motor at a time


Gliding assay: motors stuck to glass move fluorescent microtubules. This is how kinesin was discovered (1985, in squid giant axons).
Optical trap: a laser holds a bead carrying one kinesin; the bead is followed to ~1 nm. It shows 8-nm steps, one ATP per step and the stall force.
Single-molecule fluorescence: a motor tagged with a bright dye can be followed as it walks along a microtubule.


The numbers on the last slide come from experiments with single molecules. The first is the gliding assay. Purified motors are stuck to a glass slide, fluorescent microtubules are added with ATP, and the microtubules glide across the glass, pushed by the motors. In 1985 Ron Vale and colleagues used this kind of assay with extracts of the squid giant axon to find kinesin. The second method is the optical trap, also called optical tweezers. A strongly focused laser beam holds a small plastic bead, as if on a spring. A single kinesin is attached to the bead and set down on a microtubule fixed to the glass. As the motor walks, it pulls the bead out of the centre of the trap, and the bead position is measured with a precision of about a nanometre. The record looks like a staircase with steps of eight nanometres. By changing the ATP concentration you can show that each step uses one ATP, and by making the trap stiffer you find the force at which the motor stalls, about six piconewtons. The same methods were later used for dynein and myosin.

title: Microtubules and motor proteins
section: Axonal transport: motors beat diffusion over long distances
text:
Axonal transport: motors beat diffusion over long distances









Distance
Diffusion of a protein (t \approx x^2/2D, D ≈ 5 µm²/s)
Kinesin (t = x/v, v ≈ 1 µm/s)




10 µm (a cell)
~10 s
~10 s


1 m (an axon)
~3000 years
~12 days (fast transport, 2–5 µm/s: 2–6 days)




Now we can answer the question from the start. In the axon all microtubules point their plus end towards the tip, so kinesins carry new synaptic vesicle precursors, membrane proteins and mitochondria outward. This is called anterograde transport. Dynein carries endosomes, worn-out parts on their way to lysosomes, and signals from the target tissue, such as growth factors, back to the cell body: retrograde transport. Compare the two ways of moving along a line. Diffusion along one dimension takes about x squared over 2D; a motor takes x over v. Over ten micrometres both take about ten seconds for a protein, so in a small cell diffusion is good enough. But because diffusion grows with the square of the distance, one metre would take thousands of years, while a kinesin at one micrometre per second needs about twelve days, and fast axonal transport in neurons, up to a few micrometres per second, needs two to six days. A large vesicle diffuses even more slowly than a protein, so for organelles there is no alternative to motors. Cytoskeletal proteins travel by slow axonal transport, a millimetre or so per day, because their motors pause most of the time.

title: Microtubules and motor proteins
section: Motors also place organelles
text:
Motors also place organelles


Pigment cells of fish and frogs change colour in minutes: dynein gathers the pigment granules at the centre, kinesin spreads them out.
The Golgi sits next to the centrosome because dynein pulls it towards minus ends; ER tubules are pulled outward along microtubules.
Destroy microtubules with a drug and the Golgi breaks up into small stacks spread through the cytoplasm.


Motors do not only carry cargo over long distances. They also decide where organelles sit in an ordinary cell. A beautiful example is the pigment cell of fish and frogs, the melanophore. It is full of dark pigment granules. When the animal needs to become pale, a hormone signal makes dynein carry all the granules to the centre of the cell, so the skin looks light. When the signal reverses, kinesin carries them back out along the radial microtubules, and the cell turns dark again within minutes. The same tug of war between plus-end and minus-end motors positions organelles in your own cells. The Golgi apparatus sits close to the centrosome because dynein keeps pulling Golgi membranes towards the minus ends. If you add a drug that depolymerises microtubules, such as nocodazole, the Golgi falls apart into many small stacks scattered through the cytoplasm, and comes together again when the drug is washed out. The endoplasmic reticulum is stretched out towards the cell edge along microtubules. You meet the Golgi and the ER in detail in the organelle lectures.

title: Microtubules and motor proteins
section: Cilia and flagella: microtubules that bend
text:
Cilia and flagella: microtubules that bend













Electron micrograph of cilia cut across (mouse airway). Each shows nine doublets around a central pair.


The core, the axoneme, has 9 doublet microtubules around 2 single ones (“9 + 2”). It grows from a basal body, a modified centriole.
Axonemal dynein arms on each doublet walk on the neighbouring doublet. Links stop the doublets from sliding apart, so sliding becomes bending.
Motile cilia clear mucus in the airways and move the egg in the oviduct; a flagellum drives a sperm. Most cells also have one non-moving primary cilium (9 + 0), an antenna for signals.


Cilia and flagella are hair-like extensions of the cell surface, built around a bundle of microtubules called the axoneme. Look at the electron micrograph of cilia from a mouse airway, cut across: each shows nine doublet microtubules in a ring around two single microtubules in the middle. This is the famous nine plus two pattern, and it is the same in a sperm tail, an airway cilium and a single-celled alga, so it has been conserved for more than a billion years. The axoneme grows from a basal body, which is a centriole that has moved to the cell surface. Each doublet carries two rows of dynein arms, which reach to the next doublet and walk on it towards its minus end. If the doublets were free, this would push them past each other, as in the left drawing. But they are held together by links and anchored at the base, so the sliding is converted into bending. Waves of dynein activity around the ring make the cilium beat. Airway cells carry about two hundred cilia each, which sweep mucus up and out of the lungs. Almost every cell in your body also has one primary cilium without dynein arms, which does not move but senses signals.

title: Microtubules and motor proteins
section: Why it matters: taxanes and vinca alkaloids in chemotherapy
text:
Why it matters: taxanes and vinca alkaloids in chemotherapy








Taxanes (paclitaxel, docetaxel) bind β-tubulin inside the lattice and stabilise microtubules; vinca alkaloids (vincristine, vinblastine) bind tubulin at the plus end and block growth. Used against breast, ovarian and lung cancer, leukaemias and lymphomas.
Both freeze dynamic instability: the spindle cannot capture and move chromosomes, the cell arrests in mitosis and dies (the mitosis lecture).
Side effect: peripheral neuropathy. Numb, tingling hands and feet: the longest axons depend most on microtubule transport.


 
Pacific yew (left) and Madagascar periwinkle.


Now to medicine. Two of the oldest and most used groups of cancer drugs act on tubulin, and both come from plants. Paclitaxel, sold as Taxol, was found in the bark of the Pacific yew in a large screen of plant extracts in the 1960s; docetaxel is a close relative. Taxanes bind beta-tubulin on the inside of the microtubule and lock the lattice, so microtubules cannot shrink: they behave as if catastrophes no longer happened. Vinca alkaloids, such as vincristine and vinblastine, come from the Madagascar periwinkle. They bind tubulin at the plus end and between dimers, and block growth; at high doses microtubules fall apart. The two drugs push in opposite directions, yet both work, because both stop the dynamics. A mitotic spindle needs microtubules that grow and shrink to search for and pull on chromosomes, so the cell gets stuck in mitosis and dies. Cancer cells divide often, so they are hit hardest. The most common dose-limiting side effect is peripheral neuropathy: numbness and pain in fingers and toes, because the longest axons depend most on transport along microtubules. You meet these drugs again in drug development.

title: Microtubules and motor proteins
section: Why it matters: diseases of cilia and axonal transport
text:
Why it matters: diseases of cilia and axonal transport








Disease
What goes wrong
Link to this lecture




Primary ciliary dyskinesia (about 1 in 10 000–20 000)
Mutations in axonemal dynein or its partners: motile cilia do not beat
Chronic airway infections; male infertility (sperm do not swim); in about half of patients organs on the wrong side (situs inversus), because cilia in the embryo set left and right


Polycystic kidney disease (dominant form, about 1 in 1000)
Polycystins, sensor proteins of the primary cilium in kidney tubules
The tubules lose their sense of flow and grow into fluid-filled cysts; a common inherited cause of kidney failure


Neurodegeneration
Mutations in kinesin (KIF5A), dynein/dynactin or spastin (severing); tau detaches from microtubules in Alzheimer’s disease
The longest motor neurons fail first (hereditary spastic paraplegia, some forms of ALS and Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease)



These are cell-level mechanisms only; the clinical pictures come in the course on disease mechanisms.

The machinery of this lecture also explains several inherited diseases. In primary ciliary dyskinesia, mutations in the genes for the dynein arms of the axoneme, or for proteins that build them, leave the cilia without a proper beat. Mucus is not cleared from the airways, so patients have chronic bronchitis and sinusitis. Men are usually infertile because their sperm cannot swim. And about half of the patients have their organs mirrored, heart on the right, because a small patch of rotating cilia in the early embryo creates a leftward flow that tells the embryo which side is left. In autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, the mutated proteins, polycystin 1 and 2, sit in the primary cilium of kidney tubule cells, where they sense the flow of urine. Without that signal the tubule cells keep dividing and form large cysts; it is one of the most common inherited diseases leading to kidney failure. Finally, neurons depend on axonal transport, so defects in kinesin, dynein, dynactin or the severing enzyme spastin cause diseases in which the longest axons degenerate first. In Alzheimer’s disease the stabiliser tau is modified, falls off the microtubules and forms tangles.

title: Microtubules and motor proteins
section: Summary
text:
Summary

αβ-tubulin builds a polar, hollow tube. A GTP cap keeps a growing plus end stable; losing it causes a catastrophe, regaining it a rescue: dynamic instability, seen with EB1 comets and kymographs.
γ-tubulin rings in the centrosome start microtubules and anchor minus ends. Arrays differ by cell type: radial in a fibroblast, uniform plus-out in an axon, apical-to-basal in an epithelium. MAPs stabilise, track, take apart or cut.
Kinesins walk to the plus end, dynein to the minus end, using one ATP per step (kinesin: 8 nm, ~1 µm/s), as shown in single-molecule and optical-trap assays. Over long distances, motors beat diffusion (x/v versus x²/2D): axonal transport.
In cilia and flagella (9 + 2 axoneme), dynein makes doublets slide, and links turn sliding into bending. The primary cilium is a signalling antenna.
Taxanes (stabilise) and vinca alkaloids (block growth) stop dynamics, arrest mitosis and damage long axons; ciliopathies and transport defects cause disease.

Read more (optional): Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell, 7th ed., ch. 16.
Image credits

Five take-home points. First, a microtubule is a polar, hollow tube of alpha-beta tubulin, and the GTP on beta-tubulin makes it dynamically unstable: growing ends keep a GTP cap, and when it is lost the tube shrinks fast until rescued. We see this with EB1 comets and kymographs. Second, gamma-tubulin rings, mostly in the centrosome, start microtubules and hold their minus ends, and different cells arrange their arrays to suit their shape; MAPs tune the dynamics. Third, kinesins walk to plus ends and dynein to minus ends, each step paid for with one ATP, as single-molecule experiments showed. Over long distances, transport by motors wins easily over diffusion, which is why a one-metre axon works. Fourth, in cilia and flagella, dynein arms make doublet microtubules slide, and links convert the sliding into the bending that moves mucus and sperm; the primary cilium is an antenna. Fifth, drugs that freeze microtubule dynamics are mainstays of chemotherapy, with nerve damage as the price, and defects in cilia and motors cause disease. The lecture on myosin and intermediate filaments completes the cytoskeleton, with the third motor family and the mechanics of the cell.

title: Quiz: microtubules and motor proteins
text:
Short questions to check your understanding of the lecture Microtubules and motor proteins. Try each on paper first, then open the hint or the answer. The tag after each question shows the learning outcome (ELO) it practises.

Q1. Why does a microtubule have a plus end and a minus end, and which tubulin is exposed at the plus end? [ELO 6]






Hint





Think about how the αβ dimers are lined up in a protofilament.









Answer





All αβ-tubulin dimers join head to tail and point the same way, so the two ends of the tube are different: the tube is polar. β-tubulin is exposed at the plus end, which grows and shrinks fast; α-tubulin is exposed at the minus end, which in cells is usually capped by a γ-tubulin ring and anchored.




Q2. What is the GTP cap, and what happens when a growing microtubule loses it? [ELO 6]






Hint





Dimers arrive with GTP on β-tubulin. Which is faster, adding dimers or hydrolysing GTP?









Answer





New dimers carry GTP, and the GTP on β-tubulin is hydrolysed a little after the dimer is built in. While dimers add faster than GTP is hydrolysed, the end carries a cap of GTP-tubulin that keeps the protofilaments straight. GDP-tubulin behind it is strained and wants to curve. If the cap is lost, the protofilaments peel apart and the microtubule shrinks fast: a catastrophe. If it gains a new cap, shrinking stops: a rescue.




Q3. A cell expresses EB1-GFP. You see many short bright comets moving from the centre towards the cell edge. What does each comet show, and what can you measure from the movie? [ELO 6]






Hint





EB1 binds only one kind of microtubule end.









Answer





EB1 binds only growing plus ends, so each comet is the growing end of one microtubule. Their direction shows that plus ends point outward, and their speed is the growth rate (about 10–20 µm/min). A comet that disappears marks a pause or catastrophe; shrinking ends are not labelled. A kymograph along one microtubule shows growth as a sloped line.




Q4. In which direction does most kinesin walk, and in which direction does cytoplasmic dynein walk? In an axon, which motor carries new synaptic vesicle precursors to the synapse? [ELO 6]






Hint





Where are the plus ends in an axon?









Answer





Most kinesins walk to the plus end, dynein to the minus end. In an axon all plus ends point away from the cell body, so kinesin carries new vesicles and mitochondria out to the synapse (anterograde transport), and dynein brings endosomes and signals back (retrograde transport).




Q5. How far does the cargo move per kinesin step, and how much ATP does each step cost? How was this measured? [ELO 6]






Hint





Think of the length of one tubulin dimer, and of a bead held by a laser.









Answer





8 nm per step, the length of one tubulin dimer, and one ATP per step (each head moves 16 nm, hand over hand). It was measured with an optical trap: a laser holds a bead carrying a single kinesin; the bead position, followed to about 1 nm, rises in 8-nm steps, and the step rate follows the ATP concentration.




Q6. Why can a small cell rely on diffusion for many proteins, while a neuron with a 1-m axon cannot? Use the two formulas from the lecture. [ELO 6]






Hint





Diffusion time grows as \(x^2\), motor time as \(x\).









Answer





Diffusion along a line takes about \(t \approx x^2/2D\); a motor takes \(t = x/v\). For a protein (\(D \approx 5\ \mu\text{m}^2/\text{s}\)) over 10 µm, diffusion takes about 10 s, like a kinesin at 1 µm/s. Over 1 m (\(10^6\) µm), diffusion takes about \(10^{11}\) s, thousands of years, while kinesin needs \(10^6\) s, about 12 days. Because diffusion grows with the square of the distance, only motors work over long distances.




Q7. What does “9 + 2” mean in a cilium, and how does dynein make the cilium bend rather than fall apart? [ELO 6]






Hint





What would happen to two doublets if they were not linked?









Answer





The axoneme has 9 doublet microtubules in a ring around 2 single microtubules. Axonemal dynein arms on each doublet walk on the neighbouring doublet and push the doublets to slide past each other. Because the doublets are linked to each other and anchored in the basal body, they cannot slide apart, so the sliding is turned into bending.




Q8. Paclitaxel stabilises microtubules and vinblastine stops their growth. Why do both kill dividing cancer cells, and why do both cause numb fingers and toes? [ELO 6]






Hint





What does a mitotic spindle need: stable microtubules, or microtubules that can grow and shrink?









Answer





The mitotic spindle needs dynamic microtubules that grow, shrink and search for chromosomes. Both drugs freeze dynamic instability, in opposite ways, so the spindle cannot work and the cell arrests in mitosis and dies; dividing cancer cells are hit most. Neurons with the longest axons depend most on transport along microtubules, which the drugs disturb, so peripheral neuropathy is a common side effect.

title: Study questions: myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell
text:
Study questions in the style of the written exam. Write your answer first (a few sentences, or a labelled sketch where it helps), then compare with the model answer. Each question is tagged with its learning outcome (ELO). Questions tagged [VG] are of the kind used for the higher grade: predict, compare, explain an unexpected result or design an experiment.
Useful values (frog skeletal muscle, as in the lecture): thick filament 1.6 µm (bare zone 0.2 µm), thin filament 1.0 µm on each side, Z-disc 0.05 µm.
crumbs: Myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell

title: Study questions: myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell
section: G-level questions
text:
G-level questions
1. Describe the domain structure of a myosin molecule. How do the tails of myosin II and myosin V suit their different jobs? [ELO 6]






Model answer





Every myosin has a motor domain (head) that binds actin and ATP, a lever arm (neck) stabilised by light chains that amplifies small shape changes in the head into a swing of several nanometres, and a tail. Myosin II has a long coiled-coil tail; hundreds of tails bundle into a bipolar thick filament with heads at both ends, so it pulls actin filaments of opposite polarity towards the middle: contraction (muscle, contractile ring, cell rear). Myosin V has long lever arms (36 nm steps) and a tail that binds cargo (vesicles, pigment granules); it walks processively, hand over hand, along actin.




2. Draw and explain the cross-bridge cycle of myosin II. For each step, say what happens to the nucleotide and to the head. [ELO 6]






Model answer






Rigor: no nucleotide, head bound tightly to actin. 2. ATP binds → the actin-binding cleft opens and the head releases actin. 3. ATP is hydrolysed to ADP + Pi (both stay bound) → the lever is cocked (re-primed). 4. The head binds actin weakly at a new site; Pi is released → the power stroke: the lever swings and moves the actin filament 5–10 nm towards the M-line (towards the actin minus end). ADP is released → back to rigor. One ATP is used per cycle. A sketch should show the actin filament, the thick filament, the head attached or detached, the lever position and the nucleotide in each state.





3. Draw a sarcomere and label: Z-disc, M-line, thin filament, thick filament, A band, I band, H zone. Which bands change length during contraction, and why? [ELO 6]






Model answer





The sketch: Z-discs at both ends; thin (actin) filaments anchored in each Z-disc with their plus ends, pointing to the middle; thick (myosin II) filaments in the middle, centred on the M-line, overlapping the thin filaments. A band = the thick-filament length (dark); I band = the part with only thin filaments (light), across the Z-disc; H zone = the middle part of the A band without thin filaments. During contraction the A band stays constant and the I band and H zone shrink, because the filaments keep their length and slide past each other (sliding-filament model).




4. Explain the shape of the length–tension curve of skeletal muscle (Gordon, Huxley and Julian, 1966): the descending limb, the plateau and the ascending limb. [ELO 6]






Model answer





Descending limb (above 2.25 µm): force falls in a straight line with the overlap between thin filaments and the head-bearing part of the thick filaments, reaching zero at 3.65 µm (1.6 + 2 × 1.0 + 0.05 µm), where the filaments no longer overlap. This shows that every cross-bridge contributes force independently. Plateau (2.0–2.25 µm): every head faces a thin filament; extra overlap in the bare zone, which has no heads, adds nothing. Ascending limb (below 2.0 µm): thin filaments from the two halves cross the M-line and get in each other’s way (and wrong-polarity filaments face the heads); below about 1.65 µm the thick filaments are pressed against the Z-discs, so force falls steeply.




5. Explain how Ca²⁺ controls contraction in skeletal muscle. Compare with how non-muscle myosin II is switched on. [ELO 6] [ELO 3]






Model answer





Skeletal muscle: at rest (Ca²⁺ ≈ 0.1 µM) tropomyosin lies on the actin filament and covers the myosin-binding sites. An action potential opens Ca²⁺ channels in the sarcoplasmic reticulum; Ca²⁺ rises to about 10 µM and binds troponin C; troponin moves tropomyosin aside and heads can bind. SERCA pumps return Ca²⁺ to the sarcoplasmic reticulum to relax the muscle. The switch is on the thin filament. Non-muscle myosin II (and smooth muscle) has no troponin. The switch is on myosin itself: phosphorylation of the regulatory light chain by myosin light-chain kinase (activated by Ca²⁺–calmodulin) or by Rho kinase turns the motor on and lets it form minifilaments; a phosphatase turns it off.




6. Give two jobs of non-muscle myosin II in cells and explain how it does them. [ELO 6]






Model answer






Cytokinesis: at the end of mitosis, a contractile ring of actin filaments and myosin II minifilaments forms under the plasma membrane at the cell equator. Myosin pulls the antiparallel actin filaments past each other, the ring tightens like a purse string and pinches the cell in two. (2) Cell migration: at the rear of a migrating cell, myosin II contracts the actin network, pulls the cell body and tail forward and helps detach rear adhesions, while actin polymerisation pushes the front. (Also: tension in stress fibres, which traction-force microscopy measures.)





7. Describe how intermediate filaments are assembled, and explain why they have no polarity and no motor proteins. [ELO 6]






Model answer





Each protein has a long α-helical rod with head and tail domains. Two rods wind into a parallel coiled-coil dimer. Two dimers associate side by side, antiparallel and staggered, into a tetramer. Eight tetramers pack side by side into a unit-length filament, and these join end to end and compact into a 10 nm filament. Because the tetramer is antiparallel, both ends of the filament are the same: no polarity. Motor proteins need a polar track to know which way to walk, so no motors move on intermediate filaments. They also bind no ATP or GTP; they are regulated mainly by phosphorylation.




8. Name four families of intermediate filaments and where each is found. How do intermediate filaments give an epithelium its mechanical strength? [ELO 6]






Model answer





Keratins (epithelia, e.g. skin, gut, liver), vimentin (fibroblasts, endothelium, white blood cells), desmin (muscle), neurofilaments (axons), nuclear lamins (nuclear lamina in all nucleated cells). In an epithelium, keratin filaments are anchored at desmosomes (to the next cell) and hemidesmosomes (to the basal lamina), so the networks of all cells form one continuous network that spreads force over the whole sheet. The filaments themselves can be stretched to two or three times their length before breaking and become stiffer as they stretch.




9. Choose a method to answer each question and explain briefly how it works: (a) How much force does a fibroblast exert on its surroundings? (b) How far does one myosin V molecule move per step? (c) Is the keratin network rebuilt as fast as the actin network? [ELO 1] [ELO 6]






Model answer






Traction-force microscopy: grow the cell on a soft gel of known stiffness containing fluorescent beads; measure bead displacements with and without the cell; calculate the force map (nanonewtons). (b) Optical tweezers (or single-molecule TIRF tracking of a fluorescent myosin V on surface-bound actin): a laser trap holds a bead attached to the motor or the actin filament; the bead jumps by one step (36 nm) per ATP, and the trap also measures the force (piconewtons). (c) FRAP: express GFP-keratin or GFP-actin, bleach a spot, measure how fast fluorescence recovers. Actin recovers within seconds; keratin much more slowly (minutes or longer): a more stable network.

title: Study questions: myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell
section: VG-style questions
text:
VG-style questions
10. [VG] A heart muscle cell normally works at sarcomere lengths between about 1.8 and 2.3 µm. (a) Using the length–tension curve, predict what happens to the force of contraction when the heart fills with more blood and its sarcomeres are stretched from 1.9 to 2.2 µm. (b) A patient has a mutation in cardiac myosin that releases heads from the parked (super-relaxed) state. Predict the effect on force and on ATP use, and explain why mavacamten helps. (c) Why must the dose of mavacamten be adjusted carefully? [ELO 6] [ELO 9]






Model answer






At 1.9 µm the sarcomere is on the ascending limb: thin filaments from the two halves overlap each other and force is below maximum. Stretching to 2.2 µm brings it to the plateau, where every head faces a thin filament, so force increases. (This is the cellular basis of the Frank–Starling law: a fuller heart pumps more strongly; more about it in the organ course. In real heart muscle, stretch also increases Ca²⁺ sensitivity.)
More heads are available to form cross-bridges, so at the same Ca²⁺ the muscle makes more force and uses more ATP (more cycling heads, and fewer heads in the energy-saving parked state); relaxation is slower. Over time the heart wall thickens (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy). Mavacamten binds the myosin motor domain, slows its ATPase (phosphate release) and stabilises the parked state, so fewer heads form cross-bridges and force and energy use fall back towards normal.
Mavacamten reduces force for every head it parks. Too much drug parks too many heads and the heart pumps too weakly (heart failure). Patients are therefore checked by echocardiography (how much blood the ventricle ejects), and the dose is adjusted for each person.





11. [VG] A researcher adds a drug to permeabilised muscle fibres (the membrane is made leaky, so the solution reaches the filaments directly). In the bath, Ca²⁺ is 10 µM and ATP is present, and the fibres contract normally. Predict and explain the result in each case: (a) ATP is removed from the bath; (b) ATP is replaced by a non-hydrolysable ATP analogue that binds myosin like ATP but cannot be split; (c) Ca²⁺ is lowered to 0.1 µM while ATP is present. [ELO 6]






Model answer






No ATP: heads finish their stroke and remain bound (rigor). The fibre becomes stiff and cannot relax or shorten further; it stays at whatever tension it had. This shows that ATP is needed to release heads.
Non-hydrolysable analogue: binding still makes heads let go of actin, but they cannot hydrolyse it, so the lever is not re-cocked and no power stroke follows. The fibre relaxes (becomes floppy, like a resting muscle) and produces no force, even though Ca²⁺ is high. This separates the two roles: binding releases, hydrolysis cocks.
Low Ca²⁺ with ATP: troponin loses Ca²⁺, tropomyosin covers the binding sites, heads (cocked with ADP·Pi) cannot bind: the fibre relaxes normally. Compare with (a): low Ca²⁺ relaxes a muscle only when ATP is present to detach the heads.





12. [VG] Transgenic mice that make a mutant keratin 14 in their skin, in addition to their own two normal keratin 14 genes, develop blisters after mild friction, like patients with epidermolysis bullosa simplex. (a) Explain how a mutant keratin can cause disease when plenty of normal keratin 14 is also made. (b) Design an experiment with cultured keratinocytes to test whether cells with the mutant keratin are mechanically weaker, and name the controls. [ELO 6] [ELO 9] [ELO 1]






Model answer






Keratin 14 pairs with keratin 5, and many keratin molecules are packed side by side and end to end in each filament. The mutant keratin 14 is still built into the same dimers, tetramers and filaments as the normal protein, but it disrupts filament assembly (often it changes the conserved ends of the rod that are needed for elongation). Because each filament contains many subunits, a minority of bad subunits is enough to spoil most filaments: the network collapses into clumps. This is a dominant-negative effect, which is why the human disease is usually dominant (one mutant copy is enough). Without a network anchored to desmosomes and hemidesmosomes, basal cells tear under friction.
Grow keratinocytes with normal or mutant keratin 14 (patient cells, or cells edited with CRISPR) as a sheet. Mechanical test: stretch the cells on a flexible membrane (or apply shear stress) and count broken cells, e.g. with a dye that enters only damaged cells; or detach the sheet with an enzyme, shake it and count the fragments (a weaker sheet breaks into more pieces). Imaging: immunofluorescence for keratin 14 to see network versus clumps; FRAP of GFP-keratin to compare network stability. Controls: wild-type cells; cells expressing extra normal keratin 14 at the same level (to rule out over-expression effects); unstretched cells; ideally a rescue by correcting the mutation. Repeat with several independent cell lines and test the difference statistically.

title: Study questions: myosin, intermediate filaments and the mechanical cell
section: Explore
text:
Explore
A sarcomere drawn to scale (frog filament lengths, as in the lecture), with its Z-discs, thin filaments (actin with tropomyosin and troponin), and thick filaments with their myosin heads. Set the sarcomere length with the slider or by dragging the orange point on the length–tension curve; the band labels (A, I, H) update. The bars show the three factors that multiply to give the active force: the filament overlap (how many heads face a thin filament), the binding sites exposed by Ca²⁺ on troponin, and the heads available (not parked). The muscle is held at fixed length, so the filaments do not slide; the heads go through the cross-bridge cycle at 1× real time (about one cycle per second per head, like a slow heart myosin). The geometry of the length–tension curve is accurate in shape; the Ca²⁺ and mavacamten effects are qualitative (right direction, illustrative numbers).



E1. Choose Full activation, optimal length. Read the A band, I band and H zone. Now set the sarcomere length to 3.0 µm, then to 1.7 µm. Which bands change and which do not? Read the force at each length and explain it from the drawing. [ELO 6]
E2. Choose Relaxed (rest Ca²⁺) and watch the heads for a few seconds. Then raise Ca²⁺ slowly. At which Ca²⁺ is the force half of maximum? How much does Ca²⁺ have to rise to go from about 10 % to about 90 % of the force? Why is a steep switch useful for a muscle? [ELO 6]
E3. Choose No ATP (rigor). What do the heads do, and why can the muscle not relax even though Ca²⁺ is low? Tick ATP again: what happens? Which step of the cross-bridge cycle does this show? [ELO 6]
E4. [VG] Predict first. Set the length to 3.0 µm with full Ca²⁺. Will raising Ca²⁺ from 10 to 20 µM restore the force? Will the HCM mutation? Test both, and explain which factor limits the force here. [ELO 6]
E5. [VG] Choose HCM mutation at optimal length. What is the force? Increase mavacamten until the force is back at about 100 %. What happens if you give the full dose? Explain what this means for treating patients, and why the shape of the length–tension curve does not change with the drug. [ELO 6] [ELO 9]






Solutions





E1. At 2.1 µm: A band 1.60 µm, I band 0.25 µm on each side, H zone 0.05 µm; force 100 % (plateau: every head faces a thin filament; the counter shows all 88 heads facing a thin filament). At 3.0 µm: A band still 1.60 µm, I band 0.70 µm on each side, H zone 0.95 µm; overlap 0.325 of 0.70 µm per half, so force 46 %, and only 40 of 88 heads face a thin filament. At 1.7 µm: A band 1.60 µm, I band 0.05 µm, no H zone; force 86 %: the thin filaments from the two halves overlap each other in the middle and get in the way (the demo uses the measured shape of the ascending limb). The A band never changes because the thick filaments keep their length; I and H change because the filaments slide.
E2. At rest (0.1 µM) almost no sites are exposed (0.1 %) and the heads stay cocked, waiting. Force is 50 % at 1 µM. Force goes from about 10 % (0.5 µM: 11 %) to about 90 % (2 µM: 89 %) over only a fourfold rise in Ca²⁺. The switch is steep (cooperative: several Ca²⁺ ions and neighbouring troponin–tropomyosin units act together). A steep switch makes the muscle either relaxed or fully on with a small change in Ca²⁺, and makes it insensitive to small fluctuations in resting Ca²⁺. (The demo’s curve is qualitative: K = 1 µM, Hill coefficient 3.)
E3. Without ATP, every head that faces a thin filament binds, makes its stroke and stays bound: after a few seconds all 88 heads are attached. Ca²⁺ is low, but the bound heads push tropomyosin aside, and without ATP they cannot let go, so the muscle is locked and stiff: rigor. When ATP returns, ATP binds the heads, they release, re-cock, and (at low Ca²⁺) stay detached: the muscle relaxes. This shows step 2 of the cycle: ATP binding releases the head.
E4. No to both. At 3.0 µm the overlap limits force: only 40 of 88 heads face a thin filament. Raising Ca²⁺ from 10 to 20 µM changes nothing (46 % at both), because the sites were already fully exposed (99.9 % at 10 µM). The HCM mutation raises force to 62 %, because more of the heads that face a thin filament are free to bind, but it cannot create new overlap. Force is the product of the three factors, so the smallest one (here the overlap) sets the limit.
E5. HCM mutation: force 133 % of normal (80 % of heads available instead of 60 %). Mavacamten at 30 % of the maximal effect brings force back to about 101 % (35 %: 95 %). At the full dose only 15 % of heads are available and force falls to 25 %: the heart would pump far too weakly. This is why patients get their dose adjusted step by step, with ultrasound checks of heart function. The drug acts on the heads, not on the filament geometry, so it scales the whole curve down by the same factor at every length: the shape of the length–tension curve stays the same.
