title: Study questions: protein life and death
text:
Study questions in the style of the written exam. Write your answer first (a few sentences, or a labelled sketch where it helps), then compare with the model answer. Each question is tagged with its learning outcome (ELO). Questions tagged [VG] are of the kind used for the higher grade: predict, compare, explain an unexpected result or design an experiment.
Useful relations: \(\dfrac{dP}{dt} = k_s - k_d P\), \(\;t_{1/2} = \ln 2 / k_d\), \(\;P_{ss} = k_s / k_d\); after a change, the amount moves half-way to its new steady state in one half-life and 90 % of the way in about 3.3 half-lives.

title: Study questions: protein life and death
section: G-level questions
text:
G-level questions
1. Explain why a newly made protein is at risk of aggregating in the cytosol, and how Hsp70 prevents this. Include the role of ATP. [ELO 4]






Model answer





A new chain leaves the ribosome slowly (about 5 amino acids per second) and cannot fold until a whole domain is made; meanwhile its hydrophobic stretches are exposed. The cytosol is very crowded (200–300 g protein per litre), so exposed stretches easily stick to other chains. Hsp70 binds short hydrophobic stretches. With ATP bound its lid is open and binding is loose; a J-protein (Hsp40) delivers the chain and stimulates ATP hydrolysis; with ADP the lid closes and the chain is held tightly, so the stretch is covered. A nucleotide exchange factor swaps ADP for ATP, the lid opens and the chain is released. It gets a new chance to fold, or is bound again. Hsp70 does not tell the chain how to fold; it prevents wrong contacts.




2. Describe how a chaperonin (GroEL/GroES or TRiC) helps a protein fold. How does it differ from Hsp70? [ELO 4]






Model answer





A chaperonin is a barrel of two rings with a central cavity. A misfolded chain binds hydrophobic patches at the rim of an open ring. ATP and a lid (GroES in bacteria; built into TRiC) bind; the inner wall becomes hydrophilic and the chain is released into the closed chamber, where it folds alone, without contact with other chains. After about 10 s ATP hydrolysis opens the lid and the protein leaves; if still misfolded it can enter again. Difference: Hsp70 binds short stretches of extended chains, one at a time, in the open cytosol; a chaperonin encloses a whole protein (up to about 60 kDa). In human cells TRiC is essential for actin and tubulin.




3. What is a degron? Give three different kinds and an example of how a cell uses one to regulate a protein. [ELO 4]






Model answer





A degron is a feature of a protein that an E3 ubiquitin ligase recognises, leading to ubiquitination and degradation. Kinds: (1) a phosphorylated motif (phospho-degron), (2) exposed hydrophobic stretches of a misfolded protein, recognised through chaperones and their partner E3s (quality control), (3) certain amino acids at the N-terminus (N-degron rule). Example: IκB holds NF-κB in the cytosol. A signal activates the kinase IKK, which phosphorylates two serines of IκB; the phospho-degron is bound by an E3, IκB gets a Lys48 chain and is destroyed by the proteasome; NF-κB enters the nucleus and turns on genes (including IκB: negative feedback).




4. Describe the structure of the 26S proteasome and what happens to a ubiquitinated protein from binding to the release of peptides. [ELO 4]






Model answer





The 20S core is a barrel of four stacked rings (α β β α, seven subunits each). The two β rings carry six protease active sites (β1, β2, β5 in each ring) facing the inside; the α rings form a gate, so folded proteins cannot enter. One or two 19S caps sit on the ends. The cap’s receptors bind a Lys48 ubiquitin chain (four or more ubiquitins); deubiquitinating enzymes remove the ubiquitin, which is reused; a ring of six ATPases unfolds the protein and threads it into the core. Inside, it is cut into peptides of about 3–25 amino acids, which leave and are broken down to amino acids by cytosolic peptidases (some are shown to the immune system).




5. Compare phosphorylation, acetylation and ubiquitination: which residues, which enzymes add and remove the mark, and what the mark does. [ELO 4]






Model answer





Phosphorylation: Ser, Thr, Tyr; added by protein kinases (from ATP), removed by phosphatases; adds two negative charges, changes shape, activity, binding or location within seconds. Acetylation: Lys; added by acetyltransferases (from acetyl-CoA), removed by deacetylases; removes the positive charge of lysine (on histones: loosens DNA binding, opens chromatin; also changes enzyme activity). Ubiquitination: Lys; added by E1–E2–E3, removed by deubiquitinases; Lys48 chains send the protein to the proteasome, single ubiquitin or Lys63 chains are signals (endocytosis, signalling, DNA repair). All three are reversible and are read by proteins that bind the mark.




6. A protein is made at 600 molecules per hour and has a half-life of 3 h. (a) Calculate \(k_d\) and the steady-state amount. (b) The gene is switched on at time 0 (no protein before). How long until the protein reaches half and 90 % of its steady state? (c) Synthesis is doubled. What happens to the steady state and to the time needed to reach it? [ELO 4]






Model answer






\(k_d = 0.693/3 = 0.231\) per h; \(P_{ss} = 600/0.231 \approx\) 2600 molecules. (b) \(P(t) = P_{ss}(1 - e^{-k_d t})\): half after one half-life, 3 h; 90 % after \(\ln 10 / k_d = 2.303/0.231 \approx\) 10 h (3.3 half-lives). (c) The steady state doubles (about 5200), but the time to reach it is unchanged: it depends only on \(k_d\).





7. Describe a cycloheximide chase and a pulse-chase experiment for measuring a protein’s half-life. Give one advantage of each. [ELO 1] [ELO 4]






Model answer





Cycloheximide chase: add cycloheximide, which blocks eukaryotic ribosomes, so synthesis stops. Harvest cells at several times, run SDS-PAGE and a Western blot with an antibody against the protein (plus a stable loading control). The band decays as \(e^{-k_d t}\); on a log scale a straight line, \(t_{1/2}\) where it is 50 %. Advantage: simple, needs only an antibody, no radioactivity. Pulse-chase: label newly made proteins for a short time with a labelled amino acid (classically ³⁵S-methionine), then chase with excess unlabelled amino acid; at each time immunoprecipitate the protein, run a gel and detect the label. Advantage: the cell keeps working normally (no drug), and you follow one cohort of molecules (and can see processing or movement).




8. Explain why multiple myeloma cells are especially sensitive to bortezomib. [ELO 4] [ELO 9]






Model answer





Myeloma cells are cancerous plasma cells that make huge amounts of antibody in the ER. A fraction always misfolds and is returned to the cytosol and destroyed by the proteasome (ERAD). Bortezomib blocks the β5 active site of the proteasome. Misfolded proteins then pile up, the ER is overloaded, the unfolded protein response cannot restore balance and switches to apoptosis. Normal cells make much less secreted protein and tolerate partial proteasome inhibition better, which gives a therapeutic window (side effects such as nerve damage show that all cells need proteasomes).




9. Name the misfolded proteins in Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s disease and where they accumulate. Why are neurons especially vulnerable? [ELO 4] [ELO 9]






Model answer





Alzheimer’s: amyloid-β peptide forms plaques outside neurons; hyperphosphorylated tau detaches from microtubules and forms tangles inside neurons. Parkinson’s: α-synuclein forms amyloid in Lewy bodies inside dopamine neurons of the substantia nigra; some inherited forms have mutations in parkin, an E3 ligase. Neurons are post-mitotic and live for the whole lifetime, so they cannot dilute damaged protein by dividing; chaperone and proteasome capacity also decline with age, and amyloid seeds can spread between connected cells.

title: Study questions: protein life and death
section: VG-style questions
text:
VG-style questions
10. [VG] A protein X is present at the same level in two cell types. In cell type 1 its half-life is 20 min; in cell type 2 it is 10 h. (a) What can you say about its synthesis rate in the two cell types? (b) A signal stops transcription of X in both cell types. Predict the amount of X after 1 h in each. (c) Which cell type can respond faster to an increase in synthesis, and what is the cost? [ELO 4]






Model answer






At steady state \(k_s = k_d P\). \(k_d\) is 30 times larger in type 1 (0.693/0.33 h = 2.08 per h versus 0.069 per h), so X is synthesised 30 times faster in type 1. (b) Assuming the mRNA disappears quickly: type 1, 1 h = 3 half-lives, so 1/8 (12.5 %) is left; type 2, \(e^{-0.069}\approx 0.93\), so 93 % is left. (c) Type 1: the time to approach a new steady state depends only on \(k_d\) (half-way in one half-life: 20 min versus 10 h). The cost is energy and material: the cell makes and destroys 30 times more X (ATP and GTP for synthesis, ATP for ubiquitination and the proteasome). This is why regulators (transcription factors, cyclins, p53) tend to be short-lived.





11. [VG] A new compound lowers the level of the oncogenic protein Y in cancer cells. Design experiments to find out (a) whether it acts on synthesis or on degradation of Y, (b) whether degradation goes through the proteasome, and (c) whether it works like a molecular glue via cereblon. [ELO 1] [ELO 4]






Model answer






Measure Y mRNA (RT-qPCR) with and without compound: unchanged mRNA argues against reduced transcription. Then a cycloheximide chase (or pulse-chase) with and without compound: if Y’s half-life is shorter with the compound, it increases degradation; if the decay is unchanged but the level falls, it reduces synthesis (e.g. translation). (b) Add a proteasome inhibitor (bortezomib or MG132) with the compound: if Y no longer falls, degradation needs the proteasome. Check for ubiquitinated Y (immunoprecipitate Y, blot for ubiquitin). A lysosome inhibitor (e.g. bafilomycin) is a control for the other route. (c) Use cells lacking cereblon (CRISPR knockout): if the compound no longer lowers Y, cereblon is required. Compete with excess lenalidomide or thalidomide (occupies the pocket) and test whether Y binds cereblon only in the presence of the compound (co-immunoprecipitation). Controls: vehicle, a known glue, and a protein that should not change.





12. [VG] Explain why adding bortezomib together with a PROTAC can increase the level of the PROTAC’s target protein, although each drug alone has a defined effect. Use \(P_{ss} = k_s/k_d\). [ELO 4]






Model answer





The PROTAC brings the target to an E3, which ubiquitinates it; the proteasome must still destroy it. So the PROTAC adds to \(k_d\) only through the proteasome. Bortezomib blocks the proteasome, which removes both the normal proteasomal degradation and the extra PROTAC-induced degradation. \(k_d\) then falls to the small part left (lysosomal degradation, dilution), possibly below the original \(k_d\), while \(k_s\) is unchanged, so \(P_{ss} = k_s/k_d\) rises. Example (as in the demo): original \(k_d\) = 0.35 per h; with PROTAC 2.35 per h (target down to 15 %); with 90 % proteasome block plus PROTAC 0.27 per h, so the target rises to about 130 % of its starting level. This combination is the standard control showing that a PROTAC works through the proteasome.

title: Study questions: protein life and death
section: Explore
text:
Explore
Demo: protein turnover. The plot shows the amount of two proteins in a cell over time, from the exact solution of \(dP/dt = k_s - k_d P\): a target protein (blue) and a bystander protein (grey, dashed). Set how many molecules of each are made per hour and their half-life, and start from zero (the gene is switched on at 0 h) or at steady state. At a chosen time, add cycloheximide (all synthesis stops), bortezomib (blocks part of the proteasome, for both proteins) or a PROTAC (extra degradation of the target only). Drag the cursor (or tap the plot) to read values; the table gives \(k_d\), half-life and steady state before and after the drugs. The model is simplified: constant synthesis, every molecule has the same chance per hour of being destroyed, 90 % of each protein’s own degradation goes through the proteasome and the rest through lysosomes, and drugs act at once. An optional particle view shows single molecules being made and destroyed in one cell, at real time by default (choose a faster speed to watch hours pass).



E1. Choose Gene switched on. Both proteins reach the same steady state. Move the cursor to find when each reaches 50 % and 90 % of it. Predict first: if you double the target’s synthesis rate, what happens to its steady state and to the time needed to reach 90 %? Try it. [ELO 4]
E2. Choose Cycloheximide chase and tick log scale. Read each protein’s half-life from the decay with the cursor. Why are the lines straight on a log scale? How well could you measure the bystander’s half-life if the cells could only stand cycloheximide for 4 h? [ELO 1] [ELO 4]
E3. Choose Bortezomib (90 % block at 4 h). Which protein rises faster, and how much has each risen by 24 h? Both head for the same new steady state: why, and why does the target get there much sooner? Connect this to why proteasome inhibitors quickly raise the levels of short-lived regulators such as IκB or p53. [ELO 4]
E4. Choose PROTAC. How far does the target fall, and how fast (read the new half-life)? What happens to the bystander? Then set the PROTAC strength \(k\) to 0.5 and to 5 per hour: how does the new level depend on it? [ELO 4] [ELO 9]
E5. [VG] Predict before you click: what will the target do if the PROTAC and bortezomib are given together? Then choose PROTAC + bortezomib and explain the result. Finally, choose Gene switched on and tick dividing cells: which protein’s steady state and half-life change most, and why? With dividing cells, add cycloheximide and bortezomib at 100 % block: can the bystander still disappear? [ELO 4]






Solutions





E1. Both steady states are \(k_s/k_d\) = 1000/0.347 = 100/0.0347 = 2885 molecules. The target reaches 50 % after 2 h (one half-life) and 90 % after 6.6 h; the bystander needs 20 h for 50 % and 66 h for 90 % (at 24 h it is at 1630, 56 %; use the 96 h axis to see it level off). Doubling the target’s synthesis to 2000 per hour doubles the steady state to 5771, but 50 % and 90 % are still reached after 2 h and 6.6 h: the time depends only on \(k_d\). In the particle view at 1× you see about one new target molecule every few seconds (1000 per hour is one every 3.6 s).
E2. After cycloheximide, \(P(t) = P_0 e^{-k_d (t - 4\,\text{h})}\). The target falls to 50 % (1443) at 6 h, so \(t_{1/2}\) = 2 h; the bystander reaches 50 % at 24 h, so \(t_{1/2}\) = 20 h. On a log scale \(\ln P\) falls linearly with time with slope \(-k_d\), so the lines are straight and steeper for the short-lived protein. In 4 h of chase (at 8 h) the bystander has only fallen to 87 % (2512): a 13 % drop is hard to measure precisely on a blot, so long half-lives are better measured by pulse-chase or isotope labelling over a longer time without the drug.
E3. The target rises much faster: from 2885 to about 5730 at 8 h and 11 900 at 24 h; the bystander only to 3200 at 8 h and 4400 at 24 h. Both now have \(k_d\) = 0.1 × (normal \(k_d\)) from lysosomes + 0.9 × 0.1 × (normal \(k_d\)) from the remaining proteasomes = 0.19 × normal \(k_d\), so both steady states rise 5.3-fold to 15 186. The approach is set by the new \(k_d\): new half-life 10.5 h for the target and 105 h (4.4 days) for the bystander. In absolute terms, each hour the target loses 1000 molecules of degradation it would have had, the bystander only 100: blocking degradation hits fast-turnover proteins first. This is why IκB, p53 and cyclins rise within an hour of proteasome inhibition.
E4. With \(k\) = 2 per hour the target’s \(k_d\) becomes 0.347 + 2 = 2.35 per h, a half-life of 18 min. It falls from 2885 to about 660 within 1 h and settles at 426 (15 % of before); the bystander is unchanged at 2885, because the PROTAC binds only the target. The new level is \(k_s/(k_d + k)\): with \(k\) = 0.5 it is 1180 (41 %), with \(k\) = 5 it is 187 (6.5 %). A stronger PROTAC lowers the target more, with diminishing returns.
E5. Together, the target rises instead of falling: to about 3760 (130 % of the start). The PROTAC’s extra degradation also needs the proteasome, so 90 % of it is blocked: \(k_d\) = 0.1 × (0.312 + 2) + 0.035 = 0.27 per h, lower than the original 0.347. This is the standard control showing that a degrader works through the proteasome. With dividing cells, dilution adds 0.029 per h to every \(k_d\): the target hardly changes (steady state 2663, half-life 1.8 h) but the bystander falls to 1574 and its half-life to 10.9 h, because for long-lived proteins dilution is as large as degradation. With cycloheximide and 100 % bortezomib in dividing cells, the bystander still falls with a half-life of about 21 h (lysosomal degradation plus dilution), the target with 10.9 h: blocking the proteasome cannot keep the amount per cell constant in a growing cell.

title: Sorting proteins to the right compartment
section: About this lecture
crumbs: Sorting proteins to the right compartment

title: Sorting proteins to the right compartment
section: The question: one cytosol, many addresses
text:
The question: one cytosol, many addresses


Almost every protein is made on a ribosome in the cytosol. Only 13 human proteins are made inside mitochondria.
The ribosome does not know where the protein should go. The protein carries its own address.
How is the address written? Who reads it? And how does a protein cross a membrane that ions cannot cross?


Here is the puzzle. All the cell’s ribosomes sit in the cytosol, either free or on the surface of the ER. The only exception is the small set of ribosomes inside mitochondria, which make just thirteen proteins in human cells, all parts of the respiratory chain. Everything else, including the more than one thousand other mitochondrial proteins, is made in the cytosol. The ribosome itself is the same for all proteins; it does not decide anything. So the information must be in the protein. Think of a parcel in a post office: the sorting machines read the zip code, not the content. In the same way, receptors in the cytosol and in membranes read short sequences on the protein. Three questions follow. How is the address written? Who reads it? And how can a protein, a large and often charged molecule, get through a lipid bilayer that you know from the membrane lectures stops even small ions? The answers differ for each compartment, but the logic is shared.
crumbs: Sorting proteins to the right compartment

title: Sorting proteins to the right compartment
section: Recap: two sides of every membrane
text:
Recap: two sides of every membrane


Recap from the cell tour. The nucleoplasm is joined to the cytosol through pores: it is the same space.
The ER, Golgi, vesicles and lysosomes are on the lumen side, which is topologically the outside of the cell.
Mitochondria and peroxisomes are spaces of their own: their proteins come from the cytosol.


A short recap from the cell tour, because this explains how sorting works. Look at the fill colours. The pale cytosol colour also fills the nucleus. Nuclear pores are large open channels, so the inside of the nucleus and the cytosol form one continuous space. The blue fill marks the lumen side: the inside of the ER, the gap between the two nuclear membranes, the Golgi, the vesicles and the lysosomes. Vesicles bud from one of these compartments and fuse with the next, so material moves between them without crossing a membrane, and in the end it can reach the outside of the cell. That is why the lumen side counts as topologically outside. The mitochondrial matrix and the inside of peroxisomes are separate spaces. Proteins for them are made in the cytosol and must cross one or two membranes. This one picture already tells us that a protein will use different kinds of machinery depending on which space it is going to. Keep it in mind for the rest of the lecture.
crumbs: Sorting proteins to the right compartment

title: Sorting proteins to the right compartment
section: Sorting signals are zip codes
text:
Sorting signals are zip codes

Most signals are a short stretch of amino acids. The pattern matters more than the exact sequence. Many are cut off after use; KDEL, NLS and PTS1 stay.

Here are the main sorting signals of this course. Each is drawn on a protein chain, from the N-terminus on the left to the C-terminus on the right. The ER signal peptide sits at the very start: fifteen to thirty amino acids with a core of hydrophobic ones; the one shown is from albumin, the main blood protein. A transmembrane segment is about twenty hydrophobic amino acids in a row, long enough to span the bilayer. KDEL, four amino acids at the very end, brings ER proteins back to the ER. The mannose-6-phosphate signal is different: it is not a stretch of sequence but a patch on the surface of the folded protein, which gets a sugar phosphate tag in the Golgi. The mitochondrial presequence is also at the N-terminus, but it is rich in positive arginines and hydrophobic residues and forms a helix with a positive face. The NLS is a short basic stretch that can sit almost anywhere. The NES is rich in leucines. PTS1 is the last three amino acids, serine, lysine, leucine. Notice that the receptors read a pattern, not an exact word, so many different sequences work.
crumbs: Sorting proteins to the right compartment

title: Sorting proteins to the right compartment
section: How do we know? A signal is necessary and sufficient
text:
How do we know? A signal is necessary and sufficient


Sufficient: add the signal to an unrelated protein and it moves to the new place.
Necessary: mutate the signal (one Lys → Thr) and the protein stays out.
Same logic for the ER signal peptide (Günter Blobel, Nobel Prize 1999) and every other signal. Today the readout is usually a GFP fusion in living cells.


How do we know that these short sequences are really the addresses? The test has two parts, and you will see the same logic in every field of cell biology. First, sufficiency. Take a protein that normally lives in the cytosol, for example a large enzyme, and attach the candidate signal. If the fusion protein now goes to the new compartment, the signal is enough. This was done in 1984 with the NLS of a virus protein, SV40 large T antigen, PKKKRKV, which moved a large cytosolic enzyme into the nucleus. Second, necessity. Change a single amino acid in the signal, here one lysine to threonine, and the protein stays in the cytosol. Today we fuse the protein to GFP and look at living cells by fluorescence microscopy. Notice panel one: GFP alone is small, 27 kilodaltons, and diffuses through the nuclear pores, so it fills both cytosol and nucleus. That is why the test uses a large protein. Günter Blobel used the same logic for the ER signal peptide and received the 1999 Nobel Prize for showing that proteins carry intrinsic signals for their transport.
crumbs: Sorting proteins to the right compartment

title: Sorting proteins to the right compartment
section: The three ways in
text:
The three ways in

Which machine is used depends on the topology: same space (gated), into a new space from the cytosol (transmembrane), or between lumen-side spaces (vesicular).

Now we can put the signals and the topology together. There are only three ways for a protein to move between compartments. One, gated transport, between the cytosol and the nucleus. Since these are the same space, the protein does not cross a membrane. It passes through a nuclear pore, a large gate that lets small molecules through freely and controls larger ones. The protein stays folded. Two, transmembrane transport, from the cytosol into the ER, the mitochondria or the peroxisomes. Here a protein translocator sits in the membrane, and the chain is threaded across it, usually in an unfolded state; peroxisomes are an exception, as we will see. Three, vesicular transport, from the ER onwards. Vesicles bud from one membrane and fuse with the next, carrying their cargo in the lumen or in their membrane, so the protein never crosses a membrane again. In every case the logic is the same: a signal on the protein is recognised by a receptor, and the receptor delivers it to the right machine. The vesicle machines come in the lectures on the Golgi and on endocytosis.
crumbs: Sorting proteins to the right compartment

title: Sorting proteins to the right compartment
section: Gated transport: the nuclear pore complex
text:
Gated transport: the nuclear pore complex



Human nuclear pore complex, scaffold rings (cryo-electron tomography and modelling, PDB 5IJO).






HeLa cells: a pore protein (green) outlines every nucleus; vimentin filaments (red).

About 120 MDa, ~30 different proteins (nucleoporins), each in 8 or more copies; ~3000 pores per nucleus.
The central channel is filled with FG repeats, flexible chains rich in Phe-Gly: a sieve. Proteins below ~40 kDa diffuse; larger ones need a carrier that binds the FG repeats.



The nuclear envelope has thousands of pores, each a huge protein complex of about 120 megadaltons, roughly thirty times the mass of a whole ribosome. It is built from about thirty different proteins called nucleoporins, each present in eight or more copies, arranged with eightfold symmetry. On the left is a model of the scaffold of the human pore, built by combining cryo-electron tomography of real nuclear envelopes with structures of the parts. On the right, cells stained with an antibody against a pore protein: every nucleus is outlined, because thousands of pores cover its surface. The interesting part is what fills the central channel. Many nucleoporins have long, disordered tails with repeats of phenylalanine and glycine, called FG repeats. These form a dense, sticky meshwork. Small molecules and small proteins, below roughly forty kilodaltons, diffuse through. Larger proteins are held back, unless they are bound to a nuclear transport receptor, which can dissolve into the FG meshwork. This is why it is called gated transport: the gate is open for the right partners.
crumbs: Sorting proteins to the right compartment

title: Sorting proteins to the right compartment
section: Nuclear import: NLS, importins and Ran
text:
Nuclear import: NLS, importins and Ran


Importin α reads the NLS; importin β carries the complex through the FG meshwork. The cargo stays folded.
In the nucleus, Ran-GTP binds importin β and the cargo is released. Ran-GTP is (almost) only in the nucleus, so import goes one way.


Here is the import cycle for a protein with a classical NLS. Step one, in the cytosol: importin alpha binds the NLS, and importin beta binds importin alpha. Step two: importin beta interacts with the FG repeats and slips through the pore together with its cargo. A single passage takes about ten milliseconds, and the cargo is fully folded; in the other direction, exportins even carry whole ribosomal subunits out. Step three, in the nucleus: a small GTPase called Ran, in its GTP-bound form, binds importin beta. This changes its shape, and importin alpha and the cargo let go. The cargo is now inside. Step four: importin beta, still bound to Ran-GTP, goes back to the cytosol. There, Ran splits its GTP, lets go of importin beta, and the importin is free to pick up the next cargo. Importin alpha is sent back out by its own exportin. Notice the trick. The importin binds cargo where Ran-GTP is absent and releases it where Ran-GTP is present. So the direction of transport is set by where Ran-GTP is, which is the next slide.
crumbs: Sorting proteins to the right compartment

title: Sorting proteins to the right compartment
section: The Ran gradient gives direction; export is the mirror image
text:
The Ran gradient gives direction; export is the mirror image


RanGEF sits on chromatin: Ran-GTP is made in the nucleus. RanGAP is in the cytosol: Ran-GTP is turned into Ran-GDP there.
Exportins do the opposite of importins: they bind cargo with a nuclear export signal (NES) together with Ran-GTP, and let go in the cytosol.
The energy comes from GTP hydrolysis by Ran, not from the pore.


Why is Ran-GTP only in the nucleus? Because the two enzymes that control Ran are on different sides. The exchange factor, RanGEF, which swaps GDP for GTP, is bound to chromatin, so it works only in the nucleus. The GTPase-activating protein, RanGAP, which makes Ran split its GTP, is in the cytosol and on the cytosolic face of the pore. The result is a steep gradient: lots of Ran-GTP in the nucleus, almost only Ran-GDP in the cytosol. Exportins use the same gradient the other way round. The main exportin, called CRM1 or XPO1, binds a cargo that carries a leucine-rich nuclear export signal, but only when Ran-GTP is bound too. The three-part complex leaves through the pore, Ran splits its GTP in the cytosol, and the cargo is released. Many proteins shuttle back and forth, and the cell controls where they act by masking or unmasking their NLS or NES. The pore itself uses no energy; the energy that makes transport one-way comes from Ran’s GTP. Remember XPO1: it is the drug target at the end of the lecture.
crumbs: Sorting proteins to the right compartment

title: Sorting proteins to the right compartment
section: Transmembrane transport into the ER: the first fork
text:
Transmembrane transport into the ER: the first fork


An N-terminal signal peptide is recognised by SRP as soon as it leaves the ribosome. The chain enters the ER while it is made (co-translational).
A transmembrane segment stops the transfer: the protein stays in the ER membrane. Details: the ER lecture.
Every protein of the ER, Golgi, lysosomes, plasma membrane and every secreted protein starts here.


The first and biggest decision is made during translation. If the first thing to come out of the ribosome is an ER signal peptide, a particle called SRP, the signal recognition particle, binds it and slows translation. SRP brings the whole ribosome to the ER membrane, where it docks on a protein channel, the translocator. Translation then continues and the chain is pushed through the channel into the ER lumen as it is made. An enzyme on the lumen side cuts off the signal peptide. If the protein contains a hydrophobic transmembrane segment further on, that segment stops the transfer and moves sideways into the bilayer, so the protein ends up in the membrane. Proteins without an ER signal are finished in the cytosol, and only then can other signals act. So this first fork splits all proteins into two families. Every protein of the ER, the Golgi, the lysosomes and the plasma membrane, and every secreted protein, takes the ER road. We only need the principle today; the machinery, membrane topology and folding in the ER come in the next lecture.
crumbs: Sorting proteins to the right compartment

title: Sorting proteins to the right compartment
section: Transmembrane transport into mitochondria: TOM and TIM
text:
Transmembrane transport into mitochondria: TOM and TIM


Made in the cytosol, then imported (post-translational). Chaperones keep the chain unfolded.
TOM reads the presequence; the chain passes TOM and TIM23 at a contact point. The membrane potential pulls the positive presequence; mitochondrial Hsp70 pulls the rest using ATP.
A hydrophobic segment after the presequence can stop the chain in TIM23: an inner-membrane protein.


Mitochondria have about fifteen hundred different proteins, and about ninety-nine percent of them are made in the cytosol. The precursor, with its presequence at the N-terminus, is finished by a free ribosome and kept unfolded by cytosolic chaperones of the Hsp70 family. The presequence binds receptors of the TOM complex, the translocase of the outer membrane. The chain passes through the TOM channel and, where the two membranes come close, directly into the TIM23 channel, the translocase of the inner membrane. Two forces drive import. First, the inner membrane carries a voltage of about 150 to 180 millivolts, negative on the matrix side, which you know from the transport lectures as part of the proton-motive force. It pulls the positive presequence through. Second, a mitochondrial Hsp70 in the matrix binds the incoming chain and pulls it in, using ATP. A matrix protease then cuts off the presequence and the protein folds. If a hydrophobic segment follows the presequence, it stops in TIM23 and moves sideways into the inner membrane. Other routes exist for outer-membrane proteins; you meet them in the mitochondria lecture.
crumbs: Sorting proteins to the right compartment

title: Sorting proteins to the right compartment
section: How do we know? Import into isolated mitochondria
text:
How do we know? Import into isolated mitochondria


Lane 3: the shorter, mature protein is protected from the protease: it is inside, and the presequence was cut off.
Lane 4: without a membrane potential (uncoupler CCCP) nothing gets in. Lane 5: with the membranes dissolved, protease reaches everything: a control.


This is the classic experiment that worked out mitochondrial import, and it is a method you can use for any organelle. Make the precursor protein in a test tube with radioactive amino acids, so it is the only labelled protein. Isolate mitochondria from yeast or liver cells by centrifugation, mix them with the precursor and incubate. Then add a protease. The protease cannot cross membranes, so it digests every protein that is still outside, but not proteins that are already inside. Run the samples on a gel and look for the label. Lane one: the precursor. Lane two: with mitochondria, a second, shorter band appears, the mature protein with its presequence removed. Lane three: after protease, only the mature band is left, so it is protected, which means inside. Lane four: add CCCP, an uncoupler that collapses the membrane potential; the protein is not imported and is digested. This showed that import needs the voltage. Lane five: detergent dissolves the membranes, the protease reaches everything, and no band survives. This control proves the protection was due to membranes. This gel is a schematic, not real data.
crumbs: Sorting proteins to the right compartment

title: Sorting proteins to the right compartment
section: Peroxisomes: import of folded proteins
text:
Peroxisomes: import of folded proteins



Yeast (Hansenula polymorpha) by electron microscopy. B: grown on glucose, a few small peroxisomes (P). C: grown on methanol, the cell is filled with large peroxisomes. N nucleus, M mitochondrion, V vacuole.


One membrane, no DNA, no ribosomes. Enzymes for oxidation of very long fatty acids, H₂O₂ and its breakdown by catalase, plasmalogen lipids.
PTS1 (C-terminal -SKL) is read by the receptor PEX5 in the cytosol.
Unusual: proteins are imported fully folded, even as oligomers. PEX5 enters with its cargo and is recycled.
Without working PEX genes, no import: Zellweger syndrome (the organelles lecture).



Peroxisomes are small organelles with a single membrane. They have no DNA and no ribosomes, so every protein is imported. Their enzymes break down very long fatty acids, which mitochondria cannot handle, and many of these reactions make hydrogen peroxide, which the enzyme catalase destroys. Peroxisomes also make plasmalogens, lipids that are important in myelin. The images show yeast cells. When yeast grows on glucose it has only a few small peroxisomes. When it grows on methanol, which it can only use with peroxisomal enzymes, the cell fills with large peroxisomes. Organelles grow and multiply when the cell needs them. The import signal for most matrix proteins is PTS1, the last three amino acids, serine, lysine, leucine, or similar. The cytosolic receptor PEX5 binds it and docks at the peroxisome membrane. Surprisingly, the cargo does not need to unfold: even large folded complexes enter, and PEX5 goes in with them and is recycled. How this works is still being studied. If import fails, cells have empty peroxisome membranes, which causes Zellweger syndrome.
crumbs: Sorting proteins to the right compartment

title: Sorting proteins to the right compartment
section: Vesicular transport: signals read inside the ER and Golgi
text:
Vesicular transport: signals read inside the ER and Golgi


Default: a soluble protein in the ER lumen with no further signal is secreted; a membrane protein goes to the plasma membrane.
KDEL: ER proteins (e.g. the chaperone BiP) leak to the Golgi and are brought back by the KDEL receptor: retrieval, not retention.
M6P: a mannose-6-phosphate tag is added to lysosomal enzymes in the cis-Golgi; the M6P receptor sends them to lysosomes. Lose the tag (I-cell disease): the enzymes are secreted instead.


Once a protein is in the ER lumen, it can only move on in vesicles, and the signals are now read by receptors on the lumen side. If there is no further signal, the protein follows the default route through the Golgi to the outside: it is secreted, or, if it is a membrane protein, it ends up in the plasma membrane. ER-resident proteins, such as the chaperone BiP, carry KDEL at their C-terminus. Surprisingly, KDEL does not hold them in the ER. They leave with everything else, and in the cis-Golgi the KDEL receptor binds them and sends them back in COPI vesicles. Lysosomal enzymes carry a signal patch on their folded surface. In the cis-Golgi an enzyme recognises the patch and adds a phosphate to a mannose sugar, making mannose-6-phosphate. In the trans-Golgi network the M6P receptor binds it, and clathrin-coated vesicles carry receptor and cargo to endosomes, where the acid pH releases the cargo. In I-cell disease the tagging enzyme is missing, so lysosomal enzymes are secreted into the blood and lysosomes fill with undigested material. The vesicle machines come in the Golgi and endocytosis lectures.
crumbs: Sorting proteins to the right compartment

title: Sorting proteins to the right compartment
section: When a protein has several signals: the order of reading
text:
When a protein has several signals: the order of reading

The first fork (ER or not) is made during translation. After that, only signals on the same side of the membrane as their receptor can be read. Try it: Demo: zip-code game

Real proteins can carry more than one signal, so we need a rule for which one wins. The key is timing and topology. The first decision is made while the protein is still being translated: an ER signal peptide, or a first transmembrane segment, sends the ribosome to the ER. If that happens, the protein is inside the ER or in its membrane, and from now on only signals that are read in the lumen matter: transmembrane segments, KDEL, the mannose-6-phosphate patch. An NLS or a PTS1 on such a protein is never seen by its cytosolic receptor, so it does nothing. If there is no ER signal, the protein is finished in the cytosol, and the cytosolic receptors compete: importins for the NLS, TOM for the presequence, PEX5 for PTS1. Some real proteins carry two cytosolic signals on purpose and end up in two places; then the outcome depends on details, and only an experiment can tell. This is a simplification, one protein, one route, but it predicts the location of most proteins. Try it in the zip-code game: build a protein, predict, then watch its route.
crumbs: Sorting proteins to the right compartment

title: Sorting proteins to the right compartment
section: Why it matters: selinexor blocks nuclear export
text:
Why it matters: selinexor blocks nuclear export


Many cancer cells, including multiple myeloma, make too much XPO1. Tumour suppressors such as p53 are exported and cannot act in the nucleus.
Selinexor binds XPO1 covalently (to a cysteine in the NES-binding groove). Export stops; tumour suppressors build up in the nucleus; the cancer cell dies. Approved 2019 for myeloma, with dexamethasone.


Here is a drug that acts directly on the export machine from earlier in the lecture. Many tumour-suppressor proteins, such as p53, FOXO transcription factors and IkappaB, must be in the nucleus to work: they control genes, stop the cell cycle or trigger cell death. They carry nuclear export signals and shuttle in and out. Many cancers, including multiple myeloma, a cancer of plasma cells in the bone marrow, have high levels of the exportin XPO1. So these tumour suppressors spend too much time in the cytosol, where they cannot act. Selinexor is a small molecule that fits into the groove of XPO1 where the NES normally binds, and it forms a covalent bond with a cysteine there. Export of NES cargo stops, the tumour suppressors accumulate in the nucleus, and the cancer cell is pushed into apoptosis. Normal cells are affected too, which explains side effects such as nausea and low platelet counts. Selinexor was approved in 2019 for myeloma that has relapsed after other drugs. You will meet drug development of this kind in Kliniska prövningar och läkemedelsutveckling, and myeloma in Sjukdomslära.
crumbs: Sorting proteins to the right compartment

title: Sorting proteins to the right compartment
section: Why it matters: NLS tags in CRISPR and gene therapy
text:
Why it matters: NLS tags in CRISPR and gene therapy









Cas9 with guide RNA (purple) and target DNA (blue); PDB 4OO8.


Cas9 (from bacteria, 160 kDa) has no NLS and is far too big to diffuse through a pore. Every CRISPR tool adds one or two NLS tags (often the SV40 NLS from the GFP experiment).
Gene therapy has the same problem: DNA delivered to a non-dividing cell (neuron, liver cell) must get through the pores. Dividing cells get it when the envelope breaks down in mitosis.


Our second application is in biotechnology and gene therapy. Cas9, the DNA-cutting enzyme of CRISPR, comes from bacteria, which have no nucleus, so it has no NLS. It is about 160 kilodaltons, much larger than the size limit for diffusion through the nuclear pore. If you deliver Cas9 protein or its mRNA into a human cell, it stays in the cytosol and edits almost nothing. The solution is exactly the experiment from the How do we know slide on signals: add an NLS. Most CRISPR constructs carry the SV40 NLS, often together with a second NLS from a protein called nucleoplasmin, at the ends of Cas9. The importins then carry it into the nucleus, where it finds the DNA. The same problem limits gene therapy. DNA delivered to a cell has to reach the nucleus to be transcribed. In dividing cells it can be trapped in the nucleus when the envelope reforms after mitosis, but neurons, muscle and liver cells hardly divide, so import through the pores becomes the bottleneck. Viruses used as vectors solved this problem in evolution, and you meet them in later courses.
crumbs: Sorting proteins to the right compartment

title: Sorting proteins to the right compartment
section: Summary
text:
Summary

Sorting signals are zip codes written in the protein: short patterns (signal peptide, presequence, NLS, NES, PTS1, KDEL) or a patch (M6P). Receptors read them; fusion and mutation experiments show a signal is sufficient and necessary.
Three ways in, set by topology: gated (nuclear pores, folded protein), transmembrane (a translocator: ER, mitochondria, peroxisomes), vesicular (from the ER onwards, no membrane crossed).
Nuclear transport: importins and exportins pass the FG meshwork; the Ran-GTP gradient (GEF in the nucleus, GAP in the cytosol) makes it one-way.
Mitochondria import unfolded proteins through TOM and TIM, driven by the membrane potential and ATP; peroxisomes import folded proteins with PTS1. The first fork (ER or not) is made during translation.
Drugs and tools use the rules: selinexor blocks XPO1; NLS tags take Cas9 into the nucleus.

Read more (optional): Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell, 7th ed., ch. 12.
Image credits

Five points to take home. First, a protein carries its own address as one or more sorting signals, and the cell has receptors that read each kind. You should be able to say what each signal looks like, where it sits on the protein, and how an experiment shows that it is necessary and sufficient. Second, there are three ways to move a protein between compartments, and which one is used follows from topology: gated transport between cytosol and nucleus, transmembrane transport into a new space, and vesicular transport between lumen-side compartments. Third, in nuclear transport the receptors carry folded cargo through the FG meshwork, and the Ran-GTP gradient decides the direction. Fourth, mitochondria import unfolded chains, pulled by the membrane potential and an ATP-driven motor, and peroxisomes do the unusual thing of importing folded proteins. The decision to enter the ER comes first, during translation. Fifth, these rules are targets for drugs and tools. Next, we follow the proteins that take the ER road: the endoplasmic reticulum, where they fold and are checked.
crumbs: Sorting proteins to the right compartment

title: Quiz: sorting proteins to the right compartment
text:
Short questions to check your understanding of the lecture Sorting proteins to the right compartment. Try each on paper first, then open the hint or the answer. The tag after each question shows the learning outcome (ELO) it practises.

Q1. Where are almost all of a cell’s proteins made, and what decides where each one goes? [ELO 4]






Hint





Think of a parcel in a post office: who reads the address, and where is it written?









Answer





Almost all proteins are made on ribosomes in the cytosol (free, or bound to the ER); in humans only 13 proteins are made inside mitochondria. The destination is written in the protein itself as one or more sorting signals (short amino-acid patterns or a surface patch). Receptors that recognise each kind of signal deliver the protein to the right transport machine.




Q2. Match each signal to where it sends a protein: (a) PKKKRKV, (b) C-terminal -SKL, (c) C-terminal -KDEL, (d) an N-terminal helix with several arginines and no acidic residues, (e) an N-terminal stretch with a core of 8–12 hydrophobic residues. [ELO 4]






Hint





Two of them sit at the N-terminus and are cut off after use; two sit at the very C-terminus.









Answer






NLS → nucleus. (b) PTS1 → peroxisome. (c) KDEL → returned to the ER lumen. (d) Mitochondrial presequence → mitochondrial matrix. (e) ER signal peptide → into the ER (and from there the secretory pathway).





Q3. Name the three kinds of transport between compartments. For each, give one example and say whether the protein crosses a membrane. [ELO 4]






Hint





Think of the topology: same space, a new space, or between lumen-side spaces.









Answer





Gated: cytosol ↔︎ nucleus through nuclear pores; no membrane is crossed (nucleoplasm and cytosol are one space) and the protein stays folded. Transmembrane: cytosol → ER, mitochondria or peroxisomes through a protein translocator in the membrane; the protein crosses the membrane (usually unfolded). Vesicular: ER → Golgi → lysosomes, plasma membrane or outside; vesicles bud and fuse, so the protein never crosses a membrane.




Q4. GFP alone (27 kDa) is seen in both the cytosol and the nucleus. A GFP fused to a 120 kDa cytosolic enzyme is seen only in the cytosol. Explain the difference. [ELO 4]






Hint





What fills the channel of the nuclear pore, and what can pass it without help?









Answer





The nuclear pore channel is filled with a meshwork of FG repeats that acts as a sieve. Proteins below about 40 kDa, like GFP, diffuse through and spread over cytosol and nucleus. The large fusion protein cannot pass on its own and has no NLS, so no importin carries it in: it stays in the cytosol.




Q5. What makes nuclear import go in one direction? Name the two enzymes involved and where they are. [ELO 4, 5]






Hint





Importins bind cargo in one form of the environment and release it in the other.









Answer





The Ran-GTP gradient. The exchange factor RanGEF is bound to chromatin, so Ran-GTP is made in the nucleus; RanGAP is in the cytosol, where it makes Ran hydrolyse its GTP to Ran-GDP. Importins bind cargo where there is no Ran-GTP (cytosol) and release it when Ran-GTP binds them (nucleus). The energy comes from Ran’s GTP hydrolysis, not from the pore.




Q6. Name two things that drive the import of a protein into the mitochondrial matrix. [ELO 4, 5]






Hint





One is electrical, one uses ATP.









Answer






The membrane potential across the inner membrane (matrix side negative) pulls the positively charged presequence through TIM23. (2) Mitochondrial Hsp70 in the matrix binds the incoming chain and pulls it in, using ATP. (Cytosolic chaperones also keep the precursor unfolded so it fits through TOM and TIM.)





Q7. A protein has an ER signal peptide and an NLS. Where does it go, and why? [ELO 4]






Hint





Which signal is read first, and on which side of the ER membrane is the protein afterwards?









Answer





The signal peptide is read by SRP during translation, so the protein enters the ER lumen and, with no further signal, is secreted. The NLS is never read: importins are in the cytosol, and the protein is now on the lumen side of a membrane.




Q8. What does selinexor bind, and why does that kill myeloma cells? [ELO 4, 9]






Hint





Which tumour-suppressor proteins carry an NES, and where must they be to act?









Answer





Selinexor binds the exportin XPO1 (CRM1) covalently, in the groove that binds the nuclear export signal. Export of NES proteins stops. Tumour suppressors such as p53, FOXO and IκB, which myeloma cells (with their high XPO1) keep exporting, build up in the nucleus, where they act and push the cancer cell into apoptosis.
crumbs: Sorting proteins to the right compartment

title: Study questions: principles of cell communication
text:
Study questions in the style of the written exam. Write your answer first (a few sentences, or a labelled sketch where it helps), then compare with the model answer. Each question is tagged with its learning outcome (ELO). Questions tagged [VG] are of the kind used for the higher grade: predict, compare, explain an unexpected result or design an experiment.
Useful relations: fraction of receptors occupied \(= [L]/([L]+K_d)\). A competitive antagonist at concentration \([B]\) with dissociation constant \(K_B\) shifts the agonist curve to the right by the factor \(1 + [B]/K_B\).

title: Study questions: principles of cell communication
section: G-level questions
text:
G-level questions
1. Describe endocrine, paracrine, autocrine, contact-dependent and synaptic signalling. Give one example of each. [ELO 3]






Model answer





Endocrine: a gland releases a hormone into the blood, which carries it to target cells all over the body (insulin from the pancreas, cortisol from the adrenal cortex). Paracrine: a local mediator acts on nearby cells and is quickly broken down, taken up or bound, so it does not travel far (histamine from mast cells, many growth factors). Autocrine: the cell responds to a signal it releases itself, often together with neighbouring cells of the same type (interleukin 2 from activated T cells). Contact-dependent: the signal stays bound to the membrane of the sending cell and acts only on cells that touch it (Delta binding Notch). Synaptic: a nerve ending releases a neurotransmitter into a gap of about 20 nm, acting on one target cell within milliseconds (acetylcholine at the nerve–muscle junction).




2. Compare cell-surface receptors and intracellular (nuclear) receptors: which signals use them, how the signal reaches the response, and how fast the response is. [ELO 3]






Model answer





Cell-surface receptors bind water-soluble signals that cannot cross the lipid bilayer (adrenaline, peptide hormones, growth factors, neurotransmitters). The signal binds outside, the receptor changes shape and activates proteins inside the cell (channels, G proteins, kinases). Because these proteins already exist, the response can start in milliseconds to minutes; later it may also change gene expression. Intracellular receptors bind small fat-soluble signals that diffuse through the membrane (steroid hormones such as cortisol and oestrogen, thyroid hormone, vitamin D). The receptor, in the cytosol or the nucleus, binds the hormone, binds DNA response elements and recruits co-activators: it is a transcription factor controlled by a small molecule. New RNA and proteins must be made, so the response takes hours, and it lasts long.




3. Name the three classes of cell-surface receptor. For each, describe how the signal is passed into the cell and give one example. [ELO 3]






Model answer





Ion-channel-coupled receptors (ligand-gated channels): the receptor is itself a channel; binding of the signal opens it and ions flow, changing the membrane potential within milliseconds. Example: the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (Na⁺ in). G-protein-coupled receptors: a chain that crosses the membrane seven times; the active receptor activates a trimeric G protein on the inside, which changes the activity of enzymes (such as adenylyl cyclase, which makes cAMP) or channels. Example: the β-adrenergic receptor for adrenaline. Enzyme-coupled receptors: single-pass receptors that are enzymes themselves, mostly tyrosine kinases, or that bind a kinase. The signal brings two receptors together and they phosphorylate each other, which creates docking sites for signalling proteins. Example: the insulin receptor or the EGF receptor.




4. Define the dissociation constant \(K_d\). A receptor has \(K_d\) = 5 nM. (a) What fraction of receptors is occupied at 5 nM and at 1 nM ligand? (b) What concentration is needed to occupy 90 % of the receptors? [ELO 3]






Model answer





For \(\text{R} + \text{L} \rightleftharpoons \text{RL}\), \(K_d = [\text{R}][\text{L}]/[\text{RL}]\), a concentration. It equals the free ligand concentration at which half the receptors are occupied; a low \(K_d\) means high affinity. Fraction occupied \(= [L]/([L]+K_d)\). (a) At 5 nM: 5/10 = 50 %; at 1 nM: 1/6 ≈ 17 %. (b) \([L]/([L]+5) = 0.9\) gives \([L] = 9 \times 5\) = 45 nM.




5. Sketch a dose–response curve on a log concentration axis. Mark \(E_\text{max}\) and EC₅₀. Explain the difference between potency and efficacy. [ELO 3]






Model answer





The curve is S-shaped on a log axis: little response at low concentration, a steep rise over about two orders of magnitude, then a plateau. The plateau is \(E_\text{max}\), the largest response the drug can give. EC₅₀ is the concentration on the x-axis that gives half of \(E_\text{max}\). Potency is about how much drug is needed: a lower EC₅₀ means a more potent drug (the curve lies further left). Efficacy is how large a response the drug can give once bound, seen as the height of the plateau. A drug can be potent but have low efficacy (a high-affinity partial agonist), or be less potent but fully efficacious.




6. Define full agonist, partial agonist, competitive antagonist and non-competitive antagonist. Describe how a competitive and a non-competitive antagonist change the dose–response curve of an agonist. [ELO 3]






Model answer





A full agonist binds the receptor and switches it fully on (e.g. adrenaline at β receptors, morphine at opioid receptors). A partial agonist binds but switches the receptor on only part-way, so its maximum stays below that of a full agonist even at full occupancy (buprenorphine). A competitive antagonist binds reversibly to the same site and has no efficacy: it blocks the agonist (naloxone, metoprolol). A non-competitive antagonist binds to another site and prevents activation, or binds irreversibly. A competitive antagonist shifts the agonist curve to the right in parallel, with the same maximum, because enough agonist can out-compete it (by a factor \(1+[B]/K_B\)). A non-competitive antagonist lowers the maximum, because extra agonist cannot recover the blocked receptors.




7. Describe two kinds of molecular switch used in signalling. For each, say what switches it on and what switches it off. [ELO 3]






Model answer





Phosphorylation: a protein kinase transfers a phosphate from ATP to a serine, threonine or tyrosine of a target protein, which changes its shape or creates a docking site (ON, or sometimes OFF). A protein phosphatase removes the phosphate. GTP-binding proteins (trimeric G proteins, Ras): ON with GTP bound, OFF with GDP bound. A GEF (guanine nucleotide exchange factor; an activated receptor can act as one) lets GDP out and GTP in, switching the protein on. The protein switches itself off by hydrolysing GTP to GDP; a GAP (GTPase-activating protein) speeds this up. In both cases the off route is essential: a Ras protein that cannot hydrolyse GTP stays on and drives cell division in cancer.




8. What is meant by amplification in a signalling pathway? Explain why the EC₅₀ of an agonist can be lower than its \(K_d\). [ELO 3]






Model answer





Amplification: each active molecule in a pathway activates many molecules of the next step. One active GPCR activates many G proteins in turn; each activated adenylyl cyclase makes many cAMP molecules; each active protein kinase phosphorylates many targets. A few bound hormone molecules can therefore change thousands of proteins. As a consequence, only a small fraction of receptors needs to be occupied for a full response; the rest are spare receptors (a receptor reserve). Half of the maximal response is reached at a concentration where far less than half of the receptors are occupied, so EC₅₀ < \(K_d\). EC₅₀ equals \(K_d\) only when the response is directly proportional to occupancy.




9. Explain what adaptation (desensitisation) is and describe two mechanisms. Give one clinical example. [ELO 3]






Model answer





Adaptation means that the response to a constant signal declines with time, although the signal is still present; the cell becomes less sensitive and can respond again to a stronger signal. Mechanisms: (1) receptor phosphorylation and arrestin binding: a receptor kinase phosphorylates the active GPCR, and arrestin binds and blocks coupling to the G protein (seconds to minutes); (2) receptor endocytosis and degradation in lysosomes, which lowers the number of receptors on the surface (minutes to hours); (3) negative feedback further down the pathway. Clinical examples: tolerance to opioids (higher doses needed for the same pain relief), and the weaker effect of a β₂-agonist inhaler used very often.




10. Some signals change a cell’s behaviour within seconds, others only after hours. Explain the difference in mechanism and give an example of each. [ELO 3]






Model answer





Fast responses change the activity of proteins that already exist: a ligand-gated channel opens (milliseconds; acetylcholine at the muscle), or second messengers and kinases switch enzymes on or off (seconds to minutes; adrenaline makes the liver break down glycogen). Slow responses change gene expression: the signal reaches the nucleus, genes are transcribed, the RNA is processed and translated, and the new proteins must fold and reach their place (about half an hour to many hours; cortisol acting through the glucocorticoid receptor). Decisions such as cell division or differentiation take hours to days. Many pathways have both arms: protein kinase A quickly phosphorylates enzymes and later a transcription factor.

title: Study questions: principles of cell communication
section: VG-style questions
text:
VG-style questions
11. [VG] A person who is dependent on heroin (a full agonist at the μ-opioid receptor) and still has heroin in the body is given buprenorphine. A few minutes later the person develops sudden withdrawal symptoms. (a) Explain this using affinity and efficacy. (b) Would naloxone given later easily reverse an overdose of buprenorphine? Explain. [ELO 3]






Model answer






Buprenorphine has a higher affinity for the μ-opioid receptor than heroin’s active products (a lower \(K_d\)), so it displaces them from the receptors. But it is a partial agonist with lower efficacy: each receptor it occupies is switched on only part-way. The total receptor activity falls from almost full (heroin) to the lower plateau of buprenorphine, which the dependent body experiences as withdrawal. A partial agonist therefore acts as an antagonist when a full agonist is present. (b) Not easily. Naloxone is a competitive antagonist with a lower affinity than buprenorphine (and buprenorphine leaves the receptor very slowly), so high naloxone concentrations are needed to push buprenorphine off. Fortunately, buprenorphine’s effect on breathing reaches a ceiling because of its low efficacy, so overdose alone is less dangerous than with full agonists.





12. [VG] You have a new compound that lowers the heart rate. You suspect it is an antagonist at the β₁-adrenergic receptor. Design experiments in cultured cells that express this receptor to find out (a) whether it acts on the receptor at all, and (b) whether it is a competitive or a non-competitive antagonist. [ELO 3]






Model answer






Binding: do a competition binding assay. Incubate membranes with a fixed, low concentration of a radioactive β-blocker and increasing concentrations of the compound; if the compound binds the receptor, it displaces the radioactive ligand, and the curve gives its IC₅₀ and hence its \(K_i\). Include non-specific binding controls (a large excess of a known β-blocker). As a control, cells without the receptor should show no effect of the compound on a β-agonist response. (b) Function: measure an agonist dose–response curve (for example cAMP production in response to noradrenaline or isoprenaline) without the compound and with two or three fixed concentrations of it. If the curves shift to the right in parallel and reach the same maximum, and the shift grows as \(1+[B]/K_B\), the compound is a competitive antagonist. If the maximum falls (and washing out does not restore it), it is non-competitive or irreversible. Also test the compound alone: if it raises cAMP a little, it is a partial agonist.





13. [VG] Two laboratories measure the IC₅₀ of the same competitive antagonist in the same cell line. Lab A finds 3 nM, lab B 30 nM. Both did the experiment correctly. Suggest an explanation, and say which number you would quote to describe the drug itself. [ELO 3]






Model answer





The IC₅₀ of a competitive antagonist is not a constant of the drug: it depends on how much agonist is present, because the antagonist must compete with it. Lab B probably used a higher agonist concentration (the IC₅₀ rises roughly in proportion to \(1 + [A]/K_A\) in a binding assay, and more steeply in a functional assay with spare receptors). Other differences in conditions, such as receptor number (more spare receptors) or incubation time, could also contribute. To describe the drug itself, quote its equilibrium dissociation constant (\(K_i\) or \(K_B\)), which can be calculated from the IC₅₀ and the agonist concentration, or measured from the parallel shift of the agonist curve. Always report the agonist concentration together with an IC₅₀.




14. [VG] A tissue has many spare receptors for an agonist. You add increasing amounts of an irreversible antagonist. Predict how the agonist dose–response curve changes, first at low and then at high antagonist doses, and explain why. [ELO 3]






Model answer





At low doses, the irreversible antagonist removes some receptors, but the remaining ones are still more than enough for a full response. The agonist just needs to occupy a larger fraction of them, so the curve shifts to the right with an unchanged maximum, which looks like competitive antagonism. At high doses, so many receptors are lost that even full occupancy of the rest cannot give a maximal response: the maximum falls. (In the demo, with morphine: removing 50 % of the receptors shifts the EC₅₀ from 48 to 91 pM with the maximum almost unchanged, 95 % → 91 %; removing 90 % gives a maximum of 67 %.) The same logic explains why tolerance to an opioid appears first as a need for higher doses, and why a high-efficacy agonist keeps working when receptors are lost.

title: Study questions: principles of cell communication
section: Explore
text:
Explore
Demo: dose–response. The graph shows a dose–response curve (black) with the receptor occupancy by each drug (dashed: blue for drug 1, orange for drug 2) on a log concentration axis. The triangle marks the \(K_d\) of the drug on the x-axis, and the circle the EC₅₀ or IC₅₀. Choose a receptor and up to two drugs that compete for the same site. With “drug 1: dose–response” the x-axis is drug 1, and drug 2 is added at the fixed concentration set by the slider. With “drug 2: inhibition” the x-axis is drug 2, added to a fixed concentration of drug 1. Under Change the drugs and the cell you can edit the drugs, remove receptors, and switch amplification off. The model is the binding isotherm for two competing drugs and the operational model for the response (amplification with spare receptors). \(K_d\) values are rounded literature values; efficacies and amplification are illustrative; the demo shows equilibrium only.



E1. Choose Morphine (full agonist). Read the EC₅₀, the \(K_d\) and the occupancy at the EC₅₀. Why is the black curve to the left of the blue one? Now open Change the drugs and the cell and untick amplification. What happens to the EC₅₀? [ELO 3]
E2. Choose Buprenorphine (partial agonist). Compare its \(K_d\), EC₅₀ and maximal response with morphine’s. Which drug binds more tightly? Why is buprenorphine’s EC₅₀ nevertheless not lower than morphine’s? [ELO 3]
E3. Choose Morphine + naloxone (15 nM naloxone). By what factor has the EC₅₀ moved, and has the maximum changed? Predict first: what will the EC₅₀ be with 150 nM naloxone? Check with the slider. [ELO 3]
E4. [VG] Choose Naloxone reverses morphine. Read the IC₅₀ of naloxone and compare it with naloxone’s \(K_d\). What fraction of the receptors does naloxone occupy at its IC₅₀? Then raise morphine to 10 nM. What happens to the IC₅₀, and what does this mean for treating a large opioid overdose? [ELO 3]
E5. [VG] Predict before you click: a patient with 1 nM morphine receives buprenorphine. Will the response go up, go down or stay the same? Then choose Buprenorphine on top of morphine and explain the result. [ELO 3]
E6. Choose Noradrenaline + metoprolol. Read the shift of the EC₅₀ and check it with the formula \(1 + [B]/K_B\). Then choose drug 2: inhibition and keep noradrenaline at 100 nM. How much of the response is left at 250 nM metoprolol? Finally change drug 2 to pindolol and compare noradrenaline at 100 nM and at 10 nM. What does pindolol do in each case? [ELO 3]
E7. [VG] Choose Morphine (full agonist) and reduce receptors left (under Change the drugs and the cell) to 50 % and then to 10 %, as in tolerance. Note the EC₅₀ and the maximum each time. Then change drug 1 to fentanyl at 10 % receptors. Explain the pattern. [ELO 3]






Solutions





E1. EC₅₀ = 48 pM, \(K_d\) = 1 nM, and at the EC₅₀ only 5 % of the receptors are occupied. Because of amplification, a few active receptors already give a large response, so the response curve lies left of the occupancy curve (spare receptors). Without amplification the response is proportional to occupancy: the EC₅₀ becomes 1 nM = \(K_d\) and the occupancy at the EC₅₀ is 50 %. The maximum (95 %) does not change.
E2. Buprenorphine: \(K_d\) = 200 pM (five times tighter than morphine’s 1 nM), EC₅₀ = 100 pM, maximum 50 %. Morphine: EC₅₀ 48 pM, maximum 95 %. Buprenorphine binds more tightly, but its efficacy is low: it needs to occupy about a third of the receptors to give half of its small maximum, while morphine needs only 5 %. The EC₅₀ mixes affinity, efficacy and amplification; only the \(K_d\) measures binding alone. (The demo models only the receptor; in patients, doses also depend on how a drug is absorbed and distributed.)
E3. The EC₅₀ moves from 48 pM to 520 pM, a shift of × 11 = 1 + 15/1.5. The maximum stays at 95 %: enough morphine out-competes naloxone. With 150 nM naloxone the shift is 1 + 150/1.5 = × 101, so EC₅₀ ≈ 4.8 nM; the maximum is still 95 %.
E4. IC₅₀ = 33 nM, about 20 times naloxone’s \(K_d\) of 1.5 nM. At its IC₅₀, naloxone occupies about 92 % of the receptors: because of the spare receptors, morphine on the remaining 8 % still gives half of the response. With 10 nM morphine the IC₅₀ rises to 320 nM, ten times higher: naloxone is competitive, so more agonist needs more antagonist. A large overdose (or a high-affinity opioid) can need repeated or larger naloxone doses, and since naloxone is cleared within about an hour, the opioid can take over again.
E5. The response falls from 91 % to 50 % (IC₅₀ about 2.2 nM). Buprenorphine binds more tightly than morphine and displaces it, but each receptor it occupies is switched on only part-way, so the total activity drops to buprenorphine’s own plateau. In a person dependent on opioids this drop is felt as sudden withdrawal; a partial agonist acts as an antagonist when a full agonist is present.
E6. EC₅₀ rises from 48 nM to 290 nM: × 6.0 = 1 + 250/50. With noradrenaline fixed at 100 nM, the response falls from 65 % (no metoprolol) to about 25 % at 250 nM metoprolol (IC₅₀ ≈ 150 nM). With pindolol at 100 nM noradrenaline the response falls from 65 % to 29 % (pindolol’s own plateau). At 10 nM noradrenaline, pindolol raises the response from 17 % to 29 %. A partial agonist pulls the activity towards its own level: it blocks strong stimulation (exercise, stress) but gives some stimulation at rest. Such beta-blockers lower the resting heart rate less (“intrinsic sympathomimetic activity”).
E7. 50 % receptors: EC₅₀ 91 pM, maximum 91 %; 10 %: EC₅₀ 330 pM, maximum 67 %. At first, losing receptors mainly shifts the curve to the right (more drug needed for the same effect, as in early tolerance), because spare receptors make up for the loss; only when the reserve is used up does the maximum fall. Fentanyl at 10 % receptors still reaches 86 % (EC₅₀ 140 pM): a higher-efficacy agonist needs fewer receptors, so it keeps working when a lower-efficacy agonist no longer can. (In the demo, losing receptors also covers an irreversible antagonist, question 14.)

title: Course syllabus: 3MB001
text:
Summary of the official syllabus. The syllabus itself is the binding version: https://www.umu.se/en/education/syllabus/3mb001/ (Swedish: https://www.umu.se/utbildning/kurs-och-utbildningsplan/3mb001/)



English title: Cell Biology
Swedish title: Cellbiologi
Course code: 3MB001 (replaces the earlier 3MB038 Cellbiologi)
Credits: 15 ECTS
Education level: First cycle
Main fields of study: Molecular Biology; Biomedical Sciences (both first cycle, less than 60 credits of first-cycle courses as entry requirements)
Grading scale: Three-grade scale (U / G / VG)
Responsible department: Department of Molecular Biology
Established: by PRBMT, 2025-10-27
Validity: 2027-01-18 and until further notice
First run: spring 2027, 18 January to 24 March 2027, on campus in Umeå, taught in English





Theory. Fundamental theory in modern molecular cell biology. This site covers this module.
PPT: Working Life and Career. Oral presentations, seminar discussions, problem solving, a poster on a biomedical problem for a commissioning party, and projects as a working method.
Laboratory Work. Cell biology methods: planning and running experiments, analysing and presenting data, writing results in scientific form.




Knowledge and Understanding. The student should be able to:

Describe the structure and function of the cell and explain methods used to study cell biological processes.
Explain the structure and function of cell membranes and the principles of membrane transport.
Describe fundamental principles of cell communication and signal transduction.
Describe how proteins are handled and regulated in the cell.
Compare the structure and function of different organelles and explain their roles in cellular homeostasis.
Explain the basis of cell shape, motility, and intracellular transport, and give examples of methods used to study these processes.
Describe the regulation of the cell cycle and the mechanisms of cell division.
Describe different forms of programmed cell death and their regulation.
Explain basic concepts of cell biological disease mechanisms.

Skills and Abilities. The student should be able to:

Present scientific content orally in a clear and structured manner.
Collaborate in groups to solve cell biological problems and communicate the results effectively.
Participate in structured scientific discussions and critically reflect on theoretical and practical content.
Plan and conduct basic experiments in cell biology.
Apply good laboratory practice and follow established protocols.
Analyze and present experimental data in written form.
Interpret results and draw conclusions based on scientific principles.
Demonstrate skills and the ability to identify, formulate, and propose solutions to a problem relevant to the education, based on labor market needs
Demonstrate the ability to define and describe projects as a working method.

Judgement and Approach. The student should be able to:

Identify one’s own learning needs and take responsibility for further learning




20 ECTS in chemistry, of which at least 5 ECTS in biochemistry (or 20 ECTS in chemistry combined with physics and/or mathematics, of which at least 5 ECTS in biochemistry); 20 ECTS in biology, including microbiology, molecular biology and genetics.



Lectures plus student-centred teaching: interactive seminars, case-based learning and practical work. All teaching except lectures is mandatory. Lab work requires knowing the lab safety rules and basic GLP. Taught in English (Swedish if no participant needs English).






Module
Form
ELOs
Grades




1 Theory
Individual written exam
1–9
U / G / VG


2 PPT
Individual oral presentation
10–12, 17–19
U / G


3 Lab
Written lab report
13–16
U / G



How the written exam is built (this shapes the course material):

The exam has one section per ELO (1–9). To pass an ELO, at least 60 % of its questions must be correct. All nine ELOs must be passed.
Each ELO has one VG question, marked G or VG. Exam VG = at least 5 of the 9 VG questions at VG.
A student who passes at least 6 ELOs but not the whole exam may take a group oral exam (assessed individually) on the failed ELOs, or retake the full exam.
Course VG = all mandatory parts done + written exam at VG.




Not published online. The department uses Molecular Biology of the Cell (Alberts et al.). Students should not have to read the book to follow this course; each lecture ends with optional chapter pointers.
